No Pineapple Left Behind is a strategy management game from Subaltern Games. In No Pineapple Left Behind you assume the role of Principal in nine different schools (though not at the same time). For each school you will be set a challenge that you have to complete in order to unlock the next school as well as unlock a new way to play that school. While the challenges vary in what they ask of you the general idea of the game is to manage your school in a way that maximises the grades achieved by your students. Since “Children have lots of wants, needs, and feelings” you’re going to need to transform your students into pineapples for the best results because, as everyone knows, pineapples are solely focused on working to their full potential and achieving the best grades.
Full Disclosure: A review copy was provided by the developer.
While No Pineapple Left Behind (NPLB) does look rather silly when taken at face value it does perfectly get across the issues with the current education system. The game is presumably based off of the US system (due to where the devs are based), a system I have little knowledge of but since I see the problems covered in the game that I see in the UK education system I feel I can still talk about it. Just keep in mind that I’m speaking from a UK perspective. Over the past few years there’s been a shift away from teaching kids towards getting higher in the education league tables. A shift away from doing
to doing
. While some individual teachers do still care about doing right by their students most of them are simply see their students as the grades they achieve, certainly not helped by the fact that, at least in my school, teachers are given pay bonuses based on the grades that their students achieve in their GCSEs and A-Levels.
To be successful in NPLP you have to find ways around the human nature of your students (or even stop treating them as humans, i.e. make them into pineapples), you have to figure out how you can minimise costs as well as maximise profits and most importantly you have to get the best grades possible. Sounds a lot like the real system, that’s because it is. Unfortunately NPLB’s fantastic representation of the issues with the education system isn’t quite enough to save it from its rather dull gameplay.
On to how the game actually plays, there’s just not much to the gameplay. Once you’ve figured out the strategy for a given level there’s absolutely nothing to do but execute that strategy for each day of objective, for all the schools I played whatever strategy worked on the first day worked for the rest of the objective’s duration. Some of the objectives are pretty straightforward, there’s one where you just need to earn $1000 in a certain number of days to win while another requires that you get rid of a certain trait in a child by the end of each day for a certain number of days. The basic strategies for getting through a week of school remain the same but you’ll need to tweak them to fit with what it is you need to do.
The main management/strategy in NPLB comes from the teachers in the game. You decide who to hire. You decide how much to pay them. You decide what spells and lasers they use. Spells and lasers? Yes, spells and lasers. Each school teaches a combination of a possible five subjects, how many subjects are taught has an effect on the structure of the school day but that’s not overly important, the longer the school day is just changes how complex your strategy will need to be. Every subject needs a teacher and you’re given a choice of two teachers to hire for that subject. The teachers will have different hiring costs based on their starting energy. Once you’ve picked a teacher you need to choose their spell and laser, effectively a passive and an active ability. Both of these consume the teacher’s energy, how much energy depends on the type of spell or laser and that means you’ll need to choose those two carefully so you don’t use too much energy. The lower your teacher’s energy is the less likely it is that their spell will be successful. The spells are one of the factors that decide the grades of your students and are triggered automatically at the start of a lesson block. Lasers are only used on one student (though you can use them on multiple students providing you have enough energy) and have effects such as decreasing humanity or removing a negative trait for the child.
Your teachers can have a maximum of 100 energy and chances are you’re going to use most of that in one day, especially if you’ve got three or more lesson blocks. Energy is restored by the salary you pay your teachers, the more you pay them per day the more energy is restored for the next day and energy restoration is doubled over the weekend (allowing you to reduce salaries significantly on a Friday). Paying your teachers minimum wage leads to them having less energy. Less energy means less chance of their spells being successful. If their spells don’t succeed then your students will get lower grades which means less of a money bonus or even penalties if the school’s average grade is particularly bad at the end of the day.
Pineapples may not be perfect but they do have better stats than kids. Once a child’s humanity is reduced from 100 to 0 they become a pineapple which means they’ll do better in class, in turn raising the average grade of the class. Humanity can be decreased by through the use of lasers and supplies as well as through achieving good grades while getting low grades or failing parent phone calls are among the ways of increasing humanity. Supplies are a resource in the game which can be attached to a teacher’s spell. You have one of each kind of supply and they increase in price as they get better. As I mentioned some of the supplies decrease humanity but there are quite a few different effects including increasing grades. Parent phone calls are introduced several schools in, they’re basically secondary-objectives for you to complete. A parent will call in and give you a certain objective for their child, such as make sure they achieve at least a C+ in History. Failing these phone calls usually just means you get fined $200 or $500 but every so often, failure means an increase of twenty humanity for all students, something you really want to avoid. Thankfully phone calls can be ignored by spending an influence point.
The two main reasons I’m not recommending the game are simple, the uninteresting gameplay and the presentation of the game. As I’ve said the gameplay is pretty simple because once you’ve worked out your strategy there is literally nothing to do, in my experience there aren’t any random events or anything like that to shake things up and so you’re left with about five minutes of real gameplay for each school you play. The other problem is its presentation, not as important as the gameplay but important nonetheless. There’s nothing particularly special about the actual graphics, they’re pretty bland in fact but the real problem with the presentation is with the UI. The UI is just so clunky, taking up far more screen space than it needs to. It’s also not as responsive as it should be, far too many times I found myself having to click on something two or three times for the game to register it, particularly when clicking on classrooms to access the teacher and when using the salary slider for the teachers. It’s not a big deal but something so basic should be fully functional in my eyes.
NLPB tries to tackle a serious issue with comedic and challenging gameplay. Sadly the game falls flat on both fronts, hence I’m not recommending it.
El K.

Interstellar Marines is a tactical FPS in which two teams of marines are pitted against each other in an underground simulated environment.  Some very unique features of this game include the almost immediate death and the weather mechanics.  This is a game in which the old run n' gun technique will almost always get you killed.  Often the best strategy involves using a suppressor and sneaking around until you can ambush your enemies.
Some subjective and personal positive aspects to the game I have noticed are:
Losing your HUD once you take a certain amount of damage.
In this game's multiplayer it is nearly impossible to tell friendly soldiers from your enemies without the use of your HUD.  The feature which temporarily removes use of your HUD makes being wounded even more frantic because when you turn to run you need to look twice to make sure the marine behind you is friendly.
A feature which closely accompanies the loss of your HUD is the ability to open your helmet.  By pressing "H" you are able to completely disengage your display and open your helmet.  This comes in handy when it is raining because the rain will obstruct your vision by sticking to your visor.
Operable doors.
Most FPS these days have decided to remove the idea of operable doors in their multiplayer modes.  I beleive that it is a strong suite for this game they have not decided to do that as well.  When opening a door on a map such as Dynacore you can't tell if some one is hiding on the other side.  Doors are also very useful as cover from enemy fire.  It also adds a degree of realism and dynamic gameplay.
Weather/Day night system.
This game has fully dynamic shadows and a weather system which has been expertly fleshed out.  You have different weather conditions from rain to snow to high winds.  The rain will greatly obstruct your vision while your helmet is down. The snow reduces visibility in general and plays tricks with your mind because of the movement. The winds add slightly more chaos to the area however are likely the least influential of the three.
The day and night rotations are incredibly important in any game of Interstellar Marines.  In the day time you have only a very small chance of successfully hiding.  In the dusk and at night you will have a much easier time at remaining concealed.  You will also learn that the use of a flashlight is unadvisable to say the least.  The dynamic changes in weather and time force players to change their strategies whenever the map decides that it got bored.
Lastly, the dynamic motions of elements in the maps.
Many of the multiplayer maps have different structures of elements within the maps themselves which will periodically move.  This will force players to change their routes and hiding spots as hallways are cut off and buildings rise into the air and sink into the ground.
Now for what I dislike about the game in its current state.  Please be advised everything listed below is subject to change.  Alpha = Alpha
The game has very few weapons at the moment.
I am personally very happy learning to use two different weapons proficiantly.  But for those of us who want more variation you may have a hard time excepting the lack of variety in your choice of weapons.  On top of this there is only a few small differences in the way the two current weapons handle.  The Rifle has more accuracy over the SMG but it quickly loses that with sustained fire.  The SMG has an additional 10 rounds over the Rifle bringing it to a total of 30.  It also has iron sights with a much lower magnification that allows it to be used in close quarters combat, as opposed to the 4x scope on the Rifle.  However besides these small differences the guns are essentially identical.
Movement system.
Although perfect in almost all situations, the movement system has its flaws.  The devs have nerfed sprinting and jumping by forcing you to start panting after a certain amount of either running or hopping about.  My concerns with this mechanic in its current state are as follows; Jumping rarely allows you to overcome an obstacle the first try.  After your second or third attempt you begin panting for as long as 20 seconds afterwards.  In multiplayer it can also get tiresome when you are trying to catch up with your team on the map Evacuation and you start to pant, then you encounter and enemy and your crosshair is bouncing all over the screen.
Early Access.
The game is currently in development.  Listen to me when I say that this game is in EARLY ACCESS.  That means when you buy it you are admitting that this is the product you want in its CURRENT STATE.  Although I think this game deserves all the support it needs to have a successful launch, you must understand that there is no guarantee it will ever be released, and there is no guarentee there will ever be another update.  If you decide to spend your money on this game, I would say its worth every cent.  But at the same time you must make certain you want this game and not the Interstellar Marines that you are thinking about 5 years down the line.
Please remember this is a preliminary review of an early access game which is subject to change.  Before perchasing you should look at other reviews and perhaps some video coverage of it online.
Thank you,

Here I was about to give another good review to a Gothic/Risen game...
First, this is actually a pretty fun game with good level design, character development choices, varied quests and decent visials. they even finally got over their ridiculous need for niche super twitch combat.
But, and with this company there is always a but, it totally fails in progression/scaling because, frankly, there isn't any. In a vain effort to keep both "open world" and no "bethesda style monster scaling" they made a game where after you complete a third of it, there is no longer any challenge at all from even the most powerful opponents. As soon as you have finished a major island or two you have all the xp, gear and magic potency to stomp any and all opposition, with your only recourse to be cranking up the difficulty which just makes monsters one shot you if you fail to stun lock them.

I received a review copy of this game.
If you’d prefer a video review, have a look here:
No Pineapple Left Behind is a game with attitude, humour, and, at least I believe, subtext. It’s a management game where you run a for-profit school where the higher the average grade, the more you get paid. The ultimate goal of the school is to turn its students into emotionless pineapples that follow rules and get grades, and the teachers do this by casting spells on  the children and controlling their minds. Children are troublesome; they make friends, they have off days, they sometimes skip class; while pineapples, well they’re much simpler. I think you’d need to be blind to not see that this developer is trying to say something about the way schools in the US are run, and I think the sentiment and the ideas are fantastic; I just wish it was a better video game.
Honestly I felt like the game was presented pretty terribly. It’s not particularly stylized, and looks generic. From what I could tell there was no dynamic lighting, all of the shadows seemed to sit perfectly under the sprites, the colours were really drab, though while that may have been the point it still wasn’t pleasant to look at. Really, it doesn’t have a particular art direction, and there’s nothing impressive about it technically. Where it does get some points from me, is the music theme at the title screen along with the still image art there, and the funny sound effects when you click on a child or teacher. But that’s about it. There’s not much else to say other than the fact the visuals of the game seemed like an afterthought.
Speaking of afterthoughts, the presentation was not the worst aspect of the game for me. The mechanics are horrible, and for so many reasons. There’s almost nothing good about the actual game. The UI is all over the place. It takes up so much space you’d think it was an IOS game. The UI is supposed to be helpful and make your playing experience more convenient, not clutter the screen like it does in No Pineapple Left Behind. And convenience? Let me tell you about convenience. It takes far too many mouse clicks to do almost anything. There’s no reason why I cannot change individual teacher spells or salaries from the teacher menu. It’s fine to have a menu for individual characters, but to change a spell I shouldn’t have to open the teacher menu, click on a teacher, click on the spell currently equipped, click on the new spell I want, close the spell menu, and do that 4 more times just to change all of their spells to something that isn’t televisor or memorizor. Same thing with casting lasers on individual children; I have to physically click the child I need something casted on, which is impossible at higher game speeds. Why can’t I just tell my teacher to do this from the menu?
So even if all of that was ok and convenient and worked, there’s no depth to the game. There’s one or two strategies that work for making money, and that’s it. You have to follow the exact same paths. The game tries to add in special objectives and limitations to shake things up, but it just adds to the tedium. If I absolutely had to say something positive? It would be that sometimes it’s satisfying when you manage to earn money, but it’s not because the game is designed well, but because I have a stupid ape brain that likes to see numbers go up.
Everything, and I mean everything in this game, was designed after the story was set in place. This is a game that was made to say something. Someone in the development team had some ideas, and this game was built around them. Because of that, the story is, clearly, a head-height above the other elements of the game. There’s some really funny writing in the game, such as the students learning cantaloupian, some students having the trait “fruity” that meant they are attracted to pineapples, and so on. And the game is clearly making a point with the way the school gets paid in grades, and how little you, as a player, are supposed to care about the actual needs of the children, and instead prefer that they be empty, soulless zombies that get good grades, follow the rules, and nothing else. It’s not a new idea, but it’s new for video games; I don’t think I’ve seen a criticism of the US education system to this degree in a video game. It's just such a shame that the story is so unsupported by every other element of the game.
The game is $10 which is... far far too much. I wouldn’t recommend this game to anyone. Save your money. Don’t buy the game. Again, the sentiment and message of the game is great, but great games are not just made of ideas; they’re made of an innovative, compelling presentation, solid mechanics that are satisfying to play with, and a cohesive story that makes you, laugh and/or scream and/or gasp and/or cry or maybe it just speaks to you with its message or theme which this game did for me. But a third of a great game just isn’t enough, and I’d maybe even argue that, depending on the game, the story is the weakest of those three elements.
Presentation: 4
Mechanics: 2
Story: 7
Price/Quality:
Personal Enjoyment: 2
Final: 3.8/10

Having actually enjoyed Gothic 3, and then Risen 1 and 2, I was quite surprised by how tedious I found this game, to the point where I stopped playing and unistalled it after about 10 hours. I thought for sure it would be an improvement over the previous two Risen games, or at least as good.  How long should you play a game that is boring and frustrating before throwing in the towel?
Since I played a 30 hour game for about 10 hours, take that into consideration when reading this. I was not able to finish, nor would I ever want to. But I paid for it and did not really get my money worth.
The first Risen game was pretty straight forward, with a simple plot and simple combat with a small yet interesting island to explore. Risen 2 gave you a pirate ship and a crew and added some more complexity. I guess Risen 3 had to get more complicated, giving you too much to do, too many ways to do it, and too many places to go. The combat was sloppy in the first two games, but you were able to endure it and it didn't really get in the way of progress. In this game, the combat should have been cleaned up, but instead it is still clunky and it now gets in the way of progress. The low level enemies surround you and overwhelm you with interupting attacks.
After 10 hours, I still felt like a weakling. The game starts off by taking all of your abilities away from you and leaving you with a crappy raft. You have to really work to get it back and it felt like a chore. I never did get my ship back, and I didn't want to grind my life away to get it. I never felt any sense of improvement from gaining experience and abilities. I basically felt like a helpless idiot wandering around an island getting killed by every single enemy I would encounter, doing fetch quests for the locals with little payoff. The game really is a chore. It should pay you to play it.

Once again a traditional Piranha Bytes title with all its flaws, rough around the edges, feels unfinished sometimes, very very bad beginning and end, almost only tedious fetch/kill quests, ancient facial animations and many more.
I hate almost all new mechanics like the sea fights and especially the whole underworld/ghost parts.
Just finished the game in about 40h and already forgot most of the weak story.
The different factions you can join almost make no difference as you will travel around a game world that is 90% accessible right after the prologue and you will do almost all quests of all the factions anyway.
Balancing is abysmal, I would say even worse than the early Gothic 3.
The game starts extremely hard, you will probably die most of your deaths in the forst 5 hours.
At some point when you master the combat mechanics, got some decent equipment and learned nice skills, the gameplay is actually pretty good. Sadly, it wears off after only a few hours. Most combats are the same, you will probably take the same companion with you 95% of the time and the only interesting situations will arise from glitches.
The second half of the game will be one long grind towards completing most quests, looting and killing everything there is, because skilling and learning the important stuff from trainers gets extremely expensive.
You will not see a single new creature/enemy in the second half of the game.
But you will have to suffer through the worst boss fights in the history of all PB games, which is ridiculous, because they somehow built up a reputation for having the worst end fights with Risen 1 & 2 already.
I could go on ranting about many other things, some of which were certainly designed by the Devs on purpose because they are sadists and we the fans are certainly a bit masochistic in return.
Nevertheless, once again it is somehow a good game in many aspects as well. For me mostly because the world that has been created is amongst the most atmospheric and credible game worlds I ever experienced. The factions are interesting, the islands are astonishing, the level design with the incredible attention to detail is still one of a kind.
The music is beautiful and the voice actors are solid, with a few brilliant exceptions.
While many of the main characters are boring and bland, a few save the day, for me these are the gnomes and bones.
I'm happy that I decided to give the game a few second chances when I felt like quitting and after all finished the game.
My only regret is that I wasted a lot of time collectiong stuff I never needed.
TLDR:
If you liked any other Piranha Bytes Game, get Risen 3, it is better than Risen 2 and the most impressive in regards to the game world.
If you are new and curious about this rough little gem, get it in a sale and read some beginners guides.

It's a very simple roguelike/action platformer game. Move left and right with A and D. Space bar jumps. You can jump unlimited times, eseentially flying. Arrow keys attack/use potion, block, and switch items. Most of the interesting parts of the game come from the different weapons, and outfitting yourself not only in the best gear possible, but also the best gear suited to the weapon you are using.
The axe is just a simple swing away at your enemy weapon.
The club is similar, but hits harder, and if you're "flying" around, it will send you downwards due to the force of the slam.
The katana teleports you around directly near to enemies with every slash. It is extremely dangerous to both yourself, and your enemies, but it's fun.
The dagger stealths you, and with each swing it makes you jump forwards a few feet. In addition, if you strike from behind, the enemy is pretty much done for.
Rocket launchers have auto-aim, and explosions that are dangerous to you as well as groups of enemies.
Flamethrowers: jets of flames, nuff said
Ice Wands have auto aim, and rapid fire, but you must stand still, and they only have medium range.
I think that's all the weapons. But each one besides the axe and the club are varied enough to give you different options of playing the game. There are probably around 10-15 different enemy types which is reasonable.
I wasn't blown away by the game, but I also wasn't disappointed. It's simple enough to easily get into a game, and not feel like it's going to take hours before all the secrets of the game are apparent. It's also not so simple that it's a negative. I feel like the game does what it set out to do, and is enjoyable. It may not be for everyone, but if you want a casual roguelike/action platformer where games can be very fast, and easily replayed quickly, this is your fix.

Given only the options of recommending or not recommending Tallowmere, I would lean toward the former, but very  reluctantly. Tallowmere is not a "bad" game, but it is an extremely limited one in terms of scope and long-term playability. That may seem like a strange statement to make for a $5 game, granted, but it's not one made mindlessly. The core of rogue-like and rogue-lite experiences is, beyond any specific mechanics, largely down to two concepts: "differentiation between runs" and "core gameplay solid enough to encourage many runs".
Those two areas are crucial to any rogue-like or rogue-lite, and Tallowmere is rather lacking in both.
What the game does right:
What it does wrong:
The end result of all those design decisions is a game that I would not describe as "bad" so much as "bland". Tallowmere is mechanically decent, but hampered at every turn by its extremely limited scope of design. After a few runs, the lack of variety involved kills all motivation to continue playing.
So, do I recommend it? In comparison to other rogue-likes/rogue-lites on the market, absolutely not. In a general sense, still not really. If, however, you are content with a very limited experience, and merely want to kill an hour or two here and there? In that specific case, yes. Likewise, if "higher score" is all the gameplay motivation you need, Tallowmere has that covered.
For me, personally, it was not enough. Your mileage may vary.

Highly recommended!  Where to begin?  I'm a PC gamer, but I played the previous Naruto:UNS 2 on an "aquired" Xbox360 that was trashed by a friend due to the RROD (easy fix for any PC assembler).  Anyway, I'm a big anime and Naruto fan and was really dismayed at the lack of Anime inspired games on the PC.  On XBox the previous game was incredible and you could tell that cyber connect2 folks are actual Naruto fans themselves, just by the details that went into the game.  Even with the XBox's limited capability (compared to a gaming PC), the cell shaded action looked and played great. Only drawback was the horrible "jaggies" by the low xbox resolution and no AA to help smooth the images.
In comes Naruto UNS 3 PC version!  When I heard it announced, my jaw dropped. All I can say is wow! The cell shaded graphics on PC are incredible! I have my res set at 1920x1080 with the max super sampling at 2x. The game looks like I'm playing the anime, its so sharp.  There are scenes where you'll think you are watching a Naruto Blu-Ray (especially during ultimate justsu finishes). Game play is great and even varied. There's more than just story then fight.  I'm not far into the game but there have been 3-4 different styles of game play in addition to the fights.
Some have commented on the 30 fps lock as a drawback, but its not for me.  All animations play smoothly on my rig.  The slow motion issue only comes into effect if your selected game settings exceed your GPU capability.  I know because i was getting the slomo issue, but that was due to my card overheating (dead fan) and my GPU speed was throttling down to stay cool.  Only other drawback I can think of is controller support.  This was obviously a console port. QTE and menu items are made for an xbox 360 controller (A,B,X,Y). I dont have an xbox controller and, as an old PC guy, I wont be forced to buy one either, due to laziness on the developer's part to make a good controller configurer. I use a 170Kb controller emulator .dll (x360ce) and my no name controller works great, why cant the devs make that (this is not just Cyber connect2 either...)?
Anyway, this is an awesome game, especially if you are starved for some japanese anime gaming goodness on your PC whether you are a Naruto fan or not. ...AND YES! You CAN select JAPANESE VOICES with english subs (the only way to watch and play Anime!!)

Greetings Everyone!  Today I’m going to be reviewing Crossout a game I’ve described as Twisted Metal the free to play version.  I’ll admit openly that I haven’t spent too much time on this game as I generally don’t with this style of game, the free to play with micro transactions style games.  But is it worth your time?
Paint it Black:  At the core this is a deathmatch style arena shooter where you drive vehicles instead of running around in first person; very reminiscent of Twisted Metal without the immersion of the plot.  There is a small plot, mainly that of the world seems to have ended and you are building vehicles in a Mad Maxx sense to gather supplies or to take them from others.  The game focuses around PVP with a subsection of PVE that you have to have fuel to participate in, which is gain through PVP or time.  You can purchase parts with real money or gain a lot of it through progression and loot drops.  This is the core of the game but the unique nature of the game is the building of your vehicles (in a very lego sort of way) which also lends to the unique damage mechanic.
Physics Galore:  Normally, I’d talk about the graphics and sound, both of which are passable and I honestly like the aesthetic of the steam punk meets post apocalyptic design, but I want to talk more of the unique nature of the gameplay.  The game lets you build your own vehicles and puts players into tiers based on how many ‘points’ their vehicle is, this helps the balance but also makes ‘end game’ a bit of a buyer’s market (play to win in a way).  Damaging vehicles is unique in a similar way, guns shoot from where they would on the vehicle, requiring a clear firing line and causing direct damage to the part they hit.  In this way you can shoot the tires off a vehicle or destroy the weapons; more than once I’ve seen a vehicle stranded with 1 wheel and just abandoned to stew in angst.  I find this very enjoyable and would love to see it in a game that is more…game I guess and less the feel of a mobile title.
Paid to Enjoy:  The game unfortunately has all the bells and whistles of a free to play but pay to enjoy style game; as it is 100% free to play but if you want to enjoy the game as it is intended it would be very easy to argue that you need to invest some money or a lot of time.  I don’t mind this; I understand that all games need to make revenue but it leaves the game with a level of ‘freemium’ quality instead of something with a substance that keeps me coming back, even featuring a daily login bonus to boot.  Other than that I found no real issues with the game though I do feel the match making could use some tweaking as most games feel like landslides in one direction or another.
So, lots of good, lots of bad.  But, should you invest in this game?  I’m not entirely sure, I enjoyed the game and will recommend it based on the fact that it’s not utter garbage and is free.  After that you need to decide if it is worth putting in your money or your even greater resource, time.  For myself, I will be moving on as there are games that I prefer to spend my time as well as hobbies outside of video games.  Enjoy!

Given that CCP's landmark creation, EVE Online has consecutively walked away with our annual "MMORPG of the year award" it would be safe to assume that we like this game. I would even be so bold as to say that this collective Internet cloud cherishes, loves, adores, and embraces everything about this online-romp. Eve Online is perhaps one of the most purest definitions of the genre; a definitive example of how a PC, monitor, and Internet connection can open a gateway to a virtual world.
Let's just get it out of the way - if I could, I would marry, buy a condo, and have children with Eve Online: It is just that damn sexy. With that said, let's get on with the formal make-out session I like to call a review.
Aesthetics 9/10
Given that the game is now approaching almost 9 years in age, you have to hand it to CCP for keeping EVE so visually appealing. Starting out in 2003 as a slightly emancipated, ungainly child of an MMO, the Icelandic developer has continually updated and refined their vision of space. From sweeping vistas, colourful gas arrays, and goliath ships that pound seven tons of laser out of each other - EVE Online has a graphical charm you can't help but admire.The scale and "epic" nature of the entire ensemble fights tightly with the adventures that unfold around you - couple this with an inspired soundtrack and you might just believe you are a space-faring smuggler. Since Incarna, the developer's have taken us one step closer in letting us walk around in space stations (still no direct contact) which also adds another layer of immersion, and helps create some of the most camp looking avatar's in MMO history (I prefer the sunglasses and a look that says "I'm casual but I'm ready for anything.")
Perhaps EVE Online's biggest draw however, above and beyond the new interior bits or the awe-inspiring space stations, is its scalability. Whether you have the dimmest laptop or the mightiest gaming rig, New Eden is a forgiving mistress when it comes to processing power, meaning that you won't have to earmark a thousand dollars to make the game actually run - and that's what we like, humble yet attractive.
Gameplay 10/10
Eve Online is a game in which you can run quests in the morning, build a spacecraft for lunch, and pretend to be an inter-galactic Gordon Gecko for the afternoon. No MMO has ever come quite as close in achieving the multi-faceted, "make your own adventure" that defines this genre. Starting out with a tiny ship and without a single credit to your name, it is a player’s choice and individual journey that will lead them to the height of piracy, or even a freighting-empire.
The ever-refining tutorials now streamline the process from creation to first steps with easy to follow guides, as well as nudging you to a number of missions which give a taste for the various facets of the game. While newcomers will still suffer from what is known as "Eve-istentialism" at the enormity of the experience, CCP is doing their upmost to help this feeling dissipate.
And yet if you come from any traditional online game, you will be confused and scared by EVE Online. The lack of a level system, grind, humdrum questing, or even equipment (+135 Strength YAY!!) building will shock most people. This MMO takes a different tact, skills are gained in real-time, ticking over in hours or sometimes days, meaning that progress isn't about gaining an Engineering level 4, but the bits you do in between. The biggest indicator of success is in the ship you cruise around in, and the amount of money you have in the bank - sort of like a galaxy hopping rap artists: it's all about thruster-spinners and the fuzzy space-dice.
How you achieve riches and infamy within New Eden however, will be up to you. It isn't highfaluting talk to say that you could pirate the vacuum, or mine your way to fortune. Eve Online is developed is such a way that every play style is catered for, whether you want to be an action-ready pilot or instead a docile mogul looking for that chance to make it rich.
This is also one of the last few MMORPG's to emphasize the "multiplayer" part. Making it within New Eden will require a few choice friends, and seeing some of the more dangerous and exciting sights will definitely require a buddy or two. Low secruity space offers some of the most intriguing and thrilling moments of PvP known to the genre. This FFA full loot area will see paranoid groups mining for the finest ores, or even cruising asteroid belts looking for unaware opportunists - whatever the case may be, low-sec will never provide a dull moment.
From the economy to warfare amongst corporations, the individual can influence everything, and that is where this game shines. Like Ultima Online before, this is the type of game that you can proudly nail your colours the mast and proclaim that the experiment works, and you do indeed have a second life, in a galaxy far, far away.
But is it perfect? With a score winking a mighty 10 above, I'd say that whatever few negatives pale in comparison to the sheer volume of things that this game has going for it. For whatever cat-calls of it being too slow, too group-orientated, or indeed "We play to crush, not to bake bread!" well that's just missing the entire point of EVE Online: it is a virtual world, go out there and take advantage of it in its full glory.
Innovation 10/10
Originally EVE Online was a slightly broken, online Elite with nods towards Ultima Online. Now almost 9 years later that game is the hulking Goliath that most sandbox MMORPGs look to emulate. From the exclusion of grind to the classless, limitless choices for your avatar, CCP's title is leading the way in terms of what can be achieved within the genre.
Like UO before it, the game bangs the drum of the "playing to bake bread" in that it gives you the option to play an action-packed pirate, or a simple engineer. This is the type of game that truly brings to life the idea of virtual world and finding your own place within it. Even before we exclaim about player-driven markets, low-sec space, or the countless ways its developer's have overcome the most extensive genre issues, EVE Online is first and foremost the greatest definition of the term MMORPG. Innovation is what its Icelandic studio guzzles for breakfast.
Polish 9/10
Developing an MMORPG over the course of many years must become like a routine juggling act. On the one hand, maintenance, patching, and refining must all be attempted, but tweaking one thing might cause the whole thing to fall to a crumbled mess on the floor, with several angry little people caps locking "OMFG NEWB RUINED THE GAME". To this end, CCP have done a very admirable job in keeping this game in check, whilst continually adding and tweaking in whatever way they see fit.
EVE Online will rarely splutter or stall, neither will it kick you out like a stroppy horse. Through years and years of continually bettering their product, the Icelandic developer has, with gaffer tape and lots of spittle, forged a well-made, tight game. Now just get on with remaking those newbie ships.
Longevity 9/10
Most MMORPGs are victim to what is known as the "locust player". This is the type of gamer that will not rest, sleep, eat, or poop before they can claim that they dinged 50 before the servers even opened. CCP have once again bucked the trend by offering a game that makes it not only unconquerable with days, but even within months you will still be training skills and juggling abilities.
What this means is that not only is the experience in New Eden vast, but also there are many ways in which to go back through it all, never doing the same thing twice. With so many skills and with those taking a finite amount of real-life time, unless you have dual accounts alts are essential to the experience, as well as time consuming to make: the result being that you'll be playing EVE Online for a very long time.
Final score 9.2

I have high hopes for what the future has in store for this title and here's why: I came into this game where in the back of my mind I expected to find many bugs, errors, and under-developmental progress. Did I find all of that? For the most part, yes, but that's to be expected. Did it hurt the gameplay dramatically? Not in my opinion.
Dinosaurs: A Prehistoric Adventure, hasn't hit the early access expanded version, let alone the final release. This is a free-to-play game to encourage a player base that can possibly lead to a bigger, more complete phase. Due to its current state, I wasn't expecting anything jaw dropping.
However - my jaw dropped. Why? Not because "this is the best title I've ever played," but because I didn't expect as much content as it actually gave upon the first real look at the game. A lot of complains are that there isn't enough content or that it is considered boring. It took me roughly an hour to get the complete gist of what the title has to show for, including controls, mechanics, progression, and what each of the starter dinosaurs do. Of course it would become boring quickly, the game is far from complete with no real motive quite yet. This doesn't make it a terrible game or a bad experience. It's still playable, it's still enjoyable. I, as a person who owns many dinosaur-related titles in my library, was thoroughly pleased with what I saw so far.
My biggest issue aside from the controls was the fact there is no set objective as far as I can tell except from eating, drinking, and fighting about anything you run into - or running, of course. It lacks any type of real story line or lore and the only thing I could uncover was the mutations. Though, the lack of things to actually do is expected and not a game breaker at this point of time.
PROS:
- Potential. I see a ton of potential and I look forward to seeing what will become of it!
- Unique abilities, weaknesses, and strengths. Each dinosaur has something special about it and benefits.
- Unique models, skins, and animations. I was thoroughly surprised by the quality at this stage of the game's development. I do think the block mechanic could use a little idle animation, however.
- Interesting UI. I see a lot of negativity about the UI, but I personally sort of like it. I think it's unique. Could it do for some tweaking? Sure, I'm unsure as to why human items (knife/sword/hammer) are futured in a game where you play as the dinosaur. I'd recommend something such as teeth, claws, or feet to match the game itself and its objective.
- Diverse ecosystem. There's an absolute-ton of dinosaurs to discover and unlock (through killing mutations, as it seems).
- Nice soundtrack. One of the first things I noticed and definitely appreciated.
- 15 playable dinosaurs (3 starters). Several unlockable maps (1 starter), nicely designed.
- In depth encyclopedia (exhibition mode) on the dinosaurs and mutations. Good to read up on if you want to know more about them (abilities/health/attack/weaknesses/etc). I jumped straight into adventure mode without knowing what I could take on and who-does-what, so I recommend looking into the encyclopedia first unless you prefer simply testing.
- Free access to watching a game grow over time.
CONS:
- Undeveloped and needs major rework. That's to be expected though in any demo or early access title.
- Lacks a tutorial. This can be both a good and a bad thing, some games simply shouldn't have a tutorial and you can learn it on your own. However, I feel this title needs some sort of direction or push to know what to do at first. Fighting is a bit redundant and confusing. This is one of the concepts that needs a tutorial. Upon first engaging with another dinosaur (aggressive or passive), the fighting mechanic is a little odd. The first attack (Alpha1) is a light attack, second attack (Alpha2) is a medium attack, the third (Alpha3) stuns the opponent, while the fourth (Alpha4) is a special ability. When they are used, they will have a cool down, so you have to plan how you want to go into a fight (such as which keys to hit first).
- Camera angle. This probably ruined my experience the most. It was hard to become immersed into the game, I can see the style they were going for, but it's more of a downfall than anything. It makes it hard to see what is near you - which is crucial if it's something aggressive.
- Controls. I felt like I was playing a mobile game on my desktop. WASD keys are completely thrown out the window due to your primary mode of transportation being through a mouse, much like a touch pad. I was able to alter them with ease to my liking (thankfully), but the controls are quite wonky. The attacks, drinking, and eating are labeled from Alpha1 to Alpha6, which I figured out to be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 keys (to those wondering).
- No real goal, storyline, or lore (aside from the mutations/unlocking more dinosaurs). You will find yourself likely running around aimlessly eating, drinking, and fighting.
- Weird AI behavior. The AI I wasn't too impressed with in some places, while in others I was. I had a Utahraptor decide it wanted to have a duel, no biggie, went in, killed it, victorious - wonderful, but then I realized I had an Iguanadon rushing for me. I was baffled and confused as to how to react. I'm unsure if this is intended for the AI's behavior, and if it's a mechanic meant for herds, I see no issue with that. Though, I'm unsure as to why a herbivore would defend a carnivore.
Overall: I would recommend this title. It is free - no harm in checking it out and giving feedback on it. If it's not to your fancy or you feel dissatisfied, no loss, right? I may have gotten all I needed to see within an hour or so of gameplay, but that's to say I didn't miss anything. I will be following this game to see how it improves and develops.

Early Access Review. It's a fun and solid FPS game. You fight humanoid robots. Some are melee and some have guns. There's not a lot of content yet, but what is there is good. There's a tutorial, some single player missions as well as multiplayer pvp, but I enjoyed the 4-player co-op missions the most. There's only 2 guns, and I don't think there's any melee attacks or grenades, and there's only one kind of robot so far also, but it's still pretty fun. I like the adjustable difficulty. There's Easy, Normal, Hard, and Realistic. The AI actually seems pretty good, not amazing, but good.
If they add melee attacks, grenades, more guns, more enemy types, and make it a little easier to understand where you need to go in the single player missions, I think it could be a really cool fun game. Oh yeah, it needs more story/plot/npc stuff for single player to make it more immersive/interesting. Also, the "catching your breath" sounds are good, but get really annoying after a few seconds, and it would be nice to not have to re-activate the laser sight and silencer everytime you respawn.

Wow what a game. This is the closest I've felt to D&D on the computer as far as storytelling and exploration. The world is huge but contained enough to navigate around. The graphics are pretty minimalist but with the exception of the skill tree seem to fit the story and the mechanics of the game. Fantastic balancing of the items. There wasn't really a "best" of anything but rather trade offs for most of the magical items. I've been looking for a good isometric squad based fantasy game since playing Wasteland 2 and this is the best I've found so far. Enormous amount of text and story with lots of side quests and nooks and crannies waiting to be discovered. On the down side the game lacked a lot of depth. Most characters are superficially shallow serving mostly for plot device with no real attachment to or from the player. The battle sequences can also become grinding if you don't build your party correctly. You're able to get through it but it will take you forever. I clocked my first play through at 86 hours. Probably won't play it again but I've added the other games to my wishlist as I've gotten an appetite for more.

Risen 3 marks off the end of an era in the Risen-series. As far as I'm aware, there won't be another one. However, that doesn't matter since this final game finishes the series close to perfectly. From the first moment of playing Risen to this last moment of Risen 3, the series has made me replay the games several times, that's how good they are.
There are a few noticeable differences between Risen 3 and Risen/Risen 2, apart from improved graphics of coure. In Risen 3, the combat is slightly different, as many people before me has noticed aswell. While the combat in itself is very cool and not very hard, your character is pretty weak and your NPC companion has to help you quite a bit. At least in the beginning.
In Risen 3, you don't play as the character from the previous games. You play as Patty's brother, who I hadn't heard about before playing Risen 3. But that doesn't matter too much since you get to know him during the game and there's a little surprise somewhere in the game if you've played the other games...
I highly recommend playing this game if you've played the former Risen games first, if you haven't. you risk losing out on a lot of the precious story. The combat gets better and better the more you play and it's the kind of game you just want to keep playing, even after finishing it. Even more so since there are different factions that you can join, changing the gameplay for every playthrough (to a certain point).

The best way to describe it is simply like many others have been: A roguelike platformer. You run through procedurally generated dungeon rooms one by one, slaying the enemies to drop a key to the next room. It sounds simple enough, but it gets very intense the more you go in. The game can quickly run from walk-in-the-park to hair-pulling difficult in the time of one room change, and when you die... You're dead for good, having to start over from square one. One of the really neat things I've seen in this game is how the random generation doesn't apply only to items/equipment and the dungeon rooms themselves, but also to the objectives. In one playthrough, the 7th floor required me to slay the mighty Hydra, while the second runthrough I was asked to retrieve Lady Tallowmere's flag. This is a really nice thought by the dev, as it keeps it more interesting in terms of what you have to accomplish to advance throughout Tallowmere's brutish dungeon. This is a very fun game that has hours upon hours of playability in it, and I'd recommend it to anyone who loves Rogue-likes, Rogue-lites, and Metroidvania-style RPGs. Although at times it can feel a little frustrating, you'll quickly notice the fun factor easily overshadows these moments.

So here are my honest thoughts on Dragonball Xenoverse.  Note that I have played about 24 hours of the game, have yet to beat it (Although I am on the last set of missions) and still have not done all the parallel quests or master trainings.
I ♥♥♥♥ing love this game.
However, I am also a huge fan of the universe of Dragonball.  And you really need to be a fan to get the most out of the game.  The premise of the game is that you spend your time joining the "Time Patrol" with Trunks in a place called TokiToki city, after he wishes for assistance from Shenron.  Don't know who those are?  Tough, its not explained.  Again, you really need to be somewhat familiar with the universe of DBZ to get the most out of this.
YOu then spend your time doing Time Patrol missions which are basically you going back in time to correct "errors" in the history of DBZ.  You start by helping deal with Raditz, as somehow history was being changed to allow him to dodge the Special Beam Cannon attack, killing Goku but not him.
Again, if you have no idea what I am referring to, I can't help too much.
From there you uncover who is behind the strange time distortions.  You also can do Parallel quests, which are basically side missions with alternate rules.  In one you might help Frieza beat up the Z warriors.  In another you might go and reenact the World Tournament against Yamcha, Tien, and Krillin.
You can also apprentice under various members of the DBZ Universe such as Piccolo, Vegeta, Gohan, Tien, Krillin, Android 18, Cell, Capt Ginyu, ect.  You can thus learn their moves (Vegeta teaches Galick Gun and Final Flash for example, Ginyu teaches various fighting poses).
You also level up, raise your stats, and select your own combination of moves from the ones you have unlocked via PQs or Training.
And you will be grinding.  A LOT.  You can replay EVERY mission in the game, both story and PQ as many times as you want.  And in order to level up to take on tougher challenges, and to get gear and moves, you need to grind PQs.  I personally find the fighting fun so I do not mind so much.  Collecting all the moves is a fun pastime for me.
Visually I love the art style, but I grew up on DBZ so it reminds me of happy times.
I can't speak too much on MP, as I have only been able to play in 1 single Multiplayer PQ without being kicked from the party (no idea why, maybe folks dont like Female Buus?).  But it was fun to do, and the AI partners are no where near as smart as a player (Example: AI Goku with Super Saiyan on his moves list will NEVER BLOODY USE IT!)
Nothing makes me happier then punching Frieza in his smug Frieza face then hitting him with a Kamehameha followed by Milky Cannon.  And maybe a Final Flash I dunno.
Be aware that some fights can feel cheap.  Sometimes you gotta take on 2 fighters at the same time by yourself and they can easily ping pong you and wreck you.  I cant beat PQ 32 because of this (stupid super saiyans and their stupid unlimited ultimate attacks)
So there ya go.
If you have ever dreamt of being a Z Fighter and helping to fight some of the big bads (I mean I got to face off with freaking MAJIN BUU!) then this is the game for you.
Also get the DLC.  It lets ya level to 99, adds some cool extra fighters, and more masters and moves and gear.

Hey everyone, really quick here is my personal review.  Total: 7.6 (Not Bad, could use some improvement though)
Graphics: 7
Mechanics: 6
Story: 8
Controls: 8
Gameplay: 8
Graphics - 7
Not my favourite thing, the graphics to Xenoverse are not super appealing.  The corners are a bit jagged, and I think a little more anti-aliasing and a bit less contrast would be useful, just to cut back on eye strain.
Otherwise, it is definitely Dragonball, and feels like it.
Mechanics - 6
I've heard and seen a lot of complaints about characters being too fast to hit and hit boxes not functioning.  Enemies can be a pain when they are faster if you don't have a higher level.  Also, some CPUs are inherently stupid and just fly in circles fast enough you can't hit them with any form of aimable attack.
However, the game does offer plenty in the realm of unique attacks, each with different mechanics to make it more or less useful to use for your character.  The amount of coding to go into these moves is impressive, even more when animations are accounted for.
Story - 8
Very easily the best Dragonball Game story I've seen, period.  It didn't just use Dragonball's story as a backdrop to a fighting game, it adapted the game to the story.  Every detail from Character Building, to the stages, to the XP system worked for the purpose of story progression.  A unique story in the future is by far what I'd enjoy.
The Post-Story is the one thing keeping me from putting this higher.  I dislike that Broly, a character only about as strong as Cell and weaker than Buu, ended up being the final boss after beating both Beerus and Demigra, both Gods.
Controls - 8
I'm sad to say my biggest disapointment here is that there is no run ability in Toki Toki City.  Being able to run (Or Fly) would make travel in the area so much more convienent.  Otherwise you have to walk at the slow speed to the stores or Parallel Quests before rejoining the main story.  Otherwise controls run fairly smooth.
Gameplay - 8
Between the story and other options, Custom Characters and moves work out very well as a reason to be drawn to the game.  The Mentor system makes me happy, as it highlights and mirrors Goku's own training throughout the series.  The Parallel Quests even explain a big chunk of the story, explaining why they exist is to halt the Butterfly effect from occuring due to the changes made by your very presence at events.
The big, crippling injury to Gameplay is the low drop rate of skills from Parallel Quests.  You can spend hours working on farming a skill and not get it.  In some cases it comes in a run or two, others it can take hundreds.
However, the game starts by throwing you right into the story, with the massive battles starting between Goku, Freiza, Cell, and Kid Buu.  This gives you time to test the controls out for yourself a bit before the actual tutorial, a battle against Future Trunks, takes place.
My Favourite Things, In Order:
- Character Customization
- Thrown right into action
- Each move is different
- No Character Clones
- Voice 8 Easter Egg
My Least Favourite Things, Why, and How to Fix Them:
- Male and Female characters within the same species have different stats.  This annoys me, because it makes playing a Female Strike Character not so valuable, because her stats will be lower.  Similarly (Though not usually what I dealt with) Male Ki characters were also not as strong.  Removing this system would be good for all involved, as it hinders character customization to build off gender stereotypes.  Plus with Majin, it allows a more Kid-Buu like character to be made.
- "Ki Spamming."  Super and Ultimate Moves don't have a cool-down between use to increase variation.  Some have a set-up, but others such as Ill Flash or Symphonic Destruction start almost immediately making it hard to dodge.  While I understand Ki Spammers usually get killed by someone knowing how to work around the move, it is probably better in the future to add a brief cooldown to make it more effective to vary a moveset in a DPS way.
- Characters.  I know this is going to be a sticky subject, but there are very few story characters to play as of various races.  Namekians only have one, Piccolo, and the Frieza Clan has one (technically 3) in Frieza.  Buu's three forms are present, as the only Majin as well.  While I understand the story limitations, these characters were included, plus a slightly different model between full power and standard Cell, and Goku and SSG Goku.  I feel the memory that one of the two Cells, the Freiza Henchmen, or the Saibamen used could have been better utilized to add King Cold or Dende/Slug.  Given a new series is on the way, the next installment in the Series could better use those spaces for new characters from Dragonball Super, however.  I'd reccomend going through the characters most commonly used in Online Mode, and Online Battles, on top of just Polling for which of the show/movie characters people like the most and figuring out which should be added to the Game.  I ensure you, nobody will miss Appule, Saibamen, or Cell Jr. in the Character Selection screen.
- "Grinding"  Grinding for skills is obnoxious in this game, with the Random Number Game making it hard to get some of the most desired items and skills.  I think it might be more effective to have the Randomized drops take into account average score (per player) compared to current score per mission, and number of games to help determine if a skill drops from a Quest.  Otherwise, adding more to the Skill Shop would be helpful!
- No Transformations.  Aside from Super Saiyan, only Kaioken exists for Transformation Skills.  It could find better use to add other Transformation skills to other races, especially Freiza Clan members or Majin.  Adding a better regenerative ability to Namekians (Drain Stamina for Health, maybe?) and Humans (Drain Health for Ki and Stamina) could replace the existing transformations and make sense within the story.
Overall this was a good game, and if another like it is made I will pick it up!  However, in it's current state it will really only appeal to people who are big fans of Dragonball, and not just people who like games.  This is something that time and tweaking could change.

Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I'm talking like you can play the 2013 tomb raider at the completely maxed settings kind of beastly. If you do then I hope your a dedicated fan cause your going to be dealing with a lot of typical anime to game issues. For starters you will be forced to run through an "open world" that is really just a bunch of small areas that you run through with linked load screen after load screen, until you finally get to a cutscene. When you finally do get to combat its either a normal fight like if you fought your friends, or one of the main story fights with reaction commands and amazing graphics. Why every story fight isn't like that at this point I don't know. Realistically I have been hoping to see the cinematic reactions appear in the versus modes for this game. Anyway so with a story that should have been like the first budokai (cutscene, fight, cutscene, repeat) this game took a different approach and tryed to let you "free roam" the world of naruto. Also about halfway through the game it introduces a rather annoying system where you will have to fight multiple enemies in the free roam even though your combat is basically no different than it normally is, with the exception of a bunch of moves locked out, and some replaced with almost cheezy reaction attacks. At the end that can become completely ridiculous forcing you to fight multiple bosses by yourself with no real advantage on your side as these coms beat away at you with boss level hp, infinite teleportation abilities, and complicated stacked ai programming that lets them combine their individual attacks into confusing patterns that you'll find yourself beating your head against the wall trying to never figure out. By the time you get to the last boss you feel tired of the whole system almost, and then your in for the most grueling back to back to back to back to back fight that you'll die and have to start aaaaaaaaaallllllllllllllll the way from the beginning of those encounters over, and over, and over. In the end you settle for cheap surfire tactics, struggle through the story to get all the characters, and enjoy replaying the few high res fights with reaction cinematics that the game has. Some of which you will have to do those really annoying parts to be able to play again. So in the end I have to say if your a super dedicated fan with a powerhouse gaming computer then struggle through and enjoy what you have but overall this game was a huge letdown with slightly polished graphics to the original and no change to the overall gameplay dinamic to make it more friendly to players and fun overall. This game is extremely addictive. It can get repetetive quickly, but the same is true of pretty much all roguelikes and games in general, and relatively speaking this lasts longer than some of the others I've tried.
It's got the FTL problem where it's more like a fruit machine than a game at times; if you don't get good items soon, you're completely screwed. On the other hand, its timing-based gameplay means that even with the most terrible items, it's POSSIBLE to get really far into the game. It's fun.
That said, I have one complaint, and one desire. I'd like to reorder my quick-item choosing. You can reorder the weapon wheel, but I prefer scrolling through my items, and I'd rather choose the emerald dagger to be directly next to the flamethrower, or a health-regen weapon next to my primary weapon. I'd like to remove some items from my next-weapon bar thingy, since I don't want to waste that extra second looking for the weapon I need.
My desire, of course, is more variety. Areas should change over time - say, the deeper you get the darker it becomes, or the more dirt, cracks and stuff become apparent in the walls. Stuff like that, to make it feel like I'm actually progressing. A number and more hits per enemy isn't really enough. Boss variety is good as well - perhaps a boss that attacks indirectly. Regular enemies should also really be more varied - I love (by which I mean I HATE) the flying mofo that drags you to it, because it really affects how you approach combat - if you don't pay attention, you could be beating a stunner to death when it grabs you and gives him an opening to stun you, giving everyone else an opening to curbstomp you. None of the other enemies really do that, especially in the late game.

The concept of this game is insanely awesome.  If you have enough parts you can waste away hours just on building a new ride.  The gameplay isn't bad - it certainly isn't "out of the box" or inventive in any way.  Tis your average, run of the mill arena-like pvp where they rank you according to your Power Score (the score given to your ride based on the parts you have on).  This ranking and match making mechanic is still in need of balancing, but it has improved a massive amount since i started open beta around a year ago (and now it's on steam in my country!).   The PVE side of the game is also severely under developed - but this is still open beta.  Thus far, as I gauge it, the development focus has been on direct balancing, new parts and so on.  Gameplay has been oddly untouched since i started - i say untouched in terms of expanding on the current concepts which they have.   Not a lot has deviated from setup we got at start.  They added in some "brawls", "training (or is it called exercise?)"  - very, very vanilla kind of level design (in a broad sense) at the moment.   But - this is still beta so there is hope.
There's a helluva lot of scathing in relation to the microtransactions - the use of ingame money bought by real money.  Now, i jumped into that myself and I'm also of the opinion that free players are severely robbed of the game experience here.  To get your first purple item in game, you would have to jack in around 40-60 hours (and i believe that to be a laughably conservative estimate).  BUT - this is in NO WAY pay to win.  By design it cannot be and I'd ask that you flat out ignore those assertions.  The reason is in the game's ranking system.  You will allways be matched up against and with people in and around your Power Score range - So if you go ahead and buy all the items in game, you'r going to be facing off against high ranking players whom has likely been playing a while already and you will not have a great time.  You win nothing by paying - other than the satisfaction of getting that item that you want and this is where the biggest failure of this game is to be found.
As i've eluded to above, the game has potential.  The idea behind it is awesome.   The component damage, the pace - it's all very awesome.  That awesomeness ends when you experience the actual gameplay  - not off-the-bat, but after grinding through the same old daily routine for the 6th week.  After going into another pvp game on the same map - and then also there are the meta's setting in now.  This, by the way, may open the door for clan activity to actually become meaningful.  At present it's a garbage waste of time.   However, I digress.  I don't understand the logic nor do I believe the feesibility of the game as a "free to play" setup.   Where  in War thunder I am still playing after like 3 years and not having spent a single cent.   Crossout will last you about a week if you aren't able to buy coin or packages.  The free to play side of this game is horrible - it is a remnant of a trend where games are being marketed as free to play and they technically are  - you REALLY can get all of the ingame items by grinding.  The problem is you absolutely wont and in fact, out of the 15 odd people that joined with me - i am the only one left (and i wasn't the only one who spent cash).  Those embracing the free to play side of the game is left with a bit of a deceptive taste on the tongue.  After week one you as a free player will damn-well understand that you either pay or leave.  The game will become so repetitive, so mind-numbingly boring and leaving you with no sense of accomplishment that you'd simply up and quit.  Now, for Gaijin & Targem this should be fine i think.  From their perspective I can understand if they didn't worry too much about the free players.  Where are they to get money from after all?  Usually the free-to play entrance into a game is supposed to lure people into spending.  This has not been properly executed in this game -  at least not yet.  Unfortunately this approach also is reducing the possibility of a rational gamer starting on a free to play foot with the intent to spend a little if he enjoys it.   As a paying player (and i have spent 2 AAA title's worth of cash on this)  I would absolutely insist on the game being more open for free-players.  It gives us a greater pool of players to interact with on the game.  By that I mean they need to provide more content that would be easily available and enjoyable for free players.  The horridness of free players having to literally grind for arond 400 hours (i'm thumb sucking this number!) before they get properly geared means that it will take a long time before end-tier matches are populated by anyone other than the same old faces whose paid their way there (like me - almost).
The other point I've mentioned, the gameplay it self, is where people like me and many other paying players are ending up RIGHT NOW and we are logging less and less time on the game because of it.  Always, keeping in mind that this is absolutely still just beta.  Yes,  our community of "geared" players is actually reaching a depleting phase.  Again this is something to expect during beta phases, but it is affecting the current experience.   Not an unsalvagable situation, but I would hope Gaijin and their partner acts on this as I am sure they have metrics to keep track of this.  The problem with the gameplay is the bland, vanilla approach they took.  It's kind of like Warthunder in the sense that it's vehicle based combat, you get grouped according to a "level' (Power score in Crossout and battle rating in Warthunder) and you brawl it out in a limited number of maps containing different objectives.  Again, very stock standard stuff here.  Capture a point, kill everyone, capture the flag.  The PVE experience, which I was very excited for once upon a time, is also not very imaginative. So in that regard, nothing new to see here JUST YET.
The problem with that - you' got this awesome ride you just customised and there are two options available to you - pvp missions or pve raids.  And they get old really damn fast.  PVP is fun still, but it's becoming monotonous.  My hope for this game would be that some proper level designers come on board and start creating some single and multiplayer content.  Missions you can do alone or with friends against the environment - heck, campaigns and the likes.   They already have a SMIDGE of that, but it is woefully insufficient to keep you wanting to come back.. at least after a while.
Anything that breaks the utter boredom of yet another PVP title like this.  You could even pay for expansions (dlc) to open up nicely created campaigns that last you 20 hours or more.  Anything really.  It has to have some kind of "something extra" to it.   Use the potential that is obviously there.
So, sorry for the LONG review but I thought it best to describe my own experience as best I could.  I'm still playing and probably will for another few months because i still enjoy some parts of this game.  i would however caution newcomers to this game to avoid buying packs and coins at ALL COST until you have around 30 hours of gametime in.  If by then you are about ready to tear your hair out because you've been stuck waiting for components for one damn part or if you think that buying that awesome thing you want will change your game experience - you will be sorely mistaken.   It wont.  And it is because of what I said above.  After the loot-craze (typically RPG style, right...) dissipates, you are left with a , as of yet, very bland game that is in serious need of some "fun" developments.  I just can't see something like this being considered good or healthy if you look at what they charge for their packages and what you are getting gameplay / game experience related.  \
So just be slightly careful when chucking money at this.  We made the mistake so you can learn.

Wow, where to begin...
I bought this on the Steam Christmas Sale 2014 as something to play on my awful laptop. I should perhaps mention that I had no idea what the game was about at the time, but it was cheap and scored high on Metacritic.
What did I find?
One of the best games I have played in recent years. It is difficult to explain just why it is so good without spoiling the game, suffice it to say that both the story and mechanics, as well as their execution, are without fault.
The game has a subtle, dark sense of humour which punctuates its noir storytelling. In terms of actual gameplay, I would describe it as an immersive puzzle platformer, though its beauty is that each problem can be approached in a variety of ways.
The game is not particularly long, and I completed it in roughly four hours, though my playstyle is ponderous at best. However, that should not discourage you from spending money on this gem of a game. The variety of solutions as well as the multitude of achievements will make subsequent playthroughs as riveting as the first.
In conclusion: Buy it, download it, play it, recommend it.

This was definitely the toughest HOG I've ever played. I believe some of that is on purpose, and some of that is due to the game's rough translation to English. I think certain elements of the story also suffered for the same reason, but, oddly enough, the devs were able to accurately translate a fair amount of humor (even including an Airplane! reference).
It's a smart game that forces you to pay attention and actually use your journal (unlike most HOGs). If you're going for the achievements, you're going to want to use an achievement guide (there currently is a good one on Steam) because there is an achievement for getting all the other achievements in one playthrough--and some of those achievements are easily missed.
There are a few complaints about bugs on the forums, but, personally, I only encountered one in the optional, non-story bonus backyard decoration element (which is cute, but isn't executed in the best manner). There was also one instance of a HOG item being labeled "pot" when it actually is a chain.
If you like HOGs, and you have a bit of patience, I think you'll find Evil Pumpkin enjoyable; however, unlike with most other HOGs, I highly recommend playing the game on casual as I imagine hard will have you tearing your hair out.
You really, really, really need to use your journal--I can't stress that enough.
In summation, it's a smart, enjoyable, and pretty Halloween game, although it suffers from some bad translation/spelling (the voice acting is hit-or-miss too), and it can be very difficult to connect some of the dots--and you will not get all the achievements in a single playthrough without consulting a guide.

At this juncture, I simply cannot Recommend Interstellar Marines. I played during the free weekend for about an hour and more or less saw all of the gameplay that is currently released.
This game started development in 2005. It was more or less "restarted" in 2009. Even if we're generous and take that second date, this game has an appallingly slow development cycle. There are loads of excuses from loyal fans ranging from the project having a small budget to few developers to it being ambitious in scope. These may all be true (or not), but the fact remains that they are excuses. This is a "game" that is still in a pre-alpha stage after a minimum of 5 years of development.
There was a failed kickstarter and the game has now been on Early Access for more than 18 months. If you want a mediocre space shooter that will be ready in 2020, buy it in 2020. The majority of Early Access games are never finished. This one doesn't appear to be any different.
About what's in the game itself. The gameplay is not BAD, but it's nothing special either. The shooting is competent, but nothing inspired. The enemy AI is middling at best. The game is supposed to be a highly cooperative, tactical shooter. You can't even communicate in Multiplayer matches. Most glaringly, there's an utter lack of style and content. It's bland and what is there... there's very little of it. Every mission is the same thing. There's only one enemy type. Two guns that behave very similarly. Environments that blend into eachother. The art is incredibly uninspired. This game doesn't have a unique "feel" or "look" to it whatsoever.
Don't buy this game now. Check back in a few years if you still care about this type of thing. By then, there will probably be something better than this.

Gunpoint is a fun puzzle game where you play as Conway, a freelance spy. Each level is presented as a cross-section of a building, filled with an expanding array of objects which you can use to make your stealth entry / getaway.
I really enjoyed the thoughtfulness that went into each level, and the way the game gradually introduces you to your abilities as a spy. A few missions in, you're introduced to the ability to re-wire the electronics in the level, and that is truly where the fun begins. Controlling the game is simple, but as the levels become more and more elaborate, you'll still find many creative ways to use them.
The pixel art graphics are detailed, and are a nice touch, even though things can tend to get a bit small on larger displays. I also liked the music - it lent the game a classic noir feel.
Gunpoint reminds me of a simpler, 2D version of Splinter Cell, but with more puzzle elements, and with a much more forgiving autosave / replay feature. Going in, I wasn't sure I'd like it alot, but after playing it for a bit, I can easily recommend it, especially to anyone who enjoys puzzle / stealth games, and wants to think a bit.
