Lamm is a puzzle-platformer, or to be more accurate, a platformer with a cool and unique twist that I will explain later. It's divided in several worlds, themselves composed of six to eight levels each. You access them via a nice looking hub, but progress is linear and you can't go to another world if you feel stuck. Each and every world brings something new to the table, whether it be saws, water or the simple concept of darkness.
Despite its looks, Lamm is far from a Super Meat Boy x Limbo crossover. B&W has been used in games for a very long time and its choice here is pretty relevant, accentuating the importance of the colored orbs. These are, by the way, the coolest aspect of the game ; by default, your character cannot jump. He has to pick up a colored orb to gain the ability to make a certain number of jumps (Black = 0, White = 1, Yellow = 2...). This idea is used through the whole game in different and unique ways, which I quite frankly haven't seen in another game to this date.
Everything isn't perfect, obviously. The difficulty ramps up very nicely but might be a bit too much for some, especially in later levels. The hidden fireflies in each level are sometimes tough to find, let alone get since you also have to end the level to truly "keep" them. But they unlock the best levels in the game, ranging from "easy with a twist" to "mind-twisting hard" !
I'm an experienced platformer player and I had a lot of fun with Lamm. The first levels are quite easy, but things quickly get a bit tougher and you have to think to get through levels without dying. It's never impossibly hard either, which I liked, but the last levels are a real challenge.
Even though I've read some negative feedback about the game's looks on Greenlight, it's something that doesn't really bother me. The game looks nice, every world felt fresh and I can't really ask for more. Considering its relatively cheap price, this was good. If I had to mark Lamm, it would be a solid

In this game, you play as a nameless clone warrior in the bowels of hell. The wicked creature known as Lady Tallowmere has created you for the sole purpose of tormenting inhabitants who refuse to serve her. You must arm yourself, paint the walls with the blood of innocent guards, take their possessions, and feed their souls to petrified demons to increase your power. To make things more entertaining for herself, Lady Tallowmere occasionally joins them in tormenting you by forcing you to fight her malicious pet, summoning huge monsters to attack you, doubling the patrols of guards you must slaughter, or distorting the flow of time itself. When you inevitably die, she will cackle and create another clone to set forth. Depending on how well the game suits you, you might adjust the difficulty of your path by sacrificing kittens or bargaining with the Angel of Death.
All in all, it's fun for the whole family.

Combat mechanics are well put together aside from the items which I refuse to use. Certain fights shift gears into excellently coreographed QTEs (take note every other game ever made, this is how you do QTEs).
The storyline hamfisted in between the combat almost felt tacked on and bored me to tears. I just browsed the internet half-interested in what they were saying on occasion. I can't openly advocate skipping the cutscenes though since you'll be completely lost. It just felt very slowly paced, especially if the target demographic should already know the storyline.
The horrendously tedious post-game content should be ignored EXCEPT for the side mission shards at the very end of the storyline, that is the content they added specific to this re-release.
The final fight(s)  can be impossible-tier but if you can get past the first half you'll utterly crush the rest in a satisfying fit of cathartic, indignified vengance. Oh and of course on this one fight you need to use items, you can't.
It's not a bad game by any means, why am I the only person who bought it? Perhaps everyone else got the previous versions released on console.

As a heavy fighting gamer, I was taken aback by the one button melee attacks at first, but that simply hides the surprising depth of the system of this game.
The fighting flows extremely smoothly once you have a feel for the basics, combos are basic but with the substitution system and animation cancels, it's rare you land more than a handful of hits per string, leading to kind of back and force exchange of strikes based more on evasion than blocking.
There is a bit of learning curve however, I would highly recommend playing at least 3 or 4 chapters of the story mode first before trying to play online matches.
As far as the netplay goes, the netcode is a little hit or miss. When the connection is clean, the game runs without a hitch, but when the connection chugs you'll feel it in both delay and the occaisional "Transmitting Data" popup for a moment. The gameplay flow makes laggy matches far from unplayable as there really isn't any urgency with your inputs or strict timing, but it's still an inconvenience when things slow down.
The single player story in this game shines bright, between the gorgeous graphics and the well written story (granted, it's yoinked from the show/manga, still a solid story), it's just a good experience. Also it's long. VERY. LONG. In a good way.
Overall, I'd say this game is worth a pickup for both fighting gamers and fans of the series alike. Just don't try to fight players outside of your region online.

Quite possibly the most barebones roguelite game I've ever played. However, I got a bit of enjoyment out of it, so let's go through the Pros and Cons:
+Addictive: If you're the type who delights in combat in which you are invariably victorious, you'll enjoy this game, with its rampant explosions, fancy level up decals, and flying chunks of gore.
+Variable Difficulty: There are options in place that let you make the game harder or easier. They exist, but I haven't really felt the need to use them.
+Weapon Variety: There are several classes of weapons that (despite their incongruency with each other and/or the game's hardly-there theming) are actually pretty unique when compared to each other.
-Cheap Shots: There are two actual threats to you in this game: Ogres that throw purple stunning potions, and Elite enemies, which take much longer to kill and do a lot more damage. This is how Tallowmere does difficulty.
-Enemies, or, a lack thereof. There are maybe seven enemy types in this game. They all do one thing, and have no other features other than that.
-A lack of direction. There's a character called Lady Tallowmere. She has a dangerous dungeon. You go into it. That's it. OH NO SHE GETS KIDNAPPED! Oh you just rescued her. If you love MMORPGs and anime, you'll love Mabinogi. If you love the freedom of being able to learn whatever skill you want, even if it doesn't involve combat, you'll love Mabinogi. Here are some pros and cons of the game.
Pros
--Decent tutorials that teach you how to effectively use the skills related to your chosen talent. Whether it's close combat or archery; smithing or cooking, the game will teach you how to use your skills so you aren't left wondering just what a certain skill does.
--HUGE skill tree, including plenty of "life skills." Seriously, you can do almost anything in Mabinogi. There's regular combat skills you learn as you master your previous combat skills, etc. and then there's also PLENTY of skills called life skills to learn. These life skills are generally crafting skills, such as carpentry or smithing; or it also includes skills such as how to rest or how to build a campfire. When combined, Rest and Campfire can help immensely with healing your injuries and stamina.
--Tons of quests! Mabinogi has plenty of quests for players to do! A lot of the quests are automatically received via owl, such as event quests, new skill quests, and Generation quests (storyline quests), so you oftentimes won't have to worry about finding a quest yourself. If you do the ones you already have and then turn them in, it's likely that an owl will fly over your head and drop another quest down to you sometime inbetween doing things for your current quest.
--Three playable races! Three may not seem like much, but Mabinogi delivers them rather well and I personally am in no complaint as to how many races there are! The races are as follows: The Giants, who are mainly used as warriors, and cannot equip a bow of any type, making them incapable of learning archery related skills; the Elves, who are very good at magic and archery, their specialized stats being dexterity, intelligence, and mana. However, elves are also a special race that are limited to what they can do, as they cannot dual weild any weapons, with the exception of puppets, and they cannot equip most two-handed melee weapons. The third race is, of course, the humans. Humans are a well-rounded race that can really learn any skill and equip any weapon (except Giant weapons duh)
--Frequent updates and the game almost always has an event quest of some sort!
--Free beginner mounts! Most new mounts you have to get through paying with real money (we'll get to that in the cons section) but Mabinogi gives new players two free beginner mounts almost instantly! You are given a horse and an eagle, which you can fly. This greatly helps with moving from place to place, and it's better than nothing, even if it may not be as fast as some of the payed mounts!
--Homesteads are pretty neat! Mabinogi has Homesteads, which are basically little farm type things that you get for free, and as you level it up (by planting crops on farmland and harvesting them for Kon, which is basically "Homestead Experience" to level it), it gets bigger at certain levels. There are plenty of homestead items to add, and it isn't all just for show either! You can add a fishing hole to your homestead that you can actually practice fishing in, if you can't be arsed to find some watter somewhere, and there is also a furnace, anvil, loom, spinning wheel, etc. that are all useful for practicing your life skills. So if you have all these things and you don't want to find the crafting station in a public place, just enter your homestead and there you have em.
--SUPER friendly community! Sometimes in Mabinogi you WILL have to ask for help. That's just how it is. You're never gonna complete Generation 1 (Saving the Goddess) solo. You're gonna probably have to recruit a few higher level people to help you out. This is why it is good for the game to have a good community, and it really does. I have never run into another Mabinogi player who trolled/hated/made fun of me (Hm.. except that one guy I kept beating in ... Ah well, he was just a sore loser). Everyone is super nice, and even if you ask for help and it sounds like it was a "stupid question" (there are no stupid questions) players are very friendly and will help you anyways. It is nice to sometimes just sit around a campfire with players, playing music and chatting, maybe sharing some food prepared by another player to get the bonus that it gives.
Now we're gonna get to the cons. To be honest, in my personal opinion, there aren't many cons.
--Limited freedom of movement. Unfortunately, there is not much freedom of movement in Mabinogi. There are set areas that you can go to, but you are limited to that area only, and if a hill is too steep, you cannot climb it (and it's probably the edge of the area) because there is no way to jump in Mabinogi, unless you include the little jump thing you can do when you have an umbrella open, but that's not at all what I mean... Also you can't swim, there's an invisible wall when you go down to a water source, so if you want to swim in Mabinogi, you'll be disappointed (I was.. lol).
--Still a great free to play game, but there are a few microtransaction things that are a bit of a con. Obviously this can't really be helped, I mean, how do you expect the game to make money if players aren't paying real money for at least SOMETHING in the game. The only ones that disappoint me are mounts and homestead items pretty much. Some homestead items cannot be obtained in any other way than by going through a microtransaction to get Pons, and using Pons to build the homestead item. I can understand this with the Homestead Stones, which you need to build things on your homestead, and you get 10 per day, per homestead stone, or even with the animals you can get with Pon in order to harvest their items (wool from sheep, eggs from hens, etc.)  but with DECORATIVE things you really should not have to pay real money just to decorate your homestead. Yes there are some decorative items you can get without pon, but they are mainly just trees, shrubs, etc. Things like cookie trees and lanterns and such can only be gained with pon.
-Ontop of that, mounts are mainly gained through microtransactions as well. The only mount I know of that isn't gained via microtransaction and isn't one of the starter mounts is the Pegasus, which is gained by completing all Saga Quests (which, by the way, are F*cking hard). It's a cool mount, and I would be satisfied if I had one, but some players may be disappointed in the fact that all they get for free is two beginner mounts and, if they work for it, a Pegasus mount. But like I said before, I understand the game has to make money, even though it may suck.
--Somewhat complex combat system. Okay so let's start by pointing out that when you get hit by a mob on mabinogi, regardless of size, you will pretty much, almost always, be knocked back on your A$S. That being said, the reason why the combat is a bit complex is because if you are fighting a group of enemies, it is very easy to become overwhelmed by them without the proper skills or use of skills. If you do not learn how to counter enemies' attacks and use the defense skill properly, you will be knocked over quite a bit. Trust me, I would know. It took me forever to get used to using counter, defense, and windmill to counter my enemies' attacks, and I used to always get tossed around the room. This is particularly annoying when you are a much higher level than the enemies and they are only doing ONE damage to you each time they hit, as this just causes you to be tossed around like a pinball and you can't even die, so you pretty much have to try your best to recover and kick their a$ses before your mind explodes from all the stress of not being able to stand back up before another enemy in the group hits you again.
-All that being said, the best way to go into combat is to AVOID aggroing more than 3 or 4 enemies at a time if you can help it.

Before I start, I want all of you to know that I do not own a copy of this game, but rather I've only played via free week.
This game is very interesting in terms of what it's aiming for. It's a tactical FPS that requires the player to use various, realistic feeling tacticts in order to complete objectives without dieing. The game has a very dark and errie feel to it, which, in my opinion, is a perfect thing for a game like this. You can use darkness to conceal yourself so that you aren't spotted. The animation, atleast, the characters gun, looks very fluid and realistic, and the gun play is very cool, and even satisfing to shoot. It's a very immersive experience.
However, for me, anyway, I've encountered a HUGE problem. I understand that this is early access, but this issue must be fixed before I consider buying. When you first launch the game, there is text that pops up, however, and I've expirenced this issue with other games made in the Unity Engine, but the text looks like a bunch of diffrent shaped boxes. It then puts me into the tutorial mission, which, even as a tutorial, is a very cool expirence. But, after the Campaign Simulation, the game seems like it freezes, goes to a loading screen, and puts me back into the beginning of the tutorial. At the beginning, it says that you can press Esc to access the main menu and skip the mission, but when I do, the only thing that happens is that the camera locks and you can move the mouse cursor around, but no menu.
Like I've stated, this issue has occured to me with other games made in the Unity Engine. I suspect that if this were that case, it is because I'm running with an igpu in the processer. But even then, it runs very smoothly.

You are a field medic (and the only one in this squad). You and your 8 squad members including your squad leader are in a transport truck moving to the AO. Suddenly, your vechicle gets ambushed by a Russian BTR. Your squad leader yells, "DISEMBARK, DISEMBARK, DISEMBARK". You get off the vechile in panic as the BTR blows up the transport truck. Miraculously, you survive, but not the others. Seeing 8 bodies rolling down the hill, the BTR laughs and moves on. Don't give up yet! As you have 6 bandages and 8 dying teamates at your hands. You first use one of the bandages on yourself as although the explosion didn't kill you, it injured you. Now, you must think tactically; you don't have enough bandages to revive all your teamates, but others do have bandages. You first revive your Squad Leader; he puts down a squad rally point as a spawn point. You then revive a near-by rifleman; he bandages another teamate. Repeating this process, you manage to save your squad as a medic. The squad leader applauds your for saving the squad. Your squad is now behind the unsuspecting enemy line and wrecks havoc on the enemy. You and your teamates overturn the battlefield and lead your faction to victory. - My first 10 hours in the game.

First of all I must say I am a big fan of role play games, that I started back at the date with Eye of Beholder: I consider the top of the genre Baldur's Gate (the first one), and this is the first time I play an Avernum game; I was therefore completely new to the lore, mechanics and rules used in the game.
From the beginning Avernum: Escape from the pit looks intriguing and catchy: from text to text and fight to fight, I found myself playing for 3-4 hours straight after installation without realizing it.
The art and the drawing are inspiring, there is a lot of text that really make us feel the story and the lore, dialogs are brilliant; character creation and advancement, fightings, divine and arcane spellcasting: everything it is intuitive and somehow innovative, taking clear inspiration from old paper rpgs and fusing it with "modern" skill trees.
Longevity also seems to be a strong point of this title: I played 4 hours and visited 3 cities, and I could understand from the world map how insignificant is the portion of underworld I explored so far.
The only negative feedback some people might point out is graphics, and on this I completely disagree: it is a simple retro 2d graphic but is not bad at all: on the contrary it is clear and fluent, does not disturb the eye and does not require big machines to run.
Also the music is fitting, with its epic tones: it is just a pity that there is not a bigger variety of tunes.
All in all, I would recommend this game to all rpg fans and to all retro gamers, giving it a solid 8.5 out of 10. There are not many better roleplaying experiences than this one out there :)

Ah, I hate to put a "no" review for Proteus. It's a quirky little game that has some heart to it.
Proteus is one of those 'experience' games a-la Journey where the enjoyment is in experiencing what is around you. For what it's worth, Proteus does offer a lot of charm; the background melodies combine with the various sounds of your island to create a hypnotic symphony. The wide open environment reminds a lot of Minecraft, only in a beautiful cell-shaded manner.
But unlike Minecraft or Journey, Proteus lacks any form of gameplay. It consists of wandering around until you find something that piques your curiosity, investigating it, and then leaving. And there are a couple non-standard things to find in Proteus; if a player feels like they're being led somewhere, there's probably something to find. Alas, there could stand to be way more of these curiosities, as they are too few. Exploration is all that Proteus has, yet Minecraft does it with wider worlds, more mysteries, more gameplay, and the ability to express one's own artsy fartsy tendencies rather than just experiencing those of another.
If you got the game as part of a bundle, it may be worth it to play; the experience is very serene, and the way the music synergizes with the environment is wonderful. However, even though the game may be "art," it is missing an actual game, and I would not recommend its actual purchase.
Final verdict:
Exploration games are an excellent concept, but it needed way more to be as memorable as something like Journey.
On a scale out of 10 where 4.7 is considered "average," this game would rank at a 3.5 - has potential, but doesn't necessarily meet it.

Well, let's start with facts: anyone who claims 'no coding skills required' is most likely setting standards to, say, 'mediocre to less'. Got an original idea? Code it, or have someone code it for you. That's what I've seen with 99%+ games.
That said, let me point out some
good reasons you should buy RPG Maker MV (RMMV):
1) Easy to learn, not hard to master: once you get used to it (and it's fast), you'll come into some things you'll call "limitations", then go to #2.
2) A great community, full of plugins and other resources (that's the "have someone code it for you" part, in most cases). Not enough? Check #3.

4) I bought it during a promotion, and I'd pay full price for it. It's cheap, for all it offers.
Overall, it's a
, and if you're beginning at JRPG making, you should
consider RMMV.

Looking for a review from a non-dragon ball fanboy? I'd help, but this game turned me into one. Ignoring what the franchise adds to the experience, Xenoverse is a pretty solid game. Defining it beyond that gets a little bit tricky, as the game is part fighting game and part action RPG with a dash of military flight simulator. Which, worded that way, sounds awful, but hear me out. The basic controls are simple, and the early combat can be approached by pressing the lock on button and any mix of the light and heavy attack buttons, with the occasional few energy (ki) blasts to keep them at bay because you have a button for those too.  Yes, you have a block button and a grapple command if you're feeling the need to be a professional. The actual difficulty rises pretty quickly, and this is where the real mechanics begin to shine. There's a difference between a dodge and an evade, there's also two types of dodge. The two gauges you have besides health, which are stamina and ki, are things you'll need to be constantly aware of and plan around. You might have enough ki to launch a super move, but if your opponent blocks, do you have enough stamina to block or dodge the counterattack, or have the ki to keep the pressure on? Basically, the game plays off simple controls and a wide pool of maneuvers to create the strategic atmosphere of a good fighting game without traditionally handling like one.
Despite the surprisingly simple to learn mechanics and controls, having the know how isn't enough to beat the story. To progress, you have to level your character up. This translates into grinding outside of the story. A lot. This would normally be something I would call out as a cheap substitute and a cop out in regards to difficulty when the opponents could just be higher in skill instead. I hold this back because it was only in very select few circumstances where the grinding actually felt like a chore, and those few times were when farming optional sidequests for certain gear or moves. The reward or drop rates are random, and that goes for everything in the game, aside from specially assigned quests. Items and moves are not rare in general, and overall the process of growing your character is a wholly rewarding one. Just a few level ups is enough to see a noticeable difference. This game is about progression just as much as it is about fighting, and a little bit of farming goes a long way to make rematches with bosses that interrupted your progress prior a real fun experience.  Although random drops may mean getting items or techniques your current character wouldn't benefit from, your inventory is not character specific, and the later ability to have more than one character makes it more fun to build different styles of characters later on.
While Xenoverse's RPG elements, fighting elements, and slight strategic tendencies on their own are very simple, together they add up to something there really isn't a single word for. Unique works, but it's more fun and surprisingly engaging than just calling the whole thing unique.
Flaws? If you can't forgive that a large portion of the cutscenes haven't been reworked to be lip synced to the English dub, there's that. Hate the tone of the average anime? That's kind of an oxymoron, as the only average about anime is that someone will have spiky hair. In Dragon Ball, that's pretty much everyone. Don't like shooting lasers out of your hands? Why are you even looking at this game unless you want to be Hercule.

--Plan everything. PLAN. P-L-A-N. Don't just waltz into a room and start slaughtering or you'll get very dead very fast.
--Watch and wait. Patience is very, VERY key in this game.
--Use the environment to your advantage, like smashing enemies into a spike wall or waiting for a spinning metal blade to do the job for you while you sit back and watch and enjoy.
--As soon as you get a Soul Group sprint as fast as you can to the nearest Demon Statue.
--Ponder why Lady Tallowmere is so sadistic and cruel at times.

Right now it's an arena shooter. With big artificial arenas. (But you knew that, right?)
The game touts itself as scifi. All that is scifi about it is the looks, it's not even half a believable world as Halflife was. Door switches, but no light switches. Nuff said. And everything is basically empty or a storage room. It's Early Access, they say.
I've been trying out the solo "campaign" = disjointed missions. The tutorial has the full range of glitches, from rocks clipping through walls in the station to falling through the scenery and bots that can't find doors (but keep running against the wall anyway) and that in "realistic" mode seem to score more teamkills than I do kills (ok, some people might argue that _is_ realistic). And the bot sometimes see you (and shoot you) when you're standing still and crouched in the dark. Or disappear if seen through a door when they're in plain sight and 30m away.
The levels are clearly made for co-op. They're not randomized (every keycard is where it was the last time), and if the AI shoots you, you must restart the whole mission (in co-op, there's spectator mode for you). Nice, huh? Forget immersion, you're traversing an arena, and you know it. The walls are paper thin so you can hear the bots moving next door."Reinforcements" come from who-knows-where, nobody ever notices a body lying around, you can be sneaky but the silenced gun will bring them running anyway much of the time (I wish I had Tomb Raider's bow & arrow), and when you stand still a while, you often get a bout of hyperventilation as if you had just exerted yourself. I guess it's best to not play the sniper - can't lie prone anyway. Did I mention there aren't any light switches? You can shoot out the lights, but some of them will turn back on when the weather changes. If you're doing co-op against the AI, you're going to have the same sort of fun that I had in solo.
At all that, it plays more like Slenderman gone fps. The enemies are a threat because you can hear them, because they come at you from the shadows, because they hit you from afar and kill you in a random careless moment. They often seem to know where you are, and that usually draws them out, unless their Artificial Stupidity pathing fails to find the door. At least it's a fair kind of Slenderman - one that you can shoot as it shoots you.
So, yeah, fps isn't my genre, and after seeing the tutorial I still set this at "realistic" (the highest difficulty) in the hopes the AI would be challenging then, and they definitely are. Unlike most other fps that I played, this game is not "holy cow, how many bullets does it take to kill that thing", it is "where the dickens did that come from" and then the mission restarts. I can see where they want to turn these robots into aliens later (and how that would raise their rating to where this could never be a "free week" game).
So do I like this game? After it beat my♥♥♥♥♥last night, I didn't, but today I think, it's different, it's original, and I feel challenged to beat this game, as much as I hate the interiors and the fact that the everyone in it shoots better than me. There's got to be a way to balance this with experience and smarts.
"Easy" should really give you a minimap (Descent had a nice 3D minimap, so it's been done) and a radar instead of dumbing the bots down, though. And a silent weapon. I'd definitely enjoy that.

This game is like Battlefield but slower-paced and a lot more realistic. If you've heard of the famous BF2 mod Project Reality, this game is very similar to it, in fact some of the original devs are working on Squad now from what I've been told.
If you like the Arma franchise this game is also right up your alley. The bullet ballistic is realistic, the sound design is amazing, and how the game is setup to encourage team play is wonderful. I would encourage every team-based FPS clans out there to at least give squad a shot, because Squad is very fun to play with a coordinated team.
On the note of the sound design, this game have some of the best and realistic audio for guns and explosions I've ever heard in any shooter game I've played, and I have over 15 years of playing shooters. You will hear bullet cracks if you're shot at from far away, you see explosions before you can hear it if you're far away, there's just so much attention to details. Backblast is a thing for RPGs, you can get knocked unconscious if you're hit by a car, you can bleed out if you're wounded, smoke grenades can be very effective, and much more, everything you would want in a realistic/sim/tactical FPS. A pretty good game for sure!  I got about 60 hours of fun with it using both DLCs.
The game is open world and is intent on letting you go wherever you want, with only a few areas locked off.  Unfortunatly, that means that at least half of each island is full of stuff you can defeat with your starting character!  (The fog island DLC is an exception to this.)  So, once you finish a bunch of the first island you go to, the second will be a bit easy and the others will be a LOT easy.  To counter that, you'll need to up the difficulty level as you go along - essentially doing your own level scaling.
The game has lots of crafting.  You can craft potions, rum, spell scrolls/stones/dolls, and so on.  I collected TONS of crafting ingredients but I barely used any.  Why?  See the previous paragraph.  Why bother making yourself stronger when the game isn't difficult?
While the game has major balance issues as the game goes on, don't let that throw you.  The game is fun!  Just don't make yourself too powerful and keep pushing the difficulty up.  There's much to see and many, many people to chat with!

The single player is a stand alone game which is based on the original multiplayer retired game "The Ship: Murder Party".
It has all the elements of the original game except that instead of taking part in the Murder Party (hunting and being hunted) you're making your way through to escape the ship by completing tasks which are part of a pre-defined story line. The story line is not long, I finished it in 3 hours first time, and in 1 hour the second time. The gameplay is lovely though! I highly recommend you playing this single player version. For me it's something between Postal 2 and GTA: Vice City but with it's own unique charm. Postal because you can do crazy things here, some are pretty violent, also you get to do routine stuff like eating, drinking, going to the bathroom etc. GTA because well, you have certain tasks to complete in order to progress towards your character's goals, like get a poison and inject it in someone, guard an ambassador, get in prison and kill someone, etc. In short, the gameplay is very unique, it grabbed me from the beginning and I even finished the storyline twice so that's how charming this game is. A must play in my opinion.

First Impressions...
Tallowmere is one of the better pixel art rogue-lite games that I have played.  The game is very accessible in the various options and gameplay areas.  If you find the game too hard, sacrifice some kittens and get 10 more HP per kitten killed!  Yeah, yeah!!!  It's a terrible thought, but it works well for this game.  IMO, the dev's made a rogue-lite game that works for many levels of gamers!  That is a great feat in it's own right!  If you find the game is not hard enough, there are a ton of options you can turn on or off.  The game is very configurable and that makes it fun for a lot of people.
The graphics are good for a pixel art game and look better if you turn on Anti-Aliasing.  They have a flat look to them during the turning animations, but this is not developer laziness, but part of the graphical charm of the game.  The controls are very tight and you have full control over your character during jumps.  You can use the keyboard or mouse to fight, block and choose weapons and items.
I like the game a lot so far.  I fully recommend this game to any rogue-like or rogue-lite fans.  Even if you don't like them because they are usually too hard, you can configure this game to your level of experience!   If you have a problem sacrificing kittens, then stay away from this game!  lol  Review pending more gameplay time.

Did you ever want to be a secret agent? Or a detective who is really good at hiding in the dark? Or just like to beat the living daylights out of someone? Well, Gunpoint lets you do that, and much more. Gunpoint is a 2D indie strategy puzzle game that is visually represented via pixel art (and it’s very well done, might I add) that lets you infiltrate buildings and steal top secret data. Though, unlike most games nowadays, you can’t simply walk in and take the thing. As what the category says, you have to what war veterans would say: strategize; and invent your own solution to the level. This makes the game very interesting, for there are so many options to solve each puzzle. You can turn of lights, and attack the guards in the darkness, or just come up behind them and punch them while their comrades point their guns at you. Also, you don’t take fall damage (because ♥♥♥♥ you, physics) so jumping out of 20 story buildings is okay! Sometimes, Gunpoint can provide some hilarious gameplay.
Gunpoint is exclusive with not only it’s gameplay, but also with it’s storyline. At the start, the story can be quite hard to get a grip of. But when you progress, it becomes a bit easier to understand. On that standpoint; the storyline overall, is brilliant. It’s quite interesting, dark, and sometimes humorous from time to time. Gunpoint also has a very unique little system called “Crosslink”. In this you’re able to change functions of many objects; like to link a button to open a door. This will be your main component in the game, and it’s also very fun to play with. Gunpoint is that kind of game that lets you interact with your environment and change it to your advantage. This can end up to a very interesting way to outsmart the guards, and to trick them. Each level challenges you, slowly getting harder until it’s almost cruel. All of this and more adds up to an original and superb game. To survive, you have to be smart, quick, and clever to maneuver your way around each level, can you do it?
Personal Gaming Score:
9/10
I recommend this to those who want a mind simulator, a stealth game, and/or a good story, but Gunpoint won’t suit the needs for those are looking for games with good graphics
.
… and I also can’t forget about the in-game level editor!

What do a sandbox and EVE Online have in common? They're both toys. EVE Online is a game without goals, otherwise known as a toy. If I had to describe the toy I would call it "sad." And then you begin to understand what EVE is all about. It really is a sinister place. I tried many things in the game and even bought older characters, but in the end I decided I didn't want to spend any more of my life in such a dark and sad world. Give it a shot if they really managed to pique your curiosity, but take my word for it this game is more punishment than pleasure so make sure that's what you're looking for.

A true sandbox MMO that will definitely eat up more time than you intend. There's so much to do and so many viable play styles (industry, exploration, PvE, PvP, and trade to name a few big ones) that there's really no excuse to be bored. You can micro-manage as much, or as little, as you want.
It sounds like a deal, but it's not. I bought it when I originally started playing, and trying to move that amount of stuff around as a newbie is more trouble than it's worth. Go to reddit or just about any other EVE site and ask for a trial code. That will give you 21 days to test the waters free, as opposed to the usual 14. Even if you subscribe 2 days after starting the trial, You'll retain any leftover trial days after subscribing.
Every EVE vet will tell you that skipping the tutorials is about the dumbest thing you can do. While it is a wall of text (they are fixing it...it's already better than it used to be, which is saying something), it will teach you the basics of just about everything in EVE. You'll also get a good handful of ships to fly around in and a nice chunk of money to start off with. See above - starter pack isn't worth it, and will cause more confusion than problems it solves.
It's easy to look at EVE's skilling system and say that it gives veterans an unfair advantage. It doesn't. You'll probably spend the first 2-3 months getting all of the "core" skills out of the way, during which you can still have a lot of fun and do a lot of things - a week into the game I was flying around with small PvP fleets (5-10 people) and meaningfully contributing. After the "core" stuff is out of the way, any further differences are on the scale of 2-5%. There's much more going on in combat that's going to dictate the outcome than skills.
It's easy to get caught up in the excitement of flying huge ships in massive battles, but rushing to that point is the easiest way to ruin your experience. You can fly those ships around, but you will be far from effective, which is a quick route to discouragement. Start out in the small ships, learn the game, get blown up. Frigates are cheap for a reason, and new and old players both fly them more than you'd think. Most common advice for someone interested in PvP? Fit 50 cheap frigates and go get them all blown up.
You will make tons of mistakes while playing (I know I still do), and you will lose ships. In the words of Ms. Frizzle, "Take chances, make mistakes, get messy!" It's the best way to enjoy EVE.

A game that seems amicable at first glance and for the first few weeks of playing soon turned into your personal hell. Mabinogi has a way of looking and feeling amazingly pretty until you start noticing what you've been ignoring. Over the course of six years this game has grown and showed a lot of progress, but at the same time hasn't shown progress where people want it shown. Either abuse your wallet with cosmetic items, pets, and gambling gachapon to amass your pride, or spend year after year working up to a higher place to the point where you feel you're actually good at the game to not feel content because of the amount of time you spent on it with little to show.
- Rebirthing; The ability to reset level and change age after a week, rebirthing will allow you to change your age and level, allowing you accumulate a higher cumulative level, which gives means a lot more points for skills that would normally be limited by a level cap.
- Talent System; There is no classes in Mabinogi, only talents. Every rebirth, from creation on you are forced to choose one of seventeen(fc) talents. Choosing a talent will provide bonus experience when training skills of that selected talent, and some offer unique tips and tidbits, like any of the adventure talents will show you locations of smugglers.
- The fact that there's so many talents to choose from. There's a lot to do in the game, from being a grandmaster warrior to gaining the highest magic attack, from using alchemy to dual guns. The choice of having puppets to fight for you, or using a ninja star to level the playing field. There are a ton of weapon archetypes, and if you aren't into combat, there are life skill talents such as cooking, blacksmithing, tailoring and adventure. Each of these are a welcome new change when you get tired of the usual.
- The community. Say what you will, the community is a positive and negative thing. While there are some people who  are snobby and elitists about fashion or combat, there will always be a few people you can befriend and have a great time with.
- Beginner bonuses: This game is a whole lot more friendly to new players than it was when many veterans started playing. From free skill resets to multiple character slots, being under the cumulative level of 1,000 provides a lot of nifty bonuses that surely help out.
- Events: Another positive and negative, there are a lot of events. Events, while either tedious or not viable for everyone give opportunity to get some decent items and experience, and most are repeatable within the time frame the event lasts. Most MMOs I've played have advent calenders or double experience events, but Mabinogi provides from role playing dungeon events to daily gathering/tasks to  get good rewards.
-Strong Update: While a lot of the problems I wish were solved aren't, the developers aren't stupid. They notice things that many players have issue with, and aim to fix them. Before, inventory was limited to a main 6 x 10 slotted inventory, and eventually if you paid money per month you'd be available to use additional inventory slots. Since, that's become a free service. There are constant updates that help a lot.
- Player-Based economy you will see here and in cons. The reason for this is because items are usually a bidding items in trading or selling from player to player, so it's not rare to find someone selling an item you think looks cool for an affordable price.
- Free services. While the game has a literal ton of items and pets and advantages you can get from using in real life cash, with a bit of hard work and dedication, you can get a good amount of stuff that will benefit you as much.
- Player Based economy is my biggest issue with the game. While there are good things about it, there's also the fact that not every item is in abundance, and a lot of items wont be cheap. That isn't my issue though, my issue therein lies that players are given too much power in deciding how the economy shifts. Recently, a lot of people have taken to trading in game items for real cash, upwards from fifty to over two hundred dollars. For singular cosmetic items. This is insanely limiting, and not to mention against the terms of service, but little is being done about it.
- The cash shop; It doesn't provide many things that completely shift the balance of the game, but there are some things. While you can't outright buy an end-game weapon, you may buy gachapon which offers anywhere from useless common items to rare and near end-game items with a higher grade. There are also pets, which once you have some, feel like a necessity to the game. It boosts overall speed of play as well. Why walk from one area to another when you can just get on your 3x movement speed flying horse and dash through the skies. Pets also sometimes provide a combat bonus of stats after a certain time of being summoned, or AoE attacks on summon or in their skill tab that you won't get otherwise. These save hides, and make the game a /lot/ easier. Most of these items and pets are unobtainable by others means, unless you buy them with gold from other players; and pets are not tradeable(usually).
-The voidless gap and journey to end game. For people that are casually playing this, this does not apply to you. After a while, you'll take notice to the difficulties of the game, from Basic to Heroic/Lord/Elite. It's because it's a classless system that viability becomes a problem. Chances are, if you don't stick with your initial combat-oriented talent, you won't be as strong as half the players. While combinations are great in this game, until all used combinations are maxed out, you'll be doing far below normal damage. Stats are also a pain for this. You might reach the level needed for a new difficulty, but stats are a problem. If you choose to be an Archer, chances are your damage will be insanely lacking, and this is because more than half the gainable Dexterity(source of damage for archery) comes from life skills that either you aren't looking at, or do not want to waste time and effort ranking. The only clear answer for this is a recent game mechanic, Reforging which amplifies the ability of your skills and stats on equipment. The problem with this is that the NPC-sellable kit won't make a big difference for you, and the rest of the kits are in the cash shop, as well as not definite. So, even if you do buy from players or the cash shop, there's a chance you'll need anywhere between one and a hundred kits to get the effect you want.
- Skills: Other than communication, you'll be spending your time ranking skills. Unlike most games, you don't just level up and spend your points on skills. Skills have requirements in order to be ranked that get tedious as the rank up. The requirements could go from use this skill five times to use this skill five thousand times to rank it. This is why talents are cool, it cuts requirements in half.
- Gear and crafting is a pain, if you're used to the usual "oh cool, boss dropped a rare drop. wooo, enough mats to craft my ultra legacy weapon." Mabinogi doesn't do that. Most good items are bought with currencies from doing daily quests or through crafting which is rigarous compared to other games where mats are common. Most of the mats needed are scarce and require hard mode dungeons or difficult tasks such as raids.
- Performance. The game was released in Korea in 2004. The system is ages old, and no matter how pretty they make it looks, it's easy to notice. From crashes to obscene lag there are a lot of wrongs that can grow to frustrating.

As a Naruto fan, I would like to give this game a fair shot. I really would. Unfortunately, this is not an optimized port for the PC. The framerates are an extreme nuisance; they cap out at 30 FPS, which isn't bad on it's own, but as most users will report, the game commonly locks out at ~15-20 FPS. And because the game doesn't skip frames whenever the framerate falls behind, it plays as if you're in slow-motion. This makes controls less responsive and overly tedious. There are no known sure-fire fixes to this problem as of yet.
And make no mistake; even if you have a high-end, high-performance PC, you still aren't safe. The problem is not in the graphical settings, it's something to do with the poorly executed port itself. This isn't something you can just fix by lowering your graphical settings or getting a better computer.
But don't let my review discourage you from buying the game, as I'm sure it would be absolutely fine if I had a proper chance to play it. Do a little research first, and if you really want to buy it, make sure you buy it on a console.

Escape from the Pit is the first part of the Avernum series. A true-to-the-bone oldschool RPG, it reminds me of the time I played Baldur's Gate back in 1998. The game's humble isometric visuals may scare off young players born into the 3D age, yet it shouldn't be missed because of the TONS of content it offers! The game world is huge and ripe to explore at the pace the player prefers. Locations are varied and bursting with detail, which is often offered in the form of cleverly written sections of text. NPCs are colorful and interesting as well - one of my favourites is Alice, the comely innkeep at Fort Duvno, who carefully pockets the gold pieces each time you ask her about interesting gossip, yet never hears a thing...:D Quests are fun to pursue and lead you to abandoned forts, halfway dug-out Nephil dungeons and bat-infested caves. The games controls are not too streamlined (in fact, kind of clanky sometimes), but nothing too serious. If you feel the urge to enjoy some retro role-playing, jump right into the Pit...you won't be disappointed!

Fallout: Earthdawn, the RPG. Now, I can't be sure that the creator of the game is at all familiar with Earthdawn, but the setting definitely has feels of both the post-apocalyptic-ness of Fallout, and the special flavor of the fantasy rpg Earthdawn.
The gist: You did something. The Empire was displeased enough to want you out of the Empire permanently. But, rather than bloody executions that are bad for morale, they sent you... elsewhere. The caverns of Avernum, where you are to live out the rest of your hopefully-short life. Of course, this being an RPG, you have other ideas and other options.
The game world is vast, with a world map spanning numerous screens in every direction, nearly innumerable dungeons, cities, and other places to explore. Three Major Quests, and numerous lesser ones (including, of course, the fetch quests. Where would we be without pointless fetch quests that, thankfully, you can ignore if you want to).
The system is solid: There is a great deal of customizability with your characters. You make a party of four, either from pre-gen characters or making them up from scratch from a mixture of attributes, 'feats', and skills, of which you gain more with every level-up. Sword-mage? Can do. Warrior Priest? Sure. Team of archer-priests? If that's how you want to roll it, sure. Some builds will be better than others, obviously, but especially on the normal and easy modes, you can build how you please and still make it through the game.
The graphics and sounds are not modern-quality. This is an indie game, and it shows. If you want a game that has cutscenes to ooh over, or wonderful soundtracks to slay beasts by, look elsewhere. (This isn't a slight on either the people who will look elsewhere or on the game, by the by. If you want a more visceral experience, by all means find a game that suits your wants more.) What this game does provide, however, is a lot of story. While your character is very much the anybody, allowing you to project yourself seamlessly without a pre-made backstory getting in the way, that means that all of the backstory is the setting's. NPCs there are many of. Random passersby in the towns often have their own things to say. While the atmosphere generated by the graphics engine is often lacking, entering a new place often will give you a long description instead.
In short: It's a solid indie RPG for people who like reading.
Avernum 2 and 3 presently are only available in a non-Steam even-lower-graphics-quality version, but I've heard the developer is planning on upgrading them in the near future.

To the person who has never played any games by Spiderware, this game is a well done, open world, turn-based rpg. Sure you might get lost, get murdered by gremlins, or burned to a crisp when you try to steal from a dragon, but the adventure is well worth the time you scramble around the caves of Avernum. The creativity you can put into developing your characters is also quite impressive and exhilarating as you make your company go from worthless nobodies into true heros and warriors.
To the person who has played these games before, specifically Avernum 4-6: This is very different from those, and in my honest opinion, a great improvement. I have been playing these games since it was known as the Exile series, and I have got to say that this is the highest point they have climbed in the last decade. Not gonna lie, 4-6 were kinda lacking in the realm of creativity. You had a set path and you circled around Avernum while barely having enough skill and items to make it to the next boss, making it extremely stressful and frustrating. Leveling up was by far the worst because you could barely upgrade a single skill, if any. Now, in Avernum:Escape From the Pit, they return to the style of their first real success, Avernum 3, but with even greater creativity when it comes to leveling. The alternate endings/optional factions you can join is also a nice addition.
So all in all, give this a try. It is worth it.

One for fans of classic indie RPGs. Don't just look at the graphics and think it's cheap and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ - the developer Jeff Vogel has been building this world for years, creating a detailed fantasy setting and deep plot. You have a lot of freedom in character choice and progression, though this potentially lets you cripple your party by ignoring balance and picking all sorcerers. (Don't pick all sorcerers. That's hardmode.)
My favourite part of this game is not being told how tough an enemy encounter is going to be. You might wipe the floor with those giant lizards using a single Call the Storm spell. Or you might get dazed, ensnared, and burned to a crisp by exploding slimes. The fun part is picking up from your most recent autosave, assessing where you went wrong, trying something different, and coming out on top with another strategy. (Tip: trigger fights and then retreat to a bottleneck, if possible. Don't underestimate upgraded spells, either.)
The clumsiest part of the game is the interface, which harks back to more than a decade ago, and has some annoying quirks. Can't alt-tab on Mac? Pathfinding range is limited and automatically enters dungeons if they're in the way? Isometric layout makes it difficult to click enemies in the square above you? Some of this stuff seems so obvious that it makes me think Jeff's decided it would take too much time to chip off all the rough edges, but you have to admire his dedication to making games *for a living* which means *to a budget*.
(Edit: it doesn't look like I have many hours in this game, but that's because I mostly play offline on my laptop while commuting. I estimate I've spent at least twenty on it at this point - and dozens more in Jeff's earlier "Exile" series during the mid 90s.)

In today's day and age, Spiderweb Software's games may seem like a novelty, but make no doubt that for the right audience they are exceptionally good games that offer a lot of bang for their buck. Avernum: Escape From The Pit is a modernized version of the Avernum series, and while the graphics are still not flashy the game more than makes up for it with good writing and solid turn based combat.
The game is a text heavy one, a blessing or a curse depending on the person playing. The writing is stellar and coupled with the low-key graphics it's one of the few games where you can really use your imagination if you so wish. It is worth noting that Avernum is an open-world RPG, so while I say the writing is stellar, don't expect a centralized story with deep characters--that's not what this game is. The game itself takes place in a huge underground cave complex, a joy for those like me who like underground fantasy settings and even for those who don't should still appreciate the unique and interesting world Avernum presents.
Avernum is lengthy, but if it's your type of game it will feel just right, making it a great game to pick up if you're on a budget. One playthrough alone will take  about seventy to eighty hours if you are a semi completionist, and even if you aren't I would wager it would take a good fifty hours to beat. Throw in harder difficulties and achievements and you can easily extend that playtime twofold.
The combat is fairly atypical for a turn based game, but by no means bland. Each ally/enemy gets one turn per round and there are different types of characters your party can contain (priests, mage, etc.). The game is open world as mentioned and it lets you explore the world on your own, the game guides you very loosely but the bulk of the exploration is up to you to do. As thus, you can easily find yourself faced off against baddies that are higher level than you which can keep the game challenging even on normal difficulty.
Open world exploration in the deep caves of Avernum mixed with some awesome writing and very interesting in-game encounters made this game a blast, but one of the things I liked most was how seamlessly the keyboard was integrated into the game. With the exception of needing to use my touchpad to click on a few interactive objects in the game world and assigning character stats/equipping items, just about everything you need to do in-game can be done with just the keyboard. Conversations, looting, fighting, moving--can all be done with the keyboard. If you're playing at home on your desktop, this may not mean much, but if you want to play this on a laptop without a mouse handy, this game is the one. Very few RPGs can be played on low-end laptops and even fewer can be played without a mouse, but Avernum is perhaps the only game I've played that's required mouse/touchpad input so sparsely. I feel like I could have enjoyed an amazing RPG experience from any Spiderweb game, but this one stands out to me due to the stellar keyboard integration.

It has been a long time since I first played LEGO Star Wars. My friends and I loved that game, and I have great memories. So when LEGO LOTR was on sale, I decided to pick it up for the nostalgia.
PROS:
+ Classic LEGO gaming. Whacking foes, building structures, funny cutscenes, everything. Loved it.
+ Great level design. I never felt like I was playing reskinned levels. I've noticed that in a few games I played recently, but not in this one. Every level is different.
+ Every character can do almost everything!!! LEGO Star Wars needed certain characters for certain actions. LEGO LOTR allows any character to complete *almost* any action, using items.
CONS:
- Not as funny... LEGO Star Wars was laugh-out-loud hilarious. LEGO LOTR tries, but it just isn't as funny. There were only two or three cutscenes that I really laughed at.
- Occasionally requires button-mashing. There were a couple of times where the game literally tells you to button mash. For minutes on end. Boring.
- Too easy. LEGO Star Wars had a decent difficult curve, running around completing objectives. LEGO LOTR feeds everything to you.
- Too many semi-cutscenes. Parts of the game where they show you what's coming up, but it isn't a full cutscene. They drove me crazy, since they're unskippable.
- Custom characters need to have a cape? What's up with that??
CONCLUSION:
Felt really good to play a LEGO game again. Not quite as good as LEGO Star Wars, but still very well done. Some of the new abilities are great, and I really like being able play through a level with a single character, using only items to get through.
FINAL RATING: 5/7

I come from games like Battlefield and Arma. While it could be argued that those 2 games are similar (first person shooter genre), they have very different game play. Squad can be considered a mix of the 2; tactics and teamwork/communication of Arma but with much less complexity. If you didnt know already before reading this, this is essentially a remake of Project Reality (a Battlefield 2 mod).
Do you NEED a mic to play? No, but it makes the game much better. If you don't plan on using a mic, be fast and concise with typing and listen to the SL (squad leader).
Squad is not really one of those games where you can log on with the expectation of playing for a quick 30 minutes while dinner is in the oven (I've burnt many dinners this way) and have a great experience.
Take the time to watch a few of the tutorial vids and use the in game "Firing Range" to hone your skills.
If you do have a mic, dont be shy; ask questions; talk to your SL and squad mates.
Patience is important. Check your corners. 1- 2 hits will usually kill; sometimes 3.

Interstellar Marines is no Call Of Duty, but it's not meant to be, and that's what makes it so unique.
Interstellar Marines is a great game, and while I haven't played it for very long, the short time I have played it has been good fun.  I got this game, and am writing the review, at the time of Update 17, with Free Week. I do plan to buy the full version when Free Week finishes though. Here's the short version of the review:
PROS:
-Fun, and non gory shooter
-Addictive gameplay
-Great immersive maps
-Loads of servers
-Intense battles
-It is possible to 1v1
CONS:
-Ammo clips are very small
-Lack of guns
-Sometimes the game suffers extreme lag spikes
-Servers are almost always full, so you are forced to join laggy and non-national servers
-Controls can get confusing
-Obscure controls, such as Q for silencer, F for flashlight and G for red laser pointer
-Skilled players often destroy new players with ease, therefore creating an unfair game
-Lack of Melee weapon
LONG REVIEW:
I love this game. While it is not perfect, it is still a great game and really up there. Now, being someone who has only played two First Person Shooters, them being Call of Duty: Black Ops II and Interstellar Marines, I know when I see a good one. And Interstellar Marines is a shining gem. It is extremely fun with amazing maps, and it really shows the power of Unity, all though I did experience some frame-rate drops, but I do have a rubbish computer after all. But that's not to say you should just go and buy it, because it does have its flaws, like every other game out there. For those who don't know, Interstellar Marines is an Indie, Sci-Fi, Roleplay FPS for PC.
The game has a few different modes; Singleplayer, Multiplayer, Co Op and Playground. I'll go over each one individually.
Singleplayer has a few missions at the moment, however most of them are just combat against bots with some added commentary from a robot. These can get quite challenging, but most of all frustrating as the maps are very dark and as you mow down the robots it becomes increasingly hard to track them down. Most of the time the robots actually find you, and shoot you down before you get a change to react.
Multiplayer lets you join servers, which are fun, but usually full and laggy, so sometimes you're forced to join some foreign server. Multiplayer is very fun when teams and players are balanced, but unfortunately that's not normally the case. Teams are uneven and experienced players are pitched against first-timers, creating an unfair game experience.
Co Op lets you play with up to four of your friends in each of the missions I mentioned earlier. There isn't any voice chat, sometimes making it hard to communicate with other players, but you can just voice chat with them over Steam, which feels like a waste of time.
Playground is a mode where there are lots of things to do. You can play a fan-made map called 'Get Killed By Bots' in which you fight close combat and long ranged bots. You can also go into Sandbox mode, which lets you activate features like physics and ragdoll, plus heaps more. There are some other things in Playground that I can't really remember as well.
The Tutorial level of the game is a little bit confusing, and isn't really a tutorial. It doesn't tell you the controls, or what to do - it just gives you an objective, which is a thing for on the field, not a tutorial.
Weapons is the bit of the game that I feel falls flat. There are only two, and I know this game is early access, but still, the lack of weapons gets annoying after a while. You have a regular machine gun, and a long ranged sniperish machine gun. The regular machine gun has 30 bullets each clip, whereas the second gun has 20 bullets in each clip. Reloading times is also a thing that falls flat as in the time you do that, even melee bots can have you dead. You can equip a silencer by pressing Q, which as far as I know, doesn't have any bad effects, Turn on the flashlight with F, and turn on Red Laser Sight with G. Right click activates the scope, which is really the thing that saves the combat. Another frustrating thing is that there is no Melee Weapon, therefore making it extremely hard to fight enemies in close combat, as the guns don't fare well in that situation.
Even though it has a lot of problems, Interstellar Marines is a great FPS that I definetly recommend to you if you like Sci-Fi and first person shooters. For 8 USD, this is a bargain. Good job, Devs!

You can wire devices up in a building any way you like as long as you don't cross coloured circuits, however judicious use of the aforementioned sound detectors etc. will let you do this. RPG Maker MV is more-or-less what it says it is, assuming that "the RPG of your dreams" is in top-down view, and features some form of turn-based combat. I will make several comparisons with VX Ace, the only other RPG Maker I have used, but you don't need to have used VX Ace to understand this review.
RPG Maker MV allows you to make an RPG through the use of a few major tools. The first and most obvious is the map-maker, wherein one simply draws on a grid to make the map. Different types of tiles can be used, as well as background objects such as rocks and pillars. Passability of tiles (both absolute and directional) can be altered, as well as making damaging floors, and those that partially obscure your body, akin to bushes or water. Unlike in VX Ace, it is possible to layer multiple objects on top of one another without using events, though this sometimes happens accidentally. The aforementioned events can also be placed on the map, taking the form of intreractable characters or objects, or invisible spots that cause other things to happen. The event system, while not all-powerful, is fairly robust, and can do quite a few things without any coding knowledge whatsoever.
Next up is the database, which stores all of the data needed for the game, such as party members, enemy types, attack animations, skills, system settings, and more. All of these things are fairly easy to use, though making custom attack animations still takes a bit of work. Unlike in VX Ace, preset battle and menu text (e.g. [enemy name] emerged!) can be freely altered from the database. Like VX Ace, however, enemy A.I. is still somewhat simplistic. This can likely be remedied through the use of plugins.
Plugins are another major component of game design (unless you simply choose not to use them). There are numerous plugins made by the community, and I'm pretty sure that a few come with the program itself, though all of them should be free to download. The functions of plugins are so numerous and diverse that I cannot possibly cover them here. Basically, if there's something you want to do, and the base program isn't capable of doing it, there's probably a plugin somewhere than can bridge that gap.
Unlike in VX Ace, one thing you
need a plugin for is a side-view battle system. Side-view battles are supported by default, and you can opt to use them instead of the standard first-person view.
Like VX Ace, however, RPG Maker MV features a character creator. This can be used to create new sprites and face graphics for characters in your game if you don't want to use preset ones. It also lets you export sprites for use in side-view battles. The character creator here has more options than the one in VX Ace, including more precise coloration (you can often color different parts of an outfit separately) and much better looking face graphics.
It should be noted that you can always import custom character sprites from outside the editor if you want to make something the character creator can't, as well as outside assets for map tiles, music, sound effects, attack animations, enemy battlers, and pretty much everything else. If you're willing to put in the effort, you can make a game using none of the default assets whatsoever. Of course, that assumes that you can actually find/make custom assets for everything, but there are some free-to-use assets out there on the internet for those of us who can't make them by ourselves.
On a technical level, MV has a higher resolution than VX Ace, and uses larger sprites. If you want to use sprites from VX Ace, you'll either have to carefully resize them, or use a plugin to alter the default tile size. Another technical aspect where MV differs form VX Ace is performance, Unfortunately, I cannot say that MV performs particularly better than VX Ace; despite how slow Ruby can sometimes be, the coding for MV seems to be even
and, in my experience, has
lag than VX Ace. Perhaps this lag only occurs during testing, and not the actual game, but it seems that the lag, at least on weaker computers, is a noticeable drawback.
In terms of preset assets, the music is numerous and varied, though it seems that not every tune is loaded into a project by default, so you may have to manually hunt those down. Many of them have a less video-gamey feel than the music from VX Ace; whether or not that is a good thing comes down to personal preference. The graphical assets for maps may actually look slightly
appealing than those of VX Ace, despite being fairly similar to them. Character assets are of decent quality, though nothing mind-blowing.
Overall, RPG Maker MV is a fairly powerful tool, though plugins will be needed to achieve the full extent of that power. Also, because MV provides virtually no preset database entries (whereas VX Ace had numerous pre-designed skills, weapons, and enemies) you will need to have ideas and the ability to balance the game around an arbitrary starting point in order to actually make something. Playtesting is key; if you test it enough, it will eventually work out all right. There is a little bit of an initial learning curve to master the event system, but once you figure it out, it will be easy to use. The only real inherent weakness is that gameplay will experience lag on weaker computers. Any other weakness or shortcoming can probably be overcome with the right plugin.
RPG Maker MV is fairly strong and versatile, just don't expect to start churning out high-quality games overnight. It doesn't quite work miracles, but it can still do quite a bit if you're willing to put in the effort.

I've been playing EVE for nearly a decade now. I created my first character back in 2005, but I didn't really truly appreciate the game until I created my second character in 2007. I play primarily from the launcher and not via steam due to how old my accounts are.
EVE is a game of social politics, economic conquest, and unending warfare. You can do almost anything in EVE, you can be an industrial mogul manufacturing ships and equipment, you can be an unrivaled excavator of valuable resources vital to the unending cycle of creation and destruction, you can be an explorer of the far reaches of the EVE universe's nearly 8000 fully to scale star systems and sell your knowledge of locations and acquired rare goods, you can be a feared combatant of the galaxy of your own cleverness and dedication, conduct truly scandalous acts of ruthless espionage, you can even, as I do, lead and direct truly strategic and tactical combat as a fleet commander.
In this game, the only limit is your own ambition and will to find what serves you best. I do what I love in EVE. I lead a small guerrilla style force deep into the hearts of the vast player operated nullsec empires; making hit and fade attacks via the game's vast array of ever changing and unconquerable wormhole systems.
Many will try to disuade you from your dream in EVE and tell you their less imaginative way is best. They're wrong, your own savvy, acuteness, and will to find your own way are your best assets in this game. EVE favors the bold, but make no mistake though allies are necessary to advance in EVE. This is not a game where you can ignore the universe around you and expect it not to interact with you. If you choose to inhabit this universe and then ignore it, as many do, you will often do so at your own peril.
As I said before, the only limit is your own ambition and will to find your way.

While the feature set that comes with any RPG maker is extremely limited, the ability to create, share, and download plug-ins that add new functionality to games allows developers a great deal of freedom in design. Assets are easily added to the project by simply dragging them into the folders that the program makes for you. The included assets (music, art, etc.) are great for a beginning developer, allowing them to make games that are complete, functional, and fun without having to struggle to understand complex scripting. For more experienced and ambitious developers, adding in new assets is simple and painless, and while making plug-ins might require some (or significant) knowledge of programming (JavaScript, I think?) there are many offered for free online.
If you're an indie developer or small team looking to create a professional quality 2D RPG, RPG Maker MV is an incredible tool that can bring your dream game to life.

Dude I used to love this game, and so did so many others. Like I had some of the happiest times in my life through this game; I started this game with 2 of my real life friends, found an amazingly fun guild, and made an amazing friend (though I'm sadly no longer in contact with them) as well as other great friends. Now, sorry for this giant rant, hopefully you read it. I seriously loved this game.
I went and replayed the game about a year ago, hoping to relive my happy times, and to some extent I did, but to a very small extent. I went and played on the Mari server, the once biggest server in the game. I found ALOT of fun through Martial Arts (it was boxing basically), and it was flashy, and the enemy AI (The AI used to be really smart and worked very well, but it was never upgraded to combat skills like Alchemy and Dual Guns, so it became really stupid when you used these skills) was still functional using it, but besides that, everything that made the game crumbled. There was so many damn skills, each one rendering older skills useless. Magic to a point and archery more or less were replaced with Alchemy. Then puppeting came and replaced Alchemy's biggest selling point; having a golem. Then came Dual Guns to completely replace archery (like so few people used archery, why not go and fix it?). The last thing that was added before I gave up on the game was Ninjistu, and I just gave up. It was so silly and extremely anime (yes the game's korean, but it had taste and a really nice art style; not just full fledge kawaii desu Naruto rip-off crap), and I can only imagine this replaced another skill class.
That wasn't the only thing that made me leave, there's a bit more. I could deal with a load of crap skills as long as I had some fun ones, but each new event was complete crap. Back in the old days events were so much freakin fun! Like there was a skiing event, a cotton candy sheep event, and a water balloon party event! (just to list a few). Aw man these were all great and alot of fun to me! But when I returned, it was just non-stop re-hashing of the dragon boating event (where you go down a river in a raft, fight some mobs, get a reward, rinse and repeat) and the Tara event (a japanese style event with a dart throwing mini game and a test-your-strength hammer game.) The Tara event was fun when it released, but it REALLY overstayed its welcome through it being rehashed every other week.
The economy also went to complete crap. Current day rare items would cost about 10 million+. You wanted a guitar? Better be rich, because you're gonna have to dish out about 20 million. Not only that, all old rare items went to complete commodity. Like I had a rare Leprechaun outfit that was super rare when it first came out; I was one of the maybe 20-ish people who had it on Mari, but when I rejoind they were barely even worth 100k (this is basically normal spending money in player markets). Due to Nexon just re-hashing old content, extremely rare items became to the point of being only uncommon to just somewhat rare. I used to be so proud of alot of my rare clothing; since alot of the game was about fashion and being distinct and being yourself, I felt proud walking about with some really cool n rare clothes, but now that satisfaction I had was quickly diminished.
Lastly what made me give up on the game was how lonesome and empty the servers became and how crap the once thriving and amazing community became. I played in about 2009 to 2010, and when I did, I could basically just walk up to anybody and either join in their conversation or start one, and befriend them. It wouldn't be some weird akward conversation either, people would just talk and be friends with eachother. The game used to be a huge party. You could walk down dunbarton (basically the games main town) on almost any server and find naked people running about PvPing one another, and then just down the road find a group of people participating in Elves vs. Giants war. It was great! But when I went back, the place was completely lonely. Nobody talked, there were barely any live guilds anymore, most guilds being dead, and nobody Pvp'd anymore. For the most part, the game was just deserted.
Sorry about this huge dang rant man. I just really love this game. It was really important to me. I made alot of great friends through the game, some that I'm sadly no longer in contact with, but I still have the fond memories. This game was amazing in every aspect in its prime; great combat, great community, and great events; there was something to do for everyone, and the game truly was a fantasy life. You wanna go and do something? Go do it! You can! Everything felt important and was satisfying. Even just fishing and gathering potatoes and such was fun, because you always had a friend while doing it or just someone to talk to, and a reason to doing so. I'm always hoping to find another amazing game like this; a game that'd make me excited to wake up and see what's going on, and just a sheer joy to play. I keep hearing about FF:XIV, and here's hoping that I'll be able to enjoy it like mabinogi.
Once again, sorry for this giant rant; I'm just super passionate about this game. This game meant alot to me.

Borderlands is one of my all time favourite games, and the second one was even better, but this review is about the game that started this awesome series.
There are tons of side quests that will keep you busy and get lots of loot to help you through the main story line, and with thousands of different gun combinations you will never run out of new loot.
The world of Borderlands is huge and at times feels never-ending, which is good because it makes all the side quests feel important and not just “another generic side quest”. There are also a number of different landscapes and types of areas that will keep the long story line interesting and have some sense of progression.
The character choices are also very interesting, with each class being very different than the rest. You can play a more tanky class, sharpshooter class, or even a guy with a deployable turret that eliminates anything in front of it (my favourite class). The skill trees that come with these classes also help shape the kind of build you want for your character.
