I don't know what compelled me to buy this game. All I can say for that is I have my own shortcomings.
Gameplay is nonexistent - it's a walking simulator.
Graphics look awful, especially when you look at certain objects like trees, and I don't mean that because it's pixelated. There are good ways to accomplish that art style, this ain't it.
Audio quality is alright, making it the best thing about this game by a long shot.
Now it's time for me to go into ranting. The section below has little to do with whether or not you should BUY this game, and everything to do with me being tired of seeing walking simulators tirelessly hoisted as
Games like this and Dear Esther are awful as games
. They're not games, they're virtual art exhibits, and that is the problem. If you think these games are art and the rest of gaming isn't, you are part of the problem. We view these games as art because it reminds us more of what we've already established long ago. They don't progress art except by saying "see, I can replicate the feeling of an incredibly boring film or art exhibit ON THE COMPUTER". They don't establish anything new. At all.
Still, the knee-jerk reaction across almost the entire gaming press is to heap praise and worship it. Why? Because we tend to see older types of media as having more artistic merit by default. Books are seen as having more worth than movies, movies as having more merit than games. Dear Esther, Proteus, Gone Home, and the entire library of pretentious indie titles only serve to play along with this by regressing gaming to feel more like old media, even if it's with new messages and perspectives.
How about instead of praising walking simulator after walking simulator as shining examples of games as art, we instead hoist up games that actually use more aspects unique to gaming?

Avernum: Escape from the Pit is a remake of 1999's Avernum, which in turn is a remake of Exile's Saga, developed by Spiderweb Software, a indie software house which over the years has seen certain success among fans of the "hardore" RPG.
With a structure that remembers the great classical, the player takes the control of a party of 4 characters, exiled as traitors of the empire in the Avernum, an enormous underground world in which city and factions have risen.
Overall this Avernum: Escape from the Pit proves to be a good old-fashioned RPG: an original setting and a good exploratory component, excellent longevity, a turn-based combat challenging and complex and a narration over the top, true mark of factory of Jeff Vogel's games.
This title is an excellent starting point if you want to approach the Saga of Avernum and fans of the genre should definitely not let it get away. For everyone else who would like to give it a chanche, remember that it's a good buy for the price, especially if you succeed in passing over the technical execution that is not to the height of the great productions.

My first encounter with other people for my first colony: New Mana
Trading caravan from a nearby colony approaches my territory
Colonists get excited from the promise of new foods and materials
They have been eating Beaver, rat and Cougar for so long.. Oh How they long for apples or even Alpaca!
Caravan stops before New Mana, and calls out greetings of peace and friendship
I send out my negotiator, Samantha Glut, a 25 year old entrepeneur who is an active nudist and the designated hunter. But she is VERY persuasive in speechcraft!
I trade some fine Beaver pelts for new meats and fruits, as well as a few trinkets and wool hats for the coming Winter
One of the Caravan guards expresses attraction towards Samantha, who in turn finds it cute that someone likes her
Doc White leaves the cave while mining to create room for a billiards hall, and strikes up a friendly conversation with the trader
JUST THEN!! THE PIRATES ARE COMING!!!!
5 armed brigands appear on the edge of the map, weapons drawn and charging towards my little base
Damn.. Only 3 of my colonists are armed, and one of the guns is pretty much gonna fall apart anyway
The Trader laughs heartily
"We will help you against those Red Sword Marauders!"
And so, they ready their weapons, pump the shotguns, prime the grenades
The Pirates encroach, seeing the seemingly easy target
Samantha yells her warcry and fires a shot at them
They return fire but miss her, so she runs back behind a sandbag fortification, she's too pretty to die!
As the pirates near the colony, the caravan ambushes them, bullets fly in every direction, blood splatters across the grass, and explosions disturb the otherwise peaceful and scenic enviroment.
The pirates lay slain. Absolutely Slaughtered by the heavily armed Trading Caravan
My colonists express joy over the victory and at their new friendship with Halderd
Trading Caravan says farewell. They have outstayed their welcome
They leave, feeling chipper and a sense of accomplishment at killing some pirates and helping strangers with a nudist as their spokesperson.
They get ambushed by pirates and Grizzly bears. Only 4 make it out alive.
My colonists loot the bodies, gain a few firearms and rotisserie the corpses over the bonfire that night, all the while drinking merrily and playing Horseshoe toss.
10/10 Would Trade again

I finished the game right now and well...I have mixed feelings about it. I give a thumbs up because I loved previous Risen games, and want to support the developer which is a semi indy european company, but I'm not sure if I can recommend this.
Ok, the things which Piranha does great in general, does great also in this game: the atmosphere, the exploration, the humor and the side quests. AND Risen 3 does a better job in those things which are generally bad in Piranha games, like it is more polished than previous Risen games, and finally has an approachable fighting system as well, but the story is horrible as usual (even if Risen 2 had a decent story anyway).
So what's the problem? The problem is that the game is not new. RIsen 1 was an interesting game, and then Risen 2 came out and was able to bring some freshness, so they were different and innovative experiences on their own.
But Risen 3 is not more than Risen 1+2 with an updated Risen 2 graphics. It is disappointing even if the game is very enjoyable.
Then for whatewer reason the devs cut the story and the lore of the previous games and introduced a new storyline and arch enemy. It was quiet a WTF?? What made the story more messy is that they made constant references to the happenings of the previous games even if the story line doesn't have any connection with Risen 1+2.
Because the story was uninteresting I felt the game a little longer than I wanted. It is a 40+ hour game, bear in mind.
So should I recommend this game? Well, if you love Piranha Bytes games and want to get all of them, you will buy it. If you enjoyed the previous games but you are not a hardcore fan don't buy it, becuase previous Risen games are better. If you hated them, you will hate also this one.
But for starters maybe this is the most accessable game. It is the most polished out of the 3 ones with the best fighting system, and becuase it has a different story you don't need to play the older games to get into it.
I personally enjoyed it, but I feel it completely skippable.

If you played and enjoyed Risen or Risen 2 (or any of the Gothic games, for that matter), this game will feel immediately familiar. It continues with the pirate-y themes from the second, which I wasn't crazy about, but it didn't take away from the game too much for me.
The gameplay mechanics are solid enough, and the graphics are decent. The voice acting and dialogue is almost all hilariously terrible, and the story is pretty poor, but I still found myself enjoying playing it.
Honestly, there are better games out there. There are better games trying to do this exact same thing that you could play instead. I tend to have a soft spot for wonky European RPG games though, so take this recommendation with that in mind.
In the end, should you play this? Maybe. Did you play and like the other ones, and did you want more of that? If yes, get this. You know what you're getting in to. Do you just want an open world RPG and haven't played one before? You can probably find better options. If you're looking for deep character customization or a great story, you'd be better off looking elsewhere.
Still, not bad. I enjoyed it and it's lengthy enough.

This game at it's core is fantastic. It's the best installment of a Dragon Ball fighting game since Tenkaichi and Budokai. Each character feels diverse, the combat system is very fun and has appeals for casual and harder core players, and the story mode is surprisingly interesting.
This is why it is a bleeding shame that BanDai turned it into a P2W DLC fest.
You may not care if you do not plan on playing PVP at all. If not, I completely recommend this game. However, for the full DLC package of $10 per package with 2 DLC packs out now and another one on its way, the price for winning becomes very steep very quickly. These DLC packs include equipable items and super moves that go against the design of the combat engine and make winning matches versus those without the DLC free. Some of these include a Z-Soul that recharges your stamina when your opponent deals damage to you, a super that freezes your opponent for a set amount of time and disables their ability to vanish or use escape moves (which no other move in the game disables, including *paralysis moves*), and a DLC fighter (Nuova Shenron) that is strictly better than all other default fighters.
It's unacceptable and blatant P2W, which is strictly unacceptable for a game that already costs $50.

This game used to be good. It used to be fun to make a weak bot and get paired against weak bots. Now you make a weak bot and you get paired with a huge pool of everyone. It's trash. That is only the matchmaking.
The Weapons
Oh the weapons of robocraft. Why. Why did they add anti-air. Imagine adding a weapon into Call of Duty where it can instakill anyone thats using shotguns (just as an analogy). This was added because appearently rail weapons weren't good enough to counter air. Yes, there were the small flies that were unhittable. Here's a solution instead of adding the stupidest addition to any game i've seen ever. REMOVE those stupid little tiny flying robots. 2 problems solved. But no, instead they decided to make air unusable if in the terrible matchmaking there was an enemy happened to have an anti-air. And as for the missiles. Why. Why would you make that. Doesn't matter what kind of bot you have. What kind of strategy you have. You will end up in countless situations where you are powerless against missiles even at full health. I kept thinking to myself, oh these will get nerfed or hopefully removed eventually. Nope. They added a smaller version so more people can use them. Same thing happened with flak. Oh and protoseeker, yet another gun that you don't need any skill to aim whatsoever. Just throw that one onto the pile of things that shouldn't have been in the game. And the new weapon, the gyro mortar. Unbelievable. I used to be all "why is there anti-air if there isn't antiground?" (you know, cause I hated anti-air) Well they added anti-ground and its called the gyro mortar and it pushed me to uninstall after 1 match playing against people using it. Fix. Your. Game.
Battle Arena
Regular battles used to be fun. They had their own original ideas and all. You would have to shoot the control points to capture them instead of just standing near them. How cool is that? The best part was it made it so in order to capture points you had to stop shooting at enemies. Probably one of the 3-4 balanced parts of the game. Then, once you captured all the points, you would attack the enemy base and win. Whichever team was better won the game. That's how games are supposed to be. There was opportunity for comeback, but if your team wasn't as good as the other one, you didn't win. (oh and on a side note the overclocking system was a lot of fun and made the game interesting as time passed). Now what? They threw away their idea of breaking the control points. Its a stand to capture. But I suppose the points don't matter now. Let me explain. In order to win, you must charge your annihilator to destroy the enemy base. Capture points and it charges faster. If you have all the points captured (near impossible to defend now), then you can steal energy from the enemy base. This keeps some of the previous battle arena. However, there is one part of this new battle arena that ruins everything. Periodically, a protonite core will erupt out of the ground. The team that is behind can destroy the core (which is really easy) and if they do, their charge gets matched with the winning team's charge. The entirety of the battle was now pointless and it has basically started a new game. That's garbage. I get they are trying to add new opportunity for comeback as its hard to comeback in a progressive capture mode, but this is really poorly designed. Bring the old battle arena back it was much better.

Don't buy this game if you don't have a mic. Communication is very important, and going in without one is going to make your experience harder to enjoy.
Don't buy this game if you're bored by not shooting and by dying easily. You are required to fulfil a role and that may be logistics transport, or defending a point way behind a frontline.
Other than that, it's an addictive game. What mechanics are in the game are implemented well, although there's still a very long way to go. No bugs rush to mind immediately, barring maybe your rifle having no collision with walls, so you can stick it throuh the floor, although you can't fire it through walls or anything.
It's really immersive, too. I haven't played another game with such fantastic sound design. Incoming fire makes you shrink in your chair, no joke. It's genuinely rough getting fired upon, and I can't think of another game like that - not even ArmA. Hearing vehicles move nearby also instils anxiety, and prepping AT takes a few seconds, adding to the tension. Don't even talk to me about incoming RPG and frag rounds.
The game looks great too. It's very visually impressive, although the animations in a troop transport could use some attention - having a soldier just stare at you, unmoving, unflinching, statuesque is a bit unsettling. Some idle animations would do a lot of good. Other than that, the muzzle flashes, dust, explosions, hitsparks, particle effects are all top-notch and are like something out of actual war footage.
I think there are some balance issues: for instance, US AT capability is awful compared to all other teams in the game. The US use a LAW, which drops really quickly because it only has one stage of rocket ignition. All other teams use RPGs, which have two-stage, giving them way more distance. The LAW is also weak and its sights are awful. I think the US could do with heavy AT that uses an AT4.
There's lots of map space that often goes unused as well. With the way the objectives are distributed, there's just no reason to go to these places, which can get old after a few matches of fighting in the same area. We're talking areas which would be the size of a regular Battlefield map going unused.
Games can also be surprisingly "fast" or excruciatingly slow. A slow game would be an hour and a bit, whereas a fast game would be 30, 40 minutes. It never seems to be the right length - it's either way too long, or way too short. I think this could use addressing.
I am sure that the continuing updates will change this though. The devs have some interesting ideas and they're really adding polish to the game with ongoing updates. As for anything like helicopters and MBTs, I wouldn't hold your breath. Stuff like that is way out, if it ever comes. The balance is delicate enough at the moment without having nigh-indestructible death machines hovering around.
This game won't be finished by the end of 2017, no chance, and I wouldn't buy it at full price even though I like it a lot. There just isn't enough there to justify a €40 price tag, not at the moment. If you can get it for ~€20, €25, it's well worth it.
Overall, I would give the game a 7/10, with further updates and additions giving the game a potential of 9/10, but that depends on the devs.

I played that game already many games ago.
However, I could never finish it in Singleplayer because it got quite fast boring.
Now I played the whole game including the DLCs in coop though and I have to say that I actually enjoyed it.
It makes a lot of fun with a friend. Well, as long as you dont fight about the loot, hah. Since we had different characters this wasnt as much of a deal because mostly we were interested into different weapons and items.
But what is this game even about?
Well, there is a treasure in a so called vault. You are the one who should find out about it and uncover its secrets. You are helped by a woman which stays totally secret the whole game. You dont even know who she is but she is following your actions the whole game. Until you actually find the vault. Thats more or less the story. Yeah, not that special.
The game is a open world FPS. Open world more or less. I cant tell of many corridor levels luckily. I actually enjoyed the map design. The game also has some small RPG elements. Not that many though. Mostly its about killing enemies with a very big variety of weapons to get XP, items, loot. You can also use skills to do so. Like using a eagle to kill your enemies with the hunter class. There are also other classes like siren with its phasewalk skill. You always get levels with skillpoints which you can put into a skill improvement like more damage with shotguns or whatever. There is also a big amount of missions you can do like main story missions or many side missions. Those give items and XP too. The enemies usually have a level which you should have too, to be able to mess with them. Partly the enemies seem to scale with the player but im not entirely sure about that. You always should try to do side missions for XP. Those missions can be in the whole world but usually you are in a specific area for a certain time. You can also use a teleporter or cars to move in the game. The cars also have guns.
The Engine is the Unreal Engine 3 which had, for its time, nice graphics. Its cell shading graphic though. Everything looks like in a comic if you dont know what cell shading means. There is a somewhat big amount of graphic options you can select in the game. Definitely a solid PC port which doesnt really miss much beside of Anti Aliasing or Vsync. Vsync is activateable through a simple config edit. Anti Aliasing is quite a mess with Unreal Engine 3 games. But its not like you need it. Aliasing is not that bad with the game in my opinion. Might be because of the cell graphic.
The game recently got updated with Steamworks which is really cool! Multiplayer never worked that well before with Gamespy. Also playing in coop is much fun! Thanks to the devs for the continued support after many years.
Positives:
- Many different weapons with unique statistics
- Around 40 hours playtime with DLCs, without somewhat like 30
- Good multiplayer coop action
- Interesting comic look graphic
- Interesting characters
- Nice soundtrack
- Good DLCs with nice content
- Good PC Port
- Not possible to reach max level and a so called "Secret Final Boss" with only one playthrough, good replayable!
Negative:
- Might be boring in Singleplayer
- Sometimes, especially in coop, enemies take way too many hits in my opinion, its like you have to pump like 50 shots of a shotgun into a somewhat common enemy. Im not talking about bosses. And also I talk about enemy with the same level as the player. This is kinda annoying and kinda breaks the fun. Its not that often though.
- I dont know why but one DLC got kinda messed up because in it you cant teleport and mostly have to use the car to move around. This traveling takes quite some time and you often have to do it. And sometimes you are even stopped by baricades with hordes of enemies which respawn. This was really annoying...
I personally can recommend this game. Its really fun and has a nice design and its kinda addicting. However, I personally could only fully enjoy it in coop for some reason. The singleplayer might be a bit boring for some folks.
I think I will give that game a solid 8/10 rating.
If you like good coop games, this is a must buy. Singleplayer gamers might be interested too.

I don't usually write reviews but I love this game, so here goes. *ahem*
My first colony was in a snowy map where growing food was only possible a few weeks of the year. I started with the standard crashlanded scenario, which spawns you into a random map with random terrain and random dudes with random backgrounds. Pretty nifty, built myself a comfy base next to a mountain, all was good. Until winter.
My noob mind did not understand that we needed more potatoes to survive the winter, and the food stores quickly diminished. Then, of course, a raid occured. Some pirates, not many. We managed to kill them, and we were starving so... well it turns out pirate meat is pretty good in a pinch. My colonists, however, weren't too happy when I butchered their corpses and made them into hats. So they promptly went berserk and murdered each other. Including the poor cat and dog. After this experience I was hooked in the game.
The game seems very simple on the surface, but even after 715 hours i'm still constantly finding new things out about the game I didn't know. There are a lot of dice rolls and calculations going on beneath the surface that make min-maxing your colony and your base setup really fun and interesting. There's an incredible amount of replayability in this game, no two playthroughs will ever be the same. And did I mention theres an insanely active modding community for this game? There's a mod that adds lovecraftian horrors to the game. There's mods to play AS the lovecraftian horrors, fit with human slaves to do your bidding...you name it the modding community for this game probably has it. I see this game being popular with mods for years to come. Not to mention the content the developers are going to add to the game. Sometimes I forget this is an early access game because of how complete the experience feels.
There's an absolute ton of value in this game for the asking price and I highly recommend you check it out (even for 1.9 hours, if you want to refund). If you're into games like dwarf fortress, base builders, or tower defense type games, this game will be right up your alley.

WARNING This review carry's spoilers which are not suitable for those who hate them!!!
An old school RPG with a new heart, Avernum:Escape from the Pit is a remake of the first Avernum game. Character Customization, inventory management, dilog options and tradition D&D style are the corner stone of an RPG. However what makes this game shine above the others is it's in depth story. You're basically an outcast sent to Avernum, a massive underground prison where the empire sends all their unwanted. You have a choice of freedom, staying and saving Avernum, or killing the king.
If you think this game is easy, it can be, and at times, it ups the anty. There is great reward for great risk, and small reward for little risk. Dragons are the best example of this, there are some I just would not mess with, (mostly because they were cool) but others were crude and rude. So you basically could chose if you wanted to rid the dark bowels of their evil stench, which I thought was a nice touch. Though I'm not sure if the choices you make in this game would carry over to the second, but for now, it's nice to have the option of killing what you want.
Overall, with what it does great, I give this game a 8/10. There's always room for improvement, mostly graphically, but I won't hold it against them too much, since it improved the graphics from the last game greatly. A tutorial on spells may be needed since I didn't know that friendly AOE spells wouldn't harm your party members until mid way through the game, still, it's done well.

Fairly large learning curve. I put most of my time into it from Nexons website, but logged quite a few hours on here as well.
If anything it had one of the best communities of any game I had ever played. With tons of classes and quite a few people to talk to. Literally spent my first week playing just screwing around in town with people having a good time. Its a pretty relaxed game, or at least it was.
Right now its mostly just people hanging out in town and showing off their cash shop items, chatting, and maybe dueling. Which is OK, but no one runs dungeons anymore, most just buy stuff from the cash shop. Its kind of hard to recommend playing since the community pretty much stopped doing any form of dungeons etc unless you get to the much higher levels of play where people are constantly doing dailys etc. Its also gotten quite a bit taken over by a lot of kids bregging about cash shop items and not doing anything else.
Other then those few issues however, I have had more fun on this game than any other MMO I have ever played and Nexon fixed a few quality of life issues even though the game doesn't run all that great. One of which is their rebirth system in which you reset your level down to 1, but retain all your ability points (used to level up whatever you feel like training at the time: cooking, fishing, warrior, archer, cook, tailor, lots of things.) Rebirthing helps you level up and get the ability points fast again, and now free players can do this much more often. Once a week I believe which is usually pretty perfect.
One of the best parts about the game however is that you can pretty much play however you want. I was exploring the desert for a few days, mastered some cooking, then killed some beasties in a few dungeons. Its pretty crazy what you can screw around with, and even though the community went a bit downhill, its still really good; especially compared to many other MMO's out there.
If you are looking for a fairly relaxed game with tons of options and a pretty cool community, and don't mind the constant spam of people playing clannad/sword art music. Then download this and get to chatting and dungeon crawling. Its a lot of fun when you get some people to hang out with.
Sorry if this review is a bit jumbled up, not a lot of time and its my first one. Best of luck in the world of Mabinogi!

I really enjoy this game. It is a turn-based, isometric view (Diablo-style view looking down from above), single-player fantasy roleplaying game. Let me break that down:
Turn-Based: While not in combat you move your party around exploring wilderness, dungeon, and city environments and interacting with various friendly and hostile NPCs (non-player characters controlled by the computer). When battle starts, the game goes into turn-based mode. People who like the fast and furious action of real-time games like Diablo might find turn-based combat to be slow and tedious. I like it because I can let my attention wander if need be or even walk away for a restroom break right in the middle of battle. It also allows for the formulation of tactics based on the battlefield conditions.
Isometric View: Many RPGs in the 90s used isometric view. The view is from above and slightly at an angle like the Diablo games. It's nice because you get a kind of "god's eye view" of the game area.
Single-Player: There is no multiplayer option for Avernum: Escape From the Pit.
Fantasy Roleplaying Game: The environment is traditional "Western medieval style fantasy" (i.e., swords and armor and spells and fantasy monsters). There is a bit of a twist in that the game opens up with your being exiled via magic teleportation to a supposedly inescapable underworld where criminals and political prisoners are sent when they cause problems for the Empire.
You can choose from a number of traditional classes (sorcerer, warrior, rogue, berserker, priest, etc.) or you can create your own classes. The pre-made classes are merely certain selections from the game's many abilities, skills, and powers available to characters both when they are created and as they level up. Selecting a pre-made class does not pidgeon hole your character because as you level up you can choose to improve any abilities, skills and powers.
There are multiple difficulties to choose from ranging from beginner to nightmare. You can even change difficulty whenever you wish. So things are going to easy? Notch up the difficulty. Getting frustrated by how hard the play is? Notch it down.
For $10 you absolutely cannot go wrong. This is a fantasy RPG in the tradition of 90s games. I used to play the SSI gold box D&D computer games and Avernum is a great game in the same tradition.

I really want to give this game a thumbs-up. The core gameplay is fun and the developers seem dedicated to it.
Unfortunately, the fun is crippled by an onerous unlockable content system. Character skins and game modes have to be unlocked over time, and the drop rate for unlockables is punishingly slow.
Do you want to play Rocket Run or Chainsaw Backstab online? Maybe a family member wants to have the cute puppy or scary ninja avatar. Nope, you have to unlock these.
You can only unlock by playing online matches. This adds extra frustration, as players will habitually kick people with too low or too high win percentages, or hosts will ragequit in the middle of a match, or you have to contend with hosts with slow Internet connections. There's a daily challenge against AI bots that will net you some XP, but it isn't enough.
Consequently, this game feels schizophrenic. The creamy center of this title is a fun, fast-paced, casual party game particularly designed to appeal to people with short attention spans. Yet you can't quite get to the fun without chewing through a tough, chalky, depressing, obsessive grind.
I don't want grind in my Mario Party.
The developers could fix this game easily by doing one or more of the following:
1) Unlock all common drops immediately for everybody. All common game modes, mutators, and player skins are available as soon as you buy the game. People who really love progression can still ladder up for rare and legendary skins and modes, while casuals immediately have enough fun stuff to last them for a game night or two.
2) Provide more daily challenges against the AI, and increase the XP rewards from those challenges.
3) Increase XP rewards overall.
Ameliorate the grind, and I would give this game an unqualified recommendation.

If you liked Ultima 6 and 7, or even Baldur's Gate and Fallout, this is teh game for you.

I began my journey not knowing what to expect. I awoke in an 8 bit world. I was about to have a first person atari style adventure. I was in the middle of what appeared to be a vast ocean. It was very foggy, but I could see land in the distance. I could also see a comforting and familiar sun. I choose to head towards land. Gameplay wise, there isn't much there. wasd to move and you can also look around. Initially I was annoyed at the slow pace and the fact that once I had arrived at a castle like building I could not enter. My curiousity to learn more drove me to continue my journey. There were interesting sounds and visions all around. I appeared to be on an island inhibited by many creatures and containing it's own weather system. Soon enough the clouds began to disperse and the sun began to set. With night upon me I enjoyed some light star gazing upon a snowy mountain top. I noted the slow movement of the stars.
Once again my emotions switched when I came to a small cottage down the mountain side following a dirt path. Not only could I not enter this cottage, but the door itself looked terrible. I would not be fooled....no one lives here. No one has for some time.....I started my next day much like the first, blindy moving forward in an effort to discover what, if anything, remains to be discovered. This is where I had my first encounter. A silly creature bounced gracefully away from me. It did not matter how I decided to approach, the creature was sure to make haste. Remnicient of Stan's dad in South Park attempting to "catch the Dragon" I gave chase to this creature. I followed it so long that eventually we arrived at the shore line. Sadly the creature simply hopped into the water, never to be seen again.
I happened upon numerous more of these creatures during my team on the island. My experience remained the same. I would follow until I could no longer. Eventually I found a circle of what appeared to be grave stones. Upon bumping into one I noticed a small "bend" in reality. The world in which I was located was being distorted by these things. Whilst looking around  I realized the pace of this world changing picking up. Soon I was watching as days were flying by before my eyes. Getting a grip on my bewilderment I became aware of the small circle in the center of these stones, seemingly created by wind. It seemed to call me. Feeling as though it was my destiny I entered the circle.
Opening my eyes once again I took note of a slightly new sun. Perhaps this was a new world, or perhaps I had simply traveled through time. The landscape had changed. The entire pace of things seemed to pick up entirely. Wildlife was much more abundant than the when or where from which I had traveled. I had received exactly what I had asked for, as if I had somehow  directed the growth of this existence. After taking in what this new landscape had to offer I once again happened upon the bounding bouncing creature from before. Only this time something was different. The creature appeared to have let me get ever so slightly closer before making it's escape.
I'm not sure what will happen to me now. I feel as though my only route is forward. It is as if I have put a curse on myself to make a goal of understanding this creature. I fear I may never catch it, but I also feel that I must try. It occurs to me that I may travel endless worlds in search of my goal, wandering through time and space relentlessy. It is for that reason that I leave this record of my travels. Perhaps as a warning, perhaps as an explanation. If this is to be my last correspondence, please hope for me. Hope that I have attained my goal of capturing the bouncing creature.

This is a real tough game to recommend. On one hand, it had a real chance of being the best DBZ games ever made... on the other, it fails on so many fronts. This review only takes the story/coop missions into consideration.
The game's single player campaign and Parallel Quests have a ton of scripted events. Are you powerful enough to destroy Broly with one Ultimate? Too bad, he'll just fly off and you'll have to chase him to another area. This is noticed early on, as well. There are plenty of missions where your opponent is unkillable until specific dialog triggers. You can get their health to virtually zero, but it stays there until the game tells you they can die.
Is an AI character transforming? Cutscene. Is a character flying off? Cutscene. Is a character coming into battle? Cutscene. These interuptions only last 1-2 seconds, but they happen so often that it can get annoying. Your stamina/KI continue to change during these cutscenes. If you're using a race that regenarates ki/stamina over time, then your ki/stamina will increase as these cutscenes play. Sounds nice, right? Not really. If you're in a Super Saiyan state, your KI will pointlessly deplenish as these play... or, if you're using Kaioken then your stamina will decrease. It just feels like such a waste. You charge up to full power as a Super Saiyan, a new character flies into battle... well, cool... two KI bars disappeared.
Xenoverse is also chalk full of unstaggerable enemies, and even infinite super saiyan opponents. Throughout the story mode and even parallel quests you'll run into "devil triggered" enemies that have a purple aura around them. These enemies can't be staggered until they take a certain amount of damage. Are you using a melee focused fighter? Well have fun, you'll try and combo them and they'll shrug it off and put you into a stun lock. Other opponents also have this, such as Beerus, Whis, Broly, etc. What's worse, is when AI characters have infinite super saiyan transformations. What SSJ does is that it allows you to have infinite KI during that state... this applies to the bots as well. Are you fighting against SSJ Goten, SSJ Gohan, and SSJ Goku? Guess what? All 3 of them have the ability to spam their ultimates. It's not even uncommon for them to stun lock you with their spamming. At times, it's absurd how broken they can be.
Melee fighters are terrible for story/PQ missions. Do you want to make a melee focused fighter with only melee attacks? Good luck! Some missions are borderline impossible unless you go out of your way to grind out specific moves. There are parallel quests that have to be unlocked by talking to a specific character, and then finishing that quest solo. The problem? You're often put up against multiple opponents. Sometimes those opponents even have infinite super saiyan, which can be fairly frusterating. One parallel quest expects you to beat SSJ Goku and SSJ Adult Gohan... are you using a melee only human fighter? Then it's a borderline impossible mission. I've had it happen where I died seconds after flying into the area. Goku did a Kamehameha, Gohan did one, and Goku followed that up with another one. Yeah... not fun. I never beat it as my earthling. I ended up making a Saiyan focused in KI blast Supers... I finished that quest in my first try. All I had to do, was go SSJ, fly into the area, and spam an Ultimate over and over again. Goku and Gohan barely touched me. As you can imagine, melee fighters are also fairly annoying to use against unstaggerable enemies. I'd recommend only using them in parallel quests with allies.
The reward system is fairly silly. It's based almost entirely on luck. Want to obtain 'x' ultimate? Well you have to go into parallel quest 'y', complete very easy secret requirements, and then you'll have a chance of getting an ultimate finish. If you're lucky enough to get this ultimate finish, you'll then have a chance at getting the move you want. If you're unlucky? Then you'll find yourself playing a quest over and over again, finishing with all secret requirements fulfilled, just for a slim chance of activing a secret battle. Eventually, you do get the ultimate finish, but as luck has it... the attack you wanted doesn't drop. Now it's back to grinding the mission again to merely get another chance of obtaining it.
Those are all the main issues I had. I also have smaller complaints, but I won't list them off here as they seem trivial in comparison. What about the positives? Well, the custom characters are definitely a step in the right direction. The combat is simple and fun, which is expected for a DBZ game. Personally, I'd like to see more depth to the combo system.
Overall, if the above issues seem like they'd bother you, then just wait for a sale or wait for a sequel. This game has a ton of potential, but it misses so many marks that I'd find it a hard title to recommend.

There are no more tiers meaning all the weapons do a similar amount of damage, unless you grind or pay for the top unlockable weapons. And most importantly the battles are no longer unique experiences. But that's not all, the game won't open after you close it for a first time. So every time you want to play you are going to have to reinstall.
Long story short, it has become a carbon copy of all the other games in the same genre.

You have your moments with other players, winning and losing battles and experimenting with skill sets that you collect and learn.
The big flaws being that PC has its own original issues compared to console, which hinders performance between you and other online players.

A game worth having for long-time Dragon Ball fans, but a swing and a miss to those who want to avoid redundancy.

I've only just started playing this game but thus far I really like it. A lot of the people playing are pretty friendly as long as you aren't rude and the game is pretty easy to figure out when you get in. The first thing I would want to say though is that going into this I did make 2 characters, one of them was used for learning to play the game, and the other was used to play once I figured the game out. idk if this was a good Idea but I feel like with the first character I was able to make all the mistakes I needed to make while learning and not worry about it affecting the rest of my gameplay experience.
That being said it didn't take me long to figure the game out and if you're used to most basic MMO style gameplay then you should be able to figure out a lot of the concepts and UI placement pretty quickly. When I started I played as a basic human warrior and I have to say that I had a lot of fun with the combat. The fighting style with close combat is very fun and it feels like when you're hitting things you're actually doing something. The second talent I tried was magic because I thought it might be kinda fun to use magic at a distance and then beat my enemies down with my sword when they got close. I do have to say that to me personally I didn't think that the magic felt very rewarding to me. It seemed like I was just kinda poking things and making them angry and I found myself using my swords a lot more often.
Another thing I noticed that I actually really liked is that you can go anywhere. If you want to wander into an area with mobs that are much stronger than you, the game won't tell you that you can't. I mean you will obviously get murdered going in there but I feel like it makes the game more fun when exploring because you don't know how powerful a mob is compared to you in a new area until you attack it. The sense of exploration and not knowing if you'll get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you the second you attack something makes the game a lot more fun for me personally.
Again this is all low level beginner experiences of mine and the gameplay could become much better as you become higher level. I feel that this game is probably going to become kind of an addiction for me but this is also the first 2 weeks of me playing this game. I would recommend this game to anyone that enjoys MMO style games and loves exploration in games.

I've Been playing this game since 2010, on and off. I would take a break from the game but i would always make my way back to it.
I dont know what its like to be a new pilot today compared to when i started playing but i still consider myself fairly new to the game, Although i can run an Orca with Tech II boosts i only can do level 2 security missions, The orca is an mining command ship that grants fleet bonuses to the party.
In this game  you can mine the ice fields or asteroids, attack other players, do missions which are like quests, you can harvest the resources of a planet with planetary interaction, you can form corporations and an Alliance of corporations and declare war on other corporations or alliances and be able to legally fight anywhere without police intervention.
The end game goal of the game is to be in a zero security alliance and own your own parts of space or team up with others to explore wormhole space and build your own structures at these places. At the end of your eve lifetime you could be flying capital ships or even a titan, but they take extremely long amounts of time to train for.
In this game you level up your skills with time. Instead of experience points; you get a point every second which gets multiplied by whatever your attributes are. You can use a rare remap to change your attributes to learn certain things faster than others because so many different skills require different attributes to level up faster. Let me tell you a story that will explain why I came and installed this game and ran it for 5 minutes to give it a thumbs down review. Spoiler: it's Nexon's awful customer service.
Way back when, in the before times, Mabi was my first mmo. I played it for a few months, life got in the way, and I eventually put it down. A few years later, I got interested again and played it for about 2 months. By the first month, I was having a lot of fun, and I spent over $100 in the store on various pets and consumables. But I messed something up, and some of the things I bought got applied to my original character, rather than my current one. Not the clearest store for a game that runs on microtransactions, but whatever. I made a ticket about one of the items for customer support to transfer it, then a few hours later I added an addendum to the ticket for the other items that got added to the wrong character, since I hadn't noticed immediately.
A week went by. Nothing. Not too unexpected. Two weeks. Getting a little irritating. A month. At that point I was not only frusterated with customer service's slow response, but I was also starting to see how grindy and pay2win the game was, and was losing interest. I ended up quitting again.
From then on, I would get an email every week or 2 weeks or something, that basically said "hey we have a lot of tickets, sorry about the wait". I didn't care anymore, I just wanted to see how long before they actually responded to the issue. It took 6 months. Literally 6 months. 5 months after I had stopped playing the game entirely, they responded saying they moved the items to the proper character. The kicker was that they only did it for the item I had directly submitted the ticket for, they didn't even read the addendum. So the other items I had the same issue with weren't moved. It came with the invitation to submit another ticket if I had any additional issues, and they closed the ticket.
So the response times for customer service were not only beyond unreasonable, but the response itself was the barest minimum that could have been done and didn't even fully resolve the issue. This isn't a unique story. This is Nexon. This is every Nexon game. This is an experience that any paying customer has to deal with in a Nexon game. Save your time, save your money, save the headache. There are so many other better companies, with better free games, that at least make an effort to satisfy their playerbase rather than trying to make the most possible money while paying the fewest possible staff. I'll never play another Nexon game.

Addendum: As of Nov 2016, I nominated Avernum for the “I Thought This Game Was Cool Before It Won An Award” Award.
Second remake of the classic Exile series' first part, Avernum: Escape From the Pit is classic roleplaying at its best! Basically, you play as a party of adventurers, who were exiled into a huge cavern, Avernum, far below the surface of the world. You have to find a new purpose here, which basically means doing all kinds of odd-jobs and quests for mayors, wizards and kings of the underworld and, while you're at it, trying to escape your dark prison.
The controls have been streamlined for the 2010s. Like in Avernum, the first remake, the game is still isometric and tile-based. However, you can finally control the characters efficiently with a mouse. This works splendidly, though the controls have frankly lost some of the function of the earlier games: e.g. you can no longer close doors (unless I've yet to discover how). Also, the pathfinding algorithm does some weird stuff sometimes when your preferred path is blocked, making characters run into wrong direction (and at worst, their DOOOOM). There's still no music (except in the title screen and the few cut scenes): use your favorite epic adventure music instead.
Skill system has basically been remade, though the comedic art of the skill descriptions has been appreciatively retained. Skills are now learned in trees, with a basic skill in the bottom and every subsequent skill requiring the below skills before they can be developed. Also, characters gain bonus traits every few levels gaining small bonuses to different skills and stats. It's a matter of taste if these are good or bad changes, but the whole works nevertheless quite fine.
Combat has always been a rather important part of Avernum series. Turn-based, the basics are still there. However, some additions and changes have been made. Warriors have gained special skills called battle disciplines to supplement their fighting ability, making them a bit more interesting and tactical than before. Spells have been remade as well since original Avernum. Particularly, all the blessings and curses have become area effects, and multi-hit spells are now cone or area attacks instead of simply hitting a number of targets.
Frankly, the hard-coreness of the series has dulled quite a bit with this latest installment. No longer are the dark dungeons truly dark, as you don't benefit from bringing a torch or casting light spells (which were actually removed altogether). There is no need to eat to satisfy hunger nor deal with dangerous diseases, and death is no longer so much a set-back as party is automatically resurrected and healed at a friendly town, removing the need for inns and renting rooms. You may no longer jump down ledges (which was never that healthy anyway). Identification of magical items has also been removed (albeit hilariously explained by "adventurers having better training nowadays"), and potion making has become a trade secret of alchemists, so your party can't learn it itself any longer. Spiders no longer say "hi!" in a high-pitched voice audibly. Along with these changes Avernum has lost part of its legacy and spark.
What is left, however, is an excellent RPG adventure in a unique fantasy world. The streamlining makes the game more accessible and lets the player concentrate on what's really important: dialogue, exploration and questing. And their implementation is simply brilliant. There are tens, if not hundreds, of characters in the game who all have their own dialogue trees, and several tens of dungeons and towns to explore, everyone of them extremely detailed. Enemies are still dangerous, and mini-bosses and bosses are refreshingly difficult to beat.
Game is not only high-quality, for there's also quite a lot of it. My first play-through, on Hard difficulty level, lasted about 80 hours. Want to just experience the story? Play on Normal or even Casual difficulty, and you may even change it mid-game. However, the highest difficulty level, Torment, provides an amply named challenge for an experienced player, requiring advance planning and lots of re-exploring in areas that were previously too dangerous. Seriously though, I recommend playing your first game on Hard difficulty at max, as Torment can get tedious if you don't know where to go for the next admissible challenge.
TL:DR?
Excellent dialogues.
Robust tactical combat.
Addicting exploration.
Epic questing to become true heroes.
Not convinced? You may as well give it a try.

So I was buying software from Spiderweb Software back when things were on 3.5" floppies.  I remember writing a check and MAILING it in to the developer's address.  And then I was mailed back the codes.  In an envelope.
Sigh... it was so much nicer to get that rather than the credit card offers and bills that I get today.
Graphically I have to admit that the Exile series hasn't evolved a whole lot, particularly compared to other modern games.  But what has thankfully remained the same is everything else about the Exile series: the gameplay and plotlines.
At its heart this is a turn-based RPG, though with much more freedom to explore and build your characters than most other RPGs on the market.  Want to build a mage who also enjoys wielding a sword?  Yes you can do that.  Or a barbarian who dabbles in archery?  You can do that too.
Enemies and environments are varied enough to make the game interesting.  There are fairly few recolored enemies, and each town is distinct enough that they have their own personality and such.
It is easy to get lost in the cavernous world of Avernum, but I suppose that is part of the setting.
Overall well worth at least $8 in my book, and is usually much less expensive than that!

One of the best RPGs in recent years. Honestly I'm not sure to which game should I compare it, each Piranha Bytes game is its own experience, and I love them for that.
I loved all games in Gothic series and I love all games in Risen series. From the Risen series, I would say that Risen 3 is probably the best one of them, even comparable to the golden Gothic 2.
The story of this game is solid, it is not the best, not the worst. I've been quite used to bad stereotype-like stories in RPGs (especially open world ones), like TES series, Two Worlds series, or Dragon Age series (in case of more linear ones). Each of these games suffer from black-and-white storyline (from the named ones I consider the plot one of the better ones).
The gameplay is typical for Piranha Bytes games. The combat system is something different, and very good (unless you just left-click all day long, which is a bad way to play this game and it can ruin your experience). It is better than in TES games, way better compared to Dragon Age series, but a lot worse compared to Dark Messiah of Might and Magic.
In this game you can actually dodge hits (which is very common in medeival fencing schools), but well, don't expect realistic fight simulator. But it is action enough, you won't get bored. Plus, guns are very good addition into the game.
Dialogue lines are well done, audio for them is also quite good. As for the quests, there is a whole lot of them, but I'd like more impact on game in general, and longer side quest lines. Music is one of the best, it perfectly suits the game.
Visuals are also very good, very nice fire particles, water splashes and particle effects in general. The authors did quite a job on light and shadows, each single island is in a bit different stylized art set and it works perfectly. The graphics quality can compete with any other AAA game.
Of course there are few things that look bad. One of them is, that after performing major actions to close gates to underworld, the islands look unchanged. For me, if green grass would return to that areas it would be perfect. I would see that I did some major impact on game world and it would made me even more happy.
Second thing is, I don't really see further lore connection with Risen series, yes it is in the same world, there are some of the characters that were in previous games, but the lore connection is weak. I'm comparing mainly to Gothic 1 - Gothic 2 games here, where the lore connection between those game was really strong and good.
Anyways, this game is worth it. I know it seems average, it isn't. Don't believe metacritic, as some fans of older Piranha Bytes games are downvoting, without even playing it, sadly...

My problem with RimWorld comes from my years of playing Dwarf Fortress, I find that RimWorld focuses more on tending to your whiny colonists every whim rather than building and surviving. You spend the first half an hour building and spend the rest of the game trying to keep your incredibly whiny colonists happy, I personally hate this. In Dwarf Fortress you can expand into a massive underground empire but in RimWorld you do nothing but look after a small group of colonists who always find something to complain about. RimWorld also requires a horrible amount of micromanagement.
The combat in RimWorld just sucks, your colonists require a tedious amount of micromanagement and cannot think for themselves. I hate ranged combat because my colonists never seem to be able to hit anything (Thank God ammo isn't a thing) and they are unable to move and shoot at the same time. Melee combat is better but unless you have a boat load of medical supplies you're probably going to lose a colonist since they always take massive damage.
In Dwarf Fortress if a Dwarf comes under attack all the other Dwarfs will jump in and beat the living hell out of the attacker without me telling them to. In Rimworld your colonists won't fight anything until you set them to combat mode (Draft) and by time they reach their destination the person being attacked will be mortally wounded or dead. Colonists are also pretty useless at running away, attacking humans are always faster for some reason and if your colonist takes a hit their movement speed grinds to a halt making them take even more hits. Colonists also run away from things they don't need to run away from, for example my hunter will run half way across the planet just to get away from an angry squirrel which he could kill in a few seconds. Overall, combat is really annoying and you'll lose colonists because they're unable to think for themselves.
Another thing that is definitely worth mentioning here is that some animals in RimWorld are hilariously overpowered, I once lost an entire colony to a group of Caribou, this was because my colonists can't hit anything with their guns and the Caribou do massive damage in melee combat almost immediately incapacitating my colonists. You can't hide inside your buildings because the Caribou smash down doors or wait forever for you to leave. Losing an entire colony to a group of Reindeer did nothing but edge me closer to hating RimWorld.
Colonists in RimWorld are horrendous at the prioritization of tasks. If your base is on fire you have to individually tell your colonists to put it out and there is a good chance they will either stop for no reason or they'll decide to go to sleep because its night time. I've lost enitre colonies because my colonists decided to go star gazing instead of putting out the massive fire ravaging the colony.
Forest fires are common, annoying and almost impossible to stop. If a lighting strike event starts without rain you and your whole colony is screwed because the fires rarely ever stop on their own. The fire started by the lighting strikes will destroy everything including wild life, your colonists won't do anything about it until it comes to your land and even then as I said before your colonists need specific instructions to put it out. This becomes a long and frustrating process of watching the fire while trying to maintain your stupid colonists who are complaining because its one degree colder than they would like it to be!
RimWorld is in Alpha but having nothing to build in a game where you build things is a serious problem in the long run. When you manage to setup a basic colony with temperature control and a steady food supply you will notice that you have NOTHING LEFT TO DO. The only thing you're able to do is improve security and tend to your colonists childish complaints, if you're lucky an event or something you can actually do will come along but a majority of the time you'll just be sat there with max speed on.
RimWorld does have some extra and more complicated stuff you can research but my God researching takes way too long even with a colonist who is experinced in researching! Researching basic stuff takes days and your colonists will never prioritize it, you can't even tell them to do it, you have to take one of your colonists off every single job except researching in order to make them research. If you don't have a colonist who is experinced in research its going to take you weeks to research something as basic as carpeting.
Overall, I just find RimWorld to be irritating, boring and unfair. Dwarf Fortress is a far superior game and its 100% free. I wish the devs of RimWorld good luck.
P.S. £23.79 is waaaaaay too much money!

For me RimWorld is more than a game, it's a compelling and ever unfolding set of stories. And this, I believe, is precisely its thesis statement, its goal, its raison d'etre. I cite for example the fact that you choose at the outset of any playthrough not just the game's difficulty but it's "storyteller", similar to Left 4 Dead's AI "director" but so much more.
There are two reasons RimWorld holds a unique and enduring place in my heart, and these reasons keep me playing for far more hours than I've owned it on steam (I know, naughty me). The first is a fantastic strategy/simulation game. Early on I felt like RimWorld merely scratched the SimCity itch I'd had since a child. But then I realized I kept playing RimWorld long after I would have abandonded a SimCity game. And that's because I need the hardship, I need the diseases to sweep arbitrarily through and tax my supportive care capacity. I need the blights to ruin crops and force me to find alternate food sources. I need raiders to try to pillage all I've built so I have to make the hard choices about whether to feed a prisoner, or bloody my hands with an execution.
So, the first extraordinary merit of RimWorld is thus: part city builder, part sim, part RTS, part tactics shooter, part really grim Harvest Moon, etc. And it aces them all.
The second extraordinary merit of RimWorld is the story creation. Aside from a sparse setting which admittedly borrows heavily from Firefly (no complaints here) every bit of story in RimWorld is procedural or internal to your own mind. The quirky traits, frenetic firefights, life or death struggles, finding of love between colonists, it all adds up to you following the little, pixelated lives of your characters. And as you do, you can fall in love too. At thirty years old I've grown accustomed to the fact that my parents and girlfriend don't give a hoot about the game I might be playing at the moment, but they'll occasionally give a wholehearted listen when I'm real fired up about it. RimWorld is different though. The stories come out so interesting, so varied, so lifelike, that they all love to listen. My mother will literally ask me over the phone about my RimWorld colony because she wants to hear cool stories about the zany things that may have happened in the game since last we spoke. To me that speaks of a procedural genius I will always appreciate.
Don't let the early access tag fool you, this game is beyond amazing. In over a decade of using steam it has prompted me to write my first legitimate review. I swear, I buy it again if I had someone to whom I could gift it, because it's a bargain at twice the price.

Tales from the Borderlands has to be one of the best games I have ever played. Considering all the big releases that happened in 2015, Witcher 3, Fallout 4, MGS 5 to name a few, I myself was surprised that I would consider Tales from the Borderlands to be the best game I played this year.
Tales from the Boderlands is the classic episodic game that we have come to expect from Telltale. The game is divided into 5 episodes that last around 2 hours each. If you have ever played a Telltale game before you will know what to expect in terms of gameplay. If not, there is not that much to say. Gameplay is very limited. The game plays like a movie filled with dialogue choices, quick time events, and walking sections. While these are nice alternative from just watching a two hour cut scene, I understand this can be a major turn off for those who value gameplay over story.
However, the story in this game is absolutely fantastic. In a sense, the minimal gameplay helps to accentuate how good the story is. Tales from the Borderlands is a slight departure from previous Telltale games as its writing and tone focus more on comedy rather than drama. This does not mean that the story does not get very intense as you near the final chapters.
The world of Borderlands has always been an interesting one. I always felt like Borderlands 1 and 2 (I have yet to play the Pre-Sequel) lacked in terms of narrative and character development. Tales from the Borderlands really does not have these issues. It has a clear focus on world building, and as you progress through each chapter, you will see each character change and develop as they experience the events that surround them.
The story is also very well written. It will make you smile, but it will also make you sad. As you finish each episode, you will want to immediately move on to the next one. And by the end of it all the story will be over, and you will realize, like I did, that you will never experience this game for the first time again.
The music selection is also fantastic. Each song perfectly captures the tone of each episode. I guarantee you will be listening to those songs well after you are done with the game.
I realize that I didn’t talk much about the actual game itself, and the events that unfold within the story; however, I feel like any detail can be considered a spoiler here. If you enjoy narrative focused games, do yourself a favor and play this game knowing as little as possible about the narrative.
(tldr) In the end, this is truly one of the best stories told in a game. If you love the Borderlands series or simply enjoy a good story, get this game as soon as possible. If you have never played a borderlands game (especially 2), or simply don’t enjoy games with very little gameplay, I would still suggest you get the game, but you might want to wait for a sale.

Dragon Ball Xenoverse is definitely one of the better Dragon Ball games to come out in recent years.
The basic gameplay combines the best parts of the recent games (the bigger battles of Battle of Z with more characters, but with better gameplay, more than 1 combo, an EXTREMELY better character creation system & many, many aspects taken from Dragon Ball Online)
The graphics are phenomenal, so much in fact that all the cutscenes are using ingame graphics itself!
The voice acting isn't the best from a couple of characters (like Trunks & some of the Future Warrior's voices), but for the most part, it isn't too bad. The Soundtrack is very DBZ, it blends in well to the game.
The Story is quite a fresh, interesting take on the story you know and love in the Dragon Ball Z universe (it involves time travel). I liked it a lot and loved how the characters had different interactions with you depending on your race (everyone is surprisingly racist to anyone of the Frieza race for instance).
Sadly, many battles are left out (like any with Android 16 for example) & no levels for the original Dragon Ball at all (though those are handled by an Frieza Race NPC called Percel, learned about from his dialogue).
The range of playable characters is kinda poor compared to past games (many forms & characters not playable), but unlike past ones, they all play uniquely and don't share the same animations (like Ultimate Tenkaichi). The character creation isn't halfassed like that game too. There are 5 races to choose from, and you can change all sorts of things such as their hair, eyes, nose, mouth, ears, skin color, eye color, Pupil type, and even voice! Sadly, Frieza's race is unnamed & only Saiyans have transformations outside of Kaioken. I loved how Male Voice 8 is none other than Takahata101 of Team Four Star fame, using his Ghost Nappa voice from DBZ Abridged!!!
There are hundreds of items for your character to wear (but unfortunately a large amount of them can't be recolored). There are also tons of skills to use (with Strike, Ki, Power up & other catagories). You can even train under a master, who can be one of many characters in the Dragon Ball universe. They give you skills & Z Souls if you fight enough while having them as a master.
If you want to play 2 Player, you need to go into the story mode to access it (It really should've been a separate mode). You can't call upon your other Time Patrollers to help in Parallel Quests or VS mode (only the Time Patroller you picked to play as).
Also, sadly, the game relies on the RNG system to unlock many skills & costumes (the ones that can't be bought, or given to you by your master), as well as even Dragon Balls. So you may have to complete really hard missions multiple times for even a chance of getting one piece of equipment.
As for the DLC, it's quite nice. It adds several more playable characters, more Parallel Quests (which can earn you more Skills & Costumes), more masters & more story. I like how they explain the GT missions being in the game as an alternate Timeline. It gives an excuse as to why Battle of Gods & Revival of F can exist in the same game (and a damn good one since this game heavily involves Time Travel).
Many of the missions can be quite difficult, and Strike Based characters can be at a bit of a disadvantage in certain circumstances (like 3 Saiyans spamming endless Kamehamehas until you die for instance).
Anyway, apart from some minor details, it's definitely a great game with a lot of potential. Hopefully, they expand on it in a sequel or something. I definitely reccomend it.

It's worth a look - but you may find yourself cutting your losses and bailing out of this thing for good before long. The actual 'play' portion of the game is a good time, it's easy to match up and just go. No hunting for active servers, it's just ON. Raids are grindy and even though progress can be made, you will need (literally) months of intense grinding to really get into anything other than the basic starter gear. I was a late-comer to Crossout but it's very clear some hardcore balance changes were made. While this might seem like a positive, the devs have clearly made a decision to radically nerf drop-rates, drastically increase prices (both in-game and in-wallet) to really progress or get anywhere.
The performace is a very solid 60FPS on my rig, every option is maxed, I run native at 1920x1200x60. The graphics are outstanding and the audio is certainly decent.
What will kill this game (and it's already dying) is the micro-transaction the devs have dug deep into. It's hopeless and even though I will gladly fork out real dollars for a game (P2P or flat purchase) the prices are STUPID high and speak volumes about the motivation of the devs.  Any sane person will find themselves looking at the shop and saying "You want HOW MUCH for that?!" Crossout seem like a cash-grab and little more. While it's fun to play, has interesting lore and mechanics, the great game performance and overall fun - the pricing on all sides is just totally out of wack with any (even remote) value. I can't recommend this, the grind and investment are just too high. Unless you literally have months to dig in. Unless they make better decisions about pricing and player reward, it's just best to avoid it.

Just because I know one of the people that made this game, doesn't mean I'm gonna be biased and give it a good review because they gave me a copy for free. So, ♥♥♥♥ you, Tomato. 8)
Anyway. Spears 'n' Spades is an Action Platformer game, as the description on the steam store states. When I first saw this game, I thought it looked promising. The art style of the game reminds me a lot of the original Binding of Isaac, which is a plus in my book. The soundtrack is rather catchy, too, and it suits the game, despite it's rather dark and grim setting. Also, this game has controller support! Hooray! For those that are like me, however, who prefer to use a keyboard over controller, the default controls are the arrow keys to move, and z x and c to do the assigned movements, although, you can change those to your liking.
The gameplay is as simple as it sounds. You move across the stage, jump over things, kill things, etc etc. Upon spawning at the start of the first level, you are equipped with a throwing knife and some armour. The armour can withstand one hit, before being destroyed. If you get hit again, you die. The throwing knife can be thrown, of course, in a straight line. At the end of each stage, there is a boss battle, and there is an individual who will sell you some trinkets that will possibly help you in the midst of battle. There are times when this game can be cruel and unforgiving, but that's most likely due to my lack of skill in these kinds of games. Plus, I wouldn't put it past them if the game is meant to be cruel and unforgiving, because I believe it would make it a lot more fun, in my opinion.
I would comment largely on the story of this game, but I don't think it would really matter in the end, because it is literally a case of 'Boyfriend gets stolen by bad guys, lets go rescue him.' It's a simple storyline for a simple game.
All in all, I'd say this game is worth the £2.79. It's a fun little indie game, which I believe definitely needs some recognition, as I believe this game has a LOT of potential.
Final Score: 9/10.

First Impression Gameplay:
I bought this game based on the steam trailer and artwork.  Glad I did, as I actually enjoy the game.
You can tell this game borrows game play mechanics heavily from the NES game: "Ghosts 'n Goblins."  Even the name bears a resemblance.
The art style is pretty cool (reminds me of the dupes from "Oxygen Not Included) sound track is good, and the controls are responsive.  I was able to use an Xbox controller on my PC, so that's a plus as well.  I did not encounter any glitches of any kind while playing.
Game play is fairly simplistic; with your main goal being to navigate across the levels and get to end, where you fight an end stage boss.  As you fight across the levels, there are various weapons which you can use: from throwing knives, to lobbing bombs, to melee spears.  You start out wearing a suit of armor, and when you get hit, the armor will break.  Get hit again and you're dead.
From what I can tell at this time, the story is about a girl trying to save her lover from some type of ghoulish captor.  Perhaps a reverse homage to Ghosts 'n Goblins plot.
Anyways, the game is pretty good.  If you're a fan of the genre, then I absolutely believe it is worth $4.

This is the remake of sorts from an award winning indie maker Jeff Vogel who actually made the game back during the 90es, but, for obvious reasons, the game needed to be updated to work with modern machines and OS', so after Jeff updated the engine starting from Avernum 4, he didn't want old game to be forgotten, so he rewrote the wole first game in new engine in 2011.
It's fairly easy to see old genes still imbedded onto the game. Avernum: Escape from the pit is an Ultima style isometric turn-based RPG with unique skills and magic set into richly detailed fairly unique world with awesome, engaging writing and meticulously detaild maps. Narration and dialogues are the highlight, cause the game is old-school as it gets. No grim-brown realystic 3d graphic, no CGI cutscenes, but lovely prose with lots of charm and wit. Open ended world is one of the highlights. In theory you cn traverse the whole map, or at least most of it from the get-go, but areas do have unstated level requirement and you'll be quickly slaughtered if you go to the harder area than you'r level alows. Every city map is full of details, secret passages and metroid-esque still unreachable places, so don't expect to be 100% through with even the most basic of dungeons or cities up till the very end. Level progression is smooth and T-B combad is addictive in that ancient pokemon/Xcom/Fallout1&2 kind of way.
So all in all, not to stretch this for too long, I'd warmly recommend the game for anyone wanting nice, solid T-B WRPG.

My initial opinion of this game was that it is boring and pointless... actually, that's still my opinion of the game. The experience is more like an interactive screensaver. There are no action buttons, no sprinting, no jumping and no death. You simply walk around and enjoy the ambience. There are no goals or objectives other than the ones you set for yourself. Even those were simple tasks such as, make it to the top of that mountain, chase the squirrel, or try to find that tree that played bagpipes. I owe my positive opinion of the game to a gameplay review that I was attempting to record. After several takes, the environment started to grow on me. It was amazing how long I found myself wandering around while still trying to make myself hate it. This is not for everyone, but I see the appeal now. While this is not a must buy or must play, the experience is unique and enjoyable.
