Now that I have finished this game (100% completion), I feel that I can give a good solid review of its quality.  First, you have to approach this game as if you were going to be playing an old NES title.  From the graphics to the music, this game, for all intents and purposes feels like it should be played on the console.  That being said, let me get one major issue that I hope is addressed by the developers in a future patch soon; This game has no controller support.  This is unfortunate, and I know some people will be miffed about it.  What the developers did do, is provide comprehensive key mapping.  I typically play emulators of my games when I am away from home, so I am no stranger to playing these games on a keyboard.  While the keymapping feature is a big plus, I will admit this game would have been more enjoyable with a controller in hand.
While I would like to call this game a spiritual successor to "The Battle of Olympus", I feel that it would be a disservice to the game itself.  I am personally a big fan of Battle of Olympus, and after watching the trailer for the game I immediately saw all the aspects of fun I had from that game in it (even the sound effects)  The game is not precisely what the trailer shows which was a little jarring at first.  I am not sure what part of the design process changed this, but in the end I felt that it didn't hurt or hinder the gameplay.  What you get in this package is a quasi metroidvania experience that, for the price tag, ends up simplifying alot of the complexities that made Battle of Olympus unaccessable to some players.
The game is simple, the quests are obvious, and the world itself requires little attention to really keep tabs on where all the unlockables are.  Replay-value of the game is a short comming, but if you are like me and enjoy retreading ground to try and finish the game in faster times, there is a very small amount of RNG to worry about.  Outside of that I can see the game suffering.  On a positive note, the asking price is completely reasonable for the investment.  Five American dollars for a NES Erra style 8-bit game is not a bad gig in my book.
I managed to finish this game in around 3 hours on my first playthrough (got lost a couple times, and had some extra back tracking and grinding that I discovered was completely unnessesary).  It is not a difficult game, and the most frustrating part of it is the simple technical issues that crop up every now and again.   There are occasional situations where your attack does not work, and jumps stop half way in their height.  I am not sure how to replicate the probelms, they seemed to be intermitent at best, but I did manage to eat a few enemy attacks and fall into one or two pits as a result.  They are annoying, I would love to see them fixed, but since I can't readily replicate the issues, I am not sure if they ever will be patched.  So until I see a patc; consider it a price of admission much the same as you would an NES title of the past.
This game also has some bizzare hit detection issues, but I have never had them NOT work in my favor (which was odd.)  It is rare that you can complain about a game giving the player the advantage, so I figured i would go ahead and mention it anyway, in the spirit of potential fixes that may come down the pipe-line (if the devs do patch the system)  The only other real technical problem that I encountered in the game, was in the final stage (olympus) and the second to last (forgive the lack of spelling for the name, but the waterfall area) the music decided to jump to overwhelming volumes.  It overrode all the sound in the game, and I had to reduce my head set to accomodate it.  Two areas of the game had this problem so I didn't find it a deal breaker or anything.
All and all I recommend this game to the audience that will give it a look over.  I had fun despite running into a couple of snaggs provided due to the "non-linear" options the game allows.  You can fight bosses before you are ready, and the challenge goes from significant to impossible when you do so.  So as a final warning, when playing, if you do hit a snag, don't jump to complaints like I did, just go back around the world and find the items that will make the game a cake walk.  There are no dead ends in the game, and it is a pretty solid experience, and definitely worth the price of admission.
I will hold the options to adjust the rating for the game if some of the issues with the game are addressed in future releases.  I do enjoy the game, and will probably be keeping tabs on it.  But until then, hope this helps.  If you want a further look into the game, I have a full series from start to finish that will be available on youtube starting 4/25/15.

Summary: A good quality retro metroidvania with only a few minor technical issues.
Prometheus - The Fire Thief is a retro action adventure game that plays like a sequel to the 1988 NES game Battle of Olympus. It has enough polish and modern convenience to minimize frustration while still maintaining its retro feel. There are still a few rough edges, but they're minor enough to not detract too severely from an otherwise fun experience.
Boss fights are the most impressive part of the game. Each fight is unique and well designed, providing a good challenge without going overboard. It requires practice and pattern recognition to succeed but never feels unfair. The lack of a death penalty makes trying each boss over and over a relatively painless experience, adding to the fun of of the challenge instead of punishing you like most retro titles.
The other parts of the game are well done, though lack the same level of polish as the excellent boss fights. Exploration is fulfilling, with a good variety of areas to explore. However, while the size of the world gives a lot to explore, it also makes backtracking a bit tedious. Similarly, items are well designed, but the lack of good descriptions can make them hard to use. Many items are clarified through hints from NPCs, though others remain unfortunately obtuse unless you look them up in the manual.
While the gameplay is solid, there are a few technical issues worth noting. The lack of native gamepad support is a major concern. Joytokey works fine, and I recommend giving it a try, but it's unfortunate to have to rely on a third party program for such an important feature. More options would be another good addition, particularly volume and resolution adjustments. Lastly, it would be nice to be able to adjust options during play instead of having to quit the entire game and re-launch it to get at the options screen. A quit to menu option would be a fair workaround.
Overall, Prometheus - The Fire Thief is easily worth the $5 price tag and I'd highly recommend it to fans of the genre or retro gamers in general. Even if you're not into retro, it's a fun game with enough modern conveniences to stand on its own.

Rimworld, from what I've played of it, is a masterpiece of a survival game.  What sets it apart from other games of this type is the emphasis on storytelling, with characters that interact with each other in interesting ways and a real feeling that the story is progressing.  Of course, one can't forget to talk about the freedom this game gives you to do almost anything you can think of within the game's systems and the chaos that can occur when characters don't get along.  During my colony's first year, times were tough, and my colonists had to resort to cannibalism.  Against all odds they survived the harsh winter, but then one of my original party went completely mad and had to be put down and another was killed by raccoons.  Now that we've a better farm than before, my colonists no longer have to eat human flesh, but we still feed slain enemies to the dogs so that we can save the good food for ourselves.
In conclusion, buy this game.  It's amazing.  Just make sure you're prepared to see your farms ravaged by a cold snap.

Short version:
Worth buying at 75% off, if you have friends to play it with.  Not worth full price. Don't expect to find people to play with online.
Long:
Black & White Bushido is a game heavily based on stealth.  You can play either Light (white ninjas) or Shadow (black ninja).  There are four character models, though (ironically for a game so heavily based on the popular idea of ninjas), none of them are in stereotypical ninja garb.  You then choose to play online or offline.
Offline, you can play either against bots or (presumably, since I've never tried it) couch two player.  The stage is small, so there's no need for split screen.  Online, you can try to find a match, but the matchmaking is extremely barebones. I play with my fiancee, and the only way we can find each other's matches is by coordinating over the phone.  There is no indication of who else is playing, even once you're in the match.  You don't see screen names, just "Player 1."  Also, as many other reviews have noted, there is virtually no community for this game.  If you want to play against a human, bring a friend.
You will want to play against humans, too, because the bots are particularly idiotic.  Gameplay is heavily dependent on stealth.  If you break stealth, every bot will simultaneously converge on you.  I'm not a particularly good gamer, but my kill-death ratio against the bots is usually 20-1, even outnumbered 3 to 1.   If you go into stealth, the bots just beginning patrolling their platform with no attempt to locate you or use stealth themselves.  This makes them easy pickings even for a new player.  Really, the bots are just good for learning the controls.
So what about the gameplay? That's where this game shines.  Primarily, you'll attack using your melee weapon, a very simple one-button attack.  The twist comes with the stealth mechanic.  The levels continually shift between light and shadow (white or black backgrounds, in other words).  The ninjas can, when standing still, blend into the background, making them impossible to see.  They can also move in this stealth mode, though at a greatly reduced speed.  Jumping will give away their position, as will fast movement.
The stealth is the key part.  Trying to sneak up on an opponent while your character is invisible to both you and your opponent is a lot of fun.  The game throws in a few twists for you, too.  Tired of waiting? There's a taunt mechanic to reveal your position and lure adversary out of cover. Smoke bombs, a special item, allow you to mark a location, and then basically teleport back to it later.  Drop a smoke bomb, move somewhere else, and attack from hiding.  Go back into stealth after the attack and teleport back to your old spot.  Your opponent now has no idea where you are.  On the defensive side, there are caltrops, effectively three-pointed tacks that cause your opponent to bleed when he walks over them, giving away his position. You also can pick up shurikens or spears to give yourself a ranged attack against a melee-based opponent.
Because of all this, there's a lot of flexibility against a skilled human.  Do you want to silently stalk your opponent and strike from hiding?  Do you want to depend on fast movement and aggressive attacks to get you through? Both of those are options.
There are at least three game modes that I've tried: deathmatch, capture the flag, and challenge mode, where you try to score kills based on challenges. If I run across others, I'll add them here.  Up to four players can play in a match, and each player can choose if they'll be light or shadow.
The art style is stark, but appealling.  It's heavily influenced by traditional Japanese art, contributing to the feel of the overall game.  It's simple, but it's a key part of this game, and it works.
The overall result is good, but feels like a high quality flash game.  There is literally no story, no campaign, and no way to "beat the game."  There are no ranks.  It's just pick up and play.  If you have friends who will play this with you, then the 75% off price is worth it.  I've played it for an hour so far with my fiancee, and it's worth $3.24.  It is not worth $12.99, however.  There's just not enough here to justify that price.
So, to reiterate: Buy on sale, play with friends.

Quite possilbly the pinnacle of Telltale's "Walking Dead"-style adventure games, "Tales from the Borderlands" is an tour-de-force of fantastic writing, snappy dialogue, great characters, phenomenal voice acting, and absolutely beautifully staged setpiece sequences.  (Not to mention an excellent original score by Jared Emerson-Johnson, accompanied by absolutely deft use of soundtrack songs during key moments.  So good.)
Even if you're not a serious Borderlands fan, "Tales" weaves a compelling story that manages to blend and mash up all the best elements; from heist capers to road movies, treasure hunts to shootouts, and more, all capped by a pinch of romantic comedy (or comedic romance).  My biggest complaints (aside from the usual occasional Telltale animation/3d jank) are the clumsiness of the keyboard controls.  While the mouse control is fine (even preferred), there are several sequences that have you doing something that approximates classic point and click adventuring, and controlling where your character walks in a scene is clunky, to say the least.  It's not impossible to deal with, by any means, but it does take you out of the game when your otherwise well-animated character spazzes across the room, driven only in cardinal directions.  Hardly enough to knock it, however, and it remains my favorite Telltale game to date.

I have now 2762 hours of work time with RPG maker mv now. And I can tell much of this engine of the last 2 years.
This engine has been a buggy mess form the start. From little to non-optimization from the webGL engine. This do to how the game run on your device. This do to how the engine sends work flow to CPU/GPU/RAM. If you have an .ogg file that is over 3-4mb with music it will lag your game extremely. This have been improved with time but still not perfect. Or close to acceptable.
There are some good thinks with the engine.
•	Parallax mapping.
•	Easy to use.
•	Don’t need any coding experience.
•	Much content on YouTube showing and explain how things works.
But then it’s the negative side.
•	webGL engine its run on.
•	There have been so many bugs generate by the engine in game, that creators like myself have worked around. That the community have addressed on different forums. And haven’t been fixed for 2-3 months. (Some bugs have been over 12 months) For the latest example is the “image bug” with use of in game name like “charactername.angryface.png” Where if you have more than one . in the file name, it would not show up in game anymore. I have spent over 30 hours manually fixing the problem in game now. (easy fix is to rename the file with _ instead of . But you still have to do all the in game editor. (and that’s take time.)
•	The engine in itself is overpriced. (current stream price is about right, steam summer sale)
•	Little to no help from the developers when reporting bugs with engine. (see link above, lag issue) first post is in 2015 (still not fixed)
•	Don’t use the engine for something it’s not meant to be. If you have to many parallel events running in the background it will crash or lag your game. Adding sky or weather system will lag the game. (This again do to the bad optimization)
•	The community can be toxic. (not the engine fault)
Will I recommend this game engine to a friend? NO!
My recommendation is to use unreal or unity engine that are free to use and learn how the engine works before publishing anything. Or just play around in. Have I spent over 2000+ hours in unreal engine my game would been much better than it is now.
Do I regret starting with RPG maker MV? YES!
Have I known now what I know now, I would have jumped in another game engine without a second thought.
Will my next game be in rpg maker mv? NO!
Think I have explained this more than enough now. I have moved over to the unreal game engine and I hope you do too before starting out on a game.
Will I ever use a product made from the same developer? NO!
I will never buy or use any of their product never again. This is mostly to how their treat their customers.

My god Gunpoint is fantastic. I absolutely adore every single aspect of it. From the dialogue and gameplay to the music and graphics, every bit of it is executed fantastically.
The gameplay is where Gunpoint really shines. Much of it gravitates around the concept of situational awareness, IE what objects you can chain link together to knock out a guard. This allows for a plethora of possibilities and you'll always find yourself coming up with new inventive ideas to remove guards or open closed doors with useful items. Many anticipate that the design of levels would wear thin quick, at least in terms of NPCs and objects. However almost every level you encounter introduces a new object or a new enemy type, which can be helpful or detrimental in some way.
One of my favorite memories was when I chain linked a motion detector to a door. It closed on guard 1 as guard 2 passed through the detector. This would alert guard 2 and cause them to charge towards guard 1. This is where I triumphantly kicked down said door and sent it careening into guard 2, knocking him out and clearing the floor of all guard activity. While rudimentary, it still made me absolutely lose it.
The only drawback on Gunpoint is that it's quite short, at least 3 or so hours if you try to fully stealth it first time through. However the replay value greatly outweighs that. I'd recommend buying it when it's on sale unless you're willing to chip in 10$. If you want, throw in some extra cash for the soundtrack, because it is superb.

Squad has absolutely lived up to the description that you hear about in the trailers, and go beyond what I personally thought could be done in the Military Shooter genre. They truly did bridge the gap between the Arcade style FPS shooters, and the Full-Scale Tactical Military Simulators. The game features very interesting things not seen in games that come somewhat close in similarity. Such as integrated positional VoIP, allowing communication to members outside your squad, given that they are close enough to hear you. The game can be very slow at times, then immediately ramp up to fast paced action before you can even blink. For example, you could be following a friendly tank on foot, only to be ambushed by a group of hostiles on an adjacent hill. Capturing the position isn't just about pushing off 2 or 3 guys with Sub-Machine Guns, you have to factor many pieces of info in before attacking. How many units are there? Do they have Anti-Vehicle weaponry? Do they have a FOB? Do they have Mortars? Every piece of information you accurately acquire, makes your objective clear. Once your Squad Leader formulates the strategy, you go all in for it. If your the Squad leader, its your job to create a plan that gets the job done, and keeps your friends alive. You really should put this on your wishlist. It deserves a chance to be played by everyone.

EVE Online is quite a strange phenomena and at that really, really hard to actually review because of the sheer amount of content that it amassed during it's long lifetime. Basically it's not one single game but about 3 or 4 different. You can play it and never leave a station, just trading for hours, managing and moving goods on paper - and people do. A lot. In fact the economy is objectively the most complex in video games. On the other hand there are pvp, pve, industry, exploration and corporation management just to list a few. Take part in massive battles with thousands of players or just take of with a handful of friends and roam low security systems, do missions against the AI or mine ressources to feed the marked or the industry of your corporation. You can even play this as a quite fiddly RTS when commanding large fleets or managing your corporation as CEO. So, there really is a lot to and even after years of playing you will still be facing new challanges. If you so desire and dare to leave the beaten track that you have been following so far.
The mass of content and complexity though comes with a massive downside. It is hard to pick up for new players and I can pretty much guarantee you that you will be utterly overwhelmed at first with all the freedom of choice and the possibilities that you are offered. It's a massive sandbox at it's core. The size of Tokio and you get thrown in as a toddler with a plastic shovel and every inch of that sandbox is paved in spreadsheets.
The trick is to stay focused on what you wanna do. Pick one aspect, like small industry and producing for say, and stick with it for at least some weeks if not months. Find a corporation that shares the same focus and learn from your corpmates. If you get over this initial month or so you are presented with an increadibly rich and deep game that can keep you engaged for years and years to come withoud even paying one single cent as it is entirely possible to pay the monthly subscription with ingame currency once you get to a certain level of income.
It's a difficult game with focus on attracting and keeping hardcore players and at that definitely nothing I would safely recommend for a casual player who just wants to hop in and have some instant fun every now and then. To be successful and stay on top of things it requires quite a huge amount of your free time and a certain degree of passion and personal involvement.
To put it straight in just a few words: It is a compelling, overwhelmingly deep and entirely player driven game on a massive scale with basically no borders that unfortunately suffers from an aging and less than clear UI.
- Highly recommended (if you are able to endure some early pain)

This is a remake of the original Avernum which was itself a remake of the Exile series so it's not exactly an original game. On the other hand the game itself is worthy of a remake. The story is a lot of fun, and the setting is fascinating. The game has a good mix of main quests and side quests and indeed you'll probably spend a lot of time wondering around doing side quests before you even find the main quests. On the subject of main quests there are actually three different main quest lines which can be completed independently of each other.
In terms of mechanics this remake is staying reasonably true to the original. The stupid single map thing they had in Avernum 4-6 is gone and it's back to the traditional split between overland travel and town/dungoen maps. The skill system has been simplified somewhat but the addition of Battle Disiplines for fighters more than makes up for it.

Many reviewers judged Risen 3 to be generic which I don't feel is quite fair. The fantasy Caribbean setting and use of early firearms are rarely seen in rpgs as are open world games that are free of level scaling. Risen 3 is a game where you can find a difficulty 90 lock early on and a diff 10 in the "late game". Of course early and late game are almost completely dependent on where you choose to go and when.
Exploration is a strong point of the game and you're always bound to find something useful or something funny at least, whether it's a new weapon, treasure chest, schematic or just two skeletons with apples on their heads and a bunch of throwing daggers stuck in their rib cages.
Unlike in many rpgs gold is useful in Risen 3 and you always need more of it. Even if you accumulate large amounts by the end there's some powerful weapons that you can buy in the end game that will deplete your reserve.
Conversations with NPC can sometimes feel long winded and slow but the writing also has a unique kind of derpy charm and the humor can be pretty good if a little awkward. Though the ending did feel very anti-climatic I must say, not that it matters much.
English voice acting's pretty good but the main protagonist sounded very cheesy to me. Overall both the protagonist and Patty looked/sounded a lot better in Risen 2 I think. The main character in R3 is simply generic and bland both in terms of his voice and appearance while Patty was made sluttier for no good reason. Patty was already good looking in Risen 2 but she also had more character and sass appearance wise imo.
Guns and magic make combat quite easy, healing items are overplentiful imo and some of the skills (like distilling for example) are almost useless but ultimately I found the combat and overall gameplay quite fun and that's what matters in the end. It's a shame that some Risen 2 combat elements were removed. Things like salt/sand, the parrot pet, the kick skill but magic and "power gloves" were added so it's not a net loss.
Like all the Risen games Risen 3 is a bit rough around the edges but there's plenty of fun to be had and the 3 factions even give it a decent amount of replayability.
Local Co-Op at it's finest, havent had that much fun with my friends in a while.

This is a long review, so just read the bottom paragraph for a simple summary of my thoughts.
It surprises me that the general consensus for this game is worse than Risen 2: Dark Waters. To be fair, if you hated Risen 2, there likely are not enough redeeming factors about the end of the trilogy to be worth your while. But nevertheless, some substantial improvements to the overall experience have made this a promising step in the right direction for Piranha Bytes as a developer.
Risen 2: Dark Waters was ultimately a failure as an open world, engrossing RPG. It was extremely shallow, overall having one of their smallest and most lackluster world designs to date, with most of the islands consisting of winding pathways with few interesting landmarks leading between major locations. These locations were greatly devoid of life, as the characters were as dull and two-dimensional as wooden boards. The combat wasn't the worst I've ever seen in a game, but it took forever to get the necessary skills to stay on top of combat, and by then you just got used to button mashing between prayers. Beyond combat, half the skills in the game were worthless or used in only scripted situations that were easy enough to do without.
At first glance, or maybe even for the first couple hours, Risen 3 hardly seems any different. But if you put some effort into it, you'll find much more in store here. The combat system is widely criticized for the wrong reasons. To be fair, the easiest way to fail at Risen 3 was the only way to WIN in Risen 2: button mashing is heavily discouraged in Risen 3, as timing your combos poorly results in substantially slower attacks. Instead, the game encourages you to time your attacks with precision, and focus your efforts between multiple foes instead of trying to spam them to death one at a time. It also has a dodge maneuver, which Risen 2 lacked on release (and when they patched it in, it was hardly any more useful). In fact, the dodge led to quite the opposite criticism: that combat was too easy, since dodging made you invulnerable during the animation. (A patched-in "Ultra" difficulty removes these invincibility frames, if you dare - as well as forcing a cooldown between potion uses.) Beyond that, skills you can learn from instructors give you a parry ability, faster combos, additional combo attacks, and further stat increases to make you unstoppable by the end of the game. It's still not a flawless combat system overall, but this is a world where Skyrim's dreadful DPS-focused combat dodges any ounce of criticism while a game like this is torn to pieces over a moderately tactical system.
The magic system is a bit unique, and certainly much more appealing than the lame voodoo system of Risen 2. Combat magic is available to all three factions, but much more varied to the Guardian faction. Some spells are equipped as a primary weapon and used in place of a sword - these spells can be used as a moderately-ranged attack in melee, or aimed as a projectile. Support magic can be placed in your quickbar for a single rapid cast, after which it requires a cooldown. Each faction has their unique spells which can only be acquired through the faction, but single-use versions (scrolls, voodoo dolls, runestones) can be found and used by any class as a disposable magical support with no cooldown.
The only thing that truly disappointed me about the magic was that there was hardly any difference between the different types of offensive magic. Fire and Ice did the same amount of damage, for example, and had no unique effects, such as freezing enemies or igniting them. You only switched between them if you found an enemy who was immune to one and not the other.
The world design is notably improved. The game does re-use two islands from Risen 2, and scales them down considerably, but the new locations are significantly larger, have more to explore, and have areas of the map that open up as you complete more of the story. The maps themselves are a bit more open, but still tend toward a frustratingly path-focused design that makes most of the locations seem more linear than they really are. Thankfully, they've expanded the game in a vertical direction, allowing you a BIT more freedom in climbing. It's still obvious where you can and cannot climb, for the most part, but ambitious explorers may find rewards hidden in unexpected places if you can find a way. A large assortment of books can be found throughout, attempting to expand the game's lore or close some of the plotholes left between the previous titles.
I can't say the characters have improved significantly - there are plenty of fodder characters who just seem cut and paste from the previous game, and are often indistinguishable from others, but they've greatly increased in number, and the dialog has vastly increased as well. Many of the characters are still cringe-worthy or dull as dishwater, but a few still made a note with me as I played, such as the woeful Mortimer on Fog Island, the quiet yet stoic demon hunter Kane, and the misforunate Burke, many of whom have interesting quests or even just stories to tell.
You know what to expect with the questing - most RPG's these days have the same number of fetch or exterminate quests, but even in this regard, I'd say Risen 3 at least makes some of them more interesting. If you're feeling adventurous, make sure you disable quest markers - otherwise, if you're getting bored, use them to wrap up sidequests quickly. At least Risen 3's questgivers will tell you what to do and where to go, so you don't HAVE to depend on floating arrows to guide you if you don't want them.
The number of items in the game has increased, with more variety to melee weapons, magic, and firearms. Some of the weapons are mechanically indistinguisable from each other (crossbows vs. pistols, for example) yet require different skills to use. The "legendary items" quests from Risen 2 make a return, and number slightly higher, providing potent stat increases. Unique weapons can be found in two pieces, to be reforged at a smithy - but with no clues on how to find these weapons, it's quite possible you'll have better ones by the time you find both pieces.
Unfortunately, the game again shipped with day-one DLC, with two story DLC's and one item-only one. Needless to say, developing gameplay content prior to release and charging separately for it is not a practice that consumers should ever endorse, but at least each DLC is slightly larger than Risen 2's, with a smaller price tag.
Final consensus: this game does not do enough to change the most vitriolic opinions about Risen 2. Nevertheless, Piranha Bytes appears to have taken some of the largest points of contention into consideration with Risen 3. Not everything got done that fans wanted, but in the shorter development time, dealing with internal restructuring and losing major designers, I think Piranha Bytes was able to focus on their most egregious sins and provide a substantial package that I don't regret paying for.

Here's the thing about Risen 3
Even though I've pressed the "I recommend this game" button, I don't think it fits for all situations.
The graphics are decent, the writing and voice over have their moments but are overall mediocre, the story is... meh and  the game play is tough.
This should not be confused with Dark Soul's tough but fair, as in if you die, YOU screwed this up, nope, it's more like, if you died , yeah you may have done something to prevent this, but probably your character isn't really good enough at this moment, so run away and level up.
In fact the game play is a classic zero-to-hero deal, like in the gothic series and the other risen games, if you enjoy being beaten mercilessly at the beginning only to come back 10 hours later to BEAT THE CRAP OUT OF THOSE STUPID DODO BIRDS THAT STUNLOCK THE CRAP OUT OF YOU....... yes you will enjoy this.
While exploring, you get stat points or skill points or whatever they're called, and you can spend them to raise your stats. If your stats are high enough you can buy skills, this is what in effect counts as leveling, and many of the skills make a huge difference in your character's fighting ability, and if you will be able to kill a monster or not.
You will at some point get to pick one of three factions, which will give you magic, doing it sooner rather than later will make the game easier.
The only problem (yes I know there are a number of problems, this is the only one that I cared about)  I've had with this game is that , even though I like the zero-to-hero model, towards the end it becomes very easy, in fact boringly so, I powered through it just to say that I have finished it. I guess they could have done a better job at keeping the difficulty a bit higher towards the end.
Overall I liked it, maybe my opinion is a bit biased for personal reasons, or because I played this right after the shipwreck that was sacred 3, which made me appreciate things a bit more.
Bottom Line:
If you liked the gothic games or the previous risen games, or if you like games that start out frustrating (no , not hard, there's a difference) , then this game is probably for you

I bought this for game days when I have a group of friends over we pass controllers around. In a day of playing all sorts of silly same-screen games like Speedrunners, Gang Beasts, and Towerfall, this was the only game that didn't hit. I'm sure there's fun to be had here, but we very quickly moved on to the next game.

Quite possilbly the pinnacle of Telltale's "Walking Dead"-style adventure games, "Tales from the Borderlands" is an tour-de-force of fantastic writing, snappy dialogue, great characters, phenomenal voice acting, and absolutely beautifully staged setpiece sequences.  (Not to mention an excellent original score by Jared Emerson-Johnson, accompanied by absolutely deft use of soundtrack songs during key moments.  So good.)
Even if you're not a serious Borderlands fan, "Tales" weaves a compelling story that manages to blend and mash up all the best elements; from heist capers to road movies, treasure hunts to shootouts, and more, all capped by a pinch of romantic comedy (or comedic romance).  My biggest complaints (aside from the usual occasional Telltale animation/3d jank) are the clumsiness of the keyboard controls.  While the mouse control is fine (even preferred), there are several sequences that have you doing something that approximates classic point and click adventuring, and controlling where your character walks in a scene is clunky, to say the least.  It's not impossible to deal with, by any means, but it does take you out of the game when your otherwise well-animated character spazzes across the room, driven only in cardinal directions.  Hardly enough to knock it, however, and it remains my favorite Telltale game to date.

This game lacks any heavy plot and is instead, do this and kill him basically. If you are anything like me in this game and suck at the melee combat, then the NPCs that are trying to kill you, can make it frustrating. Especially due to the lack of saving during missions. It can sometimes feel very dragged out since you basically walk anywhere. You have meters that keep track of your needs, such as, eating, drinking, sleeping, reading, talking to others, etc.
Overall the game is a decent casual game that only takes a few hours to complete. It has decent graphics, decent gameplay, and an ok story. It also comes with online multiplayer which I will not be reviewing, at least not here or now. I will, however recommend that if you buy this game, it should at least be on a 25% sale.
With all that being said, I rate this game a 6.5/10

The first DBZ game to hit Steam, and what a reputation it set for itself rather quickly.
So Dragon Ball Xenoverse is all about the original DBZ timeline, but with a twist. There is a duo going around, distorting time and collecting energy for their own malicious intent, and what they do, can cause all kinds of different alterations in time. That Raditz actually escapes from Goku's grasp and dodges(fitting) Piccolo's Special Beam Cannon, Goku never has the time to overpower Vegeta during their first encounter, everyone forgetting how to step out of the way just fittingly as Ginyu gets introduced. And naturally, they need to be stopped, so Trunks (which is your main partner throughout the game) calls for Shenron and wishes for the Ultimate Fighter to help protect history. Surprise surprise, that's you.
A tad bit cliché as it might be, your character does embed itself neatly into the story without causing any real problems with how hardcore fans experience the timelines playing out, of course that does lead to the story mode / Time Patrols to feel a bit.. dull, but that doesn't mean they can't be fun.
Overall the fighting system is solid, it handles a lot like the BT series and it's the kind of game where it takes maybe an hour or two to get the hang of, and from there you can make your own moves and combos by combining light attacks, or strong attacks. Now on to the one of the two things that people mostly care about: Can I blow an enemy up with an energy ball the size of a skyscraper? Well, yes, but sadly, it doesn't really have the DBZ feeling of looking over the battlefield mid-battle, watching all the destruction that has been going on, blasts and balls of Ki don't really leave much of a trace except on your opponent's health bar, but a whole lot of them feel really solid and will probably make you remenisce about the times you were in a park with a friend, screaming "Kamehameha!" at each other because it was so cool! There is almost all the Ki moves and possible physical moves (called Strike moves) in the game that are from the show as a whole, from Saiyan saga to even Beerus, and with clothes, z-souls and accessories to match.
Now the other part, the character customization. I myself, am a complete sucker for these things, I love being able to make my creativity flow and create a character that truly feels like mine.. or I can make a black, bald Saiyan with pink clothes, the option is there. While the options for hair, nose, mouth, eyes etc. does have a variety, I feel that there are some parts that were left out and I don't really understand why. For example, all the male characters (bar the Acrosions) have muscles, really evident ones, even when they're super short and thin. I personally would like the actual body type option to be included at some point, which also brings me over to the Majins, you can choose between either a female Majin, small, pink, cute, what's not to like? And then there's.. the male ones, which is just fat Buu.
Now, don't take that like me disliking fat Buu as a character, it's the only body type that has a different one than from "stacked" to "super stacked", but why the fat one is the only variation, when Kid Buu was his original state, is beyond me.
As for DLC, I think everyone was a bit disappointed, we get promised 3 DLC packs, that one was going to be GT, and unknown on the other two, but they actually just split it up into GT 1 & 2, even though the packs don't hold enough content together to justify the split.
All in all, this game is solid, it's fun, it certainly has some balancing issues, but they seem to be working quite hard to fix them, and they also seem relatively aware of what the community suggests and thinks. CaC are stronger than canon characters, same thing in PvP (you'll never catch me PvPing with non-canon characters), and PvE difficulty is smooth in it's increase, an occasional speedbump here and there but nothing that should make you wanna stop playing.
~8/10, DBZ fan or not, this is most probably a game you'd have fun with if you enjoy fighting games and/or DBZ.

RPGMaker MV is a software that can be leveraged to make your own RPG games when you have limited to no scripting ability.  It touts that you don't need to be an artist... or a programmer... or sound engineer.  All of these resources are built-in for you so that you just need to focus on one thing:  Making a great game.
This is true... and it isn't.
On the one hand, it's very true.  Within an hour, you can be churning out some cool maps, interesting characters, and nifty combats.  You don't in fact need to program.  The system gives you all the tools you need from a paper-doll character generator (both portraits and associated sprite animations), to a layered tile map.  Tons of assets are already included, and RPGMaker MV offers you a very flexible system to set up events to occur, letting you throw weather, pictures, screen tints, characters, puzzles, and more onto the map.
Once the initial honeymoon is over, you start seeing some of the limitations.  The graphics all have to go onto a specific grid, which can make blocky looking maps.  The selection of images starts to feel very limited when you start picking between the green grass or the brown dirt.  You have one type of repeatable tree, and a few token bushes.  Likewise, the background music is ultimately pretty limited, and when you listen to the same theme over and over again, it loses a bit of luster.  The combat interface is fairly locked in.  You may select side-view, or bottom-up, but the interface isn't going to really change beyond that.  These kinds of limitations could make even the most creative and inspired designer start to feel extremely repetitive.
That said, RPGMaker is extremely open.  If you are a pixel artist, you can import your own sprites and tiles.  If you like to draw character art, import your own. Music and sound effects may be imported.  You also have an extremely elaborate scripting system (leveraging Javascript) that will let you adjust almost every element in the game, from the battle system to the menus and interface.  This can let you essentially make almost anything you really want.  If you have one of the above mentioned skills and want to bring it to bear, you have plenty of opportunity to do so.
If you don't, that brings me to my next major pro of this software:  There is an incredible community behind it.  I've tested other game development softwares, and I've never seen a community so ready and able to jump in and help build solutions to make your game better.  The community is very invested in (and loyal to) RPGMaker, and go to great lengths to give you all the support you need to make your game succeed.  If you aren't an artist, but you really want that 3-headed dragon in your game, you need only ask on the forum and very likely someone will take up the cause and deliver a 3-headed dragon.  If you have trouble working through a particularly challenging event/puzzle, you need simply ask and the community is quick to offer suggestions in a constructive way to help you succeed.
Overall, I think this is a great software for a budding game developer to start with... one that will make it difficult to use any other after.

If you're looking for a game with an authentic tactical feel, but you're new to the genre (like me), Squad is definitely the place to start. I messed around with Arma 3 and found the menu clunky and difficult to navigate. The controls were all over the place and the combat felt choppy and awkward. Not Squad. The gameplay is smooth and it's quite easy to get the hang of, though confusing the first couple matches. The battles can get quite hectic when mortars and vehicles get involved, and they pretty much nailed the sound effects used in battle. The maps can be somewhat large, but the way they set up the objectives pretty much funnels entire teams to a couple objectives, which keeps things interesting and fast paced when you're on the front lines. Communication is key--you're going to need a mic, and you're going to have to TALK. Squad leads have their own channel, squads have their own channel, and there's a separate chat channel for radial chat (anyone nearby). It takes communication from the lowest level to have a successful objective push or game in general. The only negative thing I have to say about it is the fact that teams don't autobalance between matches. Meaning if you get stomped in one match, it's best to change teams because you will be stomped again in the next. The community is friendly and the acceptance for newer players is higher in this game than I've ever seen on PC. I've been playing this game almost daily since I got it, and hopefully you will enjoy it as much as I have. Highly Recommended.

This game is easily one of my favorites. I've not played it as long as some people, but overall I've got around (Edit) 550 hours (Including Steam & Non-Steam Hours).
The game has many stories in it, even some from Shakespeare, some of my personal favorites. There's plenty of events to keep you occupied. Even if you get bored of the game, which for me, was after around 150 hours, you'll be wanting to come back to it eventually and I played it even longer after coming back to it.
Story : 10/10 - Takes far longer to beat than plenty of games I've ever played and has multiple stories.
Graphics : 6.5/10 - The game runs on an older engine, so graphics aren't the best, but the artwork is beautiful.

Combat : 8.5/10 - While it certainly isn't as fun as the combat in TERA (Another amazing mmorpg), the combat is better than that of many mmo's I've played.
Community : 7.5/10 - The game is rather old so there's not as many players as there could be on it. Overall, the community's fun, helpful, and rather friendly.
As far as being helpful goes, many experienced players are willing to help new players get a grasp on the game's key features, especially combat.

Gameplay : 9/10 - There's enough to keep you busy for a while, so there's not much to hate about it.
Overall, this game was great and I plan to keep coming back to it. The game definitely deserves more attention & players than it gets.

Subterrain is good but I have had a weird internal voice for this review. I picked it up a while ago & I was really unsure what to make of it but as a big fan of Dark Wood, I thought "I should give this top-down horror game a chance". So I did.
Subterrain is the closest thing we'd ever get to a top-down Dead Space. I am being totally serious. Minus insanity effects, an evil church and some of the actual flavor differences- It's a lot like Dead Space.
It has body horror, it has cool space gore, it has scary zombie noises & it has pulsating flesh masses. It has Things that shoot slowdown goo, it has Bruisers that will not only break your armor but kill you instantly, it has weapon upgrades and it has a genuinely tense atmosphere. The music, the tone- The overall presentation is very clean and well-managed. The pixel work is very crisp and easily understood. I have spent a good chunk of hours in it, on normal and I am going to tell you, try it out on Easy first.
I have barely cleaned out 2/3rds of the station and I still can't make it to certain places because of how corpse-infested some of the areas are. My ideal is to make the base totally liveable, which I know is, if you play the game, what feels like a pipe dream.
There are a lot of things going for Subterrain. Really. It is scary. It is tense. It has a low-maintenace crafting system. It has base management. A part of me really wants to nag on how much of your time is spent on that actual management as opposed to just going out and exploring but I can't hold the game accountable for that because as it says, right on the tin "Manage the entire colony" I just... It's like the wind got sucked from my sails.
The game is tedious. I really hate saying that. The game is really good but it really grinds your patience. You can spend time, resources & expend effort to go get great gear for your station security so your reactors can do really good so you don't have to go out, farm more- Like now sitting down and kind of gathering my thoughts, it kind of does that thing that Fallout 4 does in a way that I remember I think Joseph Anderson described:
"You go out and kill, so you can collect, so you can come back to craft better gear so you can go out and kill things easier, etc, etc, etc~"
Upon realizing this, it does leave me in an odd opinion. In no way does that Triangle of Effort seem like a negative because many games do it and we don't notice it. Only now though do I realize that the difference mechanically in how their triangles compare is that, unlike Fallout 4, where there is the ALLEGED threat of raiders or people who will come and attack your base while you're out, the Corpsefiends in this game WILL come to you.
You Have to go out, you Have to go clear sectors. If you want to stay alive, keep the gear you work hard to get, keep your reactors working proper, you Have to leave the safety of your home & in a weird sort of way, brave the Oregon Trail of Mars.
I never thought I'd be going to that comparison and that's weird. There is hardly a plot that really forces you to stay at the base as your four crafting hubs are right downstairs. Your entire goal, is actually to leave the base. To do this you must gather the necessary components to build fuel for the ship to get off the station.
I don't know man, usually I can aptly compare, focus on what makes a game fun or unique but Subterrain has these really intense moments of where, you are breaching dark corridors filled with nightmarish meat monsters with hardly a working police baton. You're running low on oxygen, you're begging, praying just to make it to the elevator that you reactivated so you can get back to the tram platform to recover your lost health with your emergency medical gear you stashed there because one of the big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s socked you hard enough to just rock your♥♥♥♥♥and break your leg in the act. That's where it is. That's the desperation.
It's the act of survival. I suppose that's the core gameplay. Aside from crafting and combat, its' only focus is to stay alive and much like the focus on the Tree of Wants and needs that all people need, to say that you only need to survive is meaning you are scraping together the bare minimum and I think that's why I'm having a hard time finding things to say. Games don't need to be art or have a metric ton of bonus features but you need to have more than just "Survive" as a list of priorities.
If the game had more to do then going out, killing, collecting and improving your base, I'd say this would really have been an unnoticed gem. It's a good game.
It's a C+ in my book.
It totally deserves a playthrough and a purchase I just don't want people expecting too much from it.
I suppose I'll give you some tips and tricks now for your playthrough:
When you get to the central reactor hub, take all the frniture and move it to make barricades. The storage area in the top left is full of stuff and trust me, you will want to block tohse passages.
Get straight into clearing out the tech and industrial area under the base. There are a ton of crafting materials and getting your homebase cleaned up is what will save you a lot of struggle in the long run.
Work on getting your reactor upgrades first. Seriously, going out, reading the available guide that tells you where to find the power reactor upgrade, go do that. Having more power means you can run all 4 stations as opposed to like 2 to 3 at the start.
The SMG is your best friend. On average you will put out the most damage with the SMG than the shotgun and the pistol. Also SMGs are the only gun that the guard stations can use.
Learn to dodge. Remember spacebar is your second-best friend.
Always carry spare Everything. You will freeze to death, you will suffocate, you will starve, you will get infected, you will get broken bones. You will need everything.
EDIT: Enemies Will open doors. Be careful, always clear rooms and when you go back, go back to somewhere you know you are safe.
Overall: 7 out of 10, overall a decent experience but could use some more meat on its' bones.
After-Shower Thoughts & an Edit: So when I was away, I went to take a shower and I had a thought, like we all do in times of contemplation and this was it. Subterrain does a really great job at instilling claustrophobia in you with the tight corridors you have to fight in. You realize a lot of the fighting is bottlenecked and requires you to move furniture and it took me a hard minute to realize this but that was something the game did really well. Sure a lot of the games' melee combat is just kiting, but when you get to build up a corridor of cover, to chuck 'nades and fire over and through cover is when you get another one of those moments where you get to feel the gameplay shine.
Suggestions & Complaints: To the games credit, it builds its' tone and atmosphere very well and I had to kind of take a step outside of my head to realize this, but something that would have added tremendously to the game, is if the option to go OUTSIDE was there. At no point do I remember being able to go outside and roam mars. I could see Mars through the agriculture center, but I think the game would have been tremendously strengthened if you could do stuff on the surface. I know the idea was to maintain this closed, tight package but that's the problem, the game is as stifling its' surrounding which does reinforce what it does well but nobody wants to actually feel the acrid breath of rotten meat on the nape of their neck and Not want to head outside. That would have added a real, literal breath of fresh air to gameplay is if it just wasn't so oppressive.
Also, I really wish we could have had 2 player co-op, this game would have almost been a 9 for me if a buddy & I could clear the Mars station together but if the addition of 2-player & going outside were added, it'd go from Good to Great! for me.

Only for the hardcorest of the hardcore turn-based strategy lovers. I have played Suikoden I and II from start to finish, Tactics Ogre, Suikoden Tactics, and Final Fantasy Tactics 3 times, plus both GBA games and the PSP remake as well. Not to mention Civilizations I-V. I LOVE turn-based strategy, in all of its forms.
Or so I thought.
This game is a member of a disturbingly expansive group of titles I like to call Keep Away Games. Remember the old childhood game keep away, where the whole point was to keep a certain person from getting a certain item they really wanted? This is similar, in that the fun is always kept JUUUUUUST outside your grasp. Ok, that's not true. Sometimes it flies so far over your head that the Sun blinds you, and you lose track of it completely.
-Just when you're enjoying exploring the overworld, your characters get stuck because you're trying to click on the square next to you, but the game thinks you're clicking on you. Teeth starting to grate, CHECK.
-Just when you're enjoying combat, you click to move 2 squares away, and the idiotic AI decides you meant you want to take 4 turns walking completely around the level, taking the absolute most circuitous route possible to get to your destination, rather than move TWO FREAKING STEPS IN THE OTHER DIRECTION. Bonus points if this idiocy costs you a battle. Prepare for lots of bonus points. Swearing at computer in multiple languages, CHECK CHECK.
-Just when you've gotten a few dozen rounds of combat down and are feeling good about things, you hit a battle so ridiculously tough (in the same exact area you've been cleaning up) that you have to quicksave and quickload 3 dozen times, hoping to get an outcome where your entire party isn't stunned at the same time for the 3rd turn in a row again. Clicking on "Delete Local Content," oh 10 minutes ago called to give you your CHECK.
I would like to meet the person whose idea of fun is fighting 3 enemies, each of which can stun your entire group at once and summon other monsters to help, which each take 4-5 turns of your team's entire concentrated effort to kill, so that I can tattoo across their forehead in Helvetica bold "FAULTY GENETIC CODE. DO NOT SLEEP WITH."
Controls are hideous as well. You can control the whole game via keyboard, and absolutely 165% should, but even that isn't well fleshed out. Hitting I opens up the inventory, of course, but DON'T hit I again. You have to hit ESC to close the menu. Hitting I again may accidentally use the item in your inventory to which the I key got arbitrarily assigned to. Small things like that really don't make that big of a difference, but they certainly don't help a game that already left a sour taste in my mouth.
Games like this actually make me angry, because they have the potential to be SO. AWESOME. Idiotic controls, horrifically moronic AI, COMPLETE lack of direction, and stupefying difficulty spikes aside, you may enjoy this...
...if you're trapped on a desert island, or don't have enough money to afford aaaaaaaaanything else.

Why? Why Piranha Bytes, why must you hurt me like this?
It's like you've taken the good parts of their older games and thrown them all out, while at best not doing anything about the bad parts, and at worst magnifying them, or even shoehorning new ones from other games in.
The NPC Hubs, unlike the ones from about every Gothic game they made, seem empty and dead. The liveliest one is the Guardians big hold, but it's a single one, compared to the countless other ones that simply seem...barren. The inter NPC banter which made the towns in Gothic and Risen seem especially lively is almost completely missing, as is the ambiance that came with it. Most of the NPCs become completely meaningless, after you've done a sweep through their area and finished whatever quest they were involved in. Unlike the previous games, there are almost no quests that become available at a later point, making the gameworld seem even more devoid of life. Because apparently nothing happens while you're away.
Choosing a faction also has almost no impact. There is only a handfull of faction-dependant perks, most of which carry little weight. Apart from that, faction dictates which set of spells becomes permanently available to you, but during one playthrough I found a sufficient amount of scrolls to make that meaningless as well. After that, the only thing left are AFAIK about 2 quests per faction that wouldn't be available without joining. There are almost no other reactions or consequences to your choice in faction. Though that might be rooted in the choice to have no conflict between the factions, which I think is a rather boring design choice.
Along with the factions comes the comparable tiny variety of equipment. There is a miniscule selection of 3 sets of armor per faction and they don't have that much impact on gameplay, as the values of armor seem laughable (150 points of damage mitigation, of which about 115 are from character attributes and perks at the end of my playthrough).  Though there are a bit more weapons available, a good part of those are already useless at the point one can optain them.
All special abilities and perks no longer cost any learning points. All that is left is an amount of gold one has to pay for them, which undoubtably enables players to get anything they want without any need for choice. And with the Potion Brewing Perk, which costs 2000 gold pieces, the upper half of the attribute scale becomes meaningless as well. Why invest experience points into enhancing an attribute past a value of 50, if one can instead do it with not that hard to get potions?
The Sea-Battle minigame they implemented seems like a sloppy attempt of copying Assassins Creed's sea battles, but with only 3 instances happening, none of which are avoidable, I couldn't familiarize with it's mechanics enough to be particularily good. It thus simply became a chore, each one taking about 20 minutes of gametime, while not being any kind of fun or adding anything to the story. The other three minigames were less of a chore, but also weren't required at any point, which is a good thing I guess. Why the hell they decided to implement the seabattles, and do so the way they did still is beyond me.
The other, more "puzzely" possiblities of the game were mostly ignored. The "trained monkey" sequences were few in number and rarely provided anything of value (only 2 times IIRC). Same goes with the "transform into Parrot" sequences. There was only a hand full of them, and most of them only provided mediocre loot. None of them were in any part needed for any quests, neither main nor side. In fact, there weren't even meaningful possiblities to use them during the mainquest.
The final battle was (again) only a "whack the damage sponge" with the occasional "follow the damage sponge" which felt kinda anti-climatic.
While you get seven possible followers, it's of little meaning which one of them you take with you. They simply didn't add that much, appart from distracting monsters during combat and only occasional lines of banter. The game simply never made me (as a player) care that much about them. Of the three followers that I never took along, there is one whom I never found out anything but his name and his fondness of Alcohol, one I only found out that he had gotten ret-conned into a cruel, mercyless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and one that only seemed to be fond of stealing things. Nothing else. Nothing upon which I could build any feelings towards these characters but disinterest.
So I have to ask: What the hell went wrong at Piranha Bytes? Why did you build something so completely forgettable, so unbelievably mediocre, so underwhelmingly plain? After a year of being abused by many players and pirates, I think it is time to write a detailed review or an impression of the psychological rollercoaster I went through.
Eve Online is identical to real life in my opinion. You are thrown in there with little to no instructions. The learning curve is tough. You could end up mining for a guild, oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ I called it a guild, you might be shunned if you call them guilds in this game, they are called corps. Where was I? Oh yeah, you could end up working for a corp as a miner to get the ship you wanted after a very long time in the safest spot or you could end up being a pirate hunting the same miners you could have been. It most likely depends on your skills and how much time you are willing to dedicate to such a game. Why do I say that? Learning skills takes real time as opposed to game time. Skills would start building up in your queue from 3 Hours to months of real time. In case you read this far and you are wondering if it is a casual MMO, no it is not. It is rather hardcore and this is coming from someone who is not all that familiar with MMOs. Anyways, just like I said, you could ultimately do whatever you want to do in this game. Planetary exploration and material extraction, piracy, logistics, Mining, whatever. It sounds very exciting initially but it takes a really long time and money and effort. All that effort can go down the drain however. If your ship gets destroyed, all those upgrades you have spent time and blood and sweat on would go away in a heartbeat, but that's not remotely all of it. Your character's pod is thrown into space and you have to get your pod to the nearest space station to find another ship before someone destroys your pod and... Well, your character dies and loses all those skills you spent real life time on. I am repeating myself with the real life time because it is just so goddamn frustrating.
I honestly didn't expect myself to get into a game like this, I didn't expect to get into it for a long time. I rarely enjoyed it but it was like staring at pandora's box from afar, it seems so interesting your curiosity gets the better of you and well... You spend 100+ hours into it getting into more than one corps the same way you apply to a job. Perhaps even more humiliating. Getting into a corp is not easy, they interview you, sometimes skype you and assess if you are the man/woman for the position. It almost sounds crazy, and I assure you, it is when you end up hearing about people being humiliated in chat rooms filled with at least 200 players that watch a man get naked on webcam to get a position in a corp. That's how it is in the world of EVE, it sounds really interesting from afar just like the notorious battle that had thousands of players pit against each other, but when you actually get into it, you want to leave and never come back.
Perhaps I got one good thing out of it. The love of Ambient music. A year ago, I was never a fan of music that fades into the background and helps you concentrate. EVE's soundtrack is full of that. It helps the players enjoy their sweet time digging into their menus for countless of hours to EVE's soundtrack. It was well engineered to the point where you feel lonely and it is scary out there when you are traveling and expect a pirate to strike you down even in the safest spots. Ironically, the first time I encountered an NPC drone, I thought it was a pirate and panicked and abandoned my ship only to find out later that it was part of the mission.
I don't think I have anything specific in my review regarding the technicalities of EVE, but I was just surprised and my expectations have been greatly exceeded by what I saw there, and I was sure it was not for me. At the same time, all I can write here are my impressions. I finally left the game after realizing it was inevitable for me especially after a pirate corp threatened the mining corp I was in. I actually stayed with that cop for about a month or so, and it was newly formed. Later on when the pirate corp threatens it, members of my mining corp started arguing and all I could do was observe. I was a spectator the whole time and it was, admittedly enjoyable to see my own corp's members argue and argue until some of them left and it went down the drain. It's just so amazing how things could change ther-- YOUR SPACESHIP IS BEING
YOUR GUN IS FROZEN, YOUR SHIELD HAS BEEN JAMMED.... WHY? OH GOD PLEA-- *boom* Pod is still there, guess I can go and grab another ship and build millions of isks instead of buying PLEX cards with real money (60$ give or take) to get back the same ship I had with the same upgra-- *respawns* *pod destroyed* ..... *quits game* *uninstalls*
10/10 would quit after a year and be haunted by it for the rest of his life

Risen 3 – Titan Lords
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
As I have not played the previous two (2) games, I really had no idea what this game would be like.
7 hours down the track, I am absolutely amazed by it. The amount of quests I am getting in one location is just unbelievable; I am literally losing count.
This RPG is set in a world of Pirates with absolutely stunning visuals. If you enjoy taking screenshots do not look further, this game will give you plenty of opportunities to snatch great screenshots from sunset to beautiful sceneries.
Great open world and apart from quests you have a fair few of other things to do like picking up clams where you can get pearls or gathering food, vegetation for potions/magic, and a must for a good pirate, rum and other distilled substances. They are great sources of health in the game. Argh...hip Argh...hip...burp...Argh!
One thing I like so far is you do not have to worry about how many objects your character is carrying, just collect them. Anyway, you will be able to trade your goods with multiple people in each destination. And, you will be able to learn many essential skills like using a monkey! Yes you will!
Along the way you meet characters and you can invite them to your party. I already have two at this stage (different skills) and they are very useful especially during combat. However, you have to choose who you want at your side when you arrive at each location.
For the combat side of the equation, it could have been smoother but it is fine. I am just being a little bit picky here. A little bit of advice, try to upgrade your character attributes as soon as possible because some foes are quiet challenging and even with a companion at your side you just might die quickly.
The audio is good and the story is sound. A good RPG all round.
Positives:

-	Great graphics
-	Good story
-	Massive number of quests
-	In depth character options
-	Challenging adversaries
-	Good humour
-	Achievements
-	Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Combat system could have been better
A very solid RPG in my opinion. Thumbs up.

Rimworld, from what I've played of it, is a masterpiece of a survival game.  What sets it apart from other games of this type is the emphasis on storytelling, with characters that interact with each other in interesting ways and a real feeling that the story is progressing. During my colony's first year, times were tough, and my colonists had to resort to cannibalism.  Against all odds they survived the harsh winter, but then one of my original party went completely mad and had to be put down and another was killed by raccoons.  Now that we've a better farm than before, my colonists no longer have to eat human flesh, but we still feed slain enemies to the dogs so that we can save the good food for ourselves.
In conclusion, buy this game.  It's amazing.  Just make sure you're prepared to see your farms ravaged by a cold snap.

When i original saw the trailer for this game, i thought it was a very action/adventure/fighting packed game type, boy i was complete wrong.
You can divide this game in 2 parts, the story side and the vs side.
The story side obviously let you follow trough the story of the anime/manga, starting after the nagato/pain saga, returning from time to time to the 9 tails incident in the leaf 16 years before. However, this is the cool part and the sad one at the same moment. The game (if you can call it that way) has no adventure side, you follow the story in a cinematic/dialogue type, with little to no gameplay (the gameplay limits from going from 1 screen to another, and no more than 3, and this is from time to time), then, after a while, after watching a cinematic or reading the dialiogues, a confrontation between characters will happen, mostly the same fights that happened in the anime/manga. This is your gameplay, a small fight, then you go back to the cinematics/dialogues.
The sad part is that you get so little gampleay that you feel ripped off your money, however, the fighting mechanics, as basic as some button mashing can be, are quite fun, specially if you have teammates with you, which help you in battle (support characters ala mvsc), from time to time you will find some quicktime events, not actually difficult, but they might take you by surprise, since there are not that many.  Yesterday, i was "Playing" chapter 4, i watched 40 minute cinematic after a 5  minute fight.
The cool part is that if you have not watched that part of the story, you will catch up, and if you have, it doesnt matter, the game looks gorgeous, the art design is beautiful, the animation is very fluid, vivid colors, it is breath taking  watching the cinematics and the quick actions, i cant say the same about the english dub, but the original languaje is great.
The soundtrack is allright, while the main theme of this game is a very quiet/slow song, though beautiful, it does not reflect what we are used to hear in the anime. The soundtrack is good, dont get me wrong, but it lacks the punch of songs such as rising the fighting spirit, the jiraiya theme or even the orochimaru theme, the soundtrack here does not stand out, but it does set the mood for the scene in turn. (<--- Scene, geez, im reviewing a game, never expected to say that)
The controls are basic. hit, kunai, cover, kawamiri no jutsu, chakra charge, jump/dash and support buttons, not much to do there in matter of combos, just mash the b button several times and you will do a 10-12 hit combo, the cancel mechanic allows you to hit more times, but again, mashing the b button. The controller works, but its very simple.
Graphics. As i mentioned before, i cannot complain about the graphics, since the game looks awesome, however, the native resolution (1280 x 720) did not managed to stress my old radeon 3870, when i tried to get more juice from the graphics, i increased them to 1440 x 900 (MAX). My card couldnt handle tomb raider at that resolution, in this game nothing changed, nothing at all, is as if i never changed the resolution in the first place.
The controller. Although the controls work as intended, the problem is the support, i dont own a console nor a 360 controller, the game did not accepted my generic usb controller (first game that does that, never had an issue). So i had to play with my keyboard, which was very annoying to set up, allow me to explain.
When you open the game, a menu appears, you can launch the game, customize your controls, change graphics/audio. The keyboard binding is blank by default, the first time i logged in, i couldnt do anything at all, no up/down, no back, no exit, no controller detected, i had to alt+f4.
Then, i rebinded some keys (coudlnt tell what they do) and launch the game, after the first fight, i figured out some actions, i wanted to rebind to my liking now that i knew what was going on, but i couldnt do it with the rebinding options ingame, since some of the keys i was planning to use were not binded first in the pre launch menu, i had to close game to rebind (again)
Then, after i was playing for a while, the first sequence appeared, i binded a,s,z,x,space,ctrl,q,w,e,r, the 4 arrows, i know what each key do, i can manage without a problem, but the quick action was requesting to press the x -yy-b-a. i do not own a 360 controller, i dont know what is the action of those buttons, why they cant add a quick action with your current binding? why does it have to be a 360 controller layout despite you are playing with a keyboard? It is not hard to change, i have seen this type of notification changes in some games for windows, why this one cant?  Seriously, the controller issue is so annoying and extremely confusing if you are not used to an xboc controller. If you have played any Telltale game you basically know what to expect. Expect a great storyline with amazing characters and important choices that affect how the story plays out. The only difference here is the 'Borderlands' addition. It basically means take a fun, explosive, over the top coop action adventure game with great humor and write an amazing story for it. Finally, add the well known Telltale gameplay to it and tadaaa you got a gem of a game! Tales From The Borderlands constantly puts a smile on your face and gets you attached to the characters within minutes which results in you being constantly eager to play the next episode in this 5 part series!
In Tales from the Borderlands you control Fiona and Rhys, yes you play two characters which basically allows you to play coop with yourself. Rhys is a Hyperion company man which basically wants to be the boss. Fiona is a con-artists which means she only talks to people if it allows her or her sister to steal money from them. Those two meet on Pandora, a planet known for its terrible inhabitants and thug lifestyles and this results in an amazing adventure together!
My short review of every episode:
Episode 1: Introductions, an amazing episode which immediately got me hooked to the game big time!
Episode 2: Sets up the main storyline, the least fun episode of the 5 which basically consists of a lot of travelling but and main story introductions. It does have a great cliffhanger though!
Episode 3: The main story continues with more fun on Pandora!
Episode 4: Things get really really awesome, best episode introduction ever!
Episode 5: Vault hunting! What else did you expect to do in a Borderlands game? A plottwist and an
climax battle!
Everybody who likes Borderlands or its humor should totally play this game!

If you like Dragon Ball, this is a game you don't want to miss. It's not just a good DBZ game, it is also a good game in its own right. But yeah, it also helps that it's the first REALLY GOOD Dragon Ball game since Budokai Tenkaichi 3, Burst Limit or Raging Blast (your mileage may vary there, but whatever the case, we certainly haven't had a palatable Dragon Ball Z game since the early days of the PS3 generation). It's also the first Dragon Ball game to ever be published for PC, at least to my knowledge (and, at the very least, a first for Steam).
What if the Budokai / Burst Limit series from DIMPS (makers of Street Fighter IV) and the Budokai Tenkaichi / Raging Blast series from Spike were fused together into a game which has the combat system depth, attention to detail (in both character models and cutscenes) and graphics of the former and the freedom of movement and Tag (multi-character) battles of the latter? Look no further than Dragon Ball Xenoverse.
Also, the port is really good. At the very least, it supports configurable VSYNC and Antialiasing, resolution at least up to 1080p (can't confirm higher, my monitor doesn't go over that) and framerate at least up to a silky-smooth 60fps maxed out with midrange hardware (again, can't confirm higher framerate). Also, if the framerate drops below 60, the in-game speed doesn't slow down (a phenomenon that you can see in several crappy console ports).
