RPG Maker MV is by far the most conflicting entry in the series for me. Ultimately, it feels like a slight step down from Ace. It started out the gate with more noticable glitches than other entries. BGM used to lag for a second before playing, and in general it struggled with sound and such. As well, the game maker had swapped over compatibilities with file types for the sake of favoring HTML and IOS functionality. Essentially, the easy to use MP3's are now required to be OGG, which is a bit rarer of a file format, and means my songs for the game will need to be converted.
Now, for the good. There is a lot of improvements, especially with patches. Being able to copy entire event pages as HTML and then paste it elsewhere has been a life saver, especially for events so complicated they might better be consolidated to common events. As well, I am a fan of the new improved resolution, even though I have yet to work with it much as a spriter. I still can't help but feel that Ace was generally a better experience, and XP still handled tilesets the best. However, if you are new, and willing to put up with the weird file formatting, and other issues I may be forgetting, this may be a good place to start. Just note, the default stats are by far the weakest. Default libraries only have a sparse amount of pre-made skills and weapons and items, while prior RPG Makers at least had the first two tiers of levels of equipment to give players an idea of where stuff should go, as well, having stats tied to classes instead of actors is fiercly annoying.
Wow, that was a tangent getting in the way of my conclusion! Sorry, sorry, I like this. It is decent. Wait for it to go on sale, and nab it! Just be ready to learn!

I have a habit of buying games, getting bored with them after about 30 minutes, and never playing them again.
Not only has this game kept my attention, I find myself thinking, "Okay, I should probably take a break."
The crafting and loot system in this game is, imo, done perfectly. This game has a lot of loot. Usually I hate games like that, because I end up spending the vast majority of my time comparing stats with minute differences. As a result of that, nothing in those types of games ever feels like a significant upgrade because of the amount of loot saturation. This game has a lot of junk loot, but you end up wanting all of it, because recycling it is one of the main way to get crafting materials. While that sounds like a chore on the face of it, it's basically just two buttons (I should mention, the UI is also nearly perfect). This also means that when you get enough items to craft something, you're doing it because you want it. It's likely going to be a significant upgrade, and not just another component in a seemingly never ending chain of an item recipe.
The story line so far has also been interesting. I get bits and pieces here and there from journals that have been left behind. I like this mechanic, because I can collect them while exploring and keep them until I get back to my base where I can go through them and read them all. I'm not forced to constantly switch from a exploring/combat mindset to a mindset where I can appreciate the narrative. I really like that aspect of this game.
It also seems like you can progress through the game at your own pace. I like crafting the absolute best equipment before venturing out, and so far the game's allowed me to do that. I'm only on day 8, though. Maybe I'll die on day 9.

A refreshed and recoded version of the fascinating 1995 indie RPG hit Exile: Escape From the Pit. If you enjoy exploration, turn-based strategic combat, and classic RPGs, this is definitely a great investment for the price. It is classic in the sense that it is highly dialogue and lore-driven, allowing for a large imaginative world filled with legends, myth and discovery. Avernum, much like it's source material, still has an impressive world map and environment to explore with hidden or special encounters for the curious.  Considering you can also purchase an iPad version of Avernum (available on the App store), it would make a great mobile RPG for those long commutes / trips. Recommended if you don't mind simpler graphics and a decent amount of reading.

A remake of a remake of Exile, an indie RPG from the 1990s that was developed first for the Mac. This is actually a decent 2D story-driven exploration RPG in the vein of Ultima. The story (or at least setting) is original, which makes it stand out enough that I played it a lot longer than Avadon (another recent Spiderweb RPG) before getting distracted by other games.
My only complaint is that the author doesn't know to put a one millisecond sleep call in his main game loops, so be prepared for having one of your CPU cores pegged at 100% usage while playing (which is especially frustrating on laptops, where power usage and heat dissipation / fan noise are concerns). This is a ridiculous oversight for a 2D game that is not heavy on the system requirements.

EVE Online is one of those MMO's that will go down amongst gaming history as one of the greats. EVE just might be the deepest, most sophisticated game I'v ever played. Starting out it's a lot to take in and can be slow to get your bearings, but once you get going it becomes one of the greatest experiences in gaming. EVE is not for the lite hearted MMO players and should be avoided if you've never played one. This is a game that requires more commitment than even several other MMO's combined.
In your usual run of the mill MMO's, give it like a month or two and you've pretty much peaked. You'll find yourself doing redundant daily instances or tasks, maybe some dull PvP and that's it. EVE Online is a multi year commitment. Don't fret though, EVE can and will be casual at most times. You will spend a lot of time basking in the incredibly gorgeous, massive universe that is EVE Online. You will mine, trade, bounty hunt, explore, hack, lead, invest, manage, manufacture, salvage, pirate, scout, and much more. EVE Online also has one of the greatest, if not THE greatest player run economies. It's one the easiest games to become self sustaining, essentially becoming free.
The truth is, I'v only ever scratched the surface of this behemoth. Yet despite that, If I were to continue this review I'd be here all day typing away and I believe short, to the point reviews are best. If you fancy a gorgeous, truly massive, relaxing worlds in space that is full of possibilites, there is non other deserving of your attention than EVE Online. 91/100

Risen 3 got a lot of bad reviews and I totally disagree with them. I understand that the combat system may be difficult to some but it wasnt that bad. Dark Souls combat is much harder but people love it. Nevertheless, Risen 3 does a lot of good things and developers did learn a lot from Risen 2 mistakes. Lets go over what are strengths and weaknesses of the game.
Pros
- Great open world that you can explore at your will. There are 5 islands and you can truly start exploring any one of them.
- Great visuals. There is variety of environments from jungles, hils, farms, mines, and lava rivers.
- Magic is back. There is crystal mage magic, warrior rune magic, and natives voodoo magic.
- There are sea battles with monsters and ships.
- There are boss battles that require certain tactics.
- Glory advancement system.
- Better, more varied faces.
Cons
- Large difficulty curve. Some may be turned off how weak player is in the begining.
- DLC should have been included as they were available on release.
Overall it is a very good game. If you play Gothics or Risen games you probably already have it.

My problem with RimWorld comes from my years of playing Dwarf Fortress, I find that RimWorld focuses more on tending to your whiny colonists every whim rather than building and surviving. You spend the first half an hour building and spend the rest of the game trying to keep your incredibly whiny colonists happy, I personally hate this. In Dwarf Fortress you can expand into a massive underground empire but in RimWorld you do nothing but look after a small group of colonists who always find something to complain about. RimWorld also requires a horrible amount of micromanagement.
The combat in RimWorld just sucks, your colonists require a tedious amount of micromanagement and cannot think for themselves. I hate ranged combat because my colonists never seem to be able to hit anything (Thank God ammo isn't a thing) and they are unable to move and shoot at the same time. Melee combat is better but unless you have a boat load of medical supplies you're probably going to lose a colonist since they always take massive damage.
In Dwarf Fortress if a Dwarf comes under attack all the other Dwarfs will jump in and beat the living hell out of the attacker without me telling them to. In Rimworld your colonists won't fight anything until you set them to combat mode (Draft) and by time they reach their destination the person being attacked will be mortally wounded or dead. Colonists are also pretty useless at running away, attacking humans are always faster for some reason and if your colonist takes a hit their movement speed grinds to a halt making them take even more hits. Colonists also run away from things they don't need to run away from, for example my hunter will run half way across the planet just to get away from an angry squirrel which he could kill in a few seconds. Overall, combat is really annoying and you'll lose colonists because they're unable to think for themselves.
Another thing that is definitely worth mentioning here is that some animals in RimWorld are hilariously overpowered, I once lost an entire colony to a group of Caribou, this was because my colonists can't hit anything with their guns and the Caribou do massive damage in melee combat almost immediately incapacitating my colonists. You can't hide inside your buildings because the Caribou smash down doors or wait forever for you to leave. Losing an entire colony to a group of Reindeer did nothing but edge me closer to hating RimWorld.
Colonists in RimWorld are horrendous at the prioritization of tasks. If your base is on fire you have to individually tell your colonists to put it out and there is a good chance they will either stop for no reason or they'll decide to go to sleep because its night time. I've lost enitre colonies because my colonists decided to go star gazing instead of putting out the massive fire ravaging the colony.
Forest fires are common, annoying and almost impossible to stop. If a lighting strike event starts without rain you and your whole colony is screwed because the fires rarely ever stop on their own. The fire started by the lighting strikes will destroy everything including wild life, your colonists won't do anything about it until it comes to your land and even then as I said before your colonists need specific instructions to put it out. This becomes a long and frustrating process of watching the fire while trying to maintain your stupid colonists who are complaining because its one degree colder than they would like it to be!
RimWorld is in Alpha but having nothing to build in a game where you build things is a serious problem in the long run. When you manage to setup a basic colony with temperature control and a steady food supply you will notice that you have NOTHING LEFT TO DO. The only thing you're able to do is improve security and tend to your colonists childish complaints, if you're lucky an event or something you can actually do will come along but a majority of the time you'll just be sat there with max speed on.
RimWorld does have some extra and more complicated stuff you can research but my God researching takes way too long even with a colonist who is experinced in researching! Researching basic stuff takes days and your colonists will never prioritize it, you can't even tell them to do it, you have to take one of your colonists off every single job except researching in order to make them research. If you don't have a colonist who is experinced in research its going to take you weeks to research something as basic as carpeting.
Overall, I just find RimWorld to be irritating, boring and unfair. Dwarf Fortress is a far superior game and its 100% free. I wish the devs of RimWorld good luck.
P.S. £23.79 is waaaaaay too much money!

For me RimWorld is more than a game, it's a compelling and ever unfolding set of stories. And this, I believe, is precisely its thesis statement, its goal, its raison d'etre. I cite for example the fact that you choose at the outset of any playthrough not just the game's difficulty but it's "storyteller", similar to Left 4 Dead's AI "director" but so much more.
There are two reasons RimWorld holds a unique and enduring place in my heart, and these reasons keep me playing for far more hours than I've owned it on steam (I know, naughty me). The first is a fantastic strategy/simulation game. Early on I felt like RimWorld merely scratched the SimCity itch I'd had since a child. But then I realized I kept playing RimWorld long after I would have abandonded a SimCity game. And that's because I need the hardship, I need the diseases to sweep arbitrarily through and tax my supportive care capacity. I need the blights to ruin crops and force me to find alternate food sources. I need raiders to try to pillage all I've built so I have to make the hard choices about whether to feed a prisoner, or bloody my hands with an execution.
So, the first extraordinary merit of RimWorld is thus: part city builder, part sim, part RTS, part tactics shooter, part really grim Harvest Moon, etc. And it aces them all.
The second extraordinary merit of RimWorld is the story creation. Aside from a sparse setting which admittedly borrows heavily from Firefly (no complaints here) every bit of story in RimWorld is procedural or internal to your own mind. The quirky traits, frenetic firefights, life or death struggles, finding of love between colonists, it all adds up to you following the little, pixelated lives of your characters. And as you do, you can fall in love too. At thirty years old I've grown accustomed to the fact that my parents and girlfriend don't give a hoot about the game I might be playing at the moment, but they'll occasionally give a wholehearted listen when I'm real fired up about it. RimWorld is different though. The stories come out so interesting, so varied, so lifelike, that they all love to listen. My mother will literally ask me over the phone about my RimWorld colony because she wants to hear cool stories about the zany things that may have happened in the game since last we spoke. To me that speaks of a procedural genius I will always appreciate.
Don't let the early access tag fool you, this game is beyond amazing. In over a decade of using steam it has prompted me to write my first legitimate review. I swear, I buy it again if I had someone to whom I could gift it, because it's a bargain at twice the price.

A MUST PLAY FOR BORDERLANDS FANS EVERYWHERE
This was my first experience with Telltale Games. I wasn't sure if I'd be into the whole "interactive movie" experience. I heard The Walking Dead one was good, but I'm a HUGE Borderlands fan, so I just had to give this one a try.
It was simply an amazing experience... it's like a Borderlands movie (more like a miniseries technically) that fans like myself have always wanted. Only in ways, it's even better than that! You get to decide how the story plays out, and in big ways. And as you make each decision, the storyline tailors itself seamlessly. At no point did any plot development seem awkward; at no point was it obvious that the game was just branching out in a given direction simply because I picked Option B. Even just quirky little things I said or did would be referenced later in the story, and in a relevant way! An epic story formed before me, getting more complex with each choice I made and it just blew my mind. And I challenge anyone to play it and not develop an emotional attachment to AT LEAST one character.
There were so many connections to the previous Borderlands games it will make any Borderlands fanboy giddy. Tons of cameos from beloved characters, as well as quite a few small connections and references that only more devoted fans will catch. And of course, the brilliant and hilarious writing that the Borderlands series is known for remains as strong as ever. I got countless laughs out of it, and even a number of moments had me dying with laughter. Long story short, Borderlands fans will feel right at home with this game.
Yes, the game is chock full of simple "click here" moments and quick-time-events, and nobody likes those. But I knew that going in... Telltale Games has to keep the player engaged in SOME way, otherwise you really would just be watching a movie. Those moments aren't where the game's strength lies - it's in the decisions you make, which form the customized story that will make you laugh, might just make you cry, and will make any Borderlands fan JOY PUKE THEIR FACE OFF!

I don't have any hours on it currently because I play it offsteam, I only want to leave a review here.
I probably have somewhere around 60-100 hours at the time I'm writing this. Also note that I didn't spend a single cent on it and do not plan on doing so in the future.
Also, if my Engrish is bad, I'm sorry.
Yes, it's kind of PayToWin.
And here's a few things for you to know:
1. Most legendary parts (LPs) will cost you somewhere around 40$ irl cash. But if you plan on playing this game like an MMO, you could probably afford one after a few weeks completelly free of charge. It should also be said, that you could then sell it and try another one, game market is completelly unrestricted and you could buy and sell anything for ingame cash.
2. Game features a "Power Score" which balances the team forces in PVP, and most LPs have a high ones, meaning if you meet somebody with 1-3 LPs, they probably will have low HP and/or have other weaknesses.
3.There are decent "Blue builds" (rare parts only) which could easily compete in PVP. PayToWin aspects mostly touch upon endgame (clan fights, high power scores PVP). So midgame its mostly up to your craft and skill.
4. Grind doesn't feel too tedious, atleast if you don't focus on it solely. There is a lot of fun to be had midgame. There are also ways to speed it up. You could play the market (crafting and selling the hottest items for example), do season missions (especially hard ones), try to make the most of your resources, etc.
As I am writing this, there is still A LOT of balance issues, and also the ingame market flips often with new updates, so I would definitelly not recommend donating heavily. But I still recommend playing, it's a fun game.

Best military simulation game I have seen so far, at least in terms of game mechanics. SQUAD is about as realistic as it can get in terms of simulating modern battlefield within an online multiplayer game without sacrificing good gameplay. Sure the game is in Early Access, it still has bugs (I hear, I have yet to see any game breaking ones) and some would say it lacks content, but those problems are worked on, and even as it is I have seen fully released games being less complete.
In this game, taking the role of a lone wolf CoD Rambo only makes your team lose horribly. It's the squad leaders and their squadmates working together who make the team win: teamwork is essential. This game really shines on having a group of friends - a squad - to play with, and even then you can very easily make friends as it is a very social game. And military grade communication is something even the worst introvert can learn, like calling out enemy positions, which is very important.
This game can even be helpful in real life, training leadership and general teamworking skills is a very big plus for a game that is also entertaining.

Not very often I review a game, however seeing the lesser reviews, thought I would stick up for this Gem of a game.
Am a strategy lover overall, however this action star keeps me coming back for more.
It reminds me when playing Gauntlet when I was a kid at the arcade with the scaryness of Deadspace (love only seeing by my flashlight and gun flashes), and a whole host of upgrades to available your kit and beyond.
Nothing like opening the door to a host of enemy, however ready with plasma grenades and plenty of space to run, or should i employ the plasma launcher? - I enjoy the moments of your power pack running out mid firefight and flashlight running out of juice, leaving you in the dark and the times of franticly searching for a toilet as my guy needs to go!
Crafting is good, with upgrades for medical; bandages, stims, medpacks, oxygen, heat cannisters, bladed or blunt weapons (power swords later), shotgun, machinegun and pistol bodies, with upgradeable stocks and barrels, not to mention facility upgrades of oxygen, heat and then there's the system power and the reactor generators, did i mention you can upgrade the reactors with your machine guns to help with invasions....
On medium the game can seem a bit grindy, simply because this is too easy to get ahead quickly, for those moaners out there try hardcore, the game changes dramatically with only level 2 access to the machines available on the main floors and there is a never ending list of things to research and build whilst fighting the quickly growing infection. Would recommend first few hours on medium to understand dynamics, then game on hardcore to understand how this game should be played.
One of my alltime quickplay classics and recommended to all Strategy/Deadspace/Action and Craft lovers out there.

This is a game about speed, stealth, and lighting.  The lighting seems to change at random times.
You play on either the light team or the dark team.  If you stand still while in your element (a light team member in the light, a dark team member in the shadow) you disappear from sight, and can hold a button to stay hidden and move slowly.  But if you dash (your typical movement speed), your outline becomes a bit easier to see.  I've found it's easier to distinguish a moving dark team member in shadow than it was to detect a moving light team member in light, which unbalances it a bit, but it's not too bad, and I'm sure its something the devs can easily fix.
When you're attacking, it's pretty much one hit kills, though there are glancing blows.  Also, when not stealthed, you're moving fast.  This really leads to two types of tactics.  Slow, methodical, waiting ninja strikes where you remember where you are while stealthed and wait for an opponent to either pass over you, or get close enough to dash and slice them up.  It's that, or you dash around, just trying to be faster than everyone else.  I've found either tactic works well, and obviously you can change up while you play, depending on the situation.
So with the dynamics at play, it makes the game feel like you're either a ninja, hiding in wait, or a samurai trying to out iajutsu everyone else.  Tons of fun, tons of flavor for a simple 4 person multiplayer game (no story, no single player except with bots).
Just the fact that this is a PC game with local multiplayer makes me like this game, everything else about it makes me love it.

I have played a lot of Pirahna Bytes games, including every Gothic game and Risen 2.  This game is an excellent addition to their catalogue.
First, you'll love this game if you're like me and enjoy the following things:
1.  A large amount of side quests, some of which have multiple possible solutions.
2.  A fairly large world to explore, and many secrets hidden by camera perspective, geography, and whether or not you can turn into a parrot right now.
3.  Being rewarded well for such exploring.
4.  The ability to chose a faction that affects the gameplay.
5.  A challenging fighting system (at least until you max out toughness and nothing can hurt you any more).
Although I very much enjoyed my playthrough, here are some things that could be improved.
1.  The moral choices seem to have only small impacts on the game.
2.  The factions aren't developed enough, you max out your rank in no time with just a little concentrated effort.
3.  There aren't as many puzzles as I remember in Risen 2.  Exploring ruins as a pirate necessitates more puzzles and traps.
4.  The majority of the quests are the same regardless of whether or not you joined a faction.
Lastly, a piece of advice from an avid off the main path player, join a faction right away.  You get special abilities for doing so that if you wait until you've done everything else, you won't have long to enjoy.  Also, it can save you some back and forth from traveling.

At the point of writing this, I have just finished the main story (including the hidden one) but don't have the DLC content. I have 3 characters, one main that's level 60+ and 2 low level alts.
With that in mind, here we go:
First off, this is a great game and I love it. I have been dying for there to be a proper PC Dragon Ball ever since I watched the shows. I waited anxiously, waited (like many) on the Half-Life mod "Earth Special Forces" that lost its significance with this release and I don't think anyone will care now if it does come out and was stuck playing a 2003 version of that mod. Lemmingball Z was fun too, but none of these were what I truly craved.
Enter Xenoverse. I can make my own character, of 5 different races no less. That's a huge plus and its got its own unique story that puts some nice spins on the downtrodden plot that's been done so many times before.
The combat system is alright, I haven't played too many fighting games so I can't really comment on that. All I know is that it takes some time to get used to and the game makes you learn things "on the fly" as it were.
The game is hard, but not unfair. If a quest kicks your rear, you can always do some parallel quests to level up.
There's a ton of skills and attacks in the game, enveloping almost every single attack seen on Dragon Ball.
But there is a one major flaw: the character roster. Sure, the plot is that your own character has its own adventure, however, in parallel quests you can play as them and have them as team mates. Of course, any missing character won't show up in the story either.
So who is missing? Well there's some pretty big omissions such as Frieza's 2nd and 3rd form, Cell's 1st and 2nd form as well as numerous versions of Super Buu missing. But there are also entire characters amiss, these are the ones I certainly miss:
- Zarbon
- Dodoria
- Broly (regular, SSJ and Bio form anyway)
- Androids 16, 19 and 20
- Babidi and all of his crew, including Dabura
- EVERY SINGLE MOVIE VILLAIN AND THEIR HENCHMEN BUT BROLY AS LSSJ (this is a serious flaw to me, as their clothing IS in the game)
- Chiaotzu
- Turtle Hermit
- King Kai
These are characters that I miss, even though they aren't as important:
- numerous Saiyans (Bardock's crew, illusion Saiyans, etc...)
- Tarble
- Cui
- Abo, Kado and (because of that) Aka
- Kami
- Garlic Jr.
- Chilled
- Demon King Piccolo
So, as you can see, there's some big gaping holes there. I know this game focuses on your own character, which is great and all. But ultimately, for a game where you are supposed to grind levels, there's gonna be little variation of quests at some point. You will fight the same enemies over and over eventually.
In conclusion, it is a great game, but the character roster leaves much to be desired. The DLC adds a few GT characters, which is interesting if that's what you like and you can wish for a few hidden ones from Shenron. But even so, this roster is tiny.
I still recommend the game though, because of the solid character creation and fun combat. Oh and I have never had any server issues, so I guess I got lucky on that one.
TL;DR: The game is lots of fun with solid gameplay, but the character roster is lacking.

I was bored waiting and saw this in my library during free week early access promotion. This review is based on the first single player mission until I nuked the thing out.
I can easily say this game is not doing good: in fact, it is quite retаrded. Right from the start the mission is called "Assault" on some corporate facility. During the first moments you are informed by your tactical advisor that you are supposed to "infiltrate" it (alone). You are given two guns (mid-range and long-range) with nothing else and set up against many robots guarding huge area.
Now "infiltration" into facility implies usage of special equipment or exploiting a known breach in the facility to enter it secretly. What sort of infiltration tactics you can employ when you are alone, got no map of the area and no special equipment for your aid (not even binoculars)? This is not "infiltration"; it is simply an "assault": you storm the facility from its weakest point (which on the first map is an area with crates to the left, discovered by trial and error), gain the access from there and continue fighting inside. It is kind of stupid, but killing robots and opening the door doesn't trigger any alarm or alert at all: guess the security technology in the world of Interstellar Marines is just as weak as AI of your robot enemies.
Speaking of robots, their AI is very poor. Your opponents get stuck in doors, walkways, sometimes even large areas and are incapable of any intelligence. On one occassion I alerted a group of bots by killing their nearby patroling unit, they charged at me right under my spraying gun, one by one, without taking any cover. Probably because of this some areas your are supposed to "infiltrate" are completely broken, such as security building you need to access in order to open large inner door. The only option is to take stairs and shoot everything that moves hoping you won't get shot first. There's no way to snipe them out as windows in this building are not actually windows, but some sort of force-fields blocking all your bullets.
Anyway, there's no ability to save your progress, not even checkpoints. So after getting all the cards and taking stairs down to underground I got one-shot in a corridor by some bot to the left. Prepare to repeat the whole thing again, from the very start.
The multiplayer is your standard FPS with one team guarding an object and another storming it from various ways using same two weapons. There are no special tactics involved and nothing interstellar either. The mode is just as generic as it can get.
Perhaps only co-op can offer something interesting since you get to explore huge areas as a team from different sides and not alone, but I didn't have a chance to try it out.
Boring and generic: you just take cover and shoot things. Nothing "stealth" and nothing "interstellar".

Let me say first that I am not a huge fan of Borderlands. I have played and completed
the first game and it was okay. The second one was much better but I did not have anyone
who I could play it with really so I never got terribly far. The humor and the aestetic of
the game is one thing that always appealed itself to me. That being said I waited a long
while for this Tales of from Tell tale to go on a 75% off sale on steam. Finally it came
so I picked it up expecting nothing, here is my experience.
I thoroughly enjoyed myself. Tales from Borderlands season 1 stood out as a joy filled
romp through Pandora and other classic Borderlands areas. The games writing and humor are
actually incredible and very enjoyable. I found myself laughing out loud and face palming
over and over again. I binged on the first 3 episodes that took me over 7 hours and enjoyed
just about every minute of it. The game has a rare personality which lets say for example
Walking Dead season 2 sorely lacked. Telltale has out done themselves with the two main
characters in TFB, and their motives and actions are engaging and fun. This series is a
breath of fresh air in TellTales repertoire which takes itself too seriously in many cases.
In terms of narrative the episodes are paced well, and have a good amount of ups and
downs and great laughs. I respect them for sticking true to Borderlands zaney world. How-
ever, what I hated was when they tried to "make me feel" bad or sad for two characters that
to be honest I couldn't give a wet♥♥♥♥♥♥about. I hate it when you can TELL that they are
inserting "audience sighs here" "que tears" I despise that, its not genuine its a forced
set of events you can see coming miles away and it detracts incredibly from the overall
story and enjoyment. However there were some characters that made me feel a lot more than
I expected and THAT is how you do it. When you insert a character you'd never think twice
about and bring us close to said character(s). That is good writing and character
development and that balanced out the "Feel bad on purpose" moments that Telltale pushed
twice in this season.
So if you are a fan of what telltale does, buy it, if you are a fan of Borderlands
lore, story and world pick this up. I doubt either bases will be let down. One thing to
be warned the ending a massive sequel bait and honestly terrible. I am pretty sure Telltale

A WW2-themed tactical FPS that's host to a strange mix of both arcade and oddly realistic elements, Day of Defeat has always been one of the more interesting oddities in Valve's catalog. Balancing these more arcade mechanics - frantic movement speeds, excellent accuracy while not using sights, and near-perfect accuracy while LDS - with more realistic mechanics like scope sway, players dropping their weapons when they get shot in the arm, and suppressing fire that effects players' aim was undoubtedly an incredible task for the DoD team - and somehow, they pulled it off.
Pretty much every title in the DoD series is well worth a purchase for anyone interested in seeing game design mastery in action. I'd recommend the original to anyone looking to see the game's mechanics distilled to their utter basics, and Source to anyone looking to see how they improved what made the original so special. Note: the first game had factions, weapons, and maps that aren't present in its Source version at all. It's because of this that I'd honestly recommend purchasing both games, if you can.

This game is so much fun but the devs and their marketing/cash model will kill it.
Its MAD MAX Meets TWISTED METAL with very fast games, most games rarely last past the 5 minute mark so you can jump in and out if you have limited time.
UNFORTUNATLY..........
Everything in this game screams GREED. The grind is horrible, the cost to manufacture parts and and to buy them on the market is insane.
The matchmaking is a joke and the worst I have ever seen. Rarely will you have a good even, right to the wire match. Most matches one team is stacked. You are either on the stacked team or losing.
I will not say this is a P2W games as any player can be beat if they make a mistake and are ganged up on, but it is for sure a P2P. Players will stack their rig with high end weapons, and mods purchased with 100's of credits to give them a quick kill edge. Then instead of separating these players with the higher tier weapons it puts them on the same team against true F2P Players.
The player base is almost non existent, more bots than players.
The daily reward boxes are a joke you always get a white (lowest) item (hint: do not re-roll it, waste of scrap). The 14 hour box rewards are worse there is still white item in them as well and a high % to get them.
PUNISHMENT...........
This game is great for punishing you if you do good. You can rack up 4-5 badges, get 2-3 kills and be the MVP on your team but if your team loses you get nothing for experience. They punish you for your teams performance when you have no ability to control what they do (Even worst when your team is 4-5 derp bots). The experience earning should be based largly on your performance and bonus if you win. That way players who do very well will still move up the ladder even if they get put on the losing non-stacked team.
WORST.........

Why cant i make this?

A very powerful tool for creating your very own RPG adventure.
Anything your heart desires, from battling your childhood villain to teaming up with the boy/girl of your dreams, is completely possible and mostly quite easy to accomplish.
And should you get stuck and don't find how to make that item behave the way you want, do not worry! How-to tutorials and ready-to-use plugins for almost everything are widely available for newcomers and those who don't master Java programming themselves.
As good as the software is, though, one of the few things I'm disappointed at is that there aren't many options for designing non-human animal characters, which I'd love to do. There's also no in-app tutorial for new users, so if you're new to RPG Maker, do yourself a favor and look up a few tutorials before you use it for the first time.
The maker also cannot create finished .apk files for use on an Android smartphone, despite having an option for exporting your game to Android and Iphone, and requires you to do some advanced setups with your computer and other software installations to accomplish this goal.
All in all, a great software that can and will make your gaming dreams come true. Only your imagination sets the limits.

I highly recommend RPG Maker MV, because if you want to get into game making, an artistt or a really good story teller, this is a good place to start, while learning other aspects of game making.  The good thing is that you can be a child to an adult to use this and you can learn things about yourself if you really open yourself up to the experience.  Yes, there is a learning when you use this or any engine, but as I stated it is a good place to start.  If you are just starting out, I highly suggest you look around for a forum that is friendly and helpful to new people.  RPG Maker web is a really good place, actually.
PROS:  The music and graphics are much better, and you can get lots of edits.
Plugins are really easy to set up
Music formats are a bit weird, but understandable at the moment. (I am on a MAC and for some reason you need both the OGG file and M4A to use the M4As, but I am not a programmer, so I don't know why that is.)
The layering effect on RPG Maker MV is really amazing much better than RPG Maker XP and RPG Maker VX Ace
CONS:  The only people who can use the product for commercial use is the person who purchased the system
The way around this is to 'create' a studio and if you use a shared computer, they make their game, but you release it under your studio name.   They do not make that clear when you purchase the system and if someone buys it for you.... I wish they had made that clear from the beginning.
In conclusion, I suggest that if you have children who are into games, so buy RPG Maker and really get them into making games.  It is a system that grows with you, yes, even if it is a 2D engine, but it is a great 2D engine.  (=^_^=)/

Look... if you're reading the reviews for this game then you are clearly interested.  Just buy it.  Seriously.  Whatever it is that brought you to this game... a love of top down shooters, an interest in science fiction, a fan of survival horror, decent graphics, zombies, light sabres, aliens, total recall, John Carpenter's Ghosts of Mars, a desire to have the living ♥♥♥♥ scared out of you LIKE EVERY 10 GODAMN SECONDS, whatever it is that brought you here... THIS GAME NAILS IT.
First top down shooter I ever played.  I literally learned how to contort my hand and use the whole WASD movement thing because of this game.   Game has controller support but I like mouse aiming in this because HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥THERE IS A THING RIGHT NEXT TO YOU AND YOU'RE GOING TO DIE HORRIBLY.  Honsetly, never really played any horror games, or top downs, or anything with crafting...  Then I played this and was literally in awe.
This game is the movie Ghosts of Mars should have been.  I've been gaming for almost 34 years now... I honsetly can't remember a game that kept the pressure on like this one.  Even in the original Gaiden... you could stop on a ledge or something.  This game?  Every single second you waste your enemies get stronger, more numerous and somehow become even better at JUMPING OUT OF THE GODAMN SHADOWS.  I mostly laugh at horror movies.  I just find it funny.  Sort of the reverse of how people think clowns are scary.  Ya not this game.  No laughing... well actually some, but then immediately followed by creeping Lovecraftian terror.
The soundtrack is perfect.  Sci-Fi goodness just dripping with tension.
The graphics are still the best I've seen in a top down.
The story?  It certainly doesn't rip anything off and isn't just a reskin of Total Recall or Ghosts of Mars.  It falls nicely in between those two and TBH it's the only thing I felt could have been handled a little better.  The story itself is fine, i just don't think it really gets told.  There's a killer narrative behind WTF happened on Mars... but you'll be too busy trying to get just another hours sleep before you have to head out into nightmare land, to care much about narrative.
The gameplay is solid.  Like really solid.  Procedurally generated levels mean you have to go EXPLORING in the dark.  You can't read a tutorial because it's different everytime.  Dev did a great job of making static goals within in a shifting labyrinth that feels like a subterranean colony, not a game level.  Gameplay is also challenging.  Not in a 'do some weird bullishit thing for an achievement' kind of challenging, you have to plan and you constantly have to think ahead and come up with a never ending series of patches to keep your world from imploding.  Not rocket science... but you can't just mash buttons and hope to live.
This game is the first game I ever felt strongly enough about to leave a review for.  It's really good.  Instant Classic good.  Probably in my top 10 games of all time actually.  It just nails a hell of a lot of things.  I love sci-fi lit, movies, anything really.  In fact... I'm a muhfukin connoisseur.  Fritz Lang up in this ♥♥♥♥♥.  If you are too...
HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥THEN BUY THIS GAME.  Like I said... whatever it is you're into, whatever it is that brought you to this game's page... Subterrain has it in SPADES.  Can't recommend it strongly enough.

This game is one of my favourite MMOs now. I used to play Wow, but have been quit for over a year, I do not play anymore as the game is falling apart IMO.
Eve offers something different, the game, is ALL controlled by players. You are literally free to do whatever you want. The incredible size of the map allows you to explore for hours on end, and i mean hours! (AKA days). Each part of space has a different security rating which gives you a somewhat 'safe zone' roam, providing you stay in a high security sector. Although, it's never really safe, anyone can come at any time and kill you..
Unlike other games where you have to grind for levels, Eve offers a different approach, skill points(SP). SP works in real time, and it can sometimes take months to level up a few skills, or it could be a matter of 10 minutes. SP will level regardless of if you're logged on or off the game, that's the beauty of Eve. You're always leveling, as long as you have set a skill to train.(Training a skill gives SP)
Pvp, this is where the game becomes reallllyyy hardcore. I joined, i did the basic missions, but i wanted more. So i joined a low sec pvp corp. Ohmygodholycrap.jpg. My first flight with my corp was immense, around 30 of us went flying through space battling huge waves of people whilst fighting to control a sector of space. Our FC(fleet commander) was in Team Speak SHOUTING his head off whilst we were all fighting. The combat can be either fast paced or slow, depending on the size of your ship, and how many are in your fleet. Once you kill a player, you loot their ship and then you fly the hell out of there before their friends/corp come to kill you. Other aspects of PvP will include hunting people down, ratting them out, travelling through worm holes and dropping huge ships on them. If you love and thrive off of PvP like me, you will LOVE this game. The game offers some of the best PvP i have ever had.
Also, playing on a world wide server is very good too, you make friends all over the world, although time zones may be a pain, sometimes, especially for places like AU and UK.
All in all, this is a great game and i recommend trying it. It's usually on the steam christmas sale for 3 pound something, which includes 1 months sub. Speaking of sub, after a while, if you earn enough ISK(currency) then you can purchase a plex, which gives you 30 days play time. Some players provide their accounts with plexes and don't have to pay sub' at all! Fantastic, i know!

There is enough praise for how solid and fluid the game is, yes it's well made and polished, but why do none of the thumb up reviews address just how insanely grindy this game is!? It has gotten to the point where it is so absurdly repetitive that I am not sure I can force myself to get through the whole game anymore. x.x I want to say great things about how well made the game is but in about 10 hours of gameplay you will be sick of playing this and beg for content I promise you that. And here are the major reasons why.
Let me give you a breif rundown of the content you can expect in this game so I don't sound like I am rambling to much. There are 3 guns in the game, a close range but risky shotgun, a high fire rate but inaccurate smg and a slow but powerful pistol, that's it, each tier they just look cool and have better numbers. There are 4 zombie enemies in the game and 2 bug type enemies and a wiggly thing, all of them you can combat perfectly by running backwards and holding down the shoot button, that is litterly the only tactic you need in the game, each tier they just get tougher and look different. As for the base? It always looks the same, you always need to micro it the same, nothing ever changes, you just tediously micro the power, repairing the core, research and build new stuff, once you have done it once or twice that is it, the micromanagement in the game will only become monotonous from that point on. There are 4 tiers of doing all this same stuff over and over, grinding like crazy like your in some kind of MMORPG before you are 'allowed' to beat the game, you tell me if that's not repetitive and heck or not.
It's truly disheartening when the game will always be the same way no matter how many hours you burn into it and no matter how good and experience you get with it's mechanics, the same tiny amount of content is all it has to offer you when you truly just wish for more. After the first 10 hours you will have experienced all the fun the game can offer you and after that it's only 10-20 more hours of the exact same thing over and over again... same guns, same equipment, same freaking dumb zombie enemies, it truly becomes a chore. This could have easily been fixed if it wasn’t so darn long and monotonous. =/
After 20 hours of gameplay I barely even moved past the -first- tier, I don't even know how that's possible but the first three starting locations just took so freaking long due to having to go back and forth on the train for oxygen, thermal or to drop off loot due to having crappy starting equipment. The only way to do this less is to get to the next tier, which would be simple... if I knew where the data chips to do that even where! The first two chips I found which took going through and entire location each where for the farm and mine which are useless without teir 2 engineering and research and by the time I even found those I was sick of the game already and furious that I found those last. This happened because the game doesn’t tell you where the chips you want/need actually are, only hinting to where chips might be in story journals so I was mostly a lost sheep hitting my head against the wall for hours and actually getting almost nowhere. The tier system in this game is laboriously slow and very poorly planned, I would have preferred if they rail roaded me along a linear path so I was getting the upgrades I needed first to actually make progress, instead they bomb you with a pile of places you can go to, no hint to where are better places to go, you go to them, waste tons of time going through them just to end up with no idea where to go next after doing them anyway and not having the chips you need to tier. Anyone can admit this is a awful system and makes no sense, if I didn't get annoyed enough to look up a guide to a location I -should- have been at I probably would have never got to tier 2 and been overrun with 'space zombies' even faster then I did after 20 hours of wasted time and having to give up as every location was overrun by that point and it was taking to long to make anymore progress.
This might just sound like I was a clueless moron but I was just going into the game hoping to have a good time, why should you have to read guides so you don't completely fail your first run and have an awful time? Playing video games is my only pass time so if this happened to me then it can happen to anyone playing for their first time and that is a very flawed game.
There is nothing meaningful about playing this game so why should it waste so much of your time on the same monotonous game loop? I have no clue but the developer seemed to think it was a great idea making you have to go over the same shallow combat, enemies, equipment and base micromanagement for 4 long, slow tiers. I am so fed up with the game is just want to finish it so I can uninstall it at this point and that is truly a shame cas I did enjoy this game for the first 5 hours but that 'fun' ran out way quicker then I hoped and now doing anything in this game just feels like a means to an end to a very very grindy repetitive experience. I bet you anything if you made someone play this for a week straight they would go completely insane
Sure I got my 10 dollars out of this game but by no means should you ever buy this at full price, as I have already clearly mentioned there is not enough content to even justify for how long the game goes for before you can even finish it in the first place, even WoW is less repetitive then this game. I wouldn’t recommend this to anyone with a job, a gf or a life that's for sure, there is no way you will have enough time to get through it properly unless you follow a guide to a tee. Unless you have like 20 to 40+ hours to burn on 5 hours of game content then I would just play something else honestly that at least feels like it has meaningful content grind.
Thanks for reading if you did, I am going to follow a guide of someone that has more patience then most sane people and move on in my life. x.x

I really didn't want to give this game a thumbs down - and in all honesty, I did get a lot of game time for my ~$8 investment. Looking back, I just didn't get much enjoyment from it.
I *loved* the first act. There's so much that it just nails. The combat is slick, the exploration is on par with System Shock, and  there's new game mechanics being introduced that all seem to fit together really nicely.
But then as soon as you start looking for software upgrades, it becomes an epic grind. Combat is constant, and everything else is just a means to that end. Exploration becomes a chore because enemies come streaming out of every door you open, and 99% of the loot you find ends up being fed through your recyclers for materials.
Research and manufacturing are just part of the difficulty curve, and all you really get out of it are the same items with bigger numbers - weapons that do more damage, but handle the same way, more backpack space, bigger energy and oxygen stores, better armour. None of it really enhances the gameplay or breaks up the monotony of the samey combat.
Also, it's gated pretty hard. You think you're going to get ahead by getting the next research software, but then you can't really manufacture much of what you research until you've got the next manufacturing software - and then you can't really do much with that until you've got the mining and farming software to get you the next tier of resources.
But the biggest killer is the item durability and repairs. I reached a point where clearing a single floor (there's 10 at each location from memory) would burn through the durability of 3-4 weapons, and then you have to trudge back to the central core, repair your gear back up to 50/55/60/65% of it's full durability. Which takes (in game) hours of train travelling back and forth, hours to wait for the repairs, and the whole time, the infection counters are going up which means more combat to wade through.
And ultimately, it's a real shame. The game is very well polished, well written, looks great, runs well, tries to introduce some interesting mechanics, but ultimately it gets dragged down by the repetition of fight, repair, repeat, and combat mechanics that don't evolve beyond 4 basic weapons (with one late game exception). Here's hoping that Subterrain 2 addresses some of these issues.

You start off on a boat sailing to who knows where, from who knows where (possibly this information is known if you've played Risen 2, which I haven't, but I still had no idea what was going on in the beginning of the game), and seemingly out of no-where, you're attacked by pirate sea creatures STRAIGHT out of Pirates of the Caribbean. I don't have the slightest doubt in my mind that the artists had pictures from PotC up on google as they designed these guys.
B. During this intro, the game briefly shows you how to move and look around, jump, attack, unsheath your weapon, shoot your gun, dodge, etc. The controls just feel off to me. If this makes sense, which I hope it does to some of you out there; there are just some games out there with controls so fine-tuned that you could do an obsticle course, jump from object to object, avoid things swinging at you, etc, with ease (think TF2, CS:GO, CoD, Skyrim). In this game there is no way in hell I would be able to jump from object to object or dodge ANYTHING, the controls feel that lousy and unsynced. A side note added onto that... when I hold down the sprint key... I want to sprint NOW, not after a delay of 1 second.
From what I understood, you're a pirate on a jouney with your sister who, by coincidence, has huge jugs, The intro lets you play through getting attacked by a ship of sea creature pirates captained by a "Ghost pirate"... who, after losing all of his men onboard to your sword, summons Gyarados which ♥♥♥♥s your♥♥♥♥♥♥up and you're stranded on an Island straight out of the TV series "Lost". It then seems your objective is to find or chase down the pirate ghost... at least for the beginning part of the game. I didn't get that far.
Imagine the worst home made movie you've ever seen, then imagine paying those people each $1,000 to actually try to act. That's about what the voice acting is like.
A. The looting system is very off from traditional RPGs. Yes, I get games can be different from others, etc, and that's cool, that's awesome, but not having a menu pop up when you go to loot a creature and instead having it auto loot everything and spam the side of your screen
can get annoying. Strangely enough, however, if you go to loot a container, you ARE given a menu and the choice to loot whatever's in the container.
B. Despite claiming to be open world, the game is still very linear. To put into perspective, Skyrim is the obvious king of open world games, you can literally go ANYWHERE. The Witcher 2, on the other hand, is pretty linear, and isn't necessarily open world. This game isn't remotely close to The Witcher 2, and is about as linear as a CoD campaign.
C. Other RPG elements such as how the inventory is managed, quests, maps, etc... it all works, but it all feels cheap and rushed.
In conclusion, the Risen fanboys will hate me and my review, but crossing over from other RPG's like the Elder Scrolls series, the Diablo series, the Borderlands series, etc, I was not prepared for the incredibly, insultingly, low quality of the game.
TL;DR: If you're coming from Skyrim, Borderlands, Diablo, Mass Effect, The Witcher... (all high quality and finely tuned RPGs), and looking for something new whilst staying in the RPG scene, stay away from Risen 3.

If we were to focus on the porting of the game rather than the game itself then we'd get nowhere, as there's not a lot to say and not much of it good. So instead, I will focus mainly on the game itself from my experience with the Console editions, and later tie that in with the PC port.
So, as anyone who has played a game in the STORM series knows, it is the go-to series for a true-to-the-anime experience. Everything is there; the beautiful graphics, the original voice actors, the story, everything. Even the tiny details you wouldn't normally catch (Such as Tobi's subtle and goofy taunts), are present. It's really what the anime would look like if it were real.
STORM 3 was a massive step up from its predecessor, Generations, in that it took the new mechanics and elements brought to the table and refined them further, and over a year after release there are still new mechanical tactics being discovered or used in entirely new ways. There are more ways to fight in STORM 3 than there were before; many viable combinations of characters and playstyles. Although it seems at times that some are more useful or practical than others, typically it lies down to individual cunning to overcome what is ahead of them.
The story is faithful to the anime (Up until a certain point, however the anime hadn't got to this point yet so it's understandable), and really makes you feel as if you were in the Naruto universe. My main gripe is the endless chains of cutscenes, with no option to skip them all, as there is a loading sequence between each one. I love the cutscenes as they are stunning, especially with Full Burst's revamped graphics, but they lose their impact if you're replaying the story mode. It would be nice to be able to skip them all without loading up each one.
Aside from the main story, there are side missions aplenty, allowing you to learn a little more about the other characters in the universe that still tie in to the main story. Very good for anyone who enjoys the other characters and want to see more of them.
The soundtrack to the game is reminiscent of the anime and equally as awesome. No complaints what-so-ever about the audio, as it's been spot on in all of the STORM games and I'm a huge fan of each OST. (My personal favorites were STORM 2's "White hot battle at the summit" and "The Uchiha Hideout" stage music.)
Another reason people are drawn to the series is for the multiplayer. Sadly, with exception to the new roster and mechanics, STORM 3 did not bring much new to the table that was exclusive to the multiplayer, however they did take what was already there and make it just that bit better. For example, whilst there are now
of possible ninja info card and title choice to choose from, none of this is visible to other players unless it's a 1v1 fight. It subtracts a lot of the motivation to unlock these cards and then spend time personalizing it when there are only two modes in which people can even see it, and even then it's only for a few seconds before both players prepare to begin character selection.
As for the non-1v1 modes, Tournaments or Endless, Both modes had a new feature added, but neither of them were really that interesting.
Nobody plays elimination Endless (A mode where you keep playing until you lose, at which point you are kicked from the lobby) because people join endlesses to play mutliple matches with a group of people over a period of time, and being ejected from the lobby for losing, or having your opponents ejected when you win, is just like playing 1v1 modes except with a waiting list.
As for Perpetual tournaments (Tournaments where each match has two stipulations that affect both players), they can still be interesting, however the feature just wasn't taken advantage of. There could have been countless possibilities for different rules and options. They could've made it so one player is affected by one rule whilst the second player is only affected by the second one. They could have also added in many more rules, too, however you'll usually have seen it all after your 3rd or 4th tournament.
The Ranked mode has also gotten considerably worse; CyberConnect2 sacrificed a lot to try and keep the game balanced, and ultimately it went to waste as there are still the small stable roster of characters and supports you'll see in the majority of your matches (Looking at you, Kimimaro and Neji.) however unlike the past games, balancing patches have been brought out to try and quell this, however most players still stick to the familiar "meta" teams.
Disconnections (Or Ragequits) were an issue CC2 attempted to address, however there still seems to be literally no penalty for people disconnect often, as there are players with
of disconnects and people still play against them. Some people actually take pride in their disconnection frequencies now that they have no limit.
Essentially, CC2 is concerned about punishing legitimate players who accidentally disconnect, however that's exactly what's happened now; I'm still getting disconnects just like someone who ragequits. If they would just give disconnecters a loss and, or heck, even JUST give the other player a win, then nobody would be bothered by disconnections at ALL.
But not all multiplayer must be online - The offline multiplayer is fantastic. All of the tournament features are available for offline use, and with addition of Full Burst; there are plenty of challenging missions which actually net you some nicely-made wallpapers. Each battle has unique stipulations, which further begs the question of why they didn't include them in the tournament mode.
Another unforseen but very welcome addition only possible due to the PC port is the inclusion of mods. Sadly is there no official support for mods - yet (wink wink) - however the community has still managed to bring some incredible content to the table, such as unlocking characters that were once unplayable and actually caused CC2 to recieve a bit of backlash for not including. There are new costumes, new stages, new characters, new movesets, you name it.
Sadly that's where the good news stops when it comes to the PC port. On launch, the game was plagued with a terrible bug that rendered the online mode nearly unplayable. It took a rather long time to fix, but it was eventually fixed. There were also many crashes during the story mode, however one still remains as of writing this. It appears that CC2 is eager to co-operate with its community though so I expect that these issues shan't persist forever.
Another problem were the very high system requirements. Although understandable for such a stunning and complex engine, it was rather disappointing to many people that the game simply couldn't run, especially due to the very little amount of graphical settings available to the user.
With that being said, here is my conclusion;
+ Brilliant graphics.
+ Perfect OST
+ Faithful to the anime
+ Very easy to pick up and play
+ Huge and active fanbase
+ Mountains of content of all kinds
+ Community-driven developers
- PC port was rather disappointing
- Too much focus on a "balanced" online mode which didn't end up being balanced, often at the sacrifice of other, much more enjoyable features
- No official support for mods despite a thriving modding community
- poorly optimised
Overall, I love this game, and this series. I have put thousands of combined hours into the entire series on PC and consoles.There are definitely glaring issues or places where they could've really put some work in and made something incredible, however everything else that is expected of the STORM series is met in spades. I cannot wait for the next STORM game and can only pray that CC2 keep up their level of community interactivity and keep on improving on constructive feedback.

Naruto Ultimate Ninja Storm 3, in my humble opinion, is a really fun game with a few flaws keeping it from greatness. As an avid fan of the series both manga and anime, I decided to pick this game up after doing some research on it, and have been very pleased.
Disclaimer: This is my first ever Gamefaqs review; you have been warned
Graphics: 9/10
I think that the game is just beautiful! The character models are all rendered and match their anime counterparts nicely. While the graphics don't look exactly like the anime, I think thats a good thing. because it looks like a video game instead.
As you fight through the story, you will face a wide variety of characters, fight huge bosses, and you will get to visit a multitude of iconic locations from the series. Not one time in my playthrough did I say "well that doesn't look very good." The color, scenery, and vividness of the game really do an excellent job of capturing the Naruto Universe that we all know and love. Even the opening menus have a great amount of detail put into them.
Another big part of this game is the large, large, LARGE amount of cutscenes and action sequences, and I believe that they all look fantastic! There are massive explosions, high paced action, and gripping story moments that are all captured very well within the games engine.
However, there is at least one major fault, and its mainly because the game can get a little big for its britches sometimes. I don't think I experienced this at all throughout the story, but when playing in tournaments or online, if multiple jutsus and teammates start getting called, the game does have framerate issues. This is the sole reason this portion doesn't get a 10 from me.
Story: 8/10
Now, if we are just talking Naruto as the manga, I would personally give this a 10; but we're not, we are talking about Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 the game, and it does have some setbacks.
The game follows the story immediatley after Naruto's confrontation with Pain, and continues up almost to where the manga is currently. The main form of story progression is through cutscenes, which there are a ton of! Not that that is bad though. One cutscene in particular lasts at least 30 minutes, but it does a wonderful job of getting you immmersed in the story and if you are invested in the series (like me) you may even find yoursef shedding a tear or two! How many times can you say a video game has done that to you before?
My biggest qualm with the story has to do with the so called "Ultimate Decisions" you make throughout the game, as they really don't do anything to effect the way that the plot unfolds. I think that in theory it was a good idea, but basically all it does is ramp up the difficulty (slightly) on certain missions. UNS3 is not a difficult game to begin with, and I would have rather seen two different endings than come to the same road at the end for some additional replay value.
The story also expects you to already know what is going on, so if you are on the fence about getting this and don't know your Naruto lore study it up or you will not have a clue about what's going on.
Sound: 8/10
Not much to say here. I thought that the music fit the mood for the game very nicely. Sad moments had soft piano keys playing in the background, and intense moments revved it up the way you would expect a Naruto game to. Everything in between was pleasant to listen to, it's just... it wasn't the original soundtrack. As much attention to detail as was put into everything else, I really wish they had gone ahead and gotten it, because you just can't replace it. I guess there were some copyright issues preventing its use.
Gameplay: 8/10
A cast of over 80 characters unite for some seriously over the top action that you can take on in the story mode, locally with friends, or online against the rest of the world! This game is so much fun to play! So why does it get an eight instead of 10, I will explain.
One downside is the very limited free roam that is offered. I almost thought why even include it, but it does open up from otherwise linear paths after you have completed the story. Basically sometimes you will watch a cutscene, then get sent to free roam. After running a short ways you will then enter another cutscene or battle. There is really not much to it other than that. You can talk to NPC's and there are a few sidequest offered, but they really didn't seem worth it to me unless you are going for all of the trophies. It is mainly just a means to an end to get you to the next battle. And that is where the meat of the game is anyway, the battles.
The game has both single and team battles. Single being just you as your character of choice (or who is currently the story character), while team battle allows you to pick one or two support characters to help you. The combat is fast paced, but never too difficult to follow, with exceptions being online sometimes.
You primarily attack with the circle button, or B button if you are on Xbox, and have three varying combos you can perform by just pressing circle and using the analog stick. Triangle is your chakra load button, X is jump, and square is the shuriken button. You have basic, and chakra loaded moves that you can execute by pressing the chakra button followed by a different command. This is how you execute your jutsu and ultimate jutsu attacks. You can also block by holding R2, though it can be broken, and you can use a substitution jutsu by pressing L2 while being attacked.
There are a variety of cancels that you can perform when executing attacks that will allow you to create your own, flashier combos, and add some depth to the gameplay. The most common of these is the Chakra Dash Cancel (CDC). Basically, while comboing or doing another action, you can press triangle and then X immediatly after to cancel whatever you were currently doing. These cancels are what really add the tactical aspects to battles, as well as providing ways to score big damage if you know what your doing.
All that being said, you will have a blast playing through the story mode, but you may experience frustration if you try to take the game online.
For me, it has mainly been connection issues. Lag is very, very abusable in this game. I cannot tell you how many times I have eaten a jutsu because the game read one extra circle press. Basically, when you are fighting someone online you need to conserve your chakra and your substitution jutsus more than anything. Play well, make the other guy run out of substitutes, and then punish them with big damage, thats how its supposed to go. However, get into a room with a little bit of input lag, and your read on when your opponent is going to substitue turns into a Rasengan Barrage because instead of being able to block or chakra cancel, the game said you hit attack again. It is playable though, and playing in rooms with little lag is a lot of fun. Winning against a good opponent is a very rewarding experience, not to mention you get to do all with your favorite Naruto characters! Both ranked and player matches are offered, as well as a tournament mode that I haven't gotten to try yet, but has a variety of different rules.
I would also have liked for this game to have been made with a more competitive aspect to it rather than almost strictly fanservice and casual. There is a skill aspect to it, some players are simply going to be better than you should you pick up the game, but there are some mechanics, like awakenings, that I do not like.
Awakenings are very powerful "super modes" that characters can enter. Don't get me wrong, they look AWESOME and make you feel like a boss when you use them, but they need to go IMO. You could be playing the match of your life, and have your opponent down to half a bar left, but if they manage to get their awakening off they could easily turn the tide back in their favor, and I do not like mechanics that reward players for getting beaten. Great game, great concept!
Interstellar sports only half a dozen levels but as an early access game it is understandable. At this point there are two single player missions (up to 4 players can complete them), a couple of levels for a team of 4 players (designated as coop missions) and some more stages for those eager to play with even more players (multiplayer missions).
When not playing against each other you play against robots. With the submachine gun they handle they look like T-800s straight out of the Terminator franchise. Some prefer melee to shooting - on greater difficulties it is easier to die but your friends can revive you.
Level design is excellent and the environment changes constantly: changes in the weather affect visibility; suddenly it is nighttime and only your flashlight helps you but then it also reveals your position. At night light poles can aid you or if it is raining the sudden lightning can help you to eliminate your foes.
Interestingly, you only have two rifles available. One is intended to help you with targets in greater distance; both can be equipped with a suppressor and laser sight. At this point they serve their purpose but perhaps a melee weapon could be nice.
As for graphics: the good old Unity engine delivers. Lighting effects are great - with the quick steps of the approaching robots you are in for a treat due to the excellent atmosphere. In fact, the single player mission revolving around an accident can certainly give you the creeps!
Interstellar proves we have to look out for independent video game developers! I am happy to recommend this game - especially now (February 11th, 2015) when it is free to play till next week.

Where to even start? This game is the biggest racket I have ever seen. First off lets address the beta status. It has multiple DLC packs in a cash shop already. These aren't cosmetic packs but money for the ingame economy and items which can be sold on the market. Thats the established cornerstone of a pay to win game.
What is interesting to note however is the patches are obviously geared to manipulate the economy. the  8.0 patch introduce vehicle parts that could hover over the ground. Now the hover acts like a wheel but was the ONLY wheel/track item which didn't reduce cabin power so could be stacked without slowing the vehicle down while gaining more tonnage. So the top gamer meta was to not have 6 or 8 of these like you would wheels but staggeringly 20 if you could afford them as they also took half damage so acted like armor. Meaning only hover vehicles stood a serious chance of taking on other hovers discounting lucky shots into their critical systems.
The more recent patches crashed this economy making more then 6 hovers dramatically reduce the cabins torque and thus slowing them down. Putting them in line with other vehicles. Now thats good but the length of time spent in each patch and the curious lack of hotfixes for issues for weeks at a time when its obvious there is a issue. Make it seem less like a constantly balanced beta and more like a captive market or insider trading setup where the meta shifts to drive market prices as formerly terrible items are the new must haves to not just compete but to even survive a match.
Currently there is an item which projects a shield for ten seconds and the hot build is to rush or stealth up and spam point blank grenades and then use the shield when and if the enemy attacks back. Watching the market surges on the game is intense as people flocked to buy in game coins to buy hovers as when they were patched and you can only use 6 or 8 effectively caused them to halve in price.
The grind is pretty atrocious but the game at its core feels fun. There is also a very lazy attitude towards griefing and other in game harassment. Unless its done in the games general chat where it gets a quick temp mute. The progression of the game is horrificly stark as the game changes pace drammatically as your vehicle hits a higher powerscore. Where you used machine guns and cannons at first the late game has a preprodence of auto aim weapons like heat seeking missiles or drones that go out and attack, these are still extremely powerful but have recently been knocked down a peg. Keep in mind when you have slapped on a couple blue weapons and finally kick over to 5000 power score, which you can do in a few days of solid play. You will be going up against 9000-11000 top end builds with obscene weapons. Though your blue little machine gun can shoot off their $150 dollar a pop weapons if you have a steady hand.
I can't in good concious reccomend the game at this time as it seems like an out of control cash grab riding the coat tails of the early access market and obsfucates the wonky patches making unrelated tweaks to items as testing rather then possibly market manipulation.
Wait 6 months and see if its still going in Q2 2018 and where its at then. Especially if you are itching to drop cash to bypass the grind and melt faces.

Early Access review
Short and sweet:
Pros:
-Large, open maps that are densely populated with buildings, trees, etc.
-High player count
-Chaotic combat
-Simple, straight forward controls
Cons:
-Sound, and what I mean by this is not necessary the quality of gunshots and things of that nature. Obviously the developer wants to simulate realism and gunshots will take precedence over area voice and comms, because let's face it, gunshots are very loud. The biggest issue I was the fact that it is almost impossible to directionally tell whats going on where or judge distances. If a vehicle is 100 yards away from you, the volume of that vehicle "feels" like you are standing right next to it. This is problem is compounded when you are in dense city/town/forrested areas where sound does not naturally travel as far.
-Clunky movement
Over all, in my opinion, this game has great potential. If you came here looking for something large scale, teamwork driven and nothing like Call of Duty or Battlefield then you've ended up in the right place. Learn to work with teammates for the best experience (headset/mic should be mandatory to play) and in the beginning expect to die, alot. If you're a lone wolf type person, you should probably look elsewhere.

Great top down shooter/survival/crafting game. You start with a tutorial that walks you through the plot and game mecanics, and from there you establish a small base of operations where storage, crafting, sleeping,  etc. take place.
The game is broken into several hubs. Each are procedurally generated Diablo-like labyrinths that are individually powered by your own base. Each has an infection rate that increases over time,  which determines the strength and number of mobs, and how quickly infection spreads to other sites. The infection decreases as you kill enemies and the rate can be slowed by minor on site repairs or by clearing out nearby hubs.
Like Diablo, you start with single shot weapons;  a powerful but slow pistol, a wildly inaccurate submachine gun and a shotgun that is powerful and aoe at close range. As the infection increases you face larger groups of enemies but gain more easy access to aoe weapons like grenades and charge guns, all of which are craftable.
You find chips in each hub that allow for upgrades to your base in order to produce higher quality equipment and produce your own raw materials.
I have put nearly 80 hours into the game and have not met with any bugs. It is a very fun way to waste your time.
