It's a good piece of software, an excellent tool for those with far too much time on their hands to make some cool stuff. It also makes for some good programming practice, at leaIst conceptually. It's pretty intuitive, and the tutorials available are pretty decent as well. There's a lot of cool stuff that makes this software a really cool tool.
That being said, I also want to point out one or two things I wish I had realized before I
used my free trial up. When I got this, I was planning on making a moderate game out of it, and I really enjoyed setting things up.
However, a few things that I came to realize over my trial period.
First, do not underestimate how much work is needed to make a full game. It requires a tremendous amount of time and effort, and I can't imagine someone who has literally anything planned out in their life having the time or the determination to complete a decently long game in this tool, start to finish. There's a reason companies are the ones who typically make games, and that's because there is sooooo much work to do. To go over the big ones, Level Design, Storywriting, Character Design, combat mechanics, quest scripting, event programming, artwork, music, debugging, and dialogue scripting. Even if you knew exactly what you wanted and did everything almost perfectly, for every hour of playtime of your finished product, you can probably expect at least 10 hours of work on
of these. It's extremely difficult to make a game without help, and alone, I honestly can't imagine how dedicated someone has to be to do this by theirselves.
Second, making a game can be fun, but there are boring parts as well. It's really rewarding to make something as cool as a game. Video games, when you think about it, are incredible things. It's so incredible that you can make something as complex as, for example, FFVII, and then have it have so much success, and influence so many people. That being said, I wished that someone had told me that I could tell the same story, but all I would have to do is write it down, and maybe learn how to draw manga. Video games are awesome, but there's a lot of awesome stuff out there to do as well. I find now that I can tell the story I have in my head much better through a different medium. I'm learning to draw manga and writing the script/story on Google Docs in the meantime. It's much less work, still rewarding, and I'm still able to tell the story I want to tell.
Lastly, I want to mention that part of me just wanted to have the RPG adventure that all RPG video games never were able to truly give me. I wanted the SAO experience, where I'm actually controlling everything about the game. I wanted a game that let me do anything, with only simple rules dictating a nearly infinite combination of possibilities, and the closest that I had ever gotten to that is probably something like modded Skyrim or Fallout 4. I wish that someone had made me more excited about Dungeons and Dragons earlier. There is no video game, at least now, that can even come close to D&D style tabletop games in the freedom you have to play. It's only using the human brain's imagination that you can have a truly epic immersion in a game, until we can figure out how to combine our technology and our imagination (literally, like SAO style). D&D might be the most fun you can possibly have in life, and I wish someone had told me earlier. It's the RPG I had been looking for forever, where the only limits to what you can do is what the DM says, and what you can think of. It's truly the best RPG experience that I think anyone can have, and I wish more people knew that.
Overall, I don't want to diminish how cool of a tool this game is. It's really a fantastic, if slightly limited and underpowered, software that is great for making (or practicing making) games. It's awesome. But, you might have turned to this in a desire for something that you can fulfill elsewhere. If what you want to do is just tell a story or have the best RPG experience that you know you can come up with, there might be better mediums for you to pursue that. $80 isn't cheap, and it's money that you could put towards buying art supplies or D&D equipment if what you want is can be given by one of those things. Make a smart decision after figuring out what it really is you want out of this.
It's awesome, and if your only other choice is to burn the 80$, definitely buy this software. Just know what it is you want from it.

This is a first impression of the program since I've used an older version. I'll update after I've used it a bit more.
So there are really two sides to this. I remember using XP when it first came out (I was using GameMaker and MultiMedia Fusion back then as well) and I have to say, its cool that its still going strong and providing accessible game development to people. If you are learning game development, get this, its a stepping stone and there are quite a few along the way.
Now, I've obviously grown since then in age and obviously ability but I've always been curious to see how this program has changed so I grabbed it when it was on sale. For the most part, I'm happy with the purchase since I'll probably get my dollar an hour out of it. But here are some thoughts anyway.
I feel like its a little misleading to say it exports for android. Now I could be wrong but the 5 minutes I looked at it, it seems that "Android" export is just HTML. Which is fine, but the store page explicitly says APK and I don't see a way to link the Android SDK so, I'm going to bet it can't pack APKs. Again, thats fine, you can wrap the html and build a real APK using the SDK and it won't be any different, you just have to do that your self.
Lastly, its been a long while (A LOOOONG while) since I used XP, but I don't see a difference really. I'll update more when I can.
Would I recommend it? Well that depends.
If you are just starting out with game development, yes, you should look at getting this if you are even a little interested in an RPG. Some others to look at would be ClickTeam Fusion, Construct 2 and Stencyl. GameMaker used to be good but who knows what happened to their business model (But thats a rant for another day).

. They even have it in thier FAQ. Just keep it in mind. So this engine is more for you to have fun and enjoy yourself and maybe show it off to friends and family.

Good:
- Return of three factions increases replayability.
- Diverse and effective spells/skills, many of which are unique to each faction.
- Characters and dialogue still have the old PB charm.
- Islands are large and interesting to explore.
- Expanded combat mechanics.
- You can turn into a parrot.
- You can talk to a parrot.
- Your parrot has his own questline.
- You can still deploy monkeys.
- Treasure hunting is still fun.
- DLC is way more substantial and compelling than Risen 2's.
Bad:
- Enemies only attack one at a time, making groups of enemies far less threatening than they used to be.
- Morality system encourages metagaming rather than making choices you genuinely believe in.
- Patty looks like a stripper.
- Chani is more white.
- You play as a new protagonist with a silly voice.
- Combat still has the old PB jank.
- Skill checks rarely offer alternative quest solutions.
- Naval boss battles are annoying.
- Lots of recycled content from Risen 2.
- Lockpicking minigames are still tedious (though this is true of minigames in general).
Conclusion: If you enjoyed the previous Risen games, you will very likely enjoy Risen 3. If you didn't enjoy them, Risen 3 won't change your mind.

Risen 3 offers great entertainment value. It was designed to be fun and enjoyable to play for a more casual gamer, or a gamer that enjoys some pleasant and relaxed gameplay once in a while.
What sets this game apart from other action-rpgs is the beautiful handcrafted world that is a joy to explore, no other developer can compete with Piranha Bytes in this respect.
The game offers a light-hearted story that is well told, and a lot of side quests.
You eventually get a good ship and start building your crew of companions, each with their own stories, personalities and side quests.
The assortment of skills and spells is very nice and varies somewhat depending on what faction you chose to join.
The character progression is fairly fast compared to previous games.
The one thing that is most important about the combat is to NOT tap the attack button repeatedly. Tap once, wait for the move to reach its peak then tap again, with a bit of practice you will get the timing which is very forgiving. You can also tap by listening to the sound. The dodge move has 100% invincibility window, making it very efficient when you want to get away from a tough spot.
If you are looking for pleasant gameplay and good entertainment this is the best game you can get.

I purchased, installed and attempted to play Risen 3 - Titan Lords today.
Playing a game is as far as I'm concerned a way to enjoy yourself. Just finished four hours playing Risen 3, and it was not fun. The graphics are nice, and the audio is fine. My source of irritation was with the 'combat' system. My apologies for the single quotes, but that was what it felt like.
First my gaming background. I've played (and enjoyed) Morrowind, Oblivion, Skyrim, Kingdoms of Amalur, Fallout:New Vegas, Dishonored, Fable: The Lost Chapters, The Witcher. All on PC.  Each with a slightly varying combat system, showing that I can adjust to different systems.
Please remember that I'm giving my experience with the game; these are not criticisms, just reasons why someone who thinks and plays like myself may want to give this game a pass.
My expectation in playing any game where combat is involved is that the combat is straightforward. That is, the laws of physics apply (I press 'Hit', my character attempts to swing), not the laws of combos (you can only swing at the right time as decided by the game).  And this is my reason for writing this review: Risen 3's combat system is not straightforward as far as I can tell.
Here are the things I observed:
- in a number of instances (during combat) when I click the left mouse button to attack, my character just stands there.
- during combat, my character decides to sheath his sword (I believe I can say with confidence that I did not click the middle mouse button by mistake when this occurred).
- more that 50% of the time, a standard attack from any creature resulted in my character taking damage, even while parrying/blocking.
- my character would strike a creature, then perform a 180 degree pivot and strike the person behind me. I only clicked the left mouse button once. Force of habit with games like Kingdom of Amalur meant my left hand was firmly pressing the 'W' key to keep moving forward ... didn't work apparently.
- the creatures at level 1 are incredibly fast. I like a challenge, but the lapse in response time by my character just meant many cycles of: Kill a creature, save, get killed. restore, kill another creature, save, get killed ... you get the idea.
- in most of the games I mentioned above, there was always 'wiggle' room; you could choose which encounters you wanted, when you were prepared for them. In Risen 3, encounters are about every 50 feet, no getting around them. This would seem that the developers were more focused on combat than anything else. In the one quest where I was escorting Balbor, there were a minimum of 15 different creatures all within a 150 foot radius. (the distace is a guess, it's just to show it felt close) And when attempting to follow him away from the water source, you had no choice (not even sneaking worked, even though it is an available skill) but to engage the animals. I partially blame Balbor, as he went out of his way to 'pull' them towards me.
Altogether not enjoyable. I've read a few comments by some folks in the community here, and some have expressed the thought that this would be solved by 'training harder'. I believe that can be interpreted to mean 'learn how the combat system works and you'll be fine'. My response would be 'but I have'. I know how to attack by pressing the left mouse button. I know how to parry/block by pressing the right mouse button. However, the actions I see on the screen are not consistent with what I want my character to do.
Let me explain myself a bit, using Skyrim as an example (it's still one of my favorite games). If I meet an NPC whose skill level with his chosen weapon is higher than my skill level with my chosen weapon, it's quite likely I'll lose the battle. But I'll lose it because the NPC is better skilled than I am. I can still swing a sword at him, it just won't do as much damage due to my lower skill level. I can still fight and block, until he gets the better of me and overwhelms me. I don't mind losing to a superior foe, as long as I put up a good fight.
But when ALL of the creatures are superior foes, and my character is effectively incapacitated during combat, it's no longer a challenge, it's a chore. And perhaps some might think me lazy, but the 'click the attack button, wait two seconds then click it again, wait three seconds and then press the Ctrl key as you click the attack button again  to perform the Super/Ultra combo' formula doesn't mean that you've mastered the game as I see it. It means it's mastered you.

Except for the combat, unfortunately a crucial part of the game, it was. It would have been a great game to play otherwise.

I will not give the ''not recommend stamp'' just because you shouldn't buy it on Steam, i tottaly recomend everyone to try it first. Then you should buy it on EVE-Online webpage.
With that said, i'm writing this review after playing this game for 8 years now.
Preparations:
This game isn't for everyone. You need to have some kind of way to deal with loss because you will loose. You will loose money, pacience, time and most of all hair!... lots of it.
Lets say after 2 months you are still playing it. you dealt with all the frustration the game brings to you everyday. You still have a steep learning curve, after that time you haven't yet scratch the surface, you are starting to read all the big battle news, and look to your ship, and its crap!
You will need time, to learn and to train the skills, because to train the skills needed to fly and use modules, it takes time, lots of it. I don't know currently, but when i started playing to have a character fully trained you had to wait about 30 years. That doens't mean you can't have fun after 3 or 4 months.
This game isn't a simulation. Everyone thinks it is, its not. Flying ships is point and click.
Depending of the first career path will dictate what kind of wallet you'll have in the first year, allways full, allways empty, there is not a middle ground.
Keep in mind that this game is in the making for 11 years now, you have alot of mechanics and systems that were implemented along ago.
The market is the most powerfull mechanic of this game, just because to you have any ship ingame, someone had to mine all the materials, and built it. The supply/demand of the items ingame are very balanced, CCP ensures that their market systems are the most stable possible. It is one of the most rewarding ways to play this game, just by ''marketing''.
Combat: Refined, PVE is dull and boring like in every mmo, it have been improving in later years, but the true sugar is in the PVP part of the game. Because you can destroy someone's hard earned money's ship. It is very satisfying to see the tears after someone lost a big, pricey ship to and epic spaceship popcorn explosion. :D
Devs, updates, new mechanics: I'm yet to see a full year passing by without a major game expansion or update. This game is growing still. You have new stuff coming in almost every 6 months.
That said, there are too many things that should be looked at. But in general the game is very stable and improving.
The 1 universe: So this game only have one server that matter (it has more, but its test and other purpuse servers). Meanwhile you have diferent people playing from diferent timezones, then you have 5000+ mapped starsystems, put 50k concurrent players, and you can have the most massive, biggest epic battles on just one place. Just because one leader woke up on the wrong side of the bed. Is that simple.
Community: One of the oldest average community i've been into gaming. Full of diplomacy, backstabbing, spying, helpfull people, crazy people.... and i think the best community of any  mmo around.
Try it.... Lets say you like it, there are so many diferent ways to play this game, that you can even play it and not pilot a single ship..... ever. You can even be the next big spy that took down the most powerfull aliance ingame! hehe

So, there I was flying my ship through space looking for a system with a decent amount of anomalies.  As an explorer I live for these sites. A few clusters of abandoned ruins ripe for the picking for those with the knowledge of how to find them.
Avoiding the High-Security systems I head to lo-sec.  The loot always tends to be more rewarding there, even with the risk of being blown apart by a fellow pilot.  I hit the system.  Afterburner on, probes launched, cloak engaged, directional scanner on full range.  The D-scan is like my little eye in the sky while I hunt down anomalies.  Anyone comes close without a cloak and I see them coming.  While I scan I see a few ships come and go. Thankfully they can't see me with my cloak engaged. Most of these guys are armed to the teeth, and I don’t even have a weapon. A weapon on my ship would be like a water pistol against these ships.  The best weapon I have is my cloak.   If I can’t be seen I can’t be shot.
Nothing good in system, just some combat sites and a lone wormhole. Combat sites would be suicide in my ship I so decide to take the WH, after all you never know what you might find. A wormhole can lead literally anywhere in the game, you might come out a few systems away or on the other side of the galaxy.  You may not even be in the galaxy anymore.
I pop out the other side and find myself in uncharted space, one of the most dangerous (and profitable) areas in the game.  I check D-scan and see one of the ships that passed me earlier, and another, and another, and another.  I run the ships against my data base to get an idea of what they’re there for.   I find an explorer (like yours truly), a weapon specialist, an electronic warfare specialist, and a cargo ship.  Four ships in what looks like a team, all after the same thing I am.
I start scanning down the sites, hoping that I might still be able to salvage something from this.  I find two data sites.  Either one could have enough loot inside to earn me a week’s worth of cash in a single haul.  I set the D-scan to filter everything but one of the sites, and the ships disappear from the scan list.  I know that the site is safe, but for how long.
The thing about WH sites like this one is that as soon as you jump in a timer starts ticking.  When it hits zero a large number of NPCs will jump in and ruin your day.  If you want to get anything from these sites you have to be fast.
I start on the first one I get to and it goes surprisingly easy.  All the practice in lo-sec is finally paying off.  I skirt around the various firewalls, bypassing any subroutines until I find the system core.  Five seconds later the cargo hatch pops open with a satisfying click.  Unsatisfyingly, the cargo bay only held about a million in loot, nice but only a fraction of what it could’ve been.  I risk it and go for the second cargo container, knowing that the NPCs or the other team could pop in at any moment.  I'm running D-scan constantly, but it will only give me about five seconds to prepare if someone comes my way.  I try to focus, looking at what points are most vulnerable in the system, trying not to set off any subsystems.  I slip up.  I surround myself in firewalls, no way out.  I abort the hack right before the NPC's spawn in.
With nowhere to go I cloak up and slowly work my way out of their range.  There isn't anywhere for me to jump to that I know is safe.  The only other place for me to go is a small gas site I found while scanning.  I set course, hit warp speed, and immediately remember that these sites also had high level NPCs.
My cloak is still on cool down, I have nowhere else to warp to, and I just landed in the middle of three high level NPCs.  My ship isn't built for combat, but they are.  I 'm stuck just watching while my ship is blown apart around me.  I eject in my capsule right as my (once) favorite ship is destroyed.  As my capsule is buffeted by the blast a notice pops in my inbox.  The insurance bureau is sorry to hear about my loss and have paid my claim in full.
As I write this I'm floating in my own debris field, too stupid to plan a proper escape route and too stubborn to self-destruct.  If that doesn't sum up Eve I don't know what will.

I do apologize for my lack of game time. I played Mabinogi directly from Nexon before it was released on Steam. Though it seems I have almost no time on the game, I guarentee I've spent at least 150+ hours on the game.
Now that that's out of the way...
This is quite possibly one of the best, if not the best, MMORPGs that I've ever played.
This game is far, FAR ahead of its time withs its massive variety of skills ranging from picking herbs to controlling puppets in combat, its INCREDIBLE organization of stats and abilities, its MASSIVE amount of customization and fashion (Hence the nickname "Fashionogi") and wonderful, active community.
Unlike other MMORPGs, where you choose a class and typically sit on it, making it stronger, creating your own skill sets, etc. Mabinogi has the unique feature in which you can be ANY CLASS. You can do anything...eventually. The game starts out fast so a new player can master one of the classes (For instance, mastering the Warrior class) and then it slows down quite a bit to increase the challenge of the game, demanding a bit more attention and dedication from the player.
Want to be a warrior? Sure.
Want to be a mage? Sure.
Want to be a ninja? Sure.
Want to be a magical ninja warrior? Sure. It'll just take more time.
However, power isn't everything. Tactics and pure skill can determine life or death as much as skills and raw power do in this game. Unlike most MMORPGs, where dungeons are scaled in a way that only players of a certain level or above can survive, Mabinogi changes the whole scene.
Going to try and clear a very difficult dungeon at a lower level? A lower level player can do it, provided he or she has the skill and appropriate knowledge of the game mechanics. But is it going to be easy? Not in the least.
Even skills that aren't combat related aren't useless in this game. As they level up, they provide increases for various stat points. No skill is totally useless, its all useful in some way whether the player uses the skill or not.
The music is simply wonderful, and the ever updating content and events are always there to keep things interesting.
My ONLY complaints in this game (And believe me, they were hard to find) is the occasional bug that comes with all MMOs and the fact that the combat system is a tad slower than I'd like it to be.
Nexon is EXTREMELY lazy when it comes to updating the combat engine, though they are making tiny updates (emphasis on "tiny") that are working on changing this.
But these flaws are insignificant and downright redundant in comparison to this game's virtues.

An absolute gem in survival horror. This game has an interesting story and a very well balanced survival system. Instead of feeling like you're constantly keeping your character fed, happy or otherwise in peak condition, you're focused right where the action is, and when you do need to pee, poo, feed or drink it will give you a gentle reminder in the form of your character muttering about how hungry he is (or whatever else his need currently is)
The game is small in size and the top down can sometimes be confusing or irritating, especially for people like me, who has a love-hate relationship towards top-down games. Regardless, this game has a depth that will keep you occupied for hours, and if you like a good story along with an ultimate goal to work towards, as opposed to just surviving for as long as possible this is definitely a recommendation I can gladly hand to you.
If they ever implemented a multiplayer system for this game, I would give this game a 10/10 rating, but as it stands right now, I'm giving it a solid 9/10
The pros:
- Very balanced need system
- Great fluent mechanics that feel intuitive (at least most of the time)
- A deep crafting system
- An interesting story
The cons:
- No multiplayer options
- Targeting (Both on enemies and containers) can be a little dodgy sometimes
- No character creation (I'm sorry, but when I play games like these, I like to immerse myself and feel like I'm the one surviving in this hell-hole. Dr. West is only reminiscent of a convict trying to survive the madness and I honestly don't really get that attached to him)

Opened up a bathroom to find 30 mutants all congregating, plotting my demise. 5/7 crapped my space suit.

So you wake up and everyone is dead or a zombie in the space station.  Sounds like you've woken up in a game that is going the have heavy crafting and survival elements.  Manage your food, water and sleep while the zombies start hitting the gym and are getting beefier by the hour.  On top of that you will also find yourself having to deal with a lack of oxygen, freezing temperatures, and a lack of power running through most locations.  Kick back and manage your high tech handy dandy crafting stations and research stations that are gonna be tedious to manage (Hit tier 2 tech as soon as possible to limit frustration).  The goal of the game is to escape this fever dream of a management nightmare using a rocket to propel us to greener pastures.
Honestly this game is a bit of a mixed bag of enjoyment with the degree of how tedious it is to manage.  Once your reach Central Control I have to say, this is where micromanagement hell begins.  Tedious busywork is what it feels like, running back and forth from the nearby facilities to access and use them.  Kill me please.  Where it does management right is the time aspect of the game.  While you rest eat sleep and go about crafting yourself better gear, researching techs.  Just remember the zombies are hitting the gym and they're inviting all their cool and hip friends too.  Essentially the longer the time you spend in the game just existing, is time the zombies are putting to growing in number and strength.  So manage your time wisely or things just might spiral out of control.
There is the usual gather up resources, materials you require to craft all your weapons armor etc.  You can also recycle items to acquire more resources as well and I highly recommend doing so in Nilson Engineering.  Where you invest your resources can end up being a bit of a quandary.  You might need to build and research better reactor modules to not have  a generator meltdown,  or maybe a better weapon to not die in the first place. Not to mention researching tech requires you to give up your newly produced long knife(as an example) to research a better one.  As well as the fact that research and production require a certain amount of the valuable resource called time. So you have to keep in mind how and when to allocate your resources to production and research.
The combat really isn't that great and can get repetitive quickly even with the introduction of new enemy types and stronger versions.  I think its mostly the restrictions that are imposed on you that force you to manage multiple factors that keep the game engaging.  You need a oxygen, thermal, and power pack to even venture into locations without functioning life support.  This pretty much keeps you on your toes and managing your finite life support. Hopefully you don't run out before you can refill or evacuate back to central control for a refill.
I really do enjoy the game despite my problems with the tedium of central control.  I find myself highly entertained playing a game where i really have to manage my time and work within the restrictions it imposes on you.  Its a constant struggle against the game trying to kick your♥♥♥♥♥♥in.  Definitely worth picking up if you don't mind the beginning's horrendous micromanagement and enjoy the idea of a game where you have to balance your crafting resources, time and the available tech you have.
Oh and this game really has no elements of horror.

I went into this expecting it to not quite be a "game", but I was still pretty disappointed.
It claims its a title about exploration, but the entire game consists of a single, small island.
As you walk near objects on the island, music plays, each object having its own distinct sound--but these sounds are somewhat poorly implemented, so rather than a seemless musical experience, it feels more like someone is trying to make organic music and not doing a very good job.
When you do certain things, i.e. stand in a certain place long enough, look at something for long enough, etc--You are shifted to different versions of the island. Each of these versions is, unfortunately, identical in structure each time, but varies in execution. For example, one version might be snowy and all of the trees "dead", one version might be fall with plants in red and orange hues, one version might be bizzare and oddly colored with strange leaves on the trees--but the layout of the island is always the same, the paths, the mountains, the rocks, essentially the same place every time but with the models for the objects on the island set to random.

For a game that is named Gunpoint, there is surprinsingly little shooting coming from you.
The main gist of the game is you are a freelance spy who does what he's supposed to do, mainly corporate espionage and the occasional people takedown.  It doesn't sound all that interesting on paper, but the main selling point of the game comes from the various ways you can tackle the level.  You can go in, kick down every single door, make a big fuss, knock out or downright kill the guards, then waltz right out to the subway before a sniper shows up to kill you.  (if you chose to dispatch the guards without using your fist or door, the sniper will show up)  Or do the traditional sneaking around, jump up on the roof, hide in the shadow, rewire the electronics in the building to your favor and etc.  The game won't really reprimand or strong arm you for going either way unlike other stealth games.  You will still get paid either way at the end of the day.  You can go for certain titles or fulfill certain achivements, but they won't unlock any fancy new gadgets or game mods.  One thing I like about the achivements in Gunpoint is that you don't have to do ridiculously complicated tasks to complete them, some are just for pure fun as well.  Maybe I just have a thing for any door related achivements.
I doubt that many would play this for the story, but it's there.  There is very little narrative going on.  You find out about events from hacking into computer and from texts sent by your employers to your phone.  You can choose to be a dickweed spy, or a fairly standup guy; in the end it doesn't really matter.  The final objective will always be the same, though you can choose to let certain events happen slightly differently.  The game will not judge you for the choices you make.
The game scales at a very reasonable rate.  The controls are very simple but to the point.  The jumping mechanics will take some getting used at the start, but they will start you out nice and easy to get you accustomed to whatever gadgets you are required to use to get through the level.  Some of the more interesting devices available in the shop also allow for a test run.  A very nice gesture that I have not seen in games recently.  If you are strapped for cash, you can also return your purchases for the ORIGINAL price.  Wow! That's some store return policy!
Enemy AIs are fairly simple.  They mainly patrol at set corridors or stand around looking stupid unless you walk into their sight, or make too much noise during your breakin attempt.  Most are fairly easy to dispatch, but frontal assaults are generally frowned upon because everyone in this game is a dead shot except for you.  (aiming time? what's that)  In the very likely scenario that your spy has perished, you can rewind time to just before you made the idiotic choice of walking into a room full of guards.  The auto save feature is very quiet and inconspicous in this game.  You can also choose to save at any time and come back later to finish the game.  Doesn't look like a big deal, but in an age where saving isn't anywhere and whenever, I highly value this sort of thing.
Other things worth mentioning are the soundtracks and the commentaries should you decide to purchase the more expensive editions.  The soundtracks are top notch and very fitting for the atmosphere.  A very worthy purchase.  If you enjoy behind the scenes stuff, the commentary mode can be turned on and off right from the menu even while ingame.  The commentaries are triggered by stationary NPC characters that you can just walk up to.  There's a color blind mode that can be switched on and off in the menu as well, but I have no idea how effective it is.  You can create multiple custom levels, but there is no way to share those with your friends to my knowledge.
Personally I bought the Exclusive Edition when it was on a big sale at 50 or 75% discount.  The game IMHO is worth $10-15.  The playtime can be short for some.  One complete run can be done in one afternoon, so it's not that long.  Achivement hunting can extend that by 2-3 hours, but still not that long.
At the time of writing this review I've had the unfortunate bug of commentary and musics tracks not playing.  A solution that worked for me was going into Gunpoint's Savegames folder and deleting the file

This "review" may be very stream of consciousness.
See, I don't think I'd call the Risen series a good game series, save maybe the first game. Well, that's probably a bit unfair. They are good in a variety of ways, just not the traditional ways most games are. The combat just kinda stinks in these games. There's no real way around it. Again, Risen had this issue too but was far lighter on combat than either of the sequels, at least for the majority of the game. It's incredibly basic and spammy, and there's far too much of it.
So why am I so compelled by this series? I think one of the things Piranha Bytes does well, is exploration. There's always nooks and crannies to explore and side quests to find. These random adventures with the sidequests are among Risen 3's strengths, are often very funny. Risen 3 lets you have almost unfettered access to the game's world once you complete the tutorial area. There's about 20 percent of the game walled off for story purposes, but other than that, you can really just do what you want. You'll have a few major goals, but they are so out of reach that often just following your wandering heart is the best course of action. You'll probably find your way into the main story eventually by sheer accident. There's a spell that turns you into a parrot that you can use
That brings me to the story. In order to account for that free form exploration, it's pretty basic. You are the son of a legendary pirate (and brother to series mainstay Patty) who gets his soul stolen by someone in the underworld, but you've managed to retain your human body. So you'll need to set out and find your soul, and in the course of doing so basically solve everyone's problems along the way. Now, the series has never had a strong story. For some reason you're a new character, despite that this new guy kinda looks like the old guy, and he's sort of a similar character (the previous hero is probably a bit more polite). So it's kinda weird that you're a new guy that's not very different from the old guy. Like you can actually read reviews for the game and people are actually confused about it, thinking it's the same character. Well, anyway, it's even weirder because like, the game is pretty heavily invested in Risen 2's story. You recruit 3 of the party members from the 2nd game. So, anyway, just a bit weird that they made this new character that's barely different and have him interact with everyone anyway. I'd get it if they were like "we don't want to reset the hero again," but they kinda do it to you anyway at the start. Just sort of a strange decision.
Speaking of things back from Risen 2, the game heavily reuses some of the areas. Most of them are vastly expanded or changed, but still felt a bit like a retread at times. There are a variety of quality of life improvements, like a fast travel system similar to something in an Ubisoft game. The game has the most ridiculously in depth quest tracking system, so if you're lost you just need to use your log and put "show map marker" so if you're not in the mood to explore, you have that option. Crafting's a bit easier now too. There's more trainers, and most trainers train multiple skills so you likely won't have to worry too much about not having access to someone to train you. Trainers and merchants are all marked on the map after you find them once.
The levelling system is largely the same but has been reorganized, and not really for the better. For instance, melee skill increases your skill in all three weapon types, so there's not much specializing. Similarly there's like a Silver Tongue (charm) and Intimidate dialogue option often, and these skills are on the same stat too. Most games would force you to pick, be a charmer or be a brute, perhaps tying them to related stats. So it's a little boring that way.
Anyways, game starts off hard, like the others. You'll need to choose a magic faction for story purposes (and also, c'mon, free magic). This magic makes the game substantially easier, at least for the faction I chose, which favors direct damage. To be honest, and I find myself saying this with complete surprise, but I'd advise people to take a melee path. The combat does ever get good but there's some fun to be had once you get the parry ability. The basic magic attacks act sort of like weapon attacks, so you can't really use them with swords. So eventually when I got bored of how easy the magic was making the game I invested in melee and only use the cooldown abilities. Combining sword, a magic attack, and then a pistol shot while dancing around enemies could actually be fun at times. Random gripe but, hey, PB, you're a PC developer. Don't give me 30 moves and make them all need to be on the 10 hotkeys. Give me a scrolling hotkey bar or something. That's something to be said about this game over Risen 2 is that you have a lot more stuff to use, and it gives you it often. Even the magic of the other factions can be used via consumable items, so it really adds to the value of exploring. In R2 it seemed pretty rare to find anything too useful outside of a sword upgrade here and there.
The game does a good job of feeling "alive." It has a small cast of characters but this allows them to do NPC scheduling. I liked that as you clear objectives like taking back a mine overrun by undead, the miners that were displaced by the undead will go back to work. That sort of stuff. Small touches a lot of games would ignore.
Voice acting is weird. The PC sounds like someone's trying to do a Bale Batman voice via Aaron Paul, and I really hated him at the start. I got used to him though, mainly because his deadpan delivery really works well given the odd stories he gets himself involved in. Most of the party members are good, and I rather love Bones' voice actor. Very strange performance in both games. Graphically it's not going to stun much but most enviroments are well done, and it seems to be far more technically sounds than Risen 2. Fairly certain I had better performance in Risen 3 than R2 on the same hardware.
Anyways, I preordered it so, a quick review of the DLC, in case you ever get the game. The Gnomes isle one is kind of bland. About 2 hours. Not much to do there, honestly, and it feels rather disconnected. One of the big appeals of the game to me was sailing into a port, finding treasure maps and quests that take me to a different island, and just bouncing around. The DLC, by nature, can't be involved in this, so it loses that. The second major DLC is the Fog Island one. This one I like better. It's more involved in the main story, and has some decent atmosphere. Also had some good treasure to be found, while the other one didn't. Still suffers from being disconnected. Both are about 2 hours each, which isn't too bad for 5 bucks, but I'd probably wait for at least a small discount.
Writing this all out sounds negative, and it kinda is, but as much as I have issues with some of it, I enjoyed my overall time. I think PB are really good at creating areas to explore. The aren't too big, not too small, and there's always something around the corner, and they give you. I just hope, now that they have the rights to Gothic back again, that we see them address the combat in the future. I don't need much when it comes to action RPGs, but something's gotta give. Even something as simple as making combat rarer.
Alright, ramble done. I don't think I can recommend it outright. Have a tolerance for Eurojank, and like pirates, humor, and good exploration? Probably worth getting. Liked Risen 2? Get it for sure. Hated Risen 2? Ehh, it's an improvement but not leaps and bounds. Wait for a sale.
Final clocked in time is 45 hours, for those that care about game time. Minus the DLC and a few deaths / idle moments I'd say most people will get 35-40 hours out of it.

Black and White Bushido is a multiplayer arena fighting game that sees you fight in teams of black or white samurai in arenas where the background is either black or white. The general idea is when standing against your colour background you are invisible allowing for all sorts of sneaky stealth kills. Controlling your character feels fairly fluid and it won’t be long before you are bouncing around the level painting the fields red.
There are 4 different characters to choose from although I must admit they did not feel radically different from each other when being played. Scattered throughout the arena is also a number of power-ups ranging from throwing stars to bombs. While these are fun to use they are generally a single use item and I felt more could have been done with them.
The stealth mechanic works well especially with 4 players as it is impossible to keep track of where everyone is. The only real problem is that after dying and re-spawning it often took me a few moments to work out where the hell I was.
The main part of the game is deathmatch split into either straight deathmatch or capture the flag game types. With only 5 arenas to choose from you do pretty quickly yearn for some more selection. Equally the challenge mode which is the games only real single player element outside deathmatch with bots feature you completing a bunch of single player objectives without dying such as kill 3 people from behind or kill 3 people using wall jumps. While a nice little distraction this equally ends up as nothing more than a side mode due to the one hit kill and inability to continue.
I love the idea of the game and with 4 friends it’s an absolute blast. I first played the game at EGX2015 and came away thinking this was definitely a highlight of the day. But in reality without having 3 other people to play against it does not quite hold the same shine. So yes for an evening of multiplayer it’s great but it burns bright and fast and will grow old quickly.
Hopefully some more maps and modes down the line can help spice it up.

So, there I was flying my ship through space looking for a system with a decent amount of anomalies.  As an explorer I live for these sites. A few clusters of abandoned ruins ripe for the picking for those with the knowledge of how to find them.
Avoiding the High-Security systems I head to lo-sec.  The loot always tends to be more rewarding there, even with the risk of being blown apart by a fellow pilot.  I hit the system.  Afterburner on, probes launched, cloak engaged, directional scanner on full range.  The D-scan is like my little eye in the sky while I hunt down anomalies.  Anyone comes close without a cloak and I see them coming.  While I scan I see a few ships come and go. Thankfully they can't see me with my cloak engaged. Most of these guys are armed to the teeth, and I don’t even have a weapon. A weapon on my ship would be like a water pistol against these ships.  The best weapon I have is my cloak.   If I can’t be seen I can’t be shot.
Nothing good in system, just some combat sites and a lone wormhole. Combat sites would be suicide in my ship I so decide to take the WH, after all you never know what you might find. A wormhole can lead literally anywhere in the game, you might come out a few systems away or on the other side of the galaxy.  You may not even be in the galaxy anymore.
I pop out the other side and find myself in uncharted space, one of the most dangerous (and profitable) areas in the game.  I check D-scan and see one of the ships that passed me earlier, and another, and another, and another.  I run the ships against my data base to get an idea of what they’re there for.   I find an explorer (like yours truly), a weapon specialist, an electronic warfare specialist, and a cargo ship.  Four ships in what looks like a team, all after the same thing I am.
I start scanning down the sites, hoping that I might still be able to salvage something from this.  I find two data sites.  Either one could have enough loot inside to earn me a week’s worth of cash in a single haul.  I set the D-scan to filter everything but one of the sites, and the ships disappear from the scan list.  I know that the site is safe, but for how long.
The thing about WH sites like this one is that as soon as you jump in a timer starts ticking.  When it hits zero a large number of NPCs will jump in and ruin your day.  If you want to get anything from these sites you have to be fast.
I start on the first one I get to and it goes surprisingly easy.  All the practice in lo-sec is finally paying off.  I skirt around the various firewalls, bypassing any subroutines until I find the system core.  Five seconds later the cargo hatch pops open with a satisfying click.  Unsatisfyingly, the cargo bay only held about a million in loot, nice but only a fraction of what it could’ve been.  I risk it and go for the second cargo container, knowing that the NPCs or the other team could pop in at any moment.  I'm running D-scan constantly, but it will only give me about five seconds to prepare if someone comes my way.  I try to focus, looking at what points are most vulnerable in the system, trying not to set off any subsystems.  I slip up.  I surround myself in firewalls, no way out.  I abort the hack right before the NPC's spawn in.
With nowhere to go I cloak up and slowly work my way out of their range.  There isn't anywhere for me to jump to that I know is safe.  The only other place for me to go is a small gas site I found while scanning.  I set course, hit warp speed, and immediately remember that these sites also had high level NPCs.
My cloak is still on cool down, I have nowhere else to warp to, and I just landed in the middle of three high level NPCs.  My ship isn't built for combat, but they are.  I 'm stuck just watching while my ship is blown apart around me.  I eject in my capsule right as my (once) favorite ship is destroyed.  As my capsule is buffeted by the blast a notice pops in my inbox.  The insurance bureau is sorry to hear about my loss and have paid my claim in full.
As I write this I'm floating in my own debris field, too stupid to plan a proper escape route and too stubborn to self-destruct.  If that doesn't sum up Eve I don't know what will.

An actually decent survival game that doesn't just make the survival aspects feel like a chore. Some people♥♥♥♥♥♥themselves when they get scared, you'll get scared when you need to♥♥♥♥♥♥in the middle of a fight with six mutants.
The game revolves around managing the gradual infestation of Mars with your typical zombie party, keeping a reactor at the heart of the colony running so you can take a tram out to explore other sectors and recover the bips and baps you need to fly a shuttle off the planet. The longer you take, the more dangerous the world around you becomes, and the stronger the enemies you'll face. Resources are fairly plentiful but don't respawn, meaning once you clear a place out you'll have to move on to another.
Crafting can be a little tedious, given that everything is largely time based and gated behind upgrading your machines to a point you can harvest, refine, and combine materials that you need, with everything being tiered, and you have to run back and forth between machines constantly to keep them busy. Fortunately you can set up queues and increase the size of production batches so you can spend more time away from the machines without losing productivity, and upgrading them increases queue sizes.
Largely it's been an enjoyable romp, with some unexpected tension from lingering too long where my thermals and oxygen ran the risk of running out, or having to make a panicked dash to a restroom I passed five minutes ago, though the damn spiders remain a point of constant annoyance. Would recommend/10

Survive and throw your unneeded junk into the recycler and fabricate more things to feed to your research machine or use for yourself to fight a little better or longer the next time you go out. You're not a superbadass space marine. You're a skinny nerd. Use your brain to make your life easier, or just get killed. Hope you like spinning plates, because you need to spin more as time goes on. Play on a harder difficulty for the real experience.

I like Subterrain.
It looks good, plays well, has atmosphere and tons to do.
The premise is simple - survive some sort of infestation on a Mars base. Eat, drink, catch some ZZZs, don't get killed and don't succumb to the infection.
Unlike other survival-horror-lite games (there's very little horror in Subterrain, I was eager to meet the next big baddie), in Subterrain you are not constantly pushing forward to some promised land, instead, you protect and upgrade your home base that houses the five systems you absolutely must use to succeed:
The Mars base is infected - enemies constantly become more numerous and powerful. You are on the clock.
Initially the enemies are weak and you can get by with what you scavenge. To venture out into the more remote areas, you must break down and research tech you find, then produce better variants of power systems, weapons, armor and tools.
It is always a balancing act between time, available tech and raw materials you have.
Bosses,
Secrets,
Cooking
Subterrain is not perfect, but it is a solid entry in the survival shoother genre and should make everyone look forward to whatever Pixellore will be releasing next.

I played EVE for about 3 weeks and a few months later I decided to write this review since by now I think I have an objective opinion of the game and I will present the rest of it now:
EVE has an unfun micromanagement issue where you need to travel and do essentially a fetch quest but the time it takes to do this quest can get unbarable. Worse yet at the begining you will be micromanaging just about everything so it's not like you can walk away and take a shower and stuff will get done. I got to the point where I could set AI to take care of somethings in high concord areas (Basically AI will protect me from evil players) but there is nothing fun about mining.
The next thing is EVE's character creator, it's AMAZING I really liked spending an hour making my character but afterwards there is nothing, nothing to it at all. You can't interact with NPCS because you aren't your character persay. Instead Interactions happen between ships this threw me off big time and I gave the game a chance in the hope that maybe they had plans to expand this stuff but I know of no such plans and I'm unwilling to dump money and time on this game because of it. Essentially instead of feeling like the Captain of my ship I feel like a ship.
The Music in EVE passes the time well but bring your own music because even good music gets boring after your 15th material haul.
Eve takes itself too seriously, the game tries way too hard and consumes way too much time, while I didn't mind it at first the back and forth between areas and having to wait for 2 days for things to complete so I could use them only to find some detail that requires something else be made before I could use it  or make something from it.  To put it briefly the game does not appreciate the value of the players time and it is not streamlined to deliver it's product to the player. The result is being pounded with self imposed fetch missions across a small portion of the galaxy which can take 20 minutes to traverse if you don't get lost.
Textures are mid to low, the character textures are mid to high though, but the game graphically is not puke worthy but it doesn't get any praises from me. Space ship fights look like something you'd see from a web game.

A solid top-down shooter with a suvirval horror theme and tone. Recommended.
It's not procedurally generated, so this is a 'one-and-done' sort of game, though you can probably get a replay or two out of the more difficult settings, if you're so inclined.
The enemies are not particularly bright, but West is alone, and merely mortal, so numbers make up for what AI lacks (or more accurately doesn't need). The need to figure out where to go, what to do and what to research, manufacture and salvage will keep the time pressure foremost in your mind, and the need to manage West's bodily needs (sleep, food, water, excretion and contamination) will not let you forget that you're always in hostile terrain. Add in a permadeath option, and suddenly the stakes go up dramatically - a several-hours playthrough can be wiped by careless indiscretions made at the beginning of the game. (did you shut off the prison to save power? Did you leave anything behind in the biosphere to salvage when your supplies start to run lower?)
If you're looking for a builder, this isn't one - it's a shooter-with-upgrades that is set in the sort of post-apoc scavanging gameplay you've come to know that I adore.
I expect to get plenty of mileage out of this one, and like it enough to recommend it to others. Shoot for a sale (full price is a bit pricy) but a good choice to pick up nonetheless.
Strikes a good balance between the daily monotony of being stranded alone with dwindling supplies and the moments of action as you explore the dark, hostile remains of the base.

This is quite possibly my favorite MMORPG.  It's simple but addictive as hell.  I'm hoping that it will become more popular because the channels seem more barren lately.  I've been playing this game off and on since 2009 and there's about 2000 hours unaccounted for by Steam.  I've spent plenty on this game, probably far more than I should have, but it is just too much fun.  Getting with the right group can make or break the experience for you.
The game has been streamlined and cuts out a lot of what was there in terms of quest based padding to get some of the earlier quest lines out of the way. I was able to get through the first story (G1) in about a day and G2 is shaping up the same way with G3 not far behind.  I'm hoping that with redoing G2 I'll get another crack at being a Paladin so I can make other skills easier to train.
There's always something to do.  There are no set classes so you can be whatever you want.  Any weapons, spell, combat skill, or life skill is available to you with only a handful of abilities segregated for race.  They've made it so that you can spam to Lv1000 and catch up quick and still be a beginnger so that you're not lagging behind the veteran players so far. Earning levels is also much easier for everyone.  Once you hit the Lv1000 and Lv2000 milestones, you can start new characters at those levels and not have to completely start over on another character.  This is a HUGE boon considering that it wasn't like this from the beginning.  There are many more free options to play so you don't even have to pay to get access to most of the options in the game unless it's something extra that you're really looking to get.  Even so, there's generally plenty of spill over from the paying players that the pay items are readily available to free players for in-game gold.
The battle system can leave a little to be desired if you're getting slammed by four or five enemies at once, but if you're in a party it evens out.  I personally really enjoy the life skills because it leads to more business options.  There's a lot of support now that wasn't there before for those who really want to focus on building life skills.  No more are we forced into battle to gain AP in order to build our life skills.  It's wonderful.  It's not for everyone, but it's a second home for me and I love it.  If you're ever on Tarlach server, look me up!

Where to begin with IM? I've got 15 hours plus change in this game at the time of this review so I feel comfortable in writing down my opions of it. First impressions were very good I got sucked into the game from the word go, it has vibes of Star Wars Republic Commando, Planetside 2, Arma, and Insurgency all good games to try and emulate! I will say that it's not going to be a game that the majority of fans of the Call of Duty or Battlefield series will possibly enjoy?
It has an excellent atmosphere which is a heavy part of the game (Or at least it is for me.) Maps change dynamically and over the course of the match, which last 10 minutes in Deadlock, you can expect to have fought through the night a few times. Weather and other sounds are simulated nicely, wind coming from giant fans in the wall and rain via sprinklers in the roof. Lightning is also simulated on a few maps and I must say a pitch black map being lit up in a lightning effect is rather cool!
The guns come in two flavors at the moment, EOTech eqiupped SMG and a 4x rifle for those longer targets. I don't know the damage they put out but the rifle has a bit more damage at longer ranges compared to the SMG. The developers have plans to implement more in the future so we'll review that as they become avaliable. Both weapons can be suppressed and I usually do unless I am trying to make noise on purpose. There is no melee in the game, but the ammount of times in 15 hours that I've thought I could use one have been far and in between; typically it's when the fisticuff robots get right on top of me.
The servers for multiplayer seem to be stable, I haven't had an issues connecting or staying connected. There are 'private' servers that you and your friends/those whom you invite can play by yourselves if you enable the option you want and connect to an empty server. Most of the servers seem to be empty with most people crowding onto a fuller on, there's never a lack of the multiplayer to go around however. You have the option of also co-oping against bots, which turns any of the single player missions into a co-op mission.
In closing, I have finally found that one early access that I am excited for and hope that it continues it's current path. I am very much looking forward to the upcoming updates and seeing what this small team can put together! In it's current state I would give it a 7.5/10, it has it's issues but that is to be expected of an early access game but what it has it feels good to play and I enjoy it!

If this game works on your PC, it's great. If you buy this and the game crashes on startup, it's best just to refund immediately.
However, it is pretty good. If you've ever played a zombie game with extremely inconvenient government intervention featuring in it, like the bridge getting bombed in Left 4 Dead 2, or the evac point always being in what for you feels like the worst possible spot, this is your chance to see if you can do a better job.
You won't. You've got a good chance of winning, sure, but you WILL get civillians killed in the process. In the beginning, you'll just be failing to evacuate people and shrug it off as an unfortunate circumstance of the outbreak, and at least you were able to save some people. As time goes on, you will eventually have to kill some people in an artillery strike, or put people at risk by having strikes near them, to protect the greater masses. By the end-game, you'll be so desensitised to those little dots you may even forget that in the game's universe, they're actually human. The way this game twists your perspective of its own events is genius.
It's not without flaws. There's two main ones that are the only ones I can think of that could legitimately be a game-ruiner:
-Horrifyingly unbalanced. Artillery are the best unit in the game with no competition. You could easily beat the entire game using nothing but Artillery and the evac helicopter. The game uses an RNG-based system for which ones you get (You always get the evac helicopter if you need to evacuate civvies, but everything else is randomly picked from your merc pool), so it's not like this is TOO horrific of a flaw, but it's still a problem. The other units in the game are far more evenly matched, but Artillery outpaces them to such an extent it's absolutely ridiculous. Even unupgraded it's a valuable unit to have, with upgrades it's nothing short of unbelievably OP.
-But sometimes, the random mercenary pool can just screw you over. I don't care if you're the best AZS player on the planet, you cannot be expected to wipe out a zombie-infested town with some mines, dynamite, and barricades.
Of course, this game's legitimate flaws are what mods are for. Though I still haven't installed any, actually, still got 25-ish hours out of it so far though. Nevertheless it's still a wholly enjoyable game despite these issues, and they only really surface in the late-game.

A small but highly entertaining package, with bags of replay value, fun and varied achievements which reward experimentation rather than simple linear story progression, and a brilliantly atmospheric soundtrack.
Gunpoint is a 2D side-scroller usually taking place in an array of office buildings, police stations and skyscrapers. You play Richard Conway; hat-lover, trenchcoat-wearer and amateur spy extraordinaire. Framed for a murder you didn't commit, you must use a mixture of gadgets, stealth, smarts and combat to clear your name. Then, you must clear the name of the person you accidentally framed while clearing yourself. Whoops.
The graphical style makes use of small sprites, barely an inch high, that are nonetheless colourful and easy to distinguish. This is fortunate because it allows the zoomed-out camera angle to take in the entirety of the buildings comprising each level. In each stage, Conway must evade/knock-out/kill/trap/etc. the various types of guards in his way to secure his objective and then escape to the subway. His first gadget to help him do this is a pair of Super Trousers which catapult him through the air as though fired from a cannon. With these he can leap enormous heights and distances, crash through plate glass windows, and land on top of enemy guards, at which point the player can render the guard unconscious with a single punch achieved by clicking the left mouse button (which performs most of the actions in the game), or pound their face into bloody mulch with repeated clicking (level of psychosis down to individual preference).
The main feature of the game - aside from the Super Jump Trousers - is the Crosslink, in which a quick scroll of the mousewheel gives players a view of all the electrical systems in the building, and enable these systems to be rewired. Rewiring these systems allows players to turn lights on and off, open and close doors, activate and deactivate security cameras, and distract or knock out guards. As the game progresses, the number and variety of electrical devices in each level increases, and the game also adds different circuits within the same building, forcing the player to become increasingly cunning and intricate in their approach to each mission.
Guard AI is fairly predictable, even with the introduction of different types of guard as the game progresses. However, the game remains challenging because while the guards can be dispatched with only one hit, so can the player, so being seen is almost certain death. Increased guard numbers in later levels combined with increasingly tricky electrical systems mean the player can quite easily open a door accidentally and allow a guard to see them, or trip an alarm and call the guards running, but while challenging the game never becomes frustrating, due to a fantastic and frequent autosave system - with no loading times anywhere to be seen - and is also never unfair: any deaths the player suffers are guaranteed to always be their own fault. Taking their time to look over the building's electrical wiring and the guard's patrol patterns should reward players with a deathless playthrough, but once upgrades and gadgets have been unlocked they can be used in earlier levels, meaning that it becomes possible to speedrun the game if preferred.
Replay value is added by the large number of achievements - only a handful of which are guaranteed to be unlocked in a single playthrough - and an intuitive level editor that allows the player to build a level every bit as complex as the story missions from the ground up. Gunpoint is a short game - the story can probably be completed in 30 minutes or so (but probably not on a first playthrough) - but the multiplicity of methods for completing each level - stealthy or loud; thoughtful or speedy; by evasion or by bloodbath, and everything in between - ensure that the game could be played through many times and still never have to become repetitive.

Gunpoint is a clever and unique puzzle game that employs stealth mechanics within a familiar, though modernized private eye narrative. The writing is genuinely funny and the level design and puzzle solutions satisfying. It's a short game, but the mission structure doesn't lend itself to marathon play sessions, so it lasts longer than its three to four hour playtime may suggest. It's charming, it's memorable, and it executes its premise flawlessly.

Basically It boils down to this. A good role playing game rewards fastidious exploration. The Risen franchise is no exception.The more you explore the more loot you get, the more loot you get, the more money you get, the more money you get, the more skills/items/equipment you get. To me, this is the attraction of the Risen franchise. Exploration=reward, pure and simple. This is a very important element in any pure single player RPG. This particular element is handled well in the  Risen series of games.
However the Risen franchise is still struggling to find a solid identity. The first Risen was very ambiguous, the second chapter, the developers, despite giving the franchise a more polished pirate themed aspect,  were still experimenting with the combat system. This 3rd chapter is wonderful to the hardcore RPG'er, the pirate element still remains but the combat remains slightly clunky and experimental if you will.
However, the exploration vs. reward idea remains solid in all 3 games. Risen 3 is a more finely polished example of where the franchise could go.
Exploration and completionism is the key in the Risen franchise.
However to be perfect the Risen franchise could do well with a lot more polishing.  Some examples being, keep working on the combat system, the combat system in Risen, being the core of the game still feels slighty clunky. I figured out the obvious pattern in the combat system early on. And there is a definite pattern still. This pattern in the obvious timed moves still hinders the combat system from feeling fluid and natural. If you attack at the wrong time, you get hit, if you attack at the right time you strike. There is no fluid inbetween. The combat feels "timed" more so than natural.
Another aspect the developers could benefit from working on.  Make the skill earning system more complex. The skill system in this game is OKAY but not perfect. It still feels slightly limited. You spend cash on new skills, and you add power points to existing skills to "level them up". However there is no complex skill tree per se. You don't get to master a whole entire set of skills in any one combat style. This all lends to a slightly limited combat system. You can get BETTER at guns...but all you'll notice if you do so is that you do more damage with ranged weapons. To be blunt, the leveling/skill system needs a serious overhaul to feel more rewarding.
Also very importan to the hardcore RPG'er is, reward all the hard work put into the game with a beautiful well thought out ending. I notice the Risen titles in this franchise have lackluster endings. I realize the games themselves tell a story. But a moving, rewarding ending for a role playing game like this, where hard work and exploration should lend to the game's ending  is needed to complete the immersion process.
I hope they continue this franchise, and fine tune the understandable flaws until they release a game that surpasses all other RPGS.
In short, this RPG does exemplary on the exploration verses reward aspect. The more you explore, the more you benefit. However this franchise still continues to fall short on the combat system, skill system and endings for the games. This game will tickle the fancy of any die-hard fan of single player RPGs, but there is still a ways to go if the developers want to perfect this franchise.

Dragon Ball Xenoverse is, imo the best DBZ game i've played in a long time. it's got some issues, and some things I'd like to have seen, I'll get to those in due time.
The premisse of the game is simple; Some one is screwing with the time line and altering the history of Dargon Ball Z, it's your job to go back set things back on track. So yes, your playing through the Saga's, again. But i don't mind so much this time. The reason being your presented with what will happen if you don't step in before you go back and beat the time line back onto the correct path.
I personally liked this.
So, I bet your wondering how this works. Is future Goku going back and saving past Goku? NOPE!! After the intro battles and cutscenes, you make your own character. So, Goku isn't the hero saving the universe this time. You Are.
You get 5 races to pick from, the 'Majin', a race of Majin Buus basicly, Saiyans, of course, Earthings, Namekians, and 'Frieza clansmen', and with the exception of the Namekians and Frieza clansmen, all have a male and female version, and gender does effect stats, to a degree. For example, female Saiyans have stronger KI attacks then Saiyan males, how ever, how much this accutally matters is debateable.
My adivce is just make the character you want and worry about stats as you level up. Which are devided between HP, Ki, Stamina, Basic Attack (you normal punches and kicks) Strike Supers (physical super moves, like stronger punches and such) and Ki Blast Supers (Kamehameha's and such.) unlike a lot of games I've played with stat allocation, what you put where matters here. So you can screw your self with your stat placement.
fortunately you can reroll them, as well as a few other things, if you summon Shenron.
While they never actually refer to your character by name in game, cause it's all voiced, they did an exellent job all things concidered taking the focus off the main DBZ cast and putting it on you.  So there's no point where you feel like your 'along for the ride' you feel like an important, and nessacry part of these battles.
The battles them selves are both simple and complex. Simple because its rather easy to figure things out and get into a groove that works. Complex, cause theres a lot of little tricks up can pull the game flat out doesn't tell you about. Like, at all. But for those picking up the controller for the first time, you'll be greeted with a combat system with I feel is just right far as 'learning curve goes. Yes I said controller. it does have KB/M support, but it's really not the type of game where KB/M is the 'optimal control scheme'. It's just not, and if that bothers you, feel free to forget this game exsists right now and be on your merry way now.
Battles, as you'd expect, take places in full 360s degrees, you will fight them in the air, you will fight them on the ground, though rarely, even in space and under water depending on the stage, and the terrian can be damaged, but sadly, only damage to buildings is 'persistant', holes in the ground vanish after a little while, which sucks. The fights them selves are usually pretty good, the controls are nice and responcive and this is probably the best system for using special and super moves and items I've seen for a game like this.
Items, as well as other funtions, like 'sensing' are bound to the control pad, meaning an item is never far away, and since you can only bring four with you into battle, chances are you'll haev what you need, when you need it no fussing about with a list like Dark Souls. just control pad right, and which ever of the X/Y/A/B buttons you have the item you wanna use on, also, the item menu closes automaticlly when an item is used so you won't have to worry about closing it. move over, you can still move around with the menu open so if you need to get out of there and avoid damage you can.
Specical and Super moves work similarly, being bound to the right trigger for Special moves, and both triggers for Supers, which means the total numer of skills you can have in use at any given time is seven (4 specials, 2 supers, 1 evasive) should be eight. theres even a slot for it, but for some reason it's not usable ... in any event, like the items you are litterally never more then two buttons away from a big attack, or something to get the other guy off you at any given time.
assuming you have the Ki or stamina to pull it off mind you.
And given how many skills your character have learn, you can really make a character thats your own. Sure your still using some one elses skills, but that's only a minor detail when you can be using pretty much any ones skills in any combonation you so desire, and with the addition of an equipable called a 'Z-Soul' you can add more effects to you character and skills, like faster Ki and Stamina regen, auto-revival on defeat, HP regen, even damage immunity for some Super moves, and so on.
Lastly, theres the diffrent outfits, a good 99% of which are just outfits worn by one DBZ character or another. like the armor Nappa and Vegeta wore when they came to earth, or Broly's clothes. There is some orgianl stuff though, but not enough for my liking.
There is also an online componant, but eh, I've never cared enough to poke at it. It was pretty broken for awhile but that's not the case now, so you shouldn't have to worry about your connection. even if it does go out or you just don't have internet access at the time you wanna play you won't be barred from anything other then online PvP battles. ALL the single player stuff and side quests can be done off line with no problems.
and now some down sides.
The character creator is far to limited for my liking. really only limited to skin color, hight, body type (thin, normal, large) and head options. I would have REALLY liked more options for my characters then that.
Some battles are stright up ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. 2 v 1 against you is fine and managable but 3 or more? it starts to be more of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥then it should be, and god help you if your fighting more then one Super Saiyan, because Super Saiyans in this game have unlimited Ki for the durration of the transformation, so Ki blast spam is a thing. Although, thankfully confined to the higher level side quests.
Clothing has stats. this might not seem like a big deal at first, but since stats per item stack you can end up losing a TON of Ki or HP, or damage output. which sadly means you ether need to be all about them stats or looking how you want, as rarely do the two meet, and when you can end up losing up to 20 points to say Ki Blast for some full sets, you need to keep an eye on that more then you should have to.
lastly, there's getting most the new skills and outfits. you have to grind for them in side quests and HOPE you get them. There are 'masters' you can learn from like Cell, or Goku (yes, you can learn moves directly from some of the villians in this game.) but they only give you skills and you have to grind side quests to fill a bar so they'll teach you the next one.
Though the plus side to the masters is some of the post battle comments, like Cell for getting the Z rank (highest)
All in all Dragon Ball Xenoverse is a good game with a decent enough twist on the usual 'DBZ game' formula as to make going through the same battles again fun and engaging, even if this is the umpteenth time we've kicked Frieza's teeth in. It's flawed, but it's flaws aren't such that I, Personally, wanted to say '♥♥♥♥ it' and put the game away for good.
I'd prefer it wasn't $60 USD + $25-30 USD for DLC, but I don't 'regret' buying the game at full price, which is rare anymore.
