Naruto Shippuden Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 Full Burst is a great fighter, once it finally clicks. When you start the story nothing is explained and you start with a pretty hectic battle, which can rather easily be won with just some button mashing. After that comes a frustratingly long battle if you have no idea what you're doing. It took me over 40 minutes to finally beat this enemy, and by that time I understood the controls slightly better. When I was halfway into the game I was still figuring things out. It would've been nice if there was some sort of tutorial; the loading screens show moves and tips but half of the time they disappear way too quickly to properly read them.
As I said, it's a great fighter with amazing visuals and cinematics (although they're a bit too long) and a bit of (linear) freedom where you can accept sidequests, find 'secrets', eat food to heal your crew and buy items that you can use during your battles.
Battles are usually relatively easy and if they're not the checkpoints seem rather limited. It took me several tries to finish the last battle, with is actually pretty long (10-20 minutes). All because it didn't have enough checkpoints. The easier battles had more checkpoints, but weren't usually needed. I thought that was a bit weird... Could be me, though.
The camera can also get in the way at times, but thankfully you can swing it the other way with the press of a button. Simple enough, but still noteworthy.
Unfortunately, I had to skip most of the cinematics (they're uncountable, there are so many). Why ? I've never seen a single episode of this show, I have only heard of it. It's not a very newbie friendly game if you're new to the show or the game. I normally watch all cinematics but I didn't understand any of it. There are so many characters and the storyline seems to be all over the place, especially at the beginning of the game. I do know that you'll be skipping at least three cinematics every 5 minutes. They just keep coming, it's unbelievable. I don't mean this in a negative way; other fighters should take note ;) I just wish I had seen some of the episodes to know what it's all about.
Behind all of the cinematics there's still enough gameplay to keep you occupied for at least a good 10 hours. Don't skip any of the movies and you can add several hours to that number. Even after finishing the game you can still finish your active sidequests, or accept new ones/ones that you hadn't found yet.
The visuals are amazing. I guess the game looks (and sounds) practically the same as the TV show. Most of the times I couldn't figure out if I was watching gameplay or a cinematic. It all works very fluently, and looks amazing. Some of the QTE battles are just gorgeous ! It's just a shame that all of this is capped to 30FPS, which is absolutely noticeable when you're not fighting, but running around in the environments.
In the end Naruto really impressed me. A lot. It just took about one hour to figure it out. It's a fun and solid game with amazing graphics, and if you love fighters, or Naruto, this game is a must. More please.

Onto the positives I guess...

The dodge mechanic and shield mechanics allow a lot of manueverability when fighting. combine these abilites with what I feel is the most entertaining weapon - the shotgun - and you can dodge in and out of melee range to blow enemies to chunky bits before they hit you at the horible danger of geting mauled to death if you mess up. the grenades also provide an entertaining and somewhat dangerous method of fighting hordes of enemies.
The survival aspect of the game is certainly well fleshed out. Food, water, sleeping, and using the restroom are all required. Injuries can include bleeding, fractured bones, etc. that all impair your ability to survive unless treated. hunting down and securing an ample supply of food and water is a must... but I cant help but feel as though the ability to produce your own food is needed (no... not that stuff from the biodome area that contaminates you and only recovers like 5% hunger and water. no, I mean food that is actualy effective at feeding you.)
You can drag furniture around. this doesnt sound like that great of a feature until you start getting your generator atacked by the mutants. You can make crude baricades that hinder their movement and can help prevent damage to your generator. this could be improved, however, by allowing us to craft our own furniture and baricades using resources instead of the limited supply availabe in the central area.
It is a nice game but I certainly wish those bugs get fixed. It seems well polished but needs a few touch ups here and there such as reducing the number of loading screens in the central area (Four loading screens? Really!? Im walking between those places every five minutes in the early game for the busywork I mentioned earlier and I have to put up with these loading screens too?)
UPDATE BELOW
The developers are also extremely cooperative and kind with my request for a refund (I cant even play with the bug I got). I say give this one a pass for now... but keep an eye out for it, once everything gets touched up and the bugs are stomped out this will be a real entertaining play.
If you are a fan of the series/game series, this is worth it.

With a title like “Ghosts of Miami” I expected something very grim dark with really boring choice of colors you’d see in a grim dark edgey triple A game complete with really cliche plot twists. Instead, I get a nice vibrant color palette  with a very diverse and interesting casts. After I was done with the game the first time I was left wanting more of Chelo’s adventures. Craving for more cases to crack. The soundtrack is pretty decent too, a shame it’s not available for sale.
For an investigation game, it’s unusual to get love interests to pursue at the same time while you are on the case. The choices are definitely interesting, 2 guys, 2 girls, 1 non-binary. They certainly are pretty balanced in terms of choices. What’s odd is that some of these character branch will be locked until you’ve beaten the game once. It’s something you’d see in some visual novels, not quite what I’d expect in a game like this. It’s not bad, just a bit surprising. So if you have your eyes set on someone right off the bat, he/she will not be immediately available due to… plot reasons. Possibly. I have not done the true ending yet.
This may be a put off for some, but I don’t mind GoM giving me limited time slots to pursue leads and romantic interests at the same time. You can choose to be a hard boiled detective only focused on your case at hand, or be a more soft boiled investigator who wants to spend more time working on her social circles. Your circle of friends actually can be very important to your investigation as well since they can indirectly give you more leads and clues. The game doesn’t require you to maintain a very rigid set of schedule if you are aiming for closing the case and still getting your love interest. There is still a good degree of flexibility which I deeply appreciate. I followed the most logical course of action and was still able to woo my love interest in one try. Nice.
Let’s talk about the design choices of this game. The interface itself is a bit screwy. While I am given the option of playing the game with a controller, I find it’s really difficult to do so. Sure, the first thing the game asks me to do when I boot it up is to configure it with the standard screen resolution, graphics quality, and input. (+ asking me which monitor to put the game on, which is pretty considerate of the developers I must say) When they ask you to input the controller and the buttons, normally you’d at least getting a prompt on what each selection will do. Not here. There are 3 columns: Control, Primary, and Secondary. Under Control it reads like this: joystick1 analog 0, joystick 1 analog 1 and so on. Primary isn’t much better: Joystick 1 axis 1, Joystick 1 axis 2 and etc. I have no clue what the selections are and which thing it corresponds with. I tried to play the game with default controller option and it was so finicky that I just went back to using the mouse and keyboard instead since it’s much faster.
Another design choice I’m not fond of is the save system. I’m a fan of multiple save slots, because I like to pursue different routes and have separate save files for when I like to muck about with the choices. You can’t do that Dave. There’s just one permanent save. You can restart a case or resume it at anytime and that’s it. I’ve also ran into this annoying bug where I just want to rewatch the ending for the final case, but I’m stuck on the log screen and unable to get out at all. Thanks game… This isn’t an isolated incident either. I restarted the game while writing this and encountered the same bug within the first 10 minutes. What’s extra hilarious is that I can still fast forward the dialogue in the background with ~ key while I’m stuck in the log screen. But of course I can’t advance the story
At this point the only way to get out is to quit the game and restart the case. Which sucks if you are almost done with the chapter.*
If you are interested in playtime length, it’s roughly 4 hours for the first playthrough. I’ll update this whenever I decide to aim for obtaining all the endings. Is this worth the full price $14.99? I enjoyed it for its content so yes, despite the annoying resume bug putting a damper on things. But I’m also the type who also doesn’t mind paying $20 for a decent VN, so your mileage may differ.
*I’m not sure how the bug happened the first 2 times since the ending + credits should’ve allowed for a proper shut down/reset of the game. The second time I was closing and opening the game to bring up the configuration menu again to write the review. The game wasn’t closed on the log screen when the bug happened after resuming the game. The third time I intentionally restarted a case, made some progress into the story,
and shut off the game by using the big X button on the game window. Sure enough, I’m bugged when I try to resume the game. I haven’t experimented enough with quitting the game via exiting to the main menu and quitting the game this way, Frankly I’m not in the mood to♥♥♥♥♥♥around more.

If you're wondering about buying this: don't. Get the Complete Saga (Star Wars) instead. If you already have that, get Pirates of the Caribean instead. Already have both? Then you don't really need more Lego games.
Here's an actual review:
My opinion for not recommending this game isn't that strong. It's not a "YOU MUST NEVER BUY THIS GAME," instead, "You probably shouldn't get this game because there are other Lego games with more polish." Continue reading if you want to know why I came to that conclusion.
I'll start with the controls. I don't know if the developers completely forgot what made the original Lego games great; it felt like there was a button for everything, though in reality, there were only four. Lego LOTR has an open world, which I'll mention why it's not terrible but was done poorly in the next paragraph. But the controls. There's weird clipping, the different walkable paths have a force field around them, swapping between characters might make you switch to your second character which isn't in the place you wanted them to, the story has weird moments where you can choose which level to play, the playable moments in the levels included some moments which really should of been a cutscene but was changed to a really awkward gameplay part which was required to have two players, . . . oh hey, that wasn't all about the controls. . . . Close enough.
Lego games were great for their simplicity, yet replayability. This was because the player had a static camera, so they didn't have to constantly reposition it. As you can tell, you need to move the camera a lot when you're in an open world, which this game features. Now, I think running around Middle-Earth when it's an open world is awesome. But why was is done so poorly? That's because you have to constantly reposition the camera. Lego games are great for their simplicity of just four buttons (and four more for movement). Adding a moveable camera requires four more. I really like the idea of moving the camera in a cutscene, but when moving the camera is keyboard only being rotated around the character you're playing as, it starts to get annoying. Especially when there's so much stuff that's required (or optional for 100%) in the overworld. A level hub would've been so much better.
And the levels are still a bit too long. Mostly the cutscene halfway through them adds a lot to their length. Not a terrible complaint, since that's pretty much every Lego game.
So, do I recommend it? As you clearly saw when you noticed that this was a negative review, no. If you're a diehard Lego fan that has to 100% every Lego game, then go ahead. For those new to Lego, try a different one.

Of all the competitive muliplayer games Valve has released on Source this one is my personal favorite.
Like TF2 it's a class based team shooter with territory control based objectives. But with a more satisfying core shooting mechanics, eg not having to shoot an enemy 6 times point blank to the head, and without no long periods of waiting ala CS:S.
Classes are effective based on location and situation they are in, making using the environment and controlling the situation keys to success. Teamplay is encouraged for accomplishing objectives and maintaing frontlines, not shoved down your throat ala TF2 where the wildly large differences in classes specialties means you cannot handle certain situations as your current class.
The core maps are fun, but where this game really shines is in the large selection of custom maps that keep the experience fresh and challenging. To my experience the commnity that play this game are usually friendly, laid back, and great fun. - Except realism.

Let me get this straight off the bat: I love Mabinogi. Character customization skill-wise is my top priority when it comes to MMORPGs, but when you start shifting the focus towards vanity items that do absolutely nothing except for making your character look good and you add a crap ton of random classes that confuse the heck out of enemy AI who've only had to deal with melee, bows, and magic, that's when I start frowning on the game. Ignore the playtime Steam has. I've played for quite awhile on the standalone launcher. Anyway, back to the review. In a nutshell, Nexon has turned Mabinogi into a cash grab with no good updates in who knows how long just to satisfy their greed. Yes, I just called Nexon out for being greedy. Yes, I will continue to point out Nexon's flaws through out this review.
| Gameplay |
The original system for Mabi's combat was a modified rock-paper-scissors match which required skill more than luck. Smash broke through Block, Counter evaded Smash's slow attack, normal melee couldn't break Block, etcetera, but with the addition of new classes and skills along with it, the AI of the mobs just can't cope. They only know the bare essentials with maybe a special skill or two for the bosses.
Outside of combat the economy of Mabi is jacked. You can hardly get started nowadays without buying something with real money from the Nexon store. Maybe, just maybe, if you find a experianced player then maybe they'll give you some gear, but with Mabi's playerbase dropping, it would be very rare.
| Graphics |
Perhaps the greatest point of Mabi is the graphics. But even then they look a tad outdated. Anime/Manga styled characters and mobs is the core concept of Mabi's graphics. Beutiful landscapes and sunsets, dark and grim dungeons, it is pretty cool, but still, it all could use a good polish.
| Community |
The second most important thing to me is the community of the game. Friendly players willing to help out the newbies, a good rivalry between guilds, the lightest touch of drama here and there... Mabi used to have all this, but with the player base dwindling, well, it's going to be hard to find a person and not a bot. And a reason behind it all is Nexon's inability to respond to support tickets.
| Summary |
Gameplay   - 3/10
Graphics     - 8/10
Community - 3/10
Average - 4.5/10

Christ, and I thought Dear Esther was bad. The game features no objectives but instead wants the player to immerse themself in an incredibly boring walking simulator. While "walking simulator" could be used as an insult towards titles such as Dear Esther, Gone Home, and Doctor Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine, it literally is what the game wants to be. I can't blame it for that, honestly. It is relaxing to venture forth this tiny, poorly designed island every time you start up the game and begin your walk on water like Jesus goddamned Christ. However, this shouldn't be seen as a game as much a tech demo for some old computer a decade ago. What really strikes me as unbelievable is the lofty price tag. It's ten dollars to walk on an island created by somebody who pointed at Minecraft and an Atari 2600 and decided they wanted to play god and create some unholy combination of the two. To summarize my point, never, ever buy this filth, but if you scored it from a humble bundle, go nuts and stumble aimlessly for all of 5 minutes before you realize you'd get the same experience taking a walk around your neighborhood, with the objective being exercise.

If you want to make a cookie cutter RPG like the rest of the steam library, buy it for the base software and go ahead, If you want to make an actual 2D game - do a decent bit of research and planning, then decide if it's RPGM you should be using or perhaps an actual game creation suite. I would however still recommend it as it's a nice platform to use, but like any project be it personal or professional, commitment is required.
-------------------
This small software suite while simple in design has become a very real, and usable tool for creating simple video game concepts or small scale games - the majority of releases (per found on steam) show the lazier side to what is capable of and should not be used as reference or review of this package.

It's hard to review this product as... well, a product; It's a vast improvement over VX/Ace because of it's intuitive UI, innate layering that makes sense, higher res and Javascript to boot, however the 6+ years of Support that Ace has had for it's community releases and is still the most favored platform for the more complex RPGM releases really outweighs MV (it can make TRPG and ARPG games, pretty hard to do that in MV currently). Honestly in my >opinion, Yanfly is one of the only reasons that MV is able to stay afloat with their free, high quality plugin releases breaking simplicity for the sake of more in depth games, but still can't branch out of the fade-screen-random-encounter RPG formulae.

RPGM releases in general requires three things,
. If you lack the input of any it shows in its results or doesn't show at all because the project is abandoned.
There are A LOT of releases with very little planning or research, but a lot of working - overworking in fact, so much working that instead of getting to a point where a project is ready to be tested, the creator has worked on nothing but making the first room look perfect, or in other obvious cases - the creator has made a 250x250 map, but instead of filling it with content, they make one, empty Tower; nothing but a ctrl+v job of a grandiose Tower with no substance.
You can spend an entire day on tilesets but still end up doing less work than doing an hour on testing. Eventually, you build an inertia to where you can work a set block of time and make progress without realising it.
Spending a little time reading why it would be better to use a simple script for math instead of using the inbuilt functions is good because it will be reusable information throughout the project no matter the stage. Watching 30 minute long parrallax tutorials for your first town in game isn't good to start off with, sure you'll have future knowledge on how to parrallax your first village - but not every town is going to look like the first, so you'll have to watch a new tutorial.
Overall, MV like any other RPGM package is a thing that you have to commit to - You don't have to treat it like a job if you don't want to, but you must treat it like a skill or hobby, it requires work and patience. You don't paint masterclass pieces after your 3rd lesson.
In closing, while it's hard to review this in terms of vidya, I'll score it in comparison to the other releases (Ace = 9, XP = 7)
Ease of use;

As with every other RPGM release, ease of use is what it aims for and it does it very well in this release.
Support;

Again, Yanfly is the shining light in the cold sea of MV plugins.
Stock Assets;
NB: I do not use stock assets in my projects as I like to work on my own assets.
The character generator is improved, the bump to 48x48 is VERY nice and allows for just that extra bit of detail. A lot of the base tilesets are back. Only gripe is the odd selection of Stock enemies, doesn't match the rest of the assets at all.
Final:

This is a game in which there are no enemies to defeat or problems to solve. Your only goal is to explore. Every time you play a new island is randomly generated. The island will have its own seasons, weather, and day/night cycles. There will also be some wildlife that will react to your presence in various ways. The soundtrack will react to your location (under a rain cloud, on top of a mountain, ect.).
This is a "walking simulator" game, and while I have no problem with walking simulator games per se (see my positive review of Dear Esther) I can't really recommend buying Proteus. The island of Dear Esther was interesting to explore because the graphics were AAA quality and the music was top notch. But Proteus suffers from low res pixel graphics (seen one pixelated tree, seen em all), a simplistic soundtrack, and the lack of interesting stuff to see. I played 20 minutes of Proteus and felt I had seen 95% of what the game had to offer; I felt no incentive to wait another 10 minutes to see what few changes the next season might bring.
Fortunately I paid just a few cents for it, and those 20 minutes I did play were enjoyable, so it wasn't a total wash. If you like exploration games and you see Proteus on sale for a few cents you might give it a try, but I wouldn't pay more than that.

The first time I played this game, it really didn't hook me, and I'm not sure why.  Because it's really, really good.
The man who designed it is very clever, and much of the story is told in interesting ways.  The achievements do a very good job of mocking achievement systems, while still being genuinely fun to collect.  In all, this is an indie game which feels like it's mocking other games, but doing it in the opposite of how most games do it - it does it by legitimately being good.
It's hard to decide whether I'd call it a platformer or a puzzle game.  It's a bit of both, and yet not quite either one, because of the large amount of stealth required.  Mainly it revolves around situational rewiring of electrical systems to make them complete tasks for you.  And jumping.  Through windows.
Anyway, it's really good, and I'm really glad I finished it.  Pick it up.

I have been a semi-serious computer gamer for decades and I don't write reviews a lot unless a game is truly unique. Subterrain is a rare standout amongst many unremarkable games out there.
Sci-fi horror story with tension-wracked decision making as you struggle to balance exploration, resource management, time management, choosing item research paths, and even some good old tower defense thrown in!  Who could ask for more than that?
I've had some very scary moments playing this game (especially on Hardcore+ difficulty with permadeath option).  As the infection spreads you truly feel the urgency of being smothered with fewer and fewer options unless you make good decisions fast.  It's a nail biter!
Much praise to Pixellore.  You put together many different gaming genres in a smooth package.
As a footnote: Fans of Subterrain may also enjoy Dungeon of the Endless in their gaming library.

The return to 3D movement in battles is nice and the original storyline in the game is a refreshing take on the franchise.

This game is fabulous and bad at the same time. If there was a neutral button toward a review, this would be the one game I'd use it on. Here are some pro's & con's.
Con's first, cause' it will grab your attention at the very finest.
PS: , I mention this later but, I have around 2500 hours on this game and I've played for four years. Don't take my hours on the steam platform for granted please :)
Cons:
*BAD support, as far as I know, only half the people in their customer/tech support system actually do their job.
*Money-hungry company, this game is 'considered' a pay to win due to the mere impossibility of doing things without money near-end game, but it's still a great experience otherwise.
*Not much customization, in outfits, near early-game, which is rather considerably okay how they deal with it. Not really a con.
//Some of these con's deal with the company that franchises it, the gameplay is, heavily, HEAVILY, different.
Pros:
*Epic combinations of skills that will leave you on your seat when you happen to get that unexpected boss kill ;D
*Best community out there for a [mainly] free2play game.
*Grand amounts of customization near mid-game, leading to epic skill combos, neat outfits, tools..
*DUAL WIELDING, do I HAVE to explain this? They handle it so well.
*It doesn't feel like a grind in the beginning or middle, near late game is where grindy stuff happens.
*Memorable times...!
*A VARIETY of amazing skills such as fishing, making a campfire, cooking even! These were added to make the game more realistic and overall bondworthy toward. It also makes some killer picnic's.
*Realistic-like PVP , or, in this case, Duels. You literally walk up to someone, ask them if they want to duel. A menu comes up, you set the pre-requisites straight forward and get dueling. You aren't FORCED to do it either, and you can make good friends off of it.
*Graphics are easy to render, a lower-end / mid-end computer could easily run 30-100FPS. The game was made around 2000-something if I recall. The graphics still look amazing though.
//
*Death penalty system is not degradeful, hated, or anything in particular. It is annoying when you die, you get Nao stones to revive on full health sometimes though, and even if you do die, you don't lose anything. There is a chance when you die you may lose your gear if its expensive and not blessed by a certain item, but you can get it back at a town hall for a .. 'reasonable yet sometimes a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ kind of price.
//
*And finally, its NOT a rage game. Well, not easily alas. Sometimes there are mobs that can truly p1ss off someone but other than that, you don't lose very much.
//\\
Oh and, don't take my hours for granted. This game was just recently platformed on steam, it used to be on the companies website, which doesn't, as you may know, transfer hours over to here.
I've played Mabinogi for four years! Highly inactive, but I at least have 2500 hours on the game and I've witnessed all the stuff they've done on it.
//\\
This is a more TL:DR Version::!!//
\\
There are plenty more cons to the game, but they are outweighed heavily by the amount of pros this game contains. The community is so well knitted together that even a child could have fun without any pervs or foul language to watch out for. It's fun, engaging, and most of all, it's made for a community. You can manage epic combos in combat, you can even have pets. Its pretty cool, and is definitely worth trying.
However, the support service/s are typically bad, but you can still manage a refund if you didn't get something you payed for. They are money hungry , as they support many different games imported from Japan, and I can understand that. When they ask for too much money though, its pretty noticable. Back on the topic of the game though, there isn't much customization in the beginning, so its kind of boring. If you keep on going though, you'll find it pretty epic overall.
--//
...An even more TL;DR version..!! ;//
\\
Fun / Engaging game; but has a bad support service / company. It is a near pay to win at the end, but it is still very fun. It's also very involved with the community, most people are friendly and you don't have to watch out for swear-a-holics. A 9 year old could play this and learn to be kind from the community, most of the time.
//
OVERALL SCORE, the moment you've been waiting for..
I give this game an 8.5 / 10  !!
The reason I knocked off 1.5 points was rather simple, just the bad service and company it is owned by in America and the 'noticable yet not overkill' hunger for money they desire to keep the game rolling. Here is a more in-depth explanation.
+1 - Great graphic design, even for a game made near 2000. It can also handle lower-end computers well.
+3 - Epic community for a free-to-play game, it is very well knitted together, its hard to rip apart. Very hard.
+4.5 - Amazing combat system, PVP, and gameplay in general. Has a killer storyline too.
-1.5 - Aside from all that, the game has a bad support system and is a mere pay to win near the end. You can still have a great time though.
Thanks for reading through this, I hope I've told you the most I could about this fabulous game.

Borderlands, the first of the series, is probably also its best. With hundreds of hours of playability and a unique loot system, this title has merged traditional RPG elements and impressive first person shooting into one great ball of squishy carnage.
Each of the playable characters has something special to offer and gives the player a different experience each time. While one gets the feeling that Gearbox wasn’t overly interested in developing the rich story of Pandora in this episode, it lays down perfectly the foundations for the events in the games to come.
Let’s talk about loot. There are literally millions of guns, shields, grenades and class-mods to hunt down through the two play-throughs, making it ever more exciting when you finally get a gold rarity weapon, or even better a pearlescent one.
Character development in this game is brilliant, if not a little overwhelming at first. Besides the skill-trees which have dominated their other FPS titles, the first Borderlands also offers the development of a player’s weapon proficiency (sadly missing from the sequels), which means the more you use a specific class of gun, the better you get at wielding it.
Finally, the 4 DLC additions give the game new and exciting worlds to play in, cataclysmic weapons and gear and challenging enemies which will really test the player’s skill and intelligence.

Overall I love this game. This is hands down the best DBZ game ever made, but take that with a grain of salt considering its former competition. I loved the RPG elements in addition to the minimalist-sandbox style of gameplay. I enjoy the custimazation and races to choose from, and the story does a great job of focusing on you instead of the same old hum-drum DBZ story line that we have all seen 10 billion times. That being said, towards the end of the Buu Saga and on, this game turns from challenging to almost impossible in certain situations. In my personal opinion it is garbage in the late game. Here are a few pet peeves I had which could have been EASILY executed better by the devs:
-The custimization of the races felt very bland. They basically took the hair, featurs, builds and voices off of most of the key characters in the show and made them interchangable. While it did add some fun customization, it was extremely generic and it was clear from the start that little effort was put into it.
-Certain skills such as Super Saiyan 1/2 and Energy Charge/Full Power Charge/Maximum Charge come WAY too late in the story progression. You can't buy Super Saiyan 1 until after clearing the Cell Saga and you can't buy Super Saiyan 2 until after the Buu Saga. It's infuriating to try and complete the Sagas without these skills as the enemies are rocking super saiyan 2 or 3 against you, and can literally rock your world in 10 seconds flat. That doesn't even consider skills like Super Vegeta 1/2 (which is the Super Saiyan equivalent to blast specialists) cannot be bought at any point and must be farmed on PQ missions at an absurdly low drop rate. I tried to get Super Vegeta 1 at least 50 times and never saw it drop once. Important skills such as Maximum Charge must either be farmed on one of the absolute worst PQ missions (prepare to rage quit A LOT) or it can only be bought when you clear the game the first time. The timing of skills being available in the shop, or even available at all was extremely discouraging for me at certain points.
-In the later PQ missions the friendly AI stands there and floats watching you get smeared by multiple ultimate attacks for incredible amounts of time. I can't even tell you how many times I threw my controller down and just watched my guy get rocked while BOTH of the friendly AI literally did not throw a single punch at any enemy.
-The computer AI is ridiculous. And I mean RIDICULOUS. I cannot even count how many times I've been perfectly comboed and rendered unable to even stand up until I'm obliterated by the computer AI (This didn't become a problem until after the Buu saga). Their attacks are flawless, they can break through your ultimate attacks like childs play. They are too overpowered overall in the later PQ missions/Story and the game crosses the line from challenging to infurating in more fights than I care to remember.
-Single player missions (by yourself) felt like a bad joke as a blast specialist. You get absolutely no time to power up and your standard attack is equivalent to a fly attacking a T-rex. Blast specialists get infuriatingly manhandled in the later story missions and you have to overlevel your character immensly. In early to mid-game my character felt incredibly overpowered often times 1 or 2 shotting most enemies. Early game I felt like a monster (which I'll admit was pretty fun for awhile) and late game I felt completely useless without a meat shield to take the focus off of me. I didn't feel a happy medium anywhere as a blast specialist.
-As a melee combat specialist your attacks do absolutely no damage until you get super saiyan and your super attacks are very difficult to chain together. The game is a bit easier (solo missions) but fights take twice as long and getting the Z rating in missions is near impossible until you hit high levels. That being said, when I hit late game and had Super Saiyan 2 it did feel pretty good.
Overall I loved the game, but with the poor execution of the fighting mechanics and AI, I don't know that I would pay full price for it had I known. Wait for summer sale and pick this game up for $10-$20. It's worth it at that point.

The game's dynamic shifts would probably stand out as the main bullet point of the back of the Interstellar Marine box. It changes everything. Suddenly the rain is teaming down, thudding off the helmet of your suit, meaning that running suddenly becomes viable, your loud footsteps masked by the sound of the rain. As the simulation changes again the rain might stop, but the light might abandon you. When it does players are forced to use flashlights for navigation, but open themselves, and their locations, up to attack.
It’s this single mindedness that marks Interstellar Marines out as more than just a standard first person shooter. This doesn’t feel like a game that is going to♥♥♥♥♥superfluous nonsense to it to draw in a crowd of Call of Duty gamers. Granted, not doing so could be detrimental to the game’s sales, but, as with the game itself, sticking to their guns and being deliberate in both message and content could attract a dedicated and loyal base.

You have bunch o these. Every person from films is present here even those who where cut
and those who weren't in films
. Each character has it's own special abilities. For example, Sam can set fire on, Orcs are strong and can pull specific lego objects, Golum climbs on the walls etc. Voicelines are good almost the same as original. This is a game in which there are no enemies to defeat or problems to solve. Your only goal is to explore. Every time you play a new island is randomly generated. The island will have its own seasons, weather, and day/night cycles. There will also be some wildlife that will react to your presence in various ways. The soundtrack will react to your location (under a rain cloud, on top of a mountain, ect.).
This is a "walking simulator" game, and while I have no problem with walking simulator games per se (see my positive review of Dear Esther) I can't really recommend buying Proteus. The island of Dear Esther was interesting to explore because the graphics were AAA quality and the music was top notch. But Proteus suffers from low res pixel graphics (seen one pixelated tree, seen em all), a simplistic soundtrack, and the lack of interesting stuff to see. I played 20 minutes of Proteus and felt I had seen 95% of what the game had to offer; I felt no incentive to wait another 10 minutes to see what few changes the next season might bring.
Fortunately I paid just a few cents for it, and those 20 minutes I did play were enjoyable, so it wasn't a total wash. If you like exploration games and you see Proteus on sale for a few cents you might give it a try, but I wouldn't pay more than that.

Hey there guys, I'd like to start by saying Proteus  isn't for everybody. It is a game, despite what some people say, there is progression, story, and gameplay all involved, it just isn't imediately noticable. A big thing to note is the soundtrack. This aspect of the game is based entirely on what season it is in game, what the time of day is, and what creatures and structures are near you. The soundtrack is entirely unique, I've never seen anything like it. Next you have the visuals, it's sort of an 8-bit style on a 3D plane. It isn't voxel as the structures are flat. It's cool to look at, and provides an interesting atmosphere. Now, bare with me here, I'm going to talk about gameplay now. The  "gameplay" isn't orthodox by any means, but it's a unique exploration based sytem. As you explore the island, you'll notice certain landmarks of interest, giant trees, graveyards, shrines, fairy circles, etc., that all contribute to the story. Every night, you'll want to look for a ring of fireflies, step into them, and then the world will in turn change, the seasons will come and go, as will the faries. After so many repeats of this process, strange things will appear or happen on the island, I won't say more, but this is the gameplay. Not a conventional game, but I find it highly enjoyable as an exploration type game, and hope you will too. Please give Proteus a chance, it's worth one.

EVE Online is one of the best games I can think of that you don't actually have to play. In fact, to play the game is actually a detriment to it as it is, ultimately, an exercise in tedium and boredom.
From a graphical standpoint, the game is very nice. Ships are detailed and impressive, the factions are varied to an extent. For example, weapon types vary between the four, though that really doesn't matter much as you can use any ship and weapon if you train the right skills. Skills take real time to learn and there are a fair number to obtain before you can be reasonably capable of operating even the most basic ship types effectively.
Where the game trips is the actual game play. Doing anything in the game takes long periods of time - from earning ingame currency to performing any action like mining, production, etc. We've all seen the videos of massive wars being waged in the game, but this is the exception. 99.93% of the game has zero action - it's been called a spreadsheet simulator and that is fairly accurate. Even that is a bit of a misnomer as even this component is more tedious than it need be. Hell, I'm a CPA - my entire worklife is spreadsheets and I find the tedium ridiculous in this game. It is quite telling when just about anybody that plays EVE will admit that they play other games WHILE playing this one. That is not exactly a glowing recommendation for the game.
The only fun to be derived is from the player corporations (and associated meta-game) and ganking people for their goods. For the anarchist out there, that sounds super and for them, if they can stand the tedium that comes with it. For the rest with a semi-neutral toward good alignment, ths game is only an exercise in tedium and frustration.

Alright, here's the thing about this program. It's amazing. As an artist, I understand how much effort has to go into each tileset and character and musical score. It makes sense that it costs money to get things for it, and the amount it gives you with the base software is fantastic for what it is. Game development is hard. A lot of people will never finish their games when they buy this, or will make a little base-pack romp and wonder why it gets bad reviews, but that's not this software's fault. The resources are there to make something amazing with this. But it's a tool. It's like buying a workshop, which includes a simple birdhouse kit, and then cursing the tools for the fact that all you can build is the birdhouse. You gotta work for it. You have to buy more wood. You have to practice your sawcuts, you need to buy better paints and brushes so the colors can be cleaner and more vibrant. With that workshop, you can build anything, but if all you can see is that one birdhouse, it'll never be what you want it to be.

I've been playing EVE off and on since 2007 (not on Steam, hence the relatively low playtime) and I STILL struggle to explain it to people. Is it an amazing game? Yes. No other MMO does such an amazing job of making you feel like the in-game world is real because no other MMORPG lets the player population have such profound, far reaching control of that world.

Having said that, is EVE a game for everyone? No. While the producers have made it immensely easier for new players to gain a foothold in the game since I first started playing, the learning curve is still extremely steep. It can be a long time before you really understand what the game is and an even longer time before you no longer feel like a tiny, helpless fish in a giant sea.

The thing is, if you can get past that, EVE Online will absolutely blow you away. If you're curious, try it. There are tons of people who love this game and love helping new players get into it. The community is by far the best I've come across in gaming.

Based on almost a thousand hours of gameplay and study, I can say that Eve Online is a game with an acquired taste. That taste can range from an upper class citizen to the lowly dregs of society, but what do they have in common?
An untreated diagnosis of Moderate to Severe Psychosis and Sociopathic tendencies.
Now this isn't to say that ALL Eve players are like this, but most are. In this virtual realm they are known as " Carebears", according to the Pirate Hierarchy. Online interactions are of course not rated by the ESRB, and trash talking is common in various MMO's, but the level of detail to a response AGAINST PvP in a PvP-centric game is shocking.
Death Threats, Deviancy, Inclining Child Abuse, Inclining Physical abuse and threats of "hacking"(ISP detection, Keylogging, Apache log manipulation and Proxies) Racism, Botting, hate groups; CCP allows this as long it remains WITHIN THE PARAMETERS of the server client, and action is only taken when external applications and domains are used in violation of the EULA. They are Lax and exhibit Sloth behaviour, not a company I would want to subscribe to.
It is a game that might of had once noble intentions, is now a den of debauchery, void of good Etiquette, and a haven for the Mentally Insane allowed online.
Now one may retort, "But if you're spouting such inane frivoulties about these psychopaths and played for such a long time, aren't you one yourself then?", to which I reply by saying:
Emulation does not equal indoctrination. I can observe and blend in to delve into the psyche of these supposed "Carebears" when in fact it is the "Evil" pirates that are the Gentlemen and Women of New Eden. This isn't propaganda to say that you should be a pirate, if anything it's a red flag that this Sandbox game is More Linear than Theme Park MMO's such as WoW or SWTOR.
The pirate Hierarchy run this game, if you want to be a pirate, more power to you, you'll find some decent folk within their ranks.
If you want to do anything else (apart from marketing and trading, which can be done solo) you will reach a dead end by AFK mining, Grinding missions over and over again, redundant Planetary Interaction, Faction Warfare Plexing etc.
There is only one proper way to play EvE in its Canonical format: PvP
If you are looking for a narrative story, PvE, a safety net, and a nice Passive Atmosphere, I suggest you find another Space Simulator.

Preface: I have a little over a hundred games in my library, and I've only reviewed the few that really stand out (around 5 of them). I only say this because I may not be as well or long spoken as most reviewers and I feel like the previous statement helps show my feelings.
Review: I LOVE this game. It has everything I want out of a survial game(my favorite genre). The basic human needs are fairly realistic and at times very hard to fufill, and it has great resource management. At the beginning of the game you have a windfall of low level items which at first seems great Ex. "Oh cool A chest with 6 guns in it!" Within about an hour of gameplay you will have either burned through the weapons or cannabalized them for research. Eventually you can nearly automate certain aspects of production and research, but you'll probably die/lose waaaaay before that. Even when you are flush with food, medicine, and weaponry, your generator is forever dying so you have to scurry around the increasingly dangerous ruins of mars to scrounge up scrap and chips to research better power cores. And with two trees of tech (which doesn't sound like a lot, but it is) to keep up with you have to manage two different resource pools, one which you can farm or mine for, and another that requires mass slaughtering of infected beasts and men. After about a week you'll be fat and full of snacks and soda but you can die from a minor infection while on the short train ride back to your safehouse, or even worse, open a bathroom stall in a fairly safe area and be smashed to smithereens by a brute (Those are the first two ways I died, but have been followed by increasingly scarier deaths).
On top of all that, you have to manage your warmth and oxygen levels when you are in most areas which is a real struggle. After a certain point you have to make some serious decisions example: You see a room full of candy wrappers and medicine chests, but in the way is a spider and a weak mutant. Not hard to deal with. BUT you know that you are running low on power charges, and if your flashlight goes out this shopping mall will be your tomb.  By the same token you have a broken leg and are bleeding out and you know that chest might have the cast or bandages you need if you need to turn tail and flee. What do you do? It doesn't matter because in the 10 seconds you were deciding you get torn open from behind. You try to dodge, but uh oh, your leg is broken so you can only walk! You whirl around and fire your shotgun 5 times into your foe. He splatters across the ground. Relief washes over you, but you are now crippled and gushing blood like a stuck pig. The blood and gun blasts alerts the spider and the mutant. As you get ready to face your death, guns blazing, you die from blood loss. Game over. *or you die from hypothermia, or suffocation, starvation, dehydration, or infection ect ect*
So now you're dead. You can load an earlier save! Whoopee! OR not. Which is another excellent feature. The game gives you the choice of difficulty(nothing new here) and permadeath mode! Now, I'm guessing 90% of people won't tinker with these but if, like me, you want to be afraid and high on adrenaline while you play because you put in 20 hours of gameplay and every door you open might be your last, then ramp up those settings, baby. Side note: I'm not particularly fast or good at these games, but I like them to be really hard because that's way more exciting and realistic.

As to negatives: None (at least none worth mentioning) I've seen people complaining(a lil bit) about graphics, music, and some things not being explained well enough. Personally I don't find any of these flaws to be real. The graphics aren't super HD, but that doesn't really matter with a top down game. Everything is very very clear and easy to distinguish and the lighting and view are very good as well. As far as music, I don't notice it at all. If you're activley listening to the music instead of playing the game, you aren't playing on a hard enough difficulty :D. And as far as things being explained, it is ALL explained at the beginning in bite sized pieces. You find great bits of stories around the game too. If you're paying even a little bit of attention to the story, you'll find really rewarding data logs all over the place. My favorite being a log from someone named "Martin" To his friend who is sent to scavenge for some equipment in the mine. He is warned up and down not to veer off the path to sate his lust for choco pie. You'll find more logs, detailing how this guy (of course) veered off his task, following his nose for pie. Eventually....well, let's just say you find him and his pie. No spoilers, but it's rewarding to follow stories like these.
All in all, I've played close to 40 hours in three days and I'm about as far as I was at hour 10 because I keep effing dying (:D). But that could have been easily avoided. So I give this game a 9(ish) out of 10. Which is how I would rate skyrim and Fallout New Vegas....maybe Terraria too. All excellent games. I'm not super far into the game, so I don't know if it will yield the hundreds of hours of gameplay like those games did for me, but I wouldn't be shocked if it came close. A piece of advice for when (not if) you get the game, be careful. And most of all, expect to be surprised. Most of the times I died I thought I was nigh invincible right up until my head was squashed. Anyways, GET TO IT!!!

A fantastic fighter, especially if you are a fan of the manga or show and even if your not. ****Transmission Error's or not.**** Scroll to the comments section to for transmission error fix.
-- Singleplayer --
If you're someone like me who can't sit through 15 seasons of filler and slow paced talking scenes the game does a great job of filling you in on most of what's happened without eating up months of your free time. Even if you have been watching or reading though it also gives you the option of picking the "Legend" route on certain fights to experience things differently; a great alternative to experiencing the same thing you've seen before but still progressing. The cut scenes are fantastically done and the option for the Japanese vocal track is always nice as I for one will punch someone if I hear Naruto say "Believe it!" one more time. Of course you are still forced to play as certain characters for certain parts that aren't always fun. Some of the boss battles can also be down right cheap, the final one for instance but hey, you only have to do it once and that's a small price to pay for how much fun is packed in there.
-- General --
Now for me considering I haven't played an Ultimate Ninja game before this was a welcome change from the Clash of Ninja fighting games, the cinematic, epic feel of every battle and the sheer complexity of the mechanics was something I wasn't expecting from an Anime fighter. If your looking for a little one on one kick-assery this is a fantastic place to land your feet. It is a little sad that you can't play even a tag mode or something similar, the complete lack of co-operative fighting does seem like an oversight considering how entertaining it could be and considering it's something Clash of Ninja has had since the get-go.
One more key thing to point out as well is the sheer amount of content here, holy crap the content. There is the massive Story Mode, the bonus Challenge Mode with 100 battles to complete, Survival Mode, Tournament Mode, the regular VS Mode and of course Online Mode. That's a a lot of things to clear. There is also an almost obsurd amount of collectables to unlock and purchase from Titles for your online Ninja Card to Ultimate Jutsu Demonstrations. The game contains 89 (correct me if I'm wrong) playable characters with only a few available as support only, as well as several characters having different costumes. Not counting same movelist, different costumes that seven versions of Sasuke to play as, rejoice Uchiha fans. It will take a while to unlock every character mind you but that can be done by either playing and earning money or clearing the entirety of the massive story mode. So if you don't like running through the sometimes tedious boss battles and the like, just hop into VS mode and beat the crap out of your friends. Which brings us to the biggest problem - I didn't say the game was perfect.
-- Multiplayer --
The game does a decent job of balancing the massive roster but at the end of the day, some characters are just down right overpowered and cheap. Which can be a problem unless you happen to have mastered the game and the other person hasn't. Roughly 60% of the matches you play online will either be against the ultimate form of Naruto, Minato or Itachi and there's a reason for that. Not that the cheap characters are unbeatable but unless you're also a high tier character prepare to have an annoyingly difficult fight; oh Itachi your crows will haunt my nightmares. Of course this being said it's not the end of the world by any means. If your fighting your friends or just playing for fun it probably won't bother you and overpowered characters is something you should be expecting going into a fighter with such a massive roster that isn't aiming to be a serious competition game. Virtua Fighter this is not.
****-- Multiplayer Section 2 --**** Scroll to the comments section to for transmission error fix.
Another key thing I have to draw attention to is something that has been completely "broken" about this game since launch: Transmission Error's. For those of you who don't know what this is, it's a disconnection error that occurs in most matches played online, example: I have played roughly 350 matches online, completing only 120 of them. While Namco-Bandai has assured us they are working on it, it has been present since launch and still isn't fixed. They have released a NA only patch for the game that, to it's credit did work somewhat, but instead of getting disconnected in some games we are presented with a slow down kind of lag and even then, sometimes are disconnected anyways. Assuming they do, at some point fix the issue the game will be downright fantastic but until then, the loyal fan base is left raging every match until you fight someone 30 times because it doesn't disconnect you for once.
-- Final Thoughts --
All in all it's not a perfect game and until they sort out the transmission errors in the online portion, it will be broken for those seeking to use it. However, it still retains a fighting experience that you simply can't get somewhere else. Trying to end an epic battle with an Ultimate Jutsu is so much fun and that terrible moment when you chakra dash right into someone elses costing you the match, leaving you yelling out curses; barely coming out of a match on top thanks to a well timed awakening and realizing you lost by 1/8th a heath bar to Rock Lee and you didn't land a hit on him. Moments like these make you forget about the shortcomings of the game.
If your looking for a solid fighter pick it up and prepare to lose the next few weeks of your life, and bring some friends. If your looking for a competitive fighting experience, best to wait till the fix the online before investing. But either way, buy it at some point, it's worth the money.

While I have played countless games throughout my life, this is the only time I want to say that I recommend it. Being a developer myself, and preparing for releasing one of my games on Steam, there are many things we notice in a game that most people usually do not. Whilst this is not exactly a good thing, it gives us the possibility for a far more deep evaluation.
I must say that the most impeccable present thing within the game are not the characters. It's not the scenery. It's not the dialogue. But the music. The soundtrack. Once you start play the game, at each episode, when the intro music comes out and a slow scene starts to open, you'll notice that it could NOT fit any better. There was NOT a single second I didn't treasure while the music was playing at the beginning of each episode.
The focus of this game is the humour. And I don't even know how to start. I'm hard to be pleased, but it is impossible to not notice the amount of work and intelligence put on the humorous scenes. You can't play this game without feeling inside a Borderlands game. It REALLY does the universe some justice. And it gives a great ending to a well deserving villain from Borderlands. This game has SERIOUS effects on the plot, I wonder how it will affect the next Game.
To put it short, if you are a fan of the series, or like the Telltale's way of storytelling, or are looking for 'something more', you should get this game. If you are looking for seeing characters you've played before in Borderland 1 and 2, you should get this game. If you are looking for some good laughs, you should get this game. If you didn't like any of the previous Telltale's games you've played, then you should wait for a discount, but you definetly should try this one. I'm sure it's one of their best so far.

Risen 1 was not that good of a game. There were few objectives other than just wondering around and not dying. The landscape didn't really change. The quests were repetitive.  And you played 99% of the game by yourself with no help from NPCs.
Risen 2 made huge strides.  Suddenly you had objectives and travelling companions.  The NPCs were unique and interesting. I saw many of the elements that made KOTR, DAO Baldurs Gate and even Mass Effect great:  The concept of having a ship/stronghold and seeking out and finding NPCs to form a crew/party capable of taking on some monumental task.  In the process you visit different lands that showcase very different environments, keeping the game from getting boring.  At the end of the day, I can say that I would replay Risen 2 a second time, and that says a lot for a game.
So when I saw Risen 3, I bought it hoping for something at least as good and hopefully better than Risen 2. Sadly I was disappointed.  You are no longer playing as the same nameless protagonist that you played in Risen 1 and 2.  Instead you are playing as the brother of the protagonists love interest.  And instead of being educated and well spoken, like someone who could just as easily be a mage or a pirate, the protagonist is a typical pirate thug. One of the games themes is overcoming your thuggish nature...
You still have a ship. You still have to gather NPCs and you still get to visit different lands, but it is not fun playing a jerk. I figured there would be a reason why they forced this on me. A plot twist or something special about being related to Steelbeard that was key to the plot.  But it never happens. At the end of the game, I said to myself, "There is no reason I could not have been the protagonist from Risen 1 and 2".
Regardless of the plot twists or other RPG elements they incorporate, this is one choice they take away from you is simply unforgivable. And since the love interest from game 2 is your sister, there is zero romance and flirting. An element that made most of the other big hit titles I mentioned so successful.
So no, I can't recommend this to people. Even if it was free, you are looking at wasting 40+ hours of your life that you will never get back.

Gunpoint is a 2D puzzle-platformer whose gameplay revolves around stealth and hacking. The game's protagonist is Richard Conway, a casual private investigator who sports a trench coat and high-tech slacks that allow him to jump incredible distances. Using his PDA, which doubles as the game's menu, Conway exchanges messages with a number of oddball characters who offer assignments involving data theft and corporate espionage. Each assignment is basically the same: infiltrate a building, find a computer, and get out without getting spotted by security.
Stealth in Gunpoint is simple enough: stay out of armed guards' line of sight or else suffer a swift, one-shot kill. The hacking mechanic is more complex, involving the use of gadgets to manipulate or rewire electronic devices found throughout each level. Everything from switches and security cameras to hand scanners and trapdoors can be adapted for Conway's own use. Using the Crosslink tool, the player may forge new circuits out of a level's existing connections-- a light switch, for example, can be rewired to open and close a security door.
Things get interesting when levels require the player to create a hierarchy of links. Because some devices operate on different circuits, and some devices can only be used by guards, it is not always enough to link a switch to a door. Sometimes an activated motion camera needs to disable a room's power, causing a guard to fiddle with a light switch, which opens a trapdoor that drops an enemy to his death. Timed elements exist as well, requiring the player to create more sophisticated circuits-- such as an elevator that disables a different security system with each floor it passes. There are countless solutions to each challenge, and it can be a lot of fun tinkering with different connections, creating infinite loops and massive, level-wide circuits. And if you get overwhelmed, you can simply knock out the guards for an easy run. Of course, this will result in a much lower end-level score, delaying you access to new gadgets and upgrades.
Fans of pixel art will love the attention to detail in Gunpoint. The blue-grey color scheme, perpetual rainfall, and sleazy jazz soundtrack create the perfect setting for a neo-noir video game. Tight controls make it easy to move Conway around, and thanks to simple drag-and-drop hacking, experimenting with circuits is a breeze. And for those moments when experimentation goes horribly wrong, Gunpoint features one of the best autosave systems I have seen. Whenever Conway dies, the player may choose to rewind the level a particular number of seconds, so that their bad decisions can be erased without losing too much progress.
Though Gunpoint is a bit short, it's an entertaining and cohesive experience. It's impressive to see such a polished game come from the hands of a single designer (except for the music, Tom Francis created everything in Gunpoint-- from the coding and animation to the pixel art and script). And the fact that Francis has made nearly all of his work transparent on his development blog-- the “Suspicious Developments Manifesto” -- shows that he cares more about supporting a culture of quality games than earning a buck. It would be nice to see more game studios following Francis' example.
TL;DR -- Creative hacking mechanics and a witty, pixel-art detective story.

Borderlands, the first of the series, is probably also its best. With hundreds of hours of playability and a unique loot system, this title has merged traditional RPG elements and impressive first person shooting into one great ball of squishy carnage.
Each of the playable characters has something special to offer and gives the player a different experience each time. While one gets the feeling that Gearbox wasn’t overly interested in developing the rich story of Pandora in this episode, it lays down perfectly the foundations for the events in the games to come.
Let’s talk about loot. There are literally millions of guns, shields, grenades and class-mods to hunt down through the two play-throughs, making it ever more exciting when you finally get a gold rarity weapon, or even better a pearlescent one.
Character development in this game is brilliant, if not a little overwhelming at first. Besides the skill-trees which have dominated their other FPS titles, the first Borderlands also offers the development of a player’s weapon proficiency (sadly missing from the sequels), which means the more you use a specific class of gun, the better you get at wielding it.
Finally, the 4 DLC additions give the game new and exciting worlds to play in, cataclysmic weapons and gear and challenging enemies which will really test the player’s skill and intelligence.

(Writing this after playing Episode 0 and 1 and waiting for the rest)
Fantastic piece of interactive fiction.
I love interactive fiction like "Spider and Web" and this game brings the genre to a whole new level with amazing voice acting.
As a hacker, you control your environment with text commands and computer interfaces while constantly talking with your partner.
It is hard to believe how frightened you can get when hearing your partner screaming for help while not being actually able to see what is going on. This is Stephen King level of scary. No jump-scares involved, just claustrophobic atmosphere and amazing voice acting.
The story has nice slow pacing. With couple of conversations, voice recordings and tons of emails we start to explore the vision of future where people are just starting to colonize other planets. You even have small pieces of data on politics.
Cracking passwords based on personal information, man in the middle attacks and hopping through network are very nice mechanics that fit very well with hacker-vibe. Other puzzles are also quite rewarding to solve.
It is not a perfect game and definitely not for everyone. It is easy to get lost with all new characters, especially given that you don't even have a picture for them while they are talking. With holo lenses and all that advanced tech, we could at least snap a photo to show it to player :)
Some puzzles require just typing stuff fast enough which can be frustrating even with all the game help like "autocomplete", but they are not too bad and make you actually feel the rush.
I feel that this game could be perceived similarly to "Life is Strange". If player likes to get into characters, both games can be very emotional and can be easily 9/10. Other people just can't stand them. I am definitely in the first group :)
I just hope that all the strange mysteries will have a nice conclusion, unlike for example in the "Lost" series.
9/10, keep up the good work!

My name is Trigger, of the Ruairi server.  I'm well known in the community, even across servers, for effectively codifying the proper use of
's Magic skill set with a comprehensive guide that underwent many, many revisions over the years (and which is still referenced and quoted to this day).  I played for over six years and sank countless thousands of dollars into the game.
is my most-played video game of all time by a nigh-incomprehensibly-large margin (just not on the Steam version, which will explain the lack of hours logged here).  I've shrugged off changes that have made similarly-tenured players quit.  And as a relatively respected player whose advice carried significant weight with newbies and old-timers alike, I have one thing to say.


's combat was originally, at its core, a rock-paper-scissors system.  Normal melee strikes are deflected by the Defense skill.  Defense can be broken with Smash.  Smash is not as fast as normal melee and will always be trumped by it.  This, combined with many different enemy AI patterns, required players to be able to read the enemy's movements well in advance and react with appropriate timing, because all attacks carry some degree of stun and enough consecutive attacks will knock a player backward.  In the original release and for some time thereafter, tanking was completely non-viable because player health was vastly outclassed by enemy damage potential, requiring
combatant to be adept at reading and reacting to enemy movements and encouraging the then-commonly-espoused battle philosophy of "don't get hit".

In the early game, this system is still mostly apparent and functions as intended.  But a number of problems have cropped up over the years that make the game's overall combat functionality less strategic and as a result less unique (and if you've not played
, yes, its original combat system literally has not been replicated anywhere else, despite its brilliance).  I will attempt to outline what I view as the most egregious of these problems below.

Mabinogi
There is an in-universe justification for the player's rise to near-godlike power, although I won't spoil it on the off chance you disregard my advice and play this game anyway.  But despite power creep actually having a treasured position in the lore (and despite its being a
good plot point), it has still negatively impacted the game in more ways than one.

The combat system underwent an overhaul back in the summer of 2012, which you may read my at-the-time opinion of
.  It was an inherently good update, and I thought it would force Nexon to consider their poor handling of the difficulty curve more seriously.  Sadly, they've done nothing but exacerbate the problem.  More and more skills keep getting added to the game with absolutely no substantial increases in content breadth or depth to match.  Since almost all skills grant permanent stats when upgraded, and since many skill sets rely on the same stats as other sets (allowing indirect upgrading of already-maxed skills), and since there are
now, there will come a point at which a player is no longer challenged by
the game has to offer.  In a game whose combat was originally defined by strategy and skill, and wherein a properly skilled player could take out a far bigger and stronger monster with ease, "difficulty" is now represented by monsters with bigger health bars and higher damage output, and virtually all of them can be laughed at upon reaching a certain power threshold, completely removing all strategy requirements from combat and reducing it to mindless grinding.
It served its purpose well in the original release -- for instance, bears and goblins were both notorious for using deceptive tactics to bait players into reacting incorrectly.  Most enemies can handle melee, magic, and archery attacks with relatively good reaction patterns.  Attacking an enemy more than once with a bolt spell or a normal bow shot, for instance, will almost always cause the enemy to charge at you directly, reducing the effectiveness of spamming, especially in the cases of fast and ultra-fast monsters.  Once alchemy was added to the game, the original AI crumbled and never recovered.  Enemies have never once had their behavior patterns updated to handle new offensive techniques or new skill sets.  They are still operating on their original AI, all of them.  If you start out focusing on melee skills initially, you'll receive a decent portion of the game's original challenge level.  If you choose something like Puppetry or Dual Guns, you will completely outsmart the AI merely by virtue of the weapons and skills you'll be using.  It isn't a total slam dunk, as most skills start out with low damage and the AoEs all start with relatively small areas of effect, but the enemy AI will still have no idea how to handle them.

This was unfortunately necessary, as the constant piling on of more and more skill sets left newcomers hopelessly behind the curve of the experienced players (and since this game has no level cap and no class system, there was no way for them to ever catch up).  The changes to leveling speed have aided everyone, though, not just the newbies, and thus the problem remains unsolved, having merely shifted in a certain direction.  Newcomers can attain a decent power level much more easily and with far less fuss than they could originally, but by the same token the old dogs can effortlessly blaze through new skill sets in a week or less, leaving anyone beyond a certain point utterly content-starved.

In case you didn't catch this in one of the previous paragraphs,
Most of the new skill sets have been added for very little reason other than bigger, badder, flashier attacks (going hand-in-hand with the attempt to shift the game's demographic from fantasy fans over to lovers of everything vapid, flashy, and hollow), and as already mentioned, enemies simply can't handle the newer stuff.  Anything designed with previous content in mind is
outclassed by the next batch of skills.
-----
That about wraps up my deconstruction of
's many current flaws, all of which contributed to my leaving the game and none of which have thus far been addressed.  I don't expect any of them to ever
addressed, either, because Nexon's Korean development team basically just develops for the Korean users, and the players on the North American servers get whatever Korea gets.  If you play this game,
You will exist merely as a cash grab for Nexon.

There are other major gripes I could have laid at Nexon's feet here, including their
overpriced cash shop, their habit of releasing a bundle of new outfits in gachapon and calling it a "content update", their poor community management, their
(of which the linked blog post is hardly the only example), and much more besides.  I tolerated all of the above for over six years because
was once a giant among MMORPGs, schooling the rest with unique mechanics and satisfying gameplay.  It's now a shadow of its former self, and it does not deserve your attention.

Crossout is a game similar to robocraft with a mad max type of feeling (wasteland) and most of the PvP is capturing a point or killing all enemies. I felt underpowered against other players because I had no idea what to do but after a bit and learning my playstyle, I was better or on par with the rest.
If you do get this game, know that all weapons can do a very good job at certain things and while you may have trouble versing a vehicle with a specific primary weapon, the learning of handling these opponents becomes better and better as you play. Everyone says that drones are OP, but they are only OP because players ignore them and shoot the drone leader (which usually has a lot of health because the drones don't get destroyed) or their cannons can't hit the little buggers. Also, drones don't aim for weapons or fuel barrels, they aim for the main core of the vehicle oh and lets not forget the autocannons. You can aim and they can destroy drones and weapons usually in one shot so don't say drones OP, drones have a hard counter.
Each weapon in crossout can be easily countered by another weapon and that diversity is great. I personally play drones and unguided rockets because I like seeing things blow up or try to kill me even when my drones are firing at them hehehe! All in all, it is worth a try and the devs are still updating the game to make the experience better. I hope they keep this insane damage though because having every vehicle seem like a glass cannon is entertaining to me knowing I could blow up at any moment XD (also the sounds are REALLY good on the weapons from firing, to hitting parts on a car, to hitting the ground)
I will warn you though, people HATE drones when they fight you and they will usually prioritize you if they remember your name for next match. Also people quit because their weapons get shot off so I will say this, BUILD AROUND YOUR WEAPONS TO KEEP THEM SAFE FROM ENEMY FIRE AND SHOOT DRONES BEFORE THE VEHICLE OTHERWISE YOU WILL LEAVE AN ANGRY DRONE REVIEW.
