Heavily recommended game! And the following play-through should make you either highly appalled or very interested:
- Started off with a monkey as a pet. Named her "Butters", but later on my pet monkey took a liking to another guy named Bones. It made me a tiny bit sad.
- Built a nice settlement, made the entire surroundings and buildings out of the easiest findable supply around: wood.
- Ended up with 5 villagers after having successfully defended our 'village' a couple of times and converted 2 of the pirate prisoners to join our cause. They eventually did.
(I'm skipping the story about the micromanagement and supply hoarding business - you'll learn about this on the spot yourself.)
- I thought I had things going smoothly. Perhaps a bit too flawless. Characters got along well and two of them actually married eachother early on. It was a joyful moment for Bones and Greta. Bones had a dislike for clothes, so he was always running around naked which was not appreciated by some. But apparently he had a passion for farming and was well endowed. Greta took the earliest opportunity and showed him some loving. Greta was listed as a lazy and weapon hating person, but not too lazy to chase down some 'bone'. Good for her.
- My self created character, named Adante, was a tireless fat miner and the other two people named Dorothy and Hunter were your average run of the mill converted prisoners from earlier battles. Dorothy could cook up some decent meals and Hunter, well, as the name implies, he was hunting down the animals for the food to make nice meals mixed up with the harvested crops from our farms. Luxurious and plentiful meals of variety. Even salt was added for flavour.
But then an event changed the atmosphere quite rapidly:
- A nasty cobra snuck into the settlement and had its fangs set on Butters, the pet Monkey, and I did not notice as I was looking to mine some shizzle.
- They battled eachother like no tomorrow and the fight lasted quite long because by the time I had actually noticed, the pet monkey had all her limbs bitten off by the snake and was crying for help while still being pounded by the Cobra.
- The sound of the monkey cries... it still traumatizes me to this day.
- Bones probably noticed long before I did, but hey, he loves being naked and probably didn't want to risk being bitten in dangling places so did nothing to help out.
- Hunter, however, eventually shot & killed the cobra before it could put a killing blow on the poor limbless cryin' monkey.
- Butters was then picked up by Hunters, carried and put in Bones' room to keep him comfortable with some painkillers while we figure out a way to get his limbs back. There are ways in this game to do so, be it four wooden pegs or made out of other technology, but it takes some craftmanship to pull this off.
- By the time that we've managed to construct these, an electric storm came down on the settlement as if it was telling us: YOUR INTENTIONS ARE NOBLE BUT THE MONKEY MUST DIE!
(Now, here's a lesson I've learned: Never make your ENTIRE settlement out of wood.)
- The storm caused fire to start and spread like wildfire.
- All villagers were alerted and commanded to extinguish the fire.
- The fire became so intense, and spread from the storages and houses straight to the farm area (and all over the entire map, all animals and trees on the entire map were burned alive.)
- Now, the house in which Butters was still 'recovering' was also hit by the fire. I sent my main character Adante to help out but the fire enclosed the area in a rapid speed. My fat miner and his slow jigglywiggly runs could not win that race by a long shot. He was a hauler, not a speedy gonzalez.
- Butters, the poor cursed monkey, just shrieked and screamed her lungs out when the fire was getting closer and closer after every second.
- So within seconds, we could hear the cries again, of a pet Monkey. Not only in pain from snake bites and losing all limbs before, but now also jumping by the belly up & down inside her once comfortable pet-bed, being on fire.
- Every villager probably had tears in the eyes from that whole ordeal once the fire started demanding the limbless body and a Monkey fighting for the last breath of her life.
- I made Bones, since he's supposedly the new master of Butters, go into the flames and try to retrieve the monkey while the plan was to let him carry the monkey into the water at a nearby lake.
- This turned Bones into a running naked man carrying a limbless monkey across the settlement, while both being on fire.
- The outcome of this is probably easy to guess. They burned together, into (what it seemed) a neverending sea of flames and emotion.
- I ordered all my other villagers to stand in the water of the lake and wait out the fire frenzy. They were all depressed and Greta simply lost it and ran into the firesea on her own accord due to severe depression.
After the fire died, I stopped playing and told the story to my girlfriend. Her eyes opened wide and then the question came: "What kind of f***ed up game is that?"

This is a fantastic game. The gameplay loop works very well, and you always feel pressure to just. keep. playing.
The research and manufacturing are awesome, the design of the self-contained mars colony makes a lot of sense, and it's neat to go to all the doomed places and find logs about the goings-on. It may not be a new thing, but Im a sucker for audio/text logs in games. I also love how the main character will point out things and give his opinion. It really helps sell that the Mars colony was a working, successful place, and not just a huge investment of money, tech, and personel that was doomed to fail.
The base-building/crafting aspects are fun as well. The constant battle, sometimes literally, to keep the power on is stressful enough to give a creeping sense of dread and pushing you to make inprovements and use your time well, without becoming an irritating slog of a task. And I love that West is like...."why are there 3 open tunnels 'accidentaly' full of radioactive waste that leave the reactor open to attack.....i dont think this was an accident"
Add to that the constant creeping increase of infection; requiring every excursion to have more and more prep, wich takes more time, which causes a greater spread! The enemies types and behaiviors are pretty basic, but it gives a great sense of mastery over them once you get the pattern down. And those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that can open doors never make it easy.
Requirements for food, drink, and rest are pretty balanced on the normal difficulty. It never feels unreasonable based on how much time is passing in game, and supplies are scarce but not unobtainable. I really appreiciate that items spawn semi-sensibly. It makes looting a lot easier than like: "Look at all these guns in the vending machine!"
One of my only negatives is that it's not well explained that the research and manufacturing stations share a chip type. I went about 15 hours without the 2nd level bio stuff and on a standard nano-repairer because it wasn't really explained that some things share software. I thought I had to find all the upgrades individually. Maybe that's just me though.
Overall a game with tons of content and an interesting idea that is well executed and overall very fun. I played my first 20 hours in 2 days!

So let me tell you, I have been binging everything point-and-click thanks to Life is Strange. I was not a fan of point-and-click games whatsoever. I thought the genre died along with Monkey Island, years ago. It was always a genre I believed was completely niche, and had no place on the mainstream market. Something that "had zero gameplay" and "no substance". Wow, I can now write this and say that, I was completely, and utterly wrong, and I apologise to these great developers who create, what I believe to now be, Triple-A titles. Which brings me to this title today, Tales from the Borderlands. When this title was announced back in 2013, there were many questions to ask. Was this going to be another Borderlands Pre-Sequel? Was Telltale about to re-invent Borderlands? Or were they about to do what people thought was impossible? Take an already established, well recognised, and hugely poplar franchise, turn it on it's head and make it into an awesome, story driven adventure?
Right from the start, we're placed in the middle of the story and introduced to the first of two protagonists in this tale. We meet Rhys (Voiced by the ever talented, and awesome Troy Baker), the Hyperion office lackey, who is trying anything and everything in his power to rise-up in the ranks to rule Helios, just like his hero, Handsome Jack. We establish that this story is after the events of Borderlands 2 here, and for those who have not completed Borderlands 2, there may be some spoilers ahead here, so you may want to look away now. Being promised a promotion from former Senior Vice President Saul Henderson, Rhys makes his way to accept said promotion, only to find that his office had been overtaken by Rhys' arch rival, Hugo Vasquez (Voiced by Puddy himself, Patrick Warburton). An egotistical, power-hungry, selfish prick of a boss, who is doing everything he can to keep you out of his way, and out of the picture. And just like any leader of the Hyperion, Vasquez is organising a real shady deal between himself, and a gang of Vault hunters down on Pandora, to acquire a vault key. Rhys taps in on this deal, and decides that he's going to go after Vasquez's deal, with a little help from his friend, Vaughn (Voiced by Nerdist CEO and Comedian, Chris Hardwick).
But as it's always been said, there are two sides of every tale. And while Rhys is planning to extract revenge on Vasquez, he has no clue that he's about to be screwed out on the deal by the second antagonist of this awesome title, Fiona (Played by Critical Role's own, Laura Bailey). The ultimate gunslinger, con-artist, who has the skill to talk her way out of, and into almost anything. She is guided by her mentor Felix, who is revealed to be the brains behind the scam, designing a fake vault key to be delivered to the Hyperion for a nice sum of cash. The deal is met by a mid-man, August (Voiced by Uncharted's Nolan North) and his partner, Sasha, who plan on delivering the goods to the Hyperion. And from here, all hell breaks loose, and you are thrown right into this amazing tale, where it's all-for-one, and none-for-all. Along the way, you meet an array of characters, that if you have played the Borderlands series before, will leave you with a range of emotions, from smiles to speechless, but we won't spoil that for you.
The title adapts right from the source material from it's artistic design. You do get the feeling that you have landed in the world of Borderlands playing this title, with the amazing cell shaded experience you would usually see in the shooter. With the title being overlooked by 2K Games, Telltale do their original character designs justice, making you believe that these characters have been canon to this series the whole time, and really do belong with the origin story of Borderlands. It does not feel forced at all. And we do get our callback characters placed within this title, like the obvious Handsome Jack, who is just as devious, cunning, and hilarious as he was in the main series. Jack's mysterious design stems to his storyline from Borderlands 2, meaning that this title makes Jack's storyline now canon within the Telltale world. So if you wanted to find out what happened to Jack after Borderlands 2, well this is it.
Now if you haven't played any Telltale games in the past, for your fear of them "Boring point-and-click games", fear not. I realise that point-and-click titles may not be for everyone, but this is a game that needs your attention. I'm talking to you, hardcore Borderlands fan. It may not be a shooter, but it's still the story that you need to know. Point-and-click titles like this show that if enough though it put into it's design, it can be quite an intuitive experience too. Not all games within the genre have to be as simple as choosing your own path, but can use it's design like quicktime events, to master it's genre, and become one-of-a-kind. Now, much like any other Telltale title, choosing your path in this game will result in some dire consequences, so be sure to choose wisely here. It will always have an impact on your result at the end, and may bite you on your♥♥♥♥♥too.
Music has always been awesome in the Borderlands universe. From Borderlands' title theme "Ain't No Rest for the Wicked" by Cage The Elephant, to the Pre-Sequels "Come with me Now" by Kongos. We get quality choice of theme music for each five episodes from this epic. Artists include Jungle, Twin Shadow, The Rapture, James Blake, and First Aid Kit. Each episodes title sequence has music to capture the vibe of the story perfectly, and places you in the mood. Personally, Episode Four's intro gave me chills from the first note hitting my ears, with it's perfectly synced visuals, and it's meaning behind it all. Just fantastic choices all round. The official soundtrack designed for the title was created by Gearbox Audio Lead Raison Varner, Cris Velasco, Jesper Kyd, Sascha Dikiciyan and Sonic Mayhem. In an interview with
, Varney stated "Jesper handled all the largest areas in the game where the player would spend a lot of time exploring. Sascha and Cris really nailed the bandit’s sound early on so they provided the aggressive bandit music. I would provide some music for boss battles and other environments that didn’t fit into that model exactly."
All-in-all, Tales from the Borderlands is a must play title. It's available on every current gen platform, Mac and PC. You may shrug this one off, and that's fine. But I'm telling you that it's your loss if you do. This title here, has everything that you are looking for in an adventure game. Amazing story, interesting characters, awesome design, a sensational soundtrack, an amazing voice cast that you would usually find in mainstream titles like The Last of Us, and fantastic gameplay. Yes, I said it. It may be a point-and-click, but it has amazing gameplay. Gameplay that keeps you on the edge of your seat, wanting more. I guarantee you, by the end of this game, you're going to want to run to Telltale's twitter, begging them for a second season. What is great though is that you can, and you will go back into this game multiple times, and change your story around for a completely different experience.
Tales from the Borderlands is a game that deserves a whole lot more attention than it's targeted market, the Telltale fans, and the Borderlands fans. Even if you haven't played any of the previous Borderlands titles, don't fret, it's a game you can play too without any prior knowledge. I will always say that, purely storyline driven titles are hard to write reviews on, but this one was easy. Just the way everything was well crafted and put together for this amazing ride, is one I will soon not forget. The Story, the characters, the amazing sequences, that had me wanting to see more amazing sequences, gripping me on the edge of my seat, wanting more. Tales from the Borderlands will be a game, that will forever be etched in my memory, as one of the best

Subterrain: Fight zombified people and alien creatures on Mars. Now why does that sound familiar?
In all seriousness though, that is pretty much the only similarity between Subterrain and Doom, minus your reliance on the flashlight if you count Doom 3...
Subterrain is a survival horror game with an empathsis on the survival part: You'll need to maintain your daily needs of food, water, rest and toilet visits, whilst also contending with a space station that's crumbling alongside its former inhabitants. Power to the different places on the station is limited, and that's including your base, so don't leave all the lights on everywhere, because you'll be using every scrapt of electricity to travel and survive.
Luckily, you'll have the basic equipment necessary for surviving soon after you escape your prison cell, including weapons, a power pack, and containers of oxygen and heat for when you delve into the broken station. Run dry on any of these and you'll soon wish you'd planned ahead a little better.
But basic equipment is not going to suffice forever, so you'll have to grab your old tools and destroy them in order to be able to research and improve them. But you can't research more advanced equipment with basic computers, so you'll have to find plans and blueprints to improve your facilities to keep up with the times. And of course, you can't build something from nothing, so do like I do: Pick up every little bit of rubbish you can and recycle them into more useful stuff.
I can go on and on about how this game works, because this is a complex game; probably the most complex survival game I've played in a long time. This means that you'll have to be prepared for some mental gymnastics to keep up with everything that's going on. It's not easy, but if you've got experience with survival games you'll probably be okay.
Frankly, I can't recommend this game enough. It's not for casual players, but it's very rewarding to manage everything you come across. Just be mindful: Most of the levels are randomised, so while that means every game is a new experience, it'll also mean that just because you know where something is now, that doesn't mean you'll know where it is next time. This also applies to the facility upgrades. Consider yourself lucky if you can find improved research and production blueprints early on, because those will likely be the most important facilities you'll have.
With all that said, I'm going to go and put my head in a bucket of water to cool down now. See ya next time!
Edit::
I found the BFG! Well it's called a plasma launcher, but come on! Slow projectile, big explosion on impact, destroys most smaller enemies; it's the BFG!
I also discovered a few things about the maps. It seems that the first level of every district is consistant on every playthrough, including the Station Hub and the facilities, meaning it's not completely randomly generated levels.
Also, while I'm at it: I said before that the facility upgrades were placed randomly across the game? Well, I was half right. The upgrades will be placed on a random level in most cases, but they're consistant in which district they appear. For example, the Lvl 2 Research upgrade will always be located in Viking Lane, though on which level is prone to change.
So my advice to new players? After you've acquainted yourself with the facilities and their uses, find the clues leading you to the Lvl 2 upgrades for each facility before you do anything else. It's just the first of three steps, but they make a big difference. Plus, if you go for the higher level upgrades before your facilities have recieved the basic upgrades first, you'll find them to be pretty much useless.
Also, pick everything up. Weapon parts, cudgels, junk, whatever you can. Trust me, you'll need the materials. And keep an extra close lookout for gems and chemicals/alcohols to get rare(-ish) materials early on. You'll gain more from the facilities when you've upgraded them, but it's a slow process. So again, pick everything up!

Gearbox's first take on a cross between diablo-like roleplaying game and a first person shooter.  I spent a lot of time in it and had a lot of fun.  However, the sequel is superior to it in nearly every possible way and is a better place to put your money and time.
As the roleplay elements are based off of diablo, killing things and gathering loot to progress what you will spend most of your time doing.  The guns, shields, and other items are randomly generated with varying rarities and manufactures which determine the performance and what numbers the gun will improve on the most.  The quest system is there and it is as in-depth as Diablo's was, which is to say there is no depth to it and it's implemented as minimally as possible.  You receive a quest with some flavor text, you may or may not have some audio going with.  It could be said this improves pacing in a game with a multiplayer focus, but the sequels demonstrate this is not the case.  There is a lot of quirk and crazy among the denizens of Pandora, but this only hides how shallow the shallow the world is in order to keep you interested.
The player characters and NPC's of Pandora have no depth to them.  Your character will only comment on combat banter, critical hits, kills, injuries, and such without any involvement in the story.  The NPC's are little more than quest dispensers which dole out money and guns as you kill stuff.  The enemies have more characterization with the psychos and bandits screaming random♥♥♥♥♥♥as they try to kill you, the effect makes combat that much more interesting.
The gunplay and combat was where the game put the most effort into.  The shooting is functional, and hardly the best among shooters of the era.  The health system is reminiscent of Halo, with regenerating shields and non-regenerating health.  The enemy AI is goofy and not at all smart, lampshaded by the aforesaid quirk of Pandora.
However, the guns you shoot are a joy to play with.  Finding a new toy to play with and killing things with your existing arsenal is going to be the thing which keeps you most motivated to play.  The different guns behave differently, fill different roles in you arsenal, and some have some wild effects.  The further into the game you get the more pronounced this is and the more of a joy it is to play with these weapons.
Grenades function similarly to grenades in any FPS where they have a dedicated button.  The difference here is they can be set up to bounce, stick, break apart, or do several other things before exploding.  They can also be set up to explode in a normal explosion or an elemental explosion.  They become another toy in the box of toys you get to play with alongside your guns.
The action skills each character has will alter combat and define the difference between each of the four characters.  Roland can set down a turret, Lilith can turn invisible and drop a PBAoE, Brick destroys things with melee, and Mordecai sends his bird to kill things.  These abilities can be further modified with skills, Roland creating an AoE ammo regen ring around his turret as an example.  The skills also set up a role, affecting the rate of fire, damage, health, shields, and other passive abilities of your character.  You also can set up some abilities which proc on events such as kills or critical hits, granting you even more pronounced benefits such as health regeneration.  This all makes you put some thought into your character's skill build and what they are equipped with.
Multiplayer is what sold this game and keeps people playing it.  If you want a game you can play with friends and sink many hours into, you can not go wrong with Borderlands. Likewise, if you like playing alone, this is a game to stay away from.  The net-code is good enough that I don't notice any problems and with the migration to steamworks, its a lot better than it used to be.  The enemies will rebalanced as more or fewer players join and leave, keeping the game from getting boring.  Other players bringing more and different things to an already chaotic combat makes combat that much more fun and chaotic.  Being one of the few games in the shoot and loot genre, it still retains a sizable community of players even with the sequels.
With all that said, why the down recommendation?  Its because Borderlands 2 exists and it does everything better, save for character balance.  If you are trying to get into the series you are better served starting with the second game.  If you do purchase this one, pick up the GotY edition as all the DLC, except for the Underdome, is worth picking up if you enjoyed playing.

I played this very briefly co-op with my cousin when it first came out, and then I stumbled across it again in a Humble Bundle.
Leaving all of the Gearbox asshattery and art style misappropriation accusations out of it, this is a very enjoyable if shallow RPG experience.  I would even argue that the art style itself, while unique, doesn't ultimately contribute much to the finished product.
Character customization is limited in terms of skills and the ability to upgrade certain proficiencies - you're basically stuck with a small tech tree and if you want to increase weapon skills you actually have to use those weapons.  It makes sense on paper, but if you're knee deep in a protracted firefight and you literally do not have the ammunition you need for a certain type of weapon, you're going to be leveling up whatever you're stuck with at the moment.  One of my biggest gripes with the game is that you can routinely end up without ammunition.
There are also some minor AI issues that can often make a campaign/quest go from impossibly difficult to stupidly easy just by respawning after you die.  It's as though once you're dead the enemies totally lose track of you. On the other hand, there is no distance you can get to where an enemy with a shotgun (a SHOTGUN) won't be able to at least graze you before he has to reload.  This can get annoying.
Aside from these 2 bits, it's a fun way to kill some hours.  And there is a ton of content - I've only played for a total of 20 or so hours and I'm barely halfway through - this doesn't count the DLC, which is refreshingly well-done and enjoyable.
Get the GOTY edition, it is worth $30.

Mabinogi has many misconceptions surrounding itself. Yeah it's more enjoyable if you pay, no it's not pay-to-win.
Yeah the combat system has some elements that are tied into the cashshop but no they really aren't that big a deal.
Yeah everything seems out of reach, but that's part of the fun of collecting, no 2 players have the exact same set of clothes for example.
Another Misconception - Dyes require USD - NO! They require USD to buy the "Normal(Paletted) Dyes" (but you can also buy them from other players) but "Fixed Color/Flashy Dyes" can easily be obtained via in-game methods.
A real misconception - The game's community sucks; Totally Untrue - The majority of the hell raisers are gone for good, and the remaining players are a friendly and helpful bunch. (note: I only have experiences on Alexina (the most popular server in the US) - I cannot speak for the other servers)
Also allow me to clarify here - The Style Tab is just an option for replacing the visual appearance of your characters model with a different set of armor/clothes than you are wearing; there is also the "Normal" Tab which can equip all the same items except for the fact that they are "really" there, and not just for show (ie style tab items don't decay or add stats, you CAN wear cute clothes you bought WITHOUT paying real money - they will not be very good for combat though)
And another rumor to be crushed: You can't use the same character to gain every skill - except for racials (of which there may be 6 between all 3 races) totally untrue, it'll just take forever to master them all.
Edit: Although I still believe it far too long for them to act, my faith in Nexon's Technical Support hass been restored hence the removal of the con on that effect.

Alright, ladies and gentlemen. I will tell you everything you have to know about this game, both good and bad.
First of all, despite the game having a long story and lots of missions, I highly recommend you playing it casually, meaning 2~3 times per week at most. This is simply because the main and side missions are 85% of the game in itself, so when you finish with those there will be little left for you to do, unless you enjoy helping people or can play fighting with friends. From what I have perceived, the game is "MMORPG~Fighting". Not at the same time, but when you are done with the mmorpg part, it becomes a fighting game. The amount of things to do might be extended by the DLC packs. Have in mind, however, that they are continuously working on the DLCs and more content, which is also why I recommend casual playing, so you don't run out of things to do until they release new stuff. Don't be fooled, endgame still has many stuff to do, specially if you want to get all the items, skills and max rank in all missions and master missions.
Grinding is....complicated. The chance for drops is completely random, tho it doesn't seem connected to the mission's rank. BUT it depends on certain factors. Now that they increased the chances of Ultimate Finish in missions, it's slightly easier. However, you must defeat some specific opponents in order to get said items. This is particularly boring, depending on the mission you are grinding, unless you try to grind 2 or 3 different missions. On the other hand it's very much rewarding.
The rankings of the missions are not really as hard as most people think. What happens is that the game greatly rewards skill and/or perseverance. This being said, if you complete a mission without taking damage in less than one minute you will be as rewarded as if you complete a mission being almost dead and with only 10 seconds. However, expect a low rank if you take an average amount of time, lose half of your health and have an overall average performance. They clearly want you to be someone above all levels or simply someone who never gives up.
Master system is an awesome idea. You get them to judge your rankings, with their own voice saying what they think of your success/failure, you can spar with them, learn their techniques and even get them to join a mission to come to your aid if things get rough. All masters actually teach you and give you advices. Except Vegeta, he's such a severe master. J/K, even Vegeta is good.
Character builds are fantastic. Each race and gender, where available, have their own innate talents. That doesn't stop you from having a giant bulky namekian dealing more damage with Ki Blasts than a petite earthling girl, for instance. You can simply make a build that suits your playstyle, instead of adapting your playstyle to a forced build. Have in mind, however, that the challenge level of the missions should not serve as a base of judgement to wether or not your build is good, mostly because the AI-controller characters accept freely many attacks that players would block or avoid.
Character customization is good, but rather limited. Not in variation, but in attributes. Most to the dismay of nearly everyone in the community, your attributes are directly linked to your character's size and physical form. Stronger and bulkier characters will have more stamina and HP, while smaller characters will have more Ki Blast power and speed, not to mention races bonuses and limitations. To increase the sadness of the community, it's not worth to become a Saiyan. They have higher attack power and lower HP, but an earthling with a full Ki bar will have even higher attack bonus.
One thing that compensates the limitation of customization are the presets. Yes, all clothes come with different attributes variations, but you can configure presets to have "battle clothes" and "lobby clothes". Have in mind that Master missions will take you in your lobby clothes. Unlike what was said in other reviews, you CAN redistribute your points, but you'd need to gather the dragonballs for that.
Pvp is, unfortunately, a complete disastrer, doomed to fail. Not because of the game, but because the humongous amount of hack users. Apparently learning to play is too much of a challenge for some people, so they have to resort to illegal programs to boost their own ego and pretend they are not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. When the stat-hack was disabled, ALL of those users were proven to be very bad players. Those who didn't stay as bad players either left the game or kept searching for other hacks, since they can't hold their own. Sadly, since pvp is one of the endgame things, and the hackers totally blew it, I'm afraid the pc community might not last long, unless the company finds an effective way to stop those kids.
Many people say the game is repetitive. That's a misconcept. ALL fighting games are highly repetitive, and MMORPGs are even worse, since they require huge amounts of grinding. Comparatively, Xenoverse is much less repetitive than both genres. True, everything in Xenoverse comes down to fighting, but since when fighting games ever had anything more than simply beating down your evemy with an invented metagaming concept such as Scorpion fighting Mileena over a teddy bear (as seen in Mortal Kombat 9's Challenge Tower - Challenge 19)? Besides, all antagonists in the Dragonball story simply try to force their way to everyone. How would you defend yourself and your friends from being murdered by a huge muscular alien who just torn down the entire military force of your planet? You'd try to do it yourself, as the last hope of your planet, right?
The story mode is fantastic. You basically get inside the anime as you try to prevent the villains from altering the storyline. This means joining in classic events of the story without stealing the lights from the main characters. That's amazing for the fans. On the other hand, however, those who are not familiar with the Dragon Ball Z story will NOT feel appealed to the game because of that. Bandai and Dimps made it unquestionably clear that the game was directed to the fans, not to new players. That's a downsize in the commercial side, because we won't have an ever-expanding community, and with the demolition of the pvp aspect because of the hackers, Xenoverse's lifespan might be very small compared to other long-lasting games like Counter-Strike.
Another misconcept is the false rumour that the company doesn't care about the players. They are actively trying to work on things that the players have complained about, like the issue with players spamming skills and stun-locking others and even the hackers themselves, they are just not announcing anything until they make their move.
Regarding character grinding, everything becomes very easier once you complete the game's main story, which is also when they allow you to create more characters. Basically the message they send with this is "now you can do this all over, but it will be very easier now".
When it comes to endgame, after you do all the missions and get all the rankings, masters and unlocks, admittedly, there will not be much to do, unless you enjoy tinkering with builds and experimenting to see what suits you even better than what you already have. Don't forget that they are constantly adding new content, so whatever boredom you might have will be temporary.
Overall this is a great game. Flawless for casuals and hardcore DBZ fans, bad for hardcore players and despicable for competitive players - thank to other players.

Interstellar Marines is pre-alpha, it promises a lot and comes short so far (written on 11.02.2015 in case this review gets outdated)
Positives? Movement is pretty solid, the two guns that are available feel pretty nice to use and it doesn't seem to be glitchy, floaty... It's immersive with what little variety it has.
OH.
The only real negative that stops the game completely is the fact that there's a LIMITED AMOUNT OF SERVERS and no way for you to setup a dedicated server as far as I know. If you want to do a full coop party of friends, you'll have to join a 3/4 server with reasonable ping, commit mutiny and "force" other players off the server. Oh, don't worry- that's the developer's fault for "focusing on developing the game" (from the forums) instead of making sure that people who bought the game can actually play it with other people.
ENEMIES:
The current enemies in the game are other players (multiplayer) and running robots that act like "sneaky" zombies or carry guns (co-op/singleplayer maps).
DIFFICULTY:
On lower than "Hard" difficulty, the game can feel a bit sloppy to be taken seriously. "Realistic" difficulty (maximum difficulty, above "Hard") makes enemy AI kill you in one or two hits, be it by gunshot or by a robosmack to the face.
STEALTH?! I LOVE STEALTH!
Eh. That's not really a thing, unless stealth to you is a "suppressant" that attracts half the robot population towards your location after you've killed one stray robot minding its own business. In multiplayer, there's a lot of maps with day/night cycles and weather effects that dirty your mask. You can actually take off the mask with H, but then all the HUD elements dissapear. This WOULD be very useful during rainy storms if you could tell your teammates from your enemies...
OTHER THAN THAT: during the night in multiplayer, lights go on! Shoot them out! Stealth = darkness.
I want to buy this game and I recommend it because it seems like a lot of fun. Just know that you probably won't get to coop with your friends since those servers are almost always occupied and that you need to go through the same painful process since servers have NO mapchange once you've exhausted the map 10 times in a row. I really hope they bring something interesting to this game later!

Obvious flaws this game has include a very non-standard control scheme that takes a good bit of getting used to, a large amount of exploitable cash shop items, preiods of long grinding that occasionally become necessary, the worst customer support I think I have ever seen in my life, and a community filled to the brim with elitest♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥with little or no interest in helping new players adjust and progress at all and a pretty limited endgame. (if you can ever get there)
Overall, however, dispite all its grevious shortcomings, Mabinogi is an amazing game. It has a massive pool of content and the options for character customization are as close to literally endless as I have ever seen in any game before short of going old school and playing D&D or some third party variant thereof. Something that I tend to use as a selling point is the games lack of a level cap. Basicly how it works is leveling up gets you ap, ap gets you skill ranks, skill ranks give you permanent stat boosts. Once per week you can rebirth, which resets your level to 1 but lets you keep all skills you ranked and all the stats they gave you. The game keeps track of your "total level", which is exactly what it sounds like, the total number of times your character has leveled up since creation. On average a powerful player can gain 100 levels or so each week between rebirthing withut any trouble, each level up grants you 1 ap, each skill on average takes 200-300 total ap to get to the maximum rank with extremes ranging from skills costing only 50 total to costing 500+ total. There are enough skills in the game that the total number of ap required to max out every skill is so high that my level 6500 main character is nowhere near achiving this, and I have participated in enough events that reward ap or double the ap gained on level up (events which are held pretty frequently) that my total amount of ap gathered is likely closer to 10,000. In addition to this they release more and more skills all the time. With this system the game rewards veteran players greatly as your characters power never stops growing. (this is even used as a theme throughout the games story) This means that with this game, unlike a game like WoW for example, the people who have put the most time into the game will be much more powerful then those who started only recently. In WoW particularly there is no diference in character power between a character that was created back at the games birth and a character that was created only a year or so ago. This does, however, lend itself to one of Mabinogis not so obvious flaws. With the way the level system is set up, considering the games age, it makes starting out seem like kind of a hopeless situation. Even my 6500 levels is relatively low for the age of the character because I have taken breaks due to events in my life or simple distraction by other games. This can be discouraging to players who, after their first few hours of gameplay, are most likely only level 30 or so if their not being assisted by stronger characters. This is, however, a problem that has in the past been addressed and adjusted for and likely will be again in the future. As of right now there is a feature in the game that gives new players whos total level is under 1000 items for easier transportation throughout the game world, items to assist in combat, free permanent ground and flying mounts, free premium service and the ability to rebirth every day rather then every week. This means that for your first 1000 levels, roughly 1/7th of what I accumulated over the course of 5 years, your progression is increased to 6 times regular speed (players over total level 1000 can rebirth only roughly once per week, every 6 days is the exact time) on top of being given other things to speed up the flow of the gameplay as a whole. This game also has a very involved and extensive crafting system and a huge range of options for gear customization and enhancement. In some cases, with good enough gear, a characters damage can be multiplied by 10. My critical hits average 12,000 damage, if I had fully upgraded and reforged gear (which takes an insane amount of time, in game gold, luck, or cash) I could potentially get criticsl hits of upwards of 100,000 damage. Currently I dont believe there is anything in the game that requires gear that good but getting gear of that quality is nearly impossible. (though I have seen it in action a few times before) Upcoming content for this game will be focusing a bit more on the endgame content, however, so we may one day in the very near future see content that does require the most carefully crafted gear possible.
I would absolutely recommend that anyone with a computer capable of running this game relatively well give it an honest chance. Break that total level 1000 mark and play after that for a while and youl realy start to get into the meat of the game. Our community could use more new players who will stick around for the longhaul. If you want to play with me personally I play on the Ruairi server and my characters name is Blortad. Its worth mentioning that the 1300 hours I have logged on this game is only my play time over the last year or so since I started playing through steam. I have been playing this game for over 5 years, nearly since its relese in the United States, so bear with me if I go a bit too fast for you at first.

The only MMO that I've ever spent more than three hours in. Going into everything I think about this game would literally be super freaking long, so I'll make it simple. Technical wise, this game is crap. But everything else is great: A player community full of people who are usually very nice, MANY classes that you can choose, and a rediculous amount of quests. Completing all 19 of the main storylines is quite the feat, and even after having played this game for 400+ hours, I still haven't done so. Just be prepared for the game to not work at all when you first install it. If that DOES happen to you, either you'll just have to go do something else, or a LOT of troubleshooting.

8/10
The game is very nice for an independent title on it's alpha (early access) stage, I'm really amazed by how every level plays out, inspired by none other than The Hunger Games, it's really fantastic, innovative and makes matches intense! There's also a whole lot of maps, and modes, really fun! And the community is great, they help each other out immedietly and will revive you if you die (unlike the Battlefield community).
Only downsides are, the game has only 2 weapons as of now (It IS in alpha stage), and the game feels very clunky in terms of movement, jumping, crouching (you won't even know that you're crouching sometimes) and object collision, you can even walk through a lot of metal objects, so it feels clunky at times, it has yet to be smoothed out, but it has great potential for it's future. I recommend getting the game if you're looking for a change in FPS games.

This game is very hard to really review. Let me go over some quick bullet points before I go throwing around my 2 cents.
Things that are objectively good:
-Absolutely GREAT Dev. Amazing guy and actually CARES about how his game's finished product will be.
-Frequent fixes, patches, and support all around.
-Gameplay is simple enough to get and so are the controls.
-Fairly cheap for what it is and how well it actually runs.
-Block based physics building WITH collision damage being a thing for once in these kind of games.
Now, Some things that are objectively terrible.
-Music. All of it but the main menu.
-AI (Which is being fixed in the update after this review, But I'm going to add it because I don't really know how much the AI will be repaired.)
-Building mechanics are VERY precise. Extremely so if working to replace one block in the middle of your ship.
-Some of the art is... I hate to admit, But it's terrible. (Something I hope to be fixed soon, Granted nobody falls down the stairs again.)
-Lacking of PASSIVE inertial dampening causes me to sometimes slam into♥♥♥♥♥♥and makes me want to die a little inside.
-NO REAL CLEAR DESCRIPTION OF ANY BLOCKS EVER. Most are straight forward, But some are just 'WHAT DOES IT DO?!'
-Drones being complete crap in battle. Really only good for repairs.
Ok, Now that those are out of the way... Let me actually go through why I would in fact recommend this game with the stuff I said is bad.
The game itself for a lacking of a better word is rather basic, And simple too play. It's got the potential to be a master-piece among the titles of 'King Arthur's gold' or 'Terraria' given time and more development. It has great replay-ability if you're into building and simple physics-y games. The mechanics of the game aren't fully flushed out yet in terms of resourcing from the feels of things, But this is something fixed over time rather then all at once. Even 'Space Engineers' took well into months of Dev with a whole team of people working on it to tweak it to be any ♥♥♥♥ing good at all.
It's actually very fun for being very simple. It feels fun all around for the most part and with new content being added each update and the updates and fixes being quite small and frequent, I usually look forward to seeing the game after each update.
One of the points that I feel though is that story mode is a little lacking and lack luster, But the open sandbox play is still quite fun.
Now, The draw backs that the game has CURRENTLY that I feel will be more influential and flushed out later are the factions. The factions to me seem reeeeeally pointless... But I think it's not a lacking of effort, and more about needing to have more time to really implement them.
Let me just mention the Dev though... He is actually REALLY nice and can really take, and often does, a lot of criticism. Really what some people need to understand is that he is only ONE GUY who does pretty much everything from what I hear, And almost never gets any outside help past some occasional forum suggestions for things he already actually has planned. Who else can say that they alone made a game that has even HALF the good things I've mentioned above?
And with all this being said, It all really boils down to, Yes the game is fun, runs great, is done by one very fantastic guy with an idea, and has just god awful music with an amazing, Passionate Dev whose not going to abandon his project just because some child doesn't understand the game creation possess.
Overall, I'd say the game deserves a chance and is actually VERY MUCH WORTH the cheap price $5.
7/10, Recommended to people who like and enjoy the simple things in games.

A game that will suck you in, Code 7 is hypnotic in it's story-telling.
Episode 0 simply throws you into a situation that you need to get out of and by Episode 1 you slowly start to realize just how much your choices really matter.
A big, FAT recommendation from me!
Story:
Code 7's strongest point by far. What starts as two people stuck on a abandoned space station quickly turns into a horror scenario in Episode 0 and once Episode 1 starts, you already come to realize how desperate the situation is, both in space and on earth. And the only thing that motivates you are two questions: What is Code 7? And will you be able to stop it?
Graphics:
As expected from a text adventure, the graphics are simple and mostly text based, but in opposition to other games, Code 7 has graphics, mini-games and a smart interface to always keep the player up to date without forcing them through annoying "Look at Shelf" shenanigans.
Audio:
Fully voiced characters, plenty of audio logs and amazing electro music always keep the game a pleasure to listen to. Turn off the lights, put on your headphones and you might just forget that you're not really a hacker trying to save the world from S.O.L.I.
Gameplay:
While being text-based, you never have to fight with the game not knowing what you want by trying out sixteen variations of "pick up". The entire language of the game works via computer-based code to navigate yourself through the network, interact with computers and servers, hack into accounts and activate doors, lights and more.
While it might need a bit of time at the beginning to get into it and really understand the logic behind it, once you're used it, it feels very natural to quickly move across the building, use a Brute Force attack to get into a computer and read through all the private mails you might want.
Additionally, you hold control over a human companion who you can ask to move or interact with the parts of the rooms that you don't have access to, allowing you full access over both digital and manual data.
What sounds incredibly complicated right now is unbelievably simple and intuitive in-game and even the very few tutorials never seem annoying or out of place.
Other:
Episode 0 and 1 hold a amazing universe full of characters and lore. Reading through the notes and mails reveals real people with wishes, dreams and relationships. Some are married, some have children, some have a really bad case of compulsive hoarding. You can spend hours simply reading and listening through everything the characters have to tell about themselves.
The main storyline meanwhile is incredibly intense, rarely allowing a break before throwing the next reveal or horrific fact at you about all the things that are going wrong. It's impossible not to care especially for the main characters Sam, Alex and Zoya as they try their best to survive and reach for help in a world that is slowly going mad.
Be prepared to be violently tossed around and left speechless at the end of EVERY episode. If you thought the end of Episode 0 is cruel, then wait for the end of Episode 1.
And considering the amazing quality so far, I am very positive that all future episodes will be no different.

It's a Pyranna Bytes open world RPG. It's got factions, day an night cycles and FLYING. (albeit as a Parrot). I went through my first run through as a Voodoo Pirate due to having the unlimited flying spell. This was one of my favorite features of the Might and Magic series and they included it in Risen 3. I hope PB keeps it for its upcoming games.
The game does have its issues however. The number one being an over relience on arcadey sequences with its boss monsters. While not as bad as the Risen 1, they are still annoying having them in my RPGs. Why did they feel their games would be improved with that addtion. The game also had some irratating video sequences. They use the same brutal combat sequence for killing baddies as they do challanging an ally. It makes no sense for an ally to get up after you slit his throat . . .
It make me ask the question, If your original template is the superior Gothic, what direction would you take to make the game better?
The game world is fairly large but needed a wider diversity of monsters. And it needed more regular human monsters/bad guys. (Remember the bandit caves in Gothic 2)  The bullet shield was wortlhess becasue there simply aren't many baddies with guns. The cities needed more people and way way way more women. And while the game was mostly set in a carribean setting, I would have preferred a couple different climates. ( I admit a preference to snow)
The UI is horrible. It needs more tabs. Some of the screen inforamation has to be scrolled when there is no need to such a thing. And some of the Voodoo Pirate magic is stored as a weapon and not as a spell. Those items should have been sold as wands not spells.
Powergamers can easily have godly avatars by the mid game if they smartly allocate but since my avatars are usually well rounded (I allocate dumbly) I didn't achieve the near invulnerable status until the end game. Many powergames who achieved that early power, looked at the game as super easy. However that is "never" a problem with me because my main enjoyment of open world RPGS is exploration.  And this game does have it. And couple open world exploration with flying and this game many times had me in RPG nirvana.
The moronic video combat sequences, the horrible UI and the far too many arcade sequences knock this game down a few notches. But the nicely implemented open world, the over all great voice acting, superior music all coupled with flying take away many of the flaws. I would rate this game 7.8 to 8.5.

I really, really wanted to write a positive review about this game. I've really enjoyed games by Piranha Bytes in the past, and Risen 1 was actually a really enjoyable game. I started but didn't finish Risen 2, because I stopped enjoying it. I was hoping that Risen 3 would have learned from the mistakes of Risen 2, and been better. I was wrong. Risen 3 is worse than Risen 2, and by a large margin.
Risen 3 has some good things. The world is lush and pretty. The theme, pirates and magic, can be a lot of fun. Okay, two good things.
It also has a lot of things that are not good, and in some cases very bad. The physical mechanics of the game are crap, frankly. You walk like you're on a flat plane that skates across the ground. There are invisi-walls all over the place. More specifically the fighting mechanics, are even worse. All the things that Assassin's Creed IV got right about fighting, such as the pace, the fluidity, and the using of different weapons, are all things that this game gets horribly, horribly wrong. You click to attack, and then there's a pause, and then there is a slow attack. There is no such thing as a fast attack. The enemies, however, do have a fast attack; and it interupts. Meaning there you are, slowly pulling your sword back for an attack, and 'whack' you get hit and have to restart the attack. I could continue on this subject, but there are so many other things wrong that I'm moving on.
This is supposed to be an open world style game. It is one, in a sense. You have the open world of the path, and the few trees on either side. But wait! What's that toward the end of a path? It's a temple complex! So you enter the temple complex, and then you have the open world of the corridor! Don't get me wrong, the world is open to you going back and forth within the path or corridor. I admit that I've only played the first area, so maybe the world becomes more open later on.
Let's talk about pop-in. Usually, pop-in is a draw distance issue where textures go from either blurry or just not there, to suddenly clear and apparant. In some horror games however, they used the sudden appearance of enemies as a scare tactic. As in, you would be walking along and suddenly BOO! an enemy jumps out at you. In this game you're walking along and enemies will suddenly pop up from the ground. It's not a slow, un-burying of an enemy. It's a quick 'look I can phase through solid matter' jump up. Not only that, but they can go from appearance to attacking instantly. Considering the time it takes for you to be able to attack, even if your reaction time is amazing, you're going to get hit multiple times before being able to land a blow. Also, this game is set on islands. Islands with rivers running across them. There is a lot of water. There are enemies that do the pop-up effect while under the water. The further problem here, is that a lot of the water has a 'foam' effect, making it opaque. That renders these popped-in enemies invisable. So then you get to fight invisiable fast-attacking enemies. I cannot, in any way, describe this as 'fun'.
There are more things wrong with this game, but honestly I think this review is long enough. So to sum-up: This game is filled with poor mechanics, has a terrible story line (sorry I didn't write a paragraph about this part), has poor voice acting and scripting (or this part), but occasionally looks pretty. On a scale of 1 to 10 I would give this game a 3. [3/10]

I just finished Risen 3 - Titan Lords for the second time, so I feel comfortable writing a review.
Risen 3 is a vast improvement over Risen 2, although I did like Risen 2 myself as well, but what can I say, I've loved PB's games ever since Gothic 2. While I do admit Risen series has been a lot worse than the original Gothic trilogy, they are still great games in their own sense. At first Risen 3 feels more like an expansion of Risen 2. Lots of assets have been recycled and even a few areas have been brought over from Risen 2. Luckily, however, that feeling vanishes pretty fast when you notice that the recycled areas aren't really that important and all the main areas are brand new, and then you notice how much better Risen 3 does everything. So it ends up feeling like Risen 2 but only less♥♥♥♥♥♥ Risen 3 is a lot bigger than Risen 2, and more refined in almost every aspect. The combat is great, the exploration is awesome and the world is actually open this time around.
It isn't without its problems however. My biggest problem with the game is that it is WAY -WAY- ---WWWAAAAYY--- too easy! It's alright in the beginning if you play without a companion, but it becomes faceroll in the end. Even on hard. On my second playthrough as a voodoo pirate, I managed to max out all my stats. All 8 stats! Maxed! Why is this even possible?
So the balance is ♥♥♥♥ed. It doesn't ruin the game, but it takes away all the tension from the last quarter of the game. Possibly even earlier if you use companions, or something else than melee. In order to get a satisfying challenge out of the game, you pretty much have to shoot yourself in the foot, by not using alchemy or companions. Alchemy is probably the biggest criminal here. It is so ridiculously overpowered it's insane.
Economy balance however, is amazingly well made. There's never enough money if you really want to get the most out of skills. If you're fine with a few skills here and there, you might end up with some extra pocket change, but that wasn't the case for me. The moment I got 10k money, I used them right away, and there were so much more I wanted.
Graphically there's a lot to say as well. The graphics are all over the place. The game looks dated and runs like♥♥♥♥♥♥ I got it running on reasonable fps only after tweaking a lot of the ConfigDefault.xml file. The level design which PB has always been amazing at, is also bit of a let down. Some places are extremely gorgeous, but some places are hideous. There's also a few narrow canyon paths too many for my taste.
The story is.... Well... The story is. It just is. It exists, but isn't important on any level. I have never cared much about PB's storylines, but I've always loved the world, and the history of it. And here it's interesting enough to keep exploring. But the storyline itself is completely irrelevant and forgettable. Combine that with a pointless ending and that's it. But it isn't the meat of the game anyway so who cares?
Some of you guys played the DLCs of Risen 2? Remember how♥♥♥♥♥♥they were? Well, the DLC of Risen 3 was a massive positive surprise to me, because both Fog Island and Uprising of the Little Guys are awesome. I enjoyed both of them thoroughly. So those are recommended if you don't have them. Nothing to say about Adventure Garb. It's a pile of gear that I don't use because it's too good for the beginning of the game. As if the game wasn't easy enough.
So all in all, it's better than Risen 2, but the difficulty holds it down. I loved it. If you're a PB fan, chances are you'll love it too. If you're not a PB fan however, you probably won't like it. I hate to see people bashing the game when they've never liked PBs games. Why do you expect this one to change your mind? The "mistakes" people claim PB makes, are all things that have always been around, and if they were magically fixed, I doubt it would be the same thing anymore. Which would make the old fans disappointed. Even moreso than they already are.
So yeah. I love it.
Sinathor out.

First of all i have played and enjoyed risen 1, and played about 20mins of the demo for risen 2 (hated it, just couldnt get into it,) but risen 3 on the other hand is amazing. I highly reccommend this game to anyone who enjoys rpg's or open world games. I pre ordered this game because it looked quite promising and it highly exceeded my expectations.
There are tons of areas to explore. The game is broken up into islands, all which have a good variety of enviornments, enemies, people, ect. There are different factions which you choose to join in the game and each gives you a unique playstyle, and quests so there is need for replayability. The game is filled with tons of quests, and many which are quite enjoyable, not the typical oh go here and collect 10 tree roots and get a reward kind of quests. There is tons of dialoge in this game and the voice acting isnt perfect but its quite acceptable in my opinion, they throw in humor sometimes too which is great. This game has a really good atmosphere to it, someting which i enjoyed about risen 1. Soundtrack in this game is also superb.
A neat twist to this game as well, you use a ship to travel from island to island, and sometimes there are random encounters and you'll have to fight off enemy ships or sea monsters. The combat in the game is a little clunky, but it just took some time getting used to. Once you build your strength abit it becomes much more enjoyable, its just a little tough in the beginning.
I usually dont take the time to write reviews, but i am enjoying this game very much, and since its an rpg theyre automatically competing with the big companies that make skyrim, dragon age, ect. So im happy to voice my opinion of the game for others to see and hopefully they will give it a try.

Proteus is not a game, it's an experience. Frankly, I think it could've been more. If you've ever played Dear Esther before, (yes, I  own it) you know it wasn't much of a game, just a "showcase" of how powerful it's engine was. Proteus is the same in many ways, but its a pixel-y game, showcasing what the developers can do.
I assume this is open world. The only reason I'm still attempting to play it is because of the music, but I'll get that later. It may just be an island, but you can walk around wherever you want and "do" whatever you want. You can't click on anything, you can just walk around, "enjoy" the art style, and enjoy (I say in a positive way) the music. There is no point to Proteus. The only main objective  is to drift away in the music, and I'd glaadly just open the game for the music. The soundtrack is pretty much the only thing it has going for it. Don't get me wrong, I kind of like the colorful, pixel world, but what really sold me was in fact the soundtrack.
If you can find the soundtrack to this "game", just get that. To be honest, I don't think that Proteus is worth it's price tag.

LOTR was my first contact with the LEGO series. It received so many good reviews I thought it would be at least mostly fun.
Alas, it is mostly boring as hell.
I admit, technically it is expertly done. It looks good, play smoothly and is overall very polished. But the gameplay mostly consists of two extremely boring features:
1) Running around the area, looking for hidden LEGOs. Could be fun if it wasn't so overwhelmingly omnipresent. Looking behind every bush is somewhat fun when it's mixed with other activities, like for example killing stuff, but on its own it is about as fun as vacuuming a very complicated room with plenty of complicated furniture. Without using hands.
2) Rewatching long scenes from the movie, rendered in the LEGO world. What was the point of this? If they did an actual parody (with actual jokes), or I don't know, did
, okay, but this? I've seen the movies, thank you very much, it looked better in the cinema, now give me stuff to do or at least let me skip the scene!
There are a lot of good elements too, I really liked the combat mechanics and some ever-changing level design (like the Black Rider motif). But when I finished Bree and I was immediately promised even more running around in search of god damn bricks, I said "Screw that" and dropped the game.
Seriously, I don't know how this title is so liked. Sure, give it a try, it might be perfect for you, but... don't say I didn't warn you.

Awesome game! Even if you don't watch Naruto or aren't even an anime watcher, this game is a must-have for melee/action gamers. With this game, you can accustom yourself to a character (or a set of characters), master him/her, and show him/her off in online battle. Unlike traditional combat games such as Street Fighter or Mortal Kombat, this game makes action sequences more simple and complex at the same time. Instead of playing in the 2D format of the aforementioned games with specific button-pushing combos, this game offers combo diversity without having to remember a ton of sequences. In this game, you can just repeatedly press the melee button and choose which direction you want to send your opponent to, and it should send them flying off to the desired direction. Moreover, this game allows you to utilize the expense of special attack energy (in this case chakra). This chakra allows players to gather up energy and expend it in a variety of ways: ninjutsu (special attack), dash, strong shuriken throws, and etc. Manipulating energy in this fashion allows for more complex gameplay, whereas others games would force players to spam attacks in order to win a game. This and many other facets of the gameplay make this game a must-buy.

A very underrated and overlooked game, that i find a true masterpiece, a gem in a massive pile that are indie survival horrors. A very detailed and developed aspects of survival system, managing your base power and integrity, trying to slow down infection rates spreading across the map, manage heating and oxygen supplies(it is a mars base afterall). Massive amount of stuff to craft and research, using the base's mining facilites, bio farms, engineering centers, etc. Very dynamic background system - just watching the map from your base, you can imagine just how much bad♥♥♥♥♥♥is happening outsite. Lore and atmosphere are fantastic, you can fully immerse yourself in the game.  It also has story and goals to achieve, so while you can play endless, its not one of those games that just throws you in endless survival for no reason, thankfully.
If you're a fan of survival horrors, especially non linear ones, where you have your own "safe" upgradeable base and have to venture for stuff, then its a must have for you. The developer have also proved to be very supportive and still keeps making big updates after the game's release.

RPG Maker MV is a great and flexible engine to bring your game ideas to life.
Being interested in game development, but failing to start because of massive setbacks such as designing characters, creating a setting, and having no direction. However, with the pre-made assets you are able to prototype, prototype, and prototype. I stress this because understanding what you're doing will make you better and faster at making a game. You don't particularly need a story, a whole bunch of characters, or designed assets - the whole point is to understand game dev, and is most definitely worth the price. If you can, get it on sale!
I'm actually interested in the battle mechanics and events. I assure you that you can make a great game if the battle system is fun! Note that I only have about 100+ hours right now, but I still want to keep making and perfecting my game even if all I am working on is battle mechanics and events. It will never be released, but nothing won't stop you if you keep learning about the mechnics of the engine. Javascript makes it extremely flexible.
And as others have said, plug-ins make the process of creation so easy, and there are many free resources online! If you're a beginner and need to experience making an RPG by all means go for this. The continued support for Javascript plug-ins doesn't hurt either.

If heaven exists, then it's Borderlands.
In fact, you can visit New and Old H(e)aven in Borderlands. The first one will be reminded as a neat sanctuary with tons of loot, the last one as pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
But truth has to be told, this game is perfect. You won't find better humour in a shooter, neither will you find more weapons and variaty of skills. Borderlands is extremly well-made, combines the feeling of a nice shooter with a story (which IS kinda flat, but still better than 90% of the shooters out there, and it isn't THAT bad - but Borderlands 2 is the better story game) which will give you tons of hours full of fun and many, many quests and challenges to complete.
Can it get even better, you ask? Well, listen here folks. 4 men co-pp experience! 4 men (or women)! You know what that means? Harder bosses, harder enemies in general, A LOT of better loot and probably the VERY BEST co-op experience you can obtain. For real. No other game will give you that much fun at some good evening with friends like Borderlands (maybe Gang Beasts will, it's pretty neat, but of course not comparable to a real co-op AAA experience). It's absurdly great.
Loot. Folks. LOOT. Prepare to jump around a rock or a house for at least 30 minutes wondering how to get on top of it because you can be sure there IS a lootchest and YOU WANT IT. Trust me, you do. That's the negative result of playing this hilarious game. In every other game which contains looting, you will see spots EVERYWHERE where you suspect a chest. Becuase that's how Borderlands is. There is loot EVERYWHERE. AND THAT'S GOOD.
The mixture of ActionRPG and shooter is good, you have many skills you can invest into, but it's still a good shooter with nice effects and many different enemies, which makes it good balanced in the first playthrough, NG+s are much easier, but I personally never played a game where this isn't the case.
And the best part: humour. It's funny as hell. Every boss has his mini intro with a cool and hilarious oneliners and also many ingame dialogs are freakin' funny. So many loveable and funny characters, you won't see this in any other game.
And last but not least: The 4 DLCs are really worth the money. Great stroy DLCs with MORE LOOT, MORE INSANE HUMOUR AND MORE STORY.
Get this game, learn to love it, be thankful to have played the very best coop and shooter experience you can get.

In contrast to my other reviews, I'll
to keep this one short. I'm getting a refund, and here's why:
This game is not complete. Not only content wise (description here is highly misleading), there are rendering bugs, weird gameflow issues, weird design decisions and probably a bonus memory leak.
I know the game's just ~2 USD (and trust me, it shows!), but since space games are my favorite theme, it really saddens me to see the wasted potential here. A month of two of polishing would've made wonders for this project.
It feels like an Alpha at most. I'd probably be way more accepting if it was Early Access, and wouldn't go for the refund.
PROS:
- Very neat concept, hunting ships and mining for new parts, then building your own ship.
- Ships and drones work as intended after built. Decent customization allowing for faster/agile ships, versus bigger and tankier ones. Drone focused, missile focused or laser focused. Balanced builds. Etc.
CONS:
- Weird UI, Weird control scheme. Constructing the ship is more annoying than it should, with a
small grid without a zoom feature.
- Graphical and sound assets are bad. I usually don't mind this, but when I see a robot-human drawn in paint it kind of hurts.
- Terrible writing, with insane amount of typos and weird content. "These are spiritual beings that possess trees for mobility" is probably one of the most intriguing things I've ever read.
- Rendering, UI and AI issues.
- Very dumb or silly AI.
Hopefully we see more updates from the devs. It seems they finished the hardest/worst part (technical issues, procgen, sandbox world, ship building, faction, quests and other systems), and didn't care for the rest..or polishing the finished systems.
WIth a dozen other similar games either released or in Early Access at the moment, Inevitability sits in a very rough spot.

I had just finished a stressful match of League of Legends and I decided that I needed to take a breather, so I loaded up Steam and remembered I had just bought this game as apart of a Humble Bundle. Figuring that it could be good, I installed it, put on my headphones, and dove in. Waking up waist deep in the pixelated ocean, I was immersed in a simple yet utterly beautiful world. I watched day turn to night and night turn to day. There were no goals, nor any rules of what I had to do. I walked around an island, listening to the world. I climbed a mountain and heard the sea wind blowing. I walked into the rain and heard a gentle drizzle land on the nearby trees. As I played-- no, not played. As I experienced Proteus, I felt my muscles relieve themselves, and even now do I feel utterly calm. I can't explain this game, because it's not a game. Walking through Proteus was a reminder that the world is beautiful, and all we have to do is take time to see it.

I think there are many iterations of LOTR games out there. Some based on single movies. Some include them all. Many I've seen poorly adapt scenes from the movie into gameplay that doesn't always fit. Or they'll force levels and gameplay that doesn't really go with the movies at all.
The Lego LOTR game is great in that it encompasses all three films with stunning attention to detail. Just about every major sequence from the films is included in this game in one form or another, either as a cutscene, or as a cleverly incorporated aspect of gameplay. You name it. It's probably in there. Remember when the hobbits meet Aragorn for the first time and escape to Weathertop? Remember "second breakfast"? Well, there's a sequence of gameplay where you actually make second breakfast (which subsequently causes the ring wraiths to spot you). It can be that granular. It's amazing. Ultimately, if you're looking for a game that gives the most fulfilling gaming experience of actually playing through all three films in a single package (and you don't mind Lego looks and humor), then this game is for you. There are tons of characters and "treasures" to unlock. And what's great is being able to traverse an open-world Middle Earth (albeit it's a bit minaturized in scale).
My only negatives are the sometimes repetitive nature of gameplay. If you've played any other modern Lego game you'll know what I'm talking about. Also, horses. There are some moments you ride horses in between levels as a part of the story, but you can't spawn a horse on command which would be GREAT for free roam. Granted, there are quite a few quick-travel locations, but there's nothing really outside of a less-than-adequate nonessential item which helps you get around quicker.
Also, the buggyness. I don't know how common it is, but there were a few points where the game graphically glitched out that caused me to have to close out completely....which was hard because the menu became invisible at this point. Also, there was a level in which you control Frodo and Sam and have to collect Orc armor to disguise yourselves to escape. Usually, you can get a character to drop a disposable object from your inventory so that the other can pick it up. Well, in this particular situation, if you grab more of the armor pieces than the character needs, you will need to restart because the game won't let you drop it for the other character to pick it up.
There's also quite a few other sporadic blips and glitches that were kind of annoying but would take too long to mention them in a review, however, when the game was running smoothly, it was a blast.

If heaven exists, then it's Borderlands.
In fact, you can visit New and Old H(e)aven in Borderlands. The first one will be reminded as a neat sanctuary with tons of loot, the last one as pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
But truth has to be told, this game is perfect. You won't find better humour in a shooter, neither will you find more weapons and variaty of skills. Borderlands is extremly well-made, combines the feeling of a nice shooter with a story (which IS kinda flat, but still better than 90% of the shooters out there, and it isn't THAT bad - but Borderlands 2 is the better story game) which will give you tons of hours full of fun and many, many quests and challenges to complete.
Can it get even better, you ask? Well, listen here folks. 4 men co-pp experience! 4 men (or women)! You know what that means? Harder bosses, harder enemies in general, A LOT of better loot and probably the VERY BEST co-op experience you can obtain. For real. No other game will give you that much fun at some good evening with friends like Borderlands (maybe Gang Beasts will, it's pretty neat, but of course not comparable to a real co-op AAA experience). It's absurdly great.
Loot. Folks. LOOT. Prepare to jump around a rock or a house for at least 30 minutes wondering how to get on top of it because you can be sure there IS a lootchest and YOU WANT IT. Trust me, you do. That's the negative result of playing this hilarious game. In every other game which contains looting, you will see spots EVERYWHERE where you suspect a chest. Becuase that's how Borderlands is. There is loot EVERYWHERE. AND THAT'S GOOD.
The mixture of ActionRPG and shooter is good, you have many skills you can invest into, but it's still a good shooter with nice effects and many different enemies, which makes it good balanced in the first playthrough, NG+s are much easier, but I personally never played a game where this isn't the case.
And the best part: humour. It's funny as hell. Every boss has his mini intro with a cool and hilarious oneliners and also many ingame dialogs are freakin' funny. So many loveable and funny characters, you won't see this in any other game.
And last but not least: The 4 DLCs are really worth the money. Great stroy DLCs with MORE LOOT, MORE INSANE HUMOUR AND MORE STORY.
Get this game, learn to love it, be thankful to have played the very best coop and shooter experience you can get.
