Heavily recommended game! And the following play-through should make you either highly appalled or very interested:
- Started off with a monkey as a pet. Named her "Butters", but later on my pet monkey took a liking to another guy named Bones. It made me a tiny bit sad.
- Built a nice settlement, made the entire surroundings and buildings out of the easiest findable supply around: wood.
- Ended up with 5 villagers after having successfully defended our 'village' a couple of times and converted 2 of the pirate prisoners to join our cause. They eventually did.
(I'm skipping the story about the micromanagement and supply hoarding business - you'll learn about this on the spot yourself.)
- I thought I had things going smoothly. Perhaps a bit too flawless. Characters got along well and two of them actually married eachother early on. It was a joyful moment for Bones and Greta. Bones had a dislike for clothes, so he was always running around naked which was not appreciated by some. But apparently he had a passion for farming and was well endowed. Greta took the earliest opportunity and showed him some loving. Greta was listed as a lazy and weapon hating person, but not too lazy to chase down some 'bone'. Good for her.
- My self created character, named Adante, was a tireless fat miner and the other two people named Dorothy and Hunter were your average run of the mill converted prisoners from earlier battles. Dorothy could cook up some decent meals and Hunter, well, as the name implies, he was hunting down the animals for the food to make nice meals mixed up with the harvested crops from our farms. Luxurious and plentiful meals of variety. Even salt was added for flavour.
But then an event changed the atmosphere quite rapidly:
- A nasty cobra snuck into the settlement and had its fangs set on Butters, the pet Monkey, and I did not notice as I was looking to mine some shizzle.
- They battled eachother like no tomorrow and the fight lasted quite long because by the time I had actually noticed, the pet monkey had all her limbs bitten off by the snake and was crying for help while still being pounded by the Cobra.
- The sound of the monkey cries... it still traumatizes me to this day.
- Bones probably noticed long before I did, but hey, he loves being naked and probably didn't want to risk being bitten in dangling places so did nothing to help out.
- Hunter, however, eventually shot & killed the cobra before it could put a killing blow on the poor limbless cryin' monkey.
- Butters was then picked up by Hunters, carried and put in Bones' room to keep him comfortable with some painkillers while we figure out a way to get his limbs back. There are ways in this game to do so, be it four wooden pegs or made out of other technology, but it takes some craftmanship to pull this off.
- By the time that we've managed to construct these, an electric storm came down on the settlement as if it was telling us: YOUR INTENTIONS ARE NOBLE BUT THE MONKEY MUST DIE!
(Now, here's a lesson I've learned: Never make your ENTIRE settlement out of wood.)
- The storm caused fire to start and spread like wildfire.
- All villagers were alerted and commanded to extinguish the fire.
- The fire became so intense, and spread from the storages and houses straight to the farm area (and all over the entire map, all animals and trees on the entire map were burned alive.)
- Now, the house in which Butters was still 'recovering' was also hit by the fire. I sent my main character Adante to help out but the fire enclosed the area in a rapid speed. My fat miner and his slow jigglywiggly runs could not win that race by a long shot. He was a hauler, not a speedy gonzalez.
- Butters, the poor cursed monkey, just shrieked and screamed her lungs out when the fire was getting closer and closer after every second.
- So within seconds, we could hear the cries again, of a pet Monkey. Not only in pain from snake bites and losing all limbs before, but now also jumping by the belly up & down inside her once comfortable pet-bed, being on fire.
- Every villager probably had tears in the eyes from that whole ordeal once the fire started demanding the limbless body and a Monkey fighting for the last breath of her life.
- I made Bones, since he's supposedly the new master of Butters, go into the flames and try to retrieve the monkey while the plan was to let him carry the monkey into the water at a nearby lake.
- This turned Bones into a running naked man carrying a limbless monkey across the settlement, while both being on fire.
- The outcome of this is probably easy to guess. They burned together, into (what it seemed) a neverending sea of flames and emotion.
- I ordered all my other villagers to stand in the water of the lake and wait out the fire frenzy. They were all depressed and Greta simply lost it and ran into the firesea on her own accord due to severe depression.
After the fire died, I stopped playing and told the story to my girlfriend. Her eyes opened wide and then the question came: "What kind of f***ed up game is that?"
Rimworld, my dear. It's Rimworld.

I enjoyed the game but wouldn't recommend it. It continues in the disappointment of the more recent DBZ entities. Terrible sophomoric writing. Incredibly corny in a bad way throughout. I
the exposition of the main story line. Why can't we have a good game set in the DBZ world that doesn't have to meet the requirements of the main DBZ story
Awesome graphics. Some of the environment can be destroyed in delightful ways, like nemekian houses. They FINALLY add multiple participants to battles (which should have always been a staple in games centered around DBZ). The battle mechanics are novel (for about 4 hours). Some of the alternative story lines are neat and thought provoking.
It's more of an action RPG, but it doesn't even do that well. You're locked on small battlefields the entire game, even when accomplishing missions like "Find the dragonballs". They're all within throwing distance of each other. The character customization is laughably non-existent, with stats being so generic they may as well not exist -- you choose which button that you spam is going to do slightly more damage.
, the special ability design is a joke. Some moves are just outright
, while others are broken and don't work. The Super Saiyan transformation breaks any semblance of a meta. It allows you to spam your ki abilities without the normal ki costs. ALL OF THEM. Not just your normal ki abilities, but your ultimates! Early in the storeline, I was able to go Super Saiyan and use Special Beam Cannon 10 times before the transformation ended, which is the equivalent damage to 5 full health Buus!
The single player mode is droll and unsatisfying. The enemy AI is just down-right awful, with forced spikes in difficulty injected in by unfair increases in enemy health(That the player can
), giving enemies the most annoying and seemingly unending super armor(They are never stunned by your attacks) and having them get up OVER and OVER again, forcing you to use healing items to have any chance of sustaining.
Strangely, in certain parallel quests the enemy AI seems to be 200% smarter and genuinely tougher. But this great AI is missing from the custom match mode. The enemies are always stupid, and you don't get to choose how strong they are. Fighting Saiyan saga vegeta is exactly as difficult as fighting buu saga Vegeta. It artificially balances everyone's power to be evened out -- even Mr. Satan! You can't set up asymmetrical fights either. You can only choose 1v1, 2v2 or 3v3 -- so forget about fighting solo against the Ginyu Force, or fighting 20 saibamen along side your favorite team. Want to fight against Vegeta and Trunks, solo? Too bad, you can't...
You could allow the player to set up custom, asymmetrical teams. While the difficulty spikes up or down, the player could be wagering differing amounts of  XP and zeni for wins.
Take a cue from old professional wrestling games and allow the player to play through a "season" or career mode. They could make small decisions, nurture relationships, rivalries and form stables. But it would still basically just be a series of fights. Easy-peesy but fun game design. You could put the player in heart-pounding impossible situations because loses can still progress the mode.

Move or Die is one of those party games that ruins friendships based on how much fun you're having. If you're not mad at at least one of your friend, you're playing it wrong.
The trailer speaks for itself, if you don't move, you die as simple as that, with a varied list of interesting gamemodes and mutators, meant to be played on the couch with friends.
But while the core mechanics are there and I did have loads of fun with it as a party game, there are some glaring oversights.
- The "move or die" mechanics is so exploitable; you can just stand in one spot and spam left and right on the same block, making it obsolete.
- Unlocking gamemodes and mutators is so boring, if you play with the same group of friends like I do, you better pray you don't get repeats (which happens way more than you think, given the list of gamemodes are too short, <9 )
- I don't entirely understand why do we unlock gamemodes and mutators through levels, that seems more orientated to playing online with strangers/ in a lobby. But let's say I'm playing with a group of friends, I don't wanna have to grind with the same people, playing the same few modes over and over again.
Maybe given a year or two when the game has been updated with healthy amount of content content, you might wanna consider getting the game.

The neglected child of the Source class multiplayer Tripartite, Day of Defeat Source is by no means a weaker game in comparison to the equally brilliant Counterstrike Source and Team Fortress 2. Released swiftly after CS:S, the game shares much in common with it. Two teams battle against each other in rounds using a variety of different weapons in well designed maps which are simple to navigate yet tactically contain hundreds of different possibilities.
DOD:S differs crucially in terms of objective however. Firstly as a class based game like TF2, each player accompanies a role of an Rifleman, Assault, Support, Machine Gunner, or Sniper class, serving vital responsibilities for the team, unlike CS:S's individualistic endeavours; simply hunting down every last enemy per round in whatever way wished. You know, it would be easy to pass Subterrain off as another boring zombie/survival/crafting game in this endless sea of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ cookie-cutter clones of this now stale genre. Yet across the blackened horizon, Subterrain is that blinking light that demands a closer inspection, and with just a few seconds of your time, you realise that this MAY be the game that rises above the rest.
Subterrain is an engrossing and extremely in-depth experience that will grip you by the balls and won’t let go. As a lone survivor aboard a massive space station you must explore, scavenge for food and materials to ensure your survival, plus research and develop powerful new equipment to aid your struggle against the ever growing infected that aims to devour the entire place, with you included.
A blend of Alien Breed, System Shock 2, Dead Space and Project Zomboid. With LOTS of backtracking required and micromanaging of your base of operations, Subterrain is not a casual game and requires a great deal of patience and perseverance to enjoy. It has a few issues with game balancing and pacing. Yet despite this, it’s extremely enjoyable and fun to play and discover for yourself.
Note: I’m playing the game on normal difficulty without reading any guides. I suggest you do the same for that fresh virgin experience and sense of discovery.
Graphics are very good and suit the game perfectly, with a 2D presentation that pays homage to top down titles of yesteryear, yet with a silky smoothness added that lets us know it’s running on modern tech. The game is fairly dark, but the colours and lighting have been used to great effect, contrasting yet subtle enough as to remain faithful to the horror theme portrayed. Newly explored areas appear spooky, with a faint mist and coldness to them, whilst areas you've conquered are bathed in sterile warmth.
The sound is well done but quite minimal: there is no spoken dialogue and only the effects of items, machines, (overly loud) guns and growling monsters play out in the world. The music is a bit too overpowering for my tastes, so I’ve had to turn it down a fair bit. Sadly, there's a lack of ambient noises, so you won’t be greeted by the bleeps of a computer console or a menacing grumble of a dark corridor. Hopefully they can add this in the future as it will greatly add to the already stellar atmosphere.
With 15 main areas to visit (some including multiple levels to explore) you can move freely between them and your main base. There’s plenty to see and discover, however it gets extremely tiresome as you constantly need to go back and forth to replenish supplies. It doesn’t help that the levels themselves are fairly large and randomly generated, some rooms leading to dead ends for logical reasons only a computer would understand. Walking simulator springs to mind.
Still, exploration is fun as you’ll need to power up elevators to ease travel plus install oxygen and thermal regulators to make areas inhabitable. As well as scavenging for food and supplies, you need to look out for keycards and dossiers that point you towards shiny new technology, essential for late game survival.
Key item locations are hinted at in journals you find throughout the game world, not only rewarding you with a sense of discovery, but also giving an incentive to move onwards. Items can still be hard to track down thanks to the massive unwieldy level design, but once you know the placement patterns it does become less tedious.
The key aspect of the game is improving your equipment and facilities to help fight against the ever evolving infected, and it’s done in a neat way. In order to improve something, you first need to lose your current item in order to research the upgraded version of it (as well as manufacture the original).
This presents a dilemma: do you sacrifice that powerful new weapon you just discovered to research, forcing you to rely on that puny pistol for a real time hour? Or do you hang onto it, hoping you’ll stumble into another copy to sacrifice to the research altar? Not only that, do you have the required facility upgrades and materials in order to construct said item? Subterrain is a game that requires you to think not just about the now, but about the future.
You can also mine your own materials and harvest your own food, each in turn can be broken down for valuable resources to aid production of equipment. You can also recycle obsolete equipment, so now you don’t need that single crate full of lvl1 weapons “just in case.” Recycle that rubbish!
You also need to balance your power output by switching off electricity to unneeded areas, replacing burnt out generators and defending them against invasions with turrets. Neglect your power levels and your generator can overload...
With most survival games, you need to eat, drink and sleep (plus♥♥♥♥♥♥, as well as quell contamination, stem bleeding and repair broken limbs. It’s all done with great restraint, so rest assured you won’t need to eat every 15 minutes or repair a broken leg after an infected so much as farts in your general direction. Now this is a basic needs system other survival games should scrutinise - present but subtle, not "eat every x seconds or die".
Despite this, I found LOADS of food, drink and medical supplies in my current playthrough, so I never really felt like I was pressured to survive like I would have done in say, Project Zomboid. This does need some balancing as it seems impossible to run out of food and water.
Your suit, weapons and electric generators lose durability over extended use, so it’s vital you pay attention to their stats and repair/replace them when necessary. Equipment can only be repaired up to a certain amount (say 50%), so you have to decide whether it’s worth repairing them, or replacing them altogether (note that you can recycle degraded gear to get back some materials in order to build a new one!).
Currently played about 13 hours and nowhere near completion (in fact I fear I may have to start a new game) but I have been blown back by the gameplay and how engrossing it is, plus how unintrusive the survival aspects have been done.
There is LOTS of time spent running back and forth, micromanaging your home base, plus exploring the often too large levels hoping to find a key item to progress the game, only to find jack♥♥♥♥♥♥ With time against your side as the infection grows stronger and stronger, it’s possible to come to a point where progression becomes virtually impossible and you may need to restart all over again, especially since you only get 1 save slot. Not for the faint of heart.
Simple enemies are bullet sponges, even with upgraded weaponary. Later on, levels are teeming with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, and it's quite a tedious affair engaging and evading them as they can mob you and pretty much♥♥♥♥♥♥your♥♥♥♥♥♥in seconds.
With multiple difficulty modes and randomly generated levels, replayability is strong with this one.
There are some minor bugs and balancing issues to be found (as well as a memory leak) however the developer seems to be on the case and frequently acknowledging player feedback. With a few minor bug fixes and some more tweaks, Subterrain is already a fantastic title that stands out from other survival games and looks to have a bright future. Highly recommended.

I started playing this game in June of 2017. I amassed easily over 200 hours in the standalone version and mostly launched the Steam version just to sync achievements. My opinion of this game started very high. I have a propensity for games that bill themselves as 1. free to play 2. highly customizable and 3. improving on gameplay as you progress as a player. Honestly, the ability to create your own Twisted Metal war-machine in any manner of strategic or goof is about as attractive a concept of a game as any. Conceptually, this game is a 10/10.
The developers of the game have demonstrated a lot of mistakes in keeping the game balanced. The ratio of people complaining about balance and actual problems with balance is about 10:1. With the right amount of real-world-dollars and in-game-know-how, you can dominate at every echelon of gameplay. It is almost pay-to-win, in that putting a lot of money in the game will reward you with amazing parts for your machines, almost as much as putting a lot of time into the game would yield the same results.
Ultimately, the gameplay is the breadwinner. There simply aren't games that exist like this. I understand the developers and publisher are raking money in hand over fist for how many whales keep this game afloat, but that rarely tarnishes my time in the Wastes. Without the pay-to-progress features, this game would be tippity-top-tier. Until then, it's still free to play, and worth checking out. Once you have your head around how the mechanics of the in-game market work.
Revisiting this game after a 2-month hiatus really demonstrated value in how well the devs can turn around and balance things, as well as make huge improvements to feel, look, and gameplay. I am onboard fully, and I've never spent a cent on this game.

Ninja storm three does a few things right, and a few things wrong. Personally, I found it highly enjoyable. The fights are beautifully animated and are accurately described as "easy to learn, hard to master." Though there are many cutscenes, I never found them obtrusive as quicktime events tended to be woven in most of them. If you really want to play a good naruto fighting game for once, and you're not a console player, I highly recommend this game.
However, I did have some serious complaints. The game is poorly optimized to work on the PC, and personally, the game runs abysmally on my system, with entire fights taking place in slow motion with the audio sync of the japanese wire-fu movies of yore. Some people might not experience this issue, but I did, so I'm making note of it. Secondly, the online part of the game is utterly dysfunctional. Online, most players can expect 2/3 online matches to disconnect before anything really happens due to server-related issues. It's incredibly frustrating, and while the developers have promised improvement, we have so far seen only one patch that did not fix the issue.
In short, if you don't care about the multiplayer much, and don't mind tinkering with your system to get the game to run as it would on a console, you'll probably have a blast with this game. However, if you wanted to play online against other people and/or you're still running a system similiar to mine (I'm running XP) you'll probably feel it's a waste of your money.
*EDIT*
In recent patches, the online segment of the game has actually been fixed... More or less. It's functional now, more often than not, and while not perfect, the multiplayer of the game is still very enjoyable.

EVE Online is a "timesink" subscription-based game in a space-economy setting that rivals every space fairing genre to date. Boasting one of the most difficult learning curves. It's not a game for the casual player. To accomplish anything you will need to dump a lot of hours into planning and coordination. For this reason, many players have referred to the game as "a second job" and "a game for lobster accountants". A lingering problem is that the developers always manage to cater to older players with their updates and changes, though they have been trying to appear more freindly to new players. Due to the enormous player-base, the servers have been time-dialated per sector load. In a heavily populated sector, this can mean nearly 60 seconds between a button press and the intended action. It's a great game so long as you play your cards right. Skill training is the biggest timesink aspect of the game, effectively piloting a Titan (largest ship type) will take a minimum of two real-world years training. If you go into this game thinking you'll try everything and kick♥♥♥♥♥doing so, you'll fail miserably. The key is early focus and long term goals.

Well, I can tell there was ALOT of love put into RPG Maker MV. It's like RPG Maker ACE, but of course, have it's present differences:
1. Javescript instead of RGSS

3. A completely new Character generator.
4. Plugins

Speaking of the character generator, it's a COMPLETE upgrade from VX Ace. The faces look much better, and the sprites aren't that bad either. Paticularlly, the faces got a real face-lift.

Rimworld offers a unique take on the survival game concept, where you take control of a colony of people rather than a single individual. As the benevolent leader of your peon colonists your goal is to survive the planet for as long as possible and eventually make it off, whether you find a space ship or build one is up to you.
The game offers several ways to play with a variety of difficulty levels and a few starting scenarios (which you can edit or download from the community) ranging from relaxing and easy to chaotic and painful. While on the topic of the community, I would be remiss if I did not mention the plethora of mods available to enhance your experience, or just make it easier.
At its core Rimworld offers a perfectly acceptable top down strategy game for fans of the genre, though what keeps me engaged is the constant updates despite being an alpha build, and the user modifications that allow for drastically different methods of play while maintaining a core similarity. Rimworld is a wonderful game that can only get better over time.

I bought this game on a whim, because I'm good like that.  Steam advertises indie games to me and like the good little consumer I am, I put my hand in my wallet without thinking "Am I wasting money on another piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥that will get uninstalled within an hour?".
Well, this is one of those rare occasions where this has been money well spent!   Although this is a 16 bit retro looking piece it has grabbed my attention!    I won't go into too much detail because (a) I'm lazy and (b) I've got other stuff to do but for a simplistic top-down interface there's SO much stuff to do!  It will keep you occupied - the initial challenge is in gaining access to areas which will allow you to research, create and harvest materials for better gear (a bit of a "hunt the key" thing, which can get a little irritating I admit).
Each area (aside from the tutorial and core areas) are also devoid of heat and oxygen so you'll have to ensure that you're well stocked with both or gtfo before they run out.  Alternatively, you can replace broken components for the heat and oxygen generators for a slightly easier life.  This will also somewhat slow down the infection rate for each area.  Quite what effect this has on gameplay, I'm not sure.  I've played for a while but have had to restart my progress several times.
If that wasn't enough, you have to manage power across each area from a fusion reactor which has decaying power cores.  Happily enough though, you are able to craft new ones - and even research upgraded versions.
The final element of challenge is with the mobs which I would describe as "Sort of Space Zombies", "Big Bugs with Little Bugs" and "Floaty eyes with little tentacles".  Thus far I have not seen much variety in the mobs but I'm far from the end game I suspect.
I have only found 1 bug so far - for some reason I was not able to enter the escape menu after alt-tabbing in and out but luckily enough I was near a manual save point (I've only found one, which is in the core area).
I'd highly recommend this game, if you like the creative element of crafting, the curiousity of researching better gear, managing resources and enjoy having a tentacled eye up your bum in the dark (the environment is, er... quite dark and situational awareness extends only to what you can see... unless you take recreational in-game drugs :)

NOTE: In order to play this game, as of the time of this review, you must install the latest OpenAL from the support site:
While short and simple, Atom Zombie Smasher (AZS) is a quirky, fun enjoyable little game that you can have fun with again and again. There is plenty of options available in the vanilla game to customize for a wide variety of playthroughs, which is greatly increased by the modding support. There is plenty enough thought to be expected on missions (where to place units, when/where to actvate traps, and how to control the flow of both zombies and humans, etc.) giving hardened and casual strategy players moments of genius and joy whenever a plan goes smoothly, and you reduce the human casualties in the single-digits.
The "story" of AZS is entertaining, but feels a lot like fluff. The vignettes are short and sweet, giving glimpses of story that, overall, is almost completely unrelated to the actual gameplay. This is more a choice of style by the developers, and thus doesn't at all affect the game negatively.
However, what does is the AI, especially for the humans. It's guaranteed that you will get angry at the humans you're saving when they move in droves towards a single zombie.There isn't any rhyme or reason, as they flow around like the zombies you're killing. Best prepare that reset button.
Conclusion:
Atom Zombie Smasher is a fun game to waste time with. Though the humans are rock-stupid, the great variety of options for setting the campaigns greatly increases its lifespan, and the potential for a new, hilarious game with each new campaign.
++Fun, hilarious mood
++Strategy gameplay that's enjoyable for both casual and hardened stategy players
++Mod support and campaign changing options made available at the start
+Simple graphical style
+Ejoyable soundtrack
--Current version is buggy and can crash on launch without the proper software (made available in support site)
--idiotic human AI

Do I really recommend it?
This isn't a game. It's an experience.
There is no end game, nor objective. There isn't an AI telling you to rescue a PoW, or an old man giving quests.
Proteus simply has one task, and that's bringing the player back to, ironically, nature. You take the place of an unkown being, and simply spend your entire playtime exploring a randomized island made almost entirely of right angles. Along the way, you're greeted by trees, frogs, owls, and much more. Temporal changes also encompass you, as your duration of one session will dictate night and day, and even the seasons. Simple movement controls take the sophistication out of what you'd call a "game"; letting WASD do the work.
Proteus boasts itself in two areas: visuals and audio. Surprisingly, the nearly 8-bit art design does well, and no fancy lighting effects or graphics to the subatomic pixel grade are necessary to proclaim this one of the more visually appealing things I've seen. The audio is nothing out of Roc Nation's professional recording studios, and you could probably make it yourself, yet how come it's one of my favorite aspects of the game? The audio reflects your journey throughout the island, changing as you climb mountains or rest on the beach. It's calming, artificial, yet real.
The developers of Proteus had one key word in mind during this project, and that is simplicity. Nothing too fancy (not saying fancy is bad) in all aspects of a "game", and it works in its favor.
Is Proteus only for hippies and tree huggers? No.
Is Proteus for gamers? Yes and no.
Is Proteus for people who want a change of pace in video games, as well as real life? Yes.
I'd give Proteus an 8.5/10 ($10 is hard to justify, wait until it goes on sale or part of a humble bundle).
After raging at Counter Strike, slaying demons, or even studying, Proteus is a calming way to reconnect yourself with sanity and holocene.
(For full experience, play it in the dark with your headphones. Trust me!)

The Ship is a decent interactive story, you find yourself trapped on a cruse ship and informed by the devious Mr. X that the only way to possibly save your life is to play his game and slay the other passengers onboard. this sets the direction for the rest of the game, simply learning the layout of the giant ship and scroungeing for weapons and neccesities to help you get off the boat. and the game does its best to create the look and feel of being on a large cruse ship with all the extras and exploration is part of the fun of the game.
now for some of the issues I had, now please note that i've only played through on easy so i dont know how or if the story changes based on difficulty. quickly after i found my target and took it out, the focus shifted away from Mr. X's game to doing oddjobs to buy passage off the boat. in fact though he says in his intro that he would be "checking in on us from time to time' hes never seen again outside of a large statue of himself onboard.
also I imagine as a way to help pace the gameplay  so the player isnt just turning into a murder hobo on a boat the game has 2 features the first is a 'needs' system in the sims vein where you have to eat/sleep/restroom/ect. or suffer consequences for letting them go on without paying attention to them. i know this was to help with interaction but it didnt really work out too well.
the second is the onboard Security. stationed throughout the ship are guards and video cameras that cant be disabled ingame or in the case of teh living guards killed, because the moment you step infront of either while wielding a weapon of any kind your instantly jailed, stripped of all weapons, fined based on the amount and variety of weapons found on you and left to roam around an empty brig. once again this is to prevent the player from going on rampage but it just slows you down  as you have to roam around to regain a useful supply of weapons to continue along the storyline.
overall its a good game and teh story was strong and intresting enough that I wanted to see it to the end.

The Ship: Singleplayer Campaign! I like it. It's very different from other Source games. You start as someone on a ship where a man named Mr. X is controlling everyone. You have a quarry you have to kill, but you are also being hunted. Seems like a good game. The first part of the game shows you what to kill and how to kill your quarry. After that, you can meet a bellboy that tells you how to get off of the ship for $100,000. Around the ship, you complete missions to collect money and get off the ship. The story is really nice. I don't think it needs polishing or anything. It's good enough. The story and game feel is nice, but the gameplay falls short. There's nothing wrong with the controls or the movement, but your character has basic human needs. Needs such as sleeping, using the restroom, personal hygiene, and talking to other people. These make the game more "realistic", but it really is impractical. Most of the time, you have to search the ship just to find a chair, or a shower, or a restroom, and it really isn't fun. It takes away from the mission! I'll mind my own business, trying to steal the Holy Grail, when all of a sudden I need to shower. There aren't many things to carry out your life processes on the ship unless you know where to look. I'm not saying these things are bad, I'm just saying that it takes away from the story.
The Ship is a good game.

TL;DR: If you love good story and have played through all of the previous Borderlands games, this is a great spinoff for you to enjoy.
Now that the TL;DR is out of the way, onwards to the actual review.
Yes, it's another episodic game from Telltale Games. Say what you like about it, I personally loved Tales from the Borderlands.
The cell-shaded graphics are here but without the fast paced action as the first person shooter variety which is much to my relief (the regular variety gave me motionsickness and a headache after a while of play time).
Much of the dialogue is hilarious and the plot is quite enrapturing. But it's definitely the characters that I love the most.
The banter is the most amusing and ties in great with the story. Of course you have your character cameos from 1, 2 and the Pre-sequel too but they're brief and mostly just there for comedy relief and plot elements.
I know this review is mostly incredibly vague, but seeming as story drives most of this game, giving it away is pretty much going to ruin any experience you'll have yourself. For me, I loved the story, characters and going through the outcomes to see what changes. It was a rollercoaster of emotions going through it the first time absolutely blind and the second time was only slightly easier but still as bad as the first. Definitely get immersed/engrossed with the characters and the story. It's very worthwhile.

text:
UNS3 is a strong fighter in it's own right, but also a good pick for people like me who more often than not, just don't enjoy fighters. This game has a very Beat-em' up feel to it.. it's also very simple by nature, with simple controls, combos and easy to perform moves. With that said, it has enough depth in the way that you can use those simple moves and turn it into a truly exciting game, full of satisfaction and devious trickery.
This game shines most in it's multiplayer. The best way to experience this game would be locally, with a mate or seven. Failing that, you can of course take to the online mode. The netcode looks like it needs work but disconnects are a thing of the past- the real beast to worry about is latency. Fighting any friend further than my own state (Western Australia) resulted in anywhere between a few milliseconds to half a second of latency, with those in my state being as responsive as a local match. Unfortunately, and this is likely due to poor Australian internet but it's still worth noting, playing any friend overseas was unplayably laggy, resulting in only frustration for both players. It kind of draws from the game, but it's more of an issue for us here.
When you do get connected, it is undoubtedly the most fun part of the game.
That is of course not to say the single player doesn't excel too, oh it does. One of the best stories in a fighting game in thanks to the rich and interesting world provided by the Naruto franchise. The story itself takes place in the same arc the currently-airing anime does at time of release, the Fourth Great Ninja War. The story is solid, it has many moments that will blow your mind and a lot of them are fully playable. Each fight is as memorable as the last, nothing feels too forced or unnecessary and the pace is set nicely too, with the exception of an almost hour-long scene that just sucks the life out of the middle of the game for a while. If I were to pick some nits I'd say that the characters are a bit too stiff and they don't move during dialogue unless it's a big scripted cutscene, but when things get good, they get fantastic. Even flashbacks are implemented into story fights as you play, giving you some GREAT perspective. Some of the story is very simpified, and it focuses more on the Main characters than the Anime does, leaving out some very interesting and emotionally impacful backstory.. but it does the job. It teaches you how to play, offers hours of entertainment and will make you excited for the franchise all over again. Sadly, the ending is a little different to what happens in canon Naruto, likely to avoid spoiler territory for the anime, and thus is a little unsatisfying. It'd be nice to have gotten that little surprise at the end- for that, I highly urge you to watch the anime, the person behind that mask.. ooh! Amazing.
For a Console port, it has it's issues. There's a lack of tweakable options.. you're given a choice of resolution and Anti-Aliasing and that's about it. RPG Maker MV is 10$ more than VX, and this is very appropriate, because MV is only slightly better than VX; about 10$ better. But that's not a bad thing. What I mean is, it isn't quite the next evolution in the rpg maker series; almost nothing has changed from vx, but that isn't a problem because vx worked well and there's no point in fixing what isn't broke. So for those who prefer and are familiar with the vx system, you will have no trouble at all adjusting to mv. And if you already have vx, I'll tell you now, I wouldm't worry about getting mv. But if you don't, here's why to consider mv over its predecessor:
1: Plug-In Support: Essentially, now you can mod RPG Maker. (Without having to root through files and perform technical gymnastics). This allows for things such as a "bestiary", a slot machine mini game, and other such add-ons, a suprising number of which freely come packaged with the game (just search through your files)
2: Improved Character Generator: overall better layout and functionality and, more importantly, the artstyle actually matches the base resources.
3: Of lesser importance, more base resources for modern-setting games. (Again, will have to be imported from the dlc files, but they're free)
Negative Points: Minor, but maybe worth consideration: you may prefer the 32-bit gba-era style graphics of vx (which I do); the music is, in my opinion, some of the poorest in the series and, as of now, there is hardly any extra resources for this game, both from the creators and made by fans.
TL;DR: Don't bother if you have VX, but if you want a new RPG Maker, you might as well pay 10 bucks extra for this.

Game story is great. You get to play through the DBZ sagas and even go into Battle of the Gods. Lots of characters which is great, fighting is generally fun.
My biggest issue is the balancing and repetition. Storyline and parallel quests range from ridiculously easy to painfully hard. Often you'll have to fight the same enemy 3 times, the enemy recovering full health between each set. Or fight 3 enemies at once, with seemingly unlimited ki and stamina. At times it can get kind of BS, not in a difficult way but in a rubber-band effect kind of way. By the end, with difficult multi-enemy scenarios that resist flinching (can't close combat because you can't combo your hits on them without them retaliating) I ended up cheesing the entire fight - flying around in circles  to dodge the CPU moves and whittling them down with ki blasts.
The other thing is that you cannot create multiple characters until you complete the game. So first time play through, if you picked buu class but decided part way through that sayian might be more fun; you're going to have to delete your progress and start from the beginning. By the time I grinded through the main quest, I just didn't have it in me to start from the beginning with a new lvl 1 character.

Subterrain will keep you hooked for some time whilst you figure out how everything works, there's crafting, resource gathering, various systems and needs to manage, exploration and combat. For a top down game I am having a blast working my way through the areas and the story as well as discovering how everything works in the crafting and resource area. I wouldn't call it horror but the clever use of lighting can create suspense and make you more cautious than you need to be. The contamination system seems to work really well and will keep you on your toes as you juggle management tasks. There's a lot to take in when you first start but the very short tutorials do the job in guiding you in the right direction.
All in all a good game so far, I may add to this once I am further along in the story depending on how it turns out. If your on the fence then grab the demo and have a crack and see what the game has to offer. Definitely worth the US$11.99 I paid for it.

Subterrain is an excellent example of what a talented dev team can do with a small toolset and a deep understanding of what makes video games fun.
This game pushes all the buttons – survival horror, sci-fi zombies, researching tech, exploring rooms and picking through containers, cutting a hole through the darkness with your flashlight, base-building, and a touch of tower defense.
The graphics are not impressive, nor are they meant to be. This is not a game you play to benchmark your new 3d card, but all that flare is hardly missed due to the complexity and urgency that the game gradually builds over time.
Semi-spoilers:
Expect plenty of tension but no cheap jump-scares, a straightforward gather/research/craft system, a quick and easy inventory interface, and a compelling narrative that unfolds via data logs and soliloquies from the main character. Top-down System Shock? Close.
If any of this sounds interesting, buy it. You’ll like this game.
Looking forward to seeing what PixelLore does next.

A mediocre, unpolished game with a core of diehard supporters/apologist. Squad is a dizzyingly unfocused game that depends really strongly on teamplay to make things sort-of work. The problem with this game is not so much Joe Public GI and his lack of teamwork, but the choices that were made in designing this game. There are numerous non-linear maps with way too many cap points, so forces become diffuse and engage in small skirmishes that greatly influence the outcome of the match but feel completely arbitary. Maps are also typically too large. This makes for smaller and shorter engagements. Vehicles in combat roles are virtually useless and are quickly destroyed without having much impact on the match. Gameplay mechanics are sub-par with guns poking thru terrain, inexplicably long reload animations and bizarre weapons switching. Medic, my usual go-to class is over-complicated and unrewarding to play.  In short, it feels like a very unfinished mod. I recently came back to this game after many months and many updates and it feels no different than it did when I left. Ironically, this game made by a group of modders, may ultimately be improved and fixed by the mod community.

Fun game, like the previous ones. Great story, let down by some dodgy voice acting and stilted dialogue. Some of the gnome voices are on the Jarjar Binks end of the annoying spectrum. Some criticize the combat system, and I can see why you'd love it or hate it as it requires a little patience. It's real-time-turn-based, if that's a thing; similar to the Gothic games. It's not a mindless hack-n-slash so you need to time blows, blocks and dodging. It's generally easy with one opponent but gets quickly impossible with 3 or more. You need a party to act as combat decoys more than you need them to assist you in fighting.
The lore is a bit of a grab-bag but I enjoyed the pirate/inquisitor/voodoo/druid/mage/aztec ruin/underworld thing they mashed together. I like sandbox sprawlers that let you jump up to seemingly inaccessible places and reward you with hidden loot. There's no character creation, but it also doesn't lock you in to classes so your character will end up evolving towards the skills you like using.

DO NOT LISTEN TO PROFESSIONAL REVIEWS, IGN and Gamespot both gave this game deceptively bad reviews. I will say that I watched some reviews whining and complaining on how bad this is or how "average" this is but I recommend you get the game on sale if you're uneasy about it. I received it as a gift and I personally think it's been unjustly panned by reviewers. The combat has a learning curve but when you get used to the timing, it can be pretty fun. The story is kinda crazy, most of the characters are nicely voiced with unique attitudes (The shaman is really weird though), but there are moments when you will see a characters face that resembles a previous character you have encountered. Some voices seem off in how the dialog is delivered and the shaman, though funny at times, can get repetitive with his one liners during combat. There is a ton of content in this game and surpirsingly the graphics look quite nice though not mindblowing as this is also on PS3. Thankfully the PC version looks and performs much better (Duh). For those who want fluid smooth animations though, you may not like the attack animations, though it's not as bad as demonicons slo-mo loaded combat. Some may also be put off by the need for gold to learn skills, but you can find places in this game where they basically throw gold at you, if you take on a lot of side quests. The story has a sort of pirate theme but it's overall a means to an end. If you want a blockbuster story, you won't find it here. You may find great gameplay and hours of quests to kill time, but not much hand holding. The map is a very appreciated addition over Risen 2, I found it frustrating that Risen 2 lacked a map, making pathfinding really tedious.
You also have 3 factions to choose from, each with unique abilities and gameplay. Overall, there are a lot of reasons to give Risen 3 a try, save for the so-so story.

It's okay. There always seems to be the wonky camera or lame angle issue with all these chess programs, but there is the 2-board in the corner, so I do appreciate & use that. Also, if you'd like to play a buddy online, you'll need to enter in their IP address -- c'mon, really!? But at least there is the means to play a friend (unlike most of these chess programs on Steam). I don't mind that the graphics aren't great -- in fact, I like that it doesn't take much effort for my pc to run it, & it reminds me of cool retro games from the 80's, so it's probably more entertaining for us old farts. There is a large variety of interesting, semi-nifty chess boards & pieces, okay music, (even though Pure Chess has the best music so far) and good chess engines with up to 9 levels. I just wish that all these chess programs would allow you to transfer your game (not just the notation) to FB, without having to record it with another program. That would be cool. Maybe if they made a patch & allowed that, it might even be worth $19.00. But right now, $10 is the maximum, & that seems accurate. Also, it's much better than all of the Fritz engines because it fairly user-friendly, especially with setting up a position. So save yourself money & get this instead. Overall, I'd say, it's decent, but you won't be thrilled & dancing around your living room by it either.

*edit* at the bottem of this review i will do a hard break down of a single combat encounter.
-----------------------------
Pros?
Litterally no level cap,
Interesting combat (can be complicated), it's skill combo based, you need to act and react according to what you, AND your enemy is doing. spamming one skill will get you killed. unless your a playing range.
Many classes, each with completely different play styles, and any skill can be used while under any "talent" as the game calls it, your talent only means your gain double xp for the skills under that talent, there is only race restrictions for some skills.
Some of the combat talents are; close combat, mage, puppeteer, Alchemist (construct, and battle), Lance, bard  (mostly buffs only one offensive move), fighter, ninja, gunslinger etc.. theres alot to pick and choose from for combat
There is many many things to do outside combat, there is alot of life skills, cooking, smithing, magic craft, etc.. the list goes on and alot of these the high end goods from these crafts can fetch a handsome price. and outside skills? there is treasure hunting on Iria, and different types of collection books to fill, such as types of food you've eaten, types fish caught, monsters you've hunted. Commerce is another thing, in which you take goods from one town and take them to another and hopefully sell for a higher price, which nets gold and ducats, ducats used to buy limited supply goods and more powerful versions of standard weapons.
MANY MANY skills, (want to be a master of milking? how about hoeing? you can do that.)
almost always 1 or more events happening,
new stuff all the time,
friendly crowd (depending on server, but over all amazing and you can usually find someone willing to help you at any time, the game is better when your friendly and make friends, just a tip.)
more clothes and styles then you can shake a stick at, (all of which can be gotten with out spending a dime, though.. sometimes the dime would be "cheaper")
great customization options (sometimes at the cost of money),
interesting lore and story (if you can read)
regular updates
------------------------
Cons?
You can find yourself spending quite a bit of money for anything from pets, pon (for character features and homesteads), limited time clothes, character cards, and such
the nice clothes, aren't cheap with ingame money. get use to it.
combat can be complicated if your coming from the typical mindless button mashing mmo.
with out spending money, there is only 2 free pets you get on start, a horse (without inventory), and a eagle mount (with out inventory). later you can get a Pegaus mount (with inventory) per character, but you have to go through a story line that can kick your butt with out the skill lvl for it. There is a biannual event where you can (after alot of work) get free pets with an sizable inventory, other then that, events where you get pets.. are rare.
With out spending money, your basic character will look pretty bland and dull. (with one or two dollars though, it can be vastly improved.)
Gachapons, can turn in to an addiction if u don't watch out.
Lag, glitches and such happen, but are completely bareable.

Overall, it's an mmo i don't plan on leaving for a while, and i've hopped from most other mmo's out there, this one, is different and i love it. For me, the best part of the game, might not be the game, alot of it is the comunity.

Gunpoint is an action puzzle game designed, coded and written by PC Gamer journalist Tom Francis who just recently, after Gunpoint proved to be a success, left the publication to fully pursue a career in game development. And the world now has another talented independent developer.
Gunpoint’s simple yet pleasing retro looks may fool you into thinking that the game is a throwback to times long past, but that couldn’t be farther from the truth. This is a wholly modern, unique and innovative game that rewards players for experimentation. The players assume the role of freelance spy Richard Conway who gets tangled up in a rather convoluted story of murder, betrayal and industrial espionage. The writing is great for the most part, it’s witty and often intentionally breaks the fourth wall. The noir atmosphere is surprisingly strong thanks to the great soundtrack and the pleasing aesthetics.
Conway’s objective usually involves breaking into a building and retrieving sensitive data. To achieve this, the players are given complete freedom to choose whichever play style fits them best. Every mission can be completed without ever making a noise or being seen by the guards, but on the flipside, you can smash through windows, break down doors and simply kill everyone standing in your way. To do either, you earn upgrades for your newly acquired pants which allow you to jump over great heights and distances. You can also move on walls and ceilings. This allows for sneaking, but can also lead to all sorts of great action such as pouncing on a guard and knocking him out of the window.
Conway can also purchase a variety of gadgets such as the Crosslink and Wirejack which introduces you to Gunpoint’s most compelling mechanic. By changing to an alternative view mode, you can rewire electric circuits. For example, you can rewire a light switch to open a door or a motion detector to turn off the lights. Later on, you can even purchase a gadget that allows you to rewire the guard’s weapons. This complete freedom of gameplay opens up numerous possibilities and the game never penalizes you for playing the way you want to play. Different clients will have different requests such as minimal violence or leaving no living witnesses, but these are completely optional objectives that only affect how the client rates you, but the mission will still be a success and you will get payed the same.
The only major drawback is that the game is pretty short. It will definitely leave you craving for more content, but at least you can play all the missions again with all the gadgets and abilities you’ve unlocked which is compelling in its own way as it lets you further experiment with all the crazy stuff you can pull off.
Gunpoint is an original and intelligent game that treats players with respect and facilitates emergent gameplay through the use of compelling, innovative and slick mechanics.

To make it easy on the common viewer, this game is very frustrating a lot of the time and relies a lot on RNG, but rewards smart and creative ideas, and has easy to pick up on mechanics and charming visuals. There's a bit of wiggle room for error, but mistakes can start adding up over time, leaving you with a few raiders miraculously digging into your dwarven fortress -- which may or may not be crawling with infuriatingly hard to kill bugs -- then stealing your silver, and kidnapping your only doctor. Of course, it can be averted if your colonists could ACTUALLY BUILD your defenses, but hey.
Aside from that, the game is a lot of fun. The game involves scrapping together a colony from basic materials, then eventually surviving long enough to either escape the planet, or make a village to comfortably house your colonists. There's a myriad of options for what you can do or where you can go, whether you're a beachside colony, or one on a sheet of ice, you can make it work.
As for the technical bits, everything works pretty well. The controls are easy enough to use, the HUD conveys enough without being cluttered, and gives enough leeway to avoid frustrating the player. The soundtrack is really easy to listen to, letting you pause time and build your colony calmly.
But, I haven't mentioned the cons. Oh boy, does the game have cons. The game can be incredibly annoying with how it throws its challenges at you. The mood system can cause serious complications, where your colonists will get into random fights because they don't like their rooms, then proceed to violently kill eachother. Raids can end up becoming overwhelming, where you either don't have enough in terms of defense, or you get horribly unlucky and end up with alien robots murdering your whole colony. Manhunter packs can catch you with your pants down, and now you're stuck inside for a few days. Fire in a raid when you built your colony out of wood? Everything's gone.
Not an amazing game by any stretch, but it's terribly addicting, and will probably suck a lot of your time from your life. The price is a bit steep, but there's a pretty good chance you'll get your money's worth.
Edit: I forgot to mention the modding and workshop support, but since it's aside from the game itself, I'll make it brief. The mods can assist with a lot of the issues mentioned, giving quality of life changes or actual additions like new weapons, new utilities, or can do so much as overhaul combat. However, if you don't enjoy the base game as a concept, mods probably won't suddenly change your mind.

This game is incredible, and I should've remembered to review it years ago.  Well-designed RTT and RTS packaged up into a tiny, pulp fiction universe that's experiencing an enormous problem with the undead.  Command a shifting roster of -unusual- mercenary squads and specialist military units amidst the chaos of the zombie apocalypse.
Supervise evacuation efforts, last-ditch defenses and all-out offensives against the surging tides of death.  As the pressure mounts, rescue wonky scientists and "ask" them to research improvements for your equipment.  Set up elaborate traps and killzones across entire downtown areas, employing mercenaries, snipers, explosives and other, more exotic weapons.  Use the zombies' behaviors against them, until desperation leads to the utilization of unlucky civilians as bait in your tactical plans.  When all else fails and the cities are alive with corpses, feel free to resort to nuclear warfare and llama bombs.
A pitch-perfect example of clever indie design and a willingness to make immensely creative games on a shoestring.  AZS is well-built on a foundation of intriguing swarm AI, hilarious art and slick, intuitive gameplay.  Take the plunge if you enjoy RTS, strategy or puzzle games; Atom Zombie Smasher won't disappoint.

Despite the trope of zombies on Mars, I had really high hopes for this game. So far it doesn't deliver, mostly because it is far too much about inventory management to be enjoyable to me. I find myself crawling through the same dark hallways (can you turn the lights back on?) over and over again to fill or empty my tiny backpack or resupply my oxygen.
I also dislike that the various crafting or research stations are separated by loading screens or animations that serves no purpose. And your research and crafting efforts, which is a very nice system, is hampered not by resources but by software cards. So before I can build a better backpack to loot more efficiently I have to loot more stuff... I'd wish for more interactions with the environment as well, such as building barricades or fixing doors.
The best about the game is the ambience. I like that I have to monitor heat and oxygen when I explore new areas, and the shrill sounds of nearby monsters. But since I sometimes fill that lootbag in less than one room, exploring/looting feels more like a chore than part of the survival.
Also, I don't agree with the save system. Just 1 slot feels like a forced ironman and I would not stomach a restart.
Combat is good enough. More detail would have been nice, but not needed. Overall it's not a bad indie game, if there were more options for finetuning the difficulty and settings (bag size, monster respawn, craft station animations, lights) for non-hardcore-fans I'd give it a solid thumbs up.

Forget Risen 2. Let it not bias you. Risen 3 is all you'd want from the Risens and the Gothics, too.
Graphics
The game is gorgeous. Sunlight/Godrays crash through the canopies of the trees; distant mountains cast their shadow on distant land realistically; fire never looked as good; water makes you want to jump right in; distant ruins beckon you to explore them; higher tier armour -- the cloth properly dancing as you move, the steel reflecting the light -- makes you drool as you stare at your hero. The physics engine is also fluid and realistic, enemies falling back after having received their killing blow will tumble over objects or droop down from them.
Gameplay
It's still what you expect from any Risen or Gothic game: The HUD is simple, and that's perfectly fine. In fact, I wouldn't have it any other way. You can now also change into a parrot with scrolls that you'll find everywhere -- specifically in high places! -- the devs silently begging you to use them as turning into a parrot makes you glide however long you want. There's a little energybar nonetheless which will slowly empty whenever you want to fly upward. It's fun! And as for the combat...
Combat
It has improved SO MUCH! If you time your attacks properly, you can swing with heavy attacks almost as fast as you would with normal attacks. This needs some practise, but once you get a feel for it, it becomes easy. For some too easy, though many players still think combat is hard. As you gain enough experience (or Glory) you'll be able to gain the Riposte skill, which, if you time it right, your parry will execute a sweet animation of your hero evading a strike and counter-attacking with a strike of his own. You can also still dodge, which is an ability that can be exploited since there's no stamina bar. I say exploited, because during a dodge you're practically invincible. A fantastic addition to the combat is the finishing move on humanoids. When you kill the last enemy in an encounter, you watch your character execute him. There are multiple finishers. Your hero pushes an enemy against a wall, rams his weapon's hilt into the face multiple times before running him through; your hero turns the enemy around and slits his throat, etc. etc. etc. My most favorite finisher is where the enemy runs toward the hero and the hero steps aside at the last moment, leaving his weapon stretched horizontally in the enemy's path... the enemy runs into the blade, stumbles past the hero and eventually drops on the ground a few strides further, quite dead. Imagine stuff like this with a perfect physics engine. Yes, if there's a ledge a few strides behind your hero in said finisher, the enemy will stumble and drop down the edge instead. Deader than dead. So awesome.
Exploration
There's so much to see and do and find in this game! Almost every NPC with a name (which is almost every NPC) has a quest or more quests. When you climb up a mountain and see these mysterious places in the far, far distance... well, that telltale feeling rushes through every RPG player -- the feeling that says: I NEED to go there and explore every nook and cranny! And I can guarantee: You WILL be rewarded for it.
Final verdict
I love this game. I am not kidding. It's the best thing in the gaming world that has happened to me in YEARS. And that's coming from a guy who fell in LOVE with Gothic 1 & 2, Risen 1 and very much disliked Risen 2. I catch myself playing this game with a content smile on my face. It's crazy. This game is phenomenal!

RPG Maker MV is the next implement of the RPG Maker franchise, a series of tools that allows you to create a classic RPG game. How that game is going to be made will be entirely up to you, enabling you to create the game you always dreamed of making. Starting off RPG Maker MV is an expensive tool set starting off at $79.99 and certain packs/DLC that follow suit are anywhere from $5.00-$20.00, which is a pretty expensive hobby overall. Once these have been purchased you are given a decent amount of starting resources to make a game. The tool itself is relatively easy to start using, but getting into scripts and how certain events work demands more advanced and seasoned users. While creating the game, you are given so many options from adding actors (the characters of your game), creating equipment, adding bosses and monsters, to states that will affect the combat, everything is up to your creative insight. The character creation tool makes its return again, but this time it feels like a much smoother system, characters created not only look better, but the sprites they produce also look pretty good. The system of creating events and maps remained more or less the same with a few new features, but overall the tool feels great. While some RPG Maker veterans will cling to the old, some will move onto the new and utilize this software to create awesome new titles that will either be sold on STEAM or remain only playable by the author.
PROS:
Loads of new resources and features
Pretty good starting music
Character creator enhanced
Allows you to create your own game
Easy to start off
CONS:
EXPENSIVE
Some features require more advanced users
Requires some of your older resources to be enlarged or changed to match the new standards.

Borderlands is a hybrid FPS / RPG that combines elements of Diablo, Halo, and the old Mad Max movie series. It tells the tale of 4 mercenaries, called Vault Hunters, who scour the planet of Pandora searching for an ancient alien vault, rumored to contain treasure and power beyond belief. Along the way, they battle bandits, soldiers, monsters, and aliens, all the while helping out different townsfolk and eccentric scientists who are always offering weapons and cash in exchange for work.
The game is huge and offers a multitude of quests, literally millions of different guns, and four distinct classes that all manipulate the battlefield differently. It can be played solo, but co-op is encouraged and can add many extra hours of replayability. It's extremely enjoyable, has great storytelling
, features a New Game+ mode, and has quite a few epic set pieces.
However, despite this, the original Borderlands is lacking in quite a few areas that make later entries in the series so spectacular...
Charismatic, hilarious villain? Nah.
Gripping storyline with plot twists and unexpected deaths? Nah.
Tons of great voice acting and dialogue? Not so much.
DLC out the♥♥♥♥♥that really expands the universe? Eh...
Huge differences between gun manufacturers and the need for high level gear? Surprisingly, no.
But what this game lacks in what many consider the defining traits of this series, it makes up for in something else...
It has Brick as a playable character.
You see that badass enemy over there? Big dude? Definitely gonna shred your♥♥♥♥♥if you try and rush him?
Brick will uppercut that guy so hard his head will
explode. The soul of Mr. Torgue lives in Brick's hands, and♥♥♥♥♥♥goes boom whenever those beautiful meat hunks connect with any fleshy or armored surface.
You see that boss over there that will blast you if you even think about coming out of cover?
Brick punches the cover. Brick then runs over to the boss. Brick punches the boss's family, friends, and entire religion. Then Brick punches the boss. The boss is now dead. The universe doesn't even register the fact that the boss ever existed.
Brick does not care about being shot. Brick does not care how badass an enemy is. Brick will punch that enemy, all the while being filled with bullets, and that enemy will
be erased from history.
Borderlands GOTY Edition is often on sale for $8. For the price of some crappy buttrock album at WalMart; for the price of some crappy latte from Starbucks; for the price of a new pair of underwear (which you aren't going to wear anyway), you can own what is arguably one of the greatest games of all time.
And you can be Brick.
Buy this game. Experience Borderlands in all its glory. Be Brick. Punch things. Win forever.

This is the game I always wanted Battlefield to be. A serious combat simulator, which is less clunky than ARMA, but more realistic than BF.
The community is largely fantastic, and there is the general understanding that this is a team game first and foremost. However I mic is an absolute must, and the game is simply pointless without one.
It's not a standard FPS and you need to be willing to literally do the grunt work in order to win, which includes spending time pulling security around a corner for three minutes while you wait for the other squads to sort themselves out, digging fortifications constantly and waiting for a medic to show up (which I've found they generally do very well).
Yes there are toxic players who believe if you are not a tier one operator with sixteen years in the SAS than you are simply not worthy of playing this game. Ignore them, because the majority of players are friendly, helpful and honestly a joy to play with.
Get this game if you're looking for a solid combat simulator, and are willing to to put the effort into literally playing as a real soldier, because the amount of times I have zoned out pulling security really did remind me of my time in the army.
My verdict, 7.5/10.

The business model of this game is to introduce nice new items, some of which are often OP, and get people to heavily invest in them. After a month or two they then go overly nerf those items into totally useless. This has happened time after time during the so called 'open beta' that has lasted slightly under half a year now. However, the game was pretty much ready even as start of open beta other some balance issues. But even those were so little that most released games have more issues. And the game does have a real money store to buy ingame stuff with packs upto 100 euro a piece. And they have also stated there will not be any more wipes coming ever.
Now in the latest patch yesterday they really outdid themselves breaking way more than ever before. Despite 40 pages of feedback on their dev blog telling them not to do it, they went for it. And didn't roll it back with another 40 pages of almost exclusively negative feedback on update discussion and high volume of negative reviews on Steam.
Basically what they did was first release all new nice stuff about two months ago, including hovers which they advertised you need at least 8 for a good build. Those who could afford them, either with approx 70 euros of real life money or months of heavy grinding, went for it and got enough of them to do well on high power score, clan wars and ranked battles. But now with this new patch they limited hovers to effectively only 4 per vehicle and they had already been nerfed before so they are very vulnerable. And do note even after these changes cars with wheels typically have 8-12 wheels on high end battles. With only 4 hovers your build will be totally unsuitable for even medium battles because losing just one hover makes you effectively immobile. This caused the ingame market value of hovers to drop like crazy and there is also 10 % tax on all sales, so effectively everything players invested into hovers resulted in loss of approx 50 % of the value. That is around 35 euros of real life money lost. They also did other very major changes into how the game works that are in no way balanced and cause huge change into what kind of builds work. That will also cause notable losses to many players.
Before this patch they have also nerfed various items to death, but the value of such has been lower. But this has happened multiple times and shows they have no intention of making everything balanced. Whenever enough people complain about something it gets nerfed to totally useless item but still remains in the game. And no-one who has invested in the item will get any reimbursement whatsoever. And those items are not boosted afterwards to be even somewhat useable. People would be fine with suitable balance changes for OP items, but not with nerfing items to death.
TL;DR
Stay far away from this game! The business model is to force people to play a lot of real money to get past the huge grinding wall. And in addition to that they regularly change items so that your precious items will no longer work and you have to pay or grind to get new items. Repeat that every month or two. And no, they do not listen to player feedback at all.

Gunpoint is an action puzzle game designed, coded and written by PC Gamer journalist Tom Francis who just recently, after Gunpoint proved to be a success, left the publication to fully pursue a career in game development. And the world now has another talented independent developer.
Gunpoint’s simple yet pleasing retro looks may fool you into thinking that the game is a throwback to times long past, but that couldn’t be farther from the truth. This is a wholly modern, unique and innovative game that rewards players for experimentation. The players assume the role of freelance spy Richard Conway who gets tangled up in a rather convoluted story of murder, betrayal and industrial espionage. The writing is great for the most part, it’s witty and often intentionally breaks the fourth wall. The noir atmosphere is surprisingly strong thanks to the great soundtrack and the pleasing aesthetics.
Conway’s objective usually involves breaking into a building and retrieving sensitive data. To achieve this, the players are given complete freedom to choose whichever play style fits them best. Every mission can be completed without ever making a noise or being seen by the guards, but on the flipside, you can smash through windows, break down doors and simply kill everyone standing in your way. To do either, you earn upgrades for your newly acquired pants which allow you to jump over great heights and distances. You can also move on walls and ceilings. This allows for sneaking, but can also lead to all sorts of great action such as pouncing on a guard and knocking him out of the window.
Conway can also purchase a variety of gadgets such as the Crosslink and Wirejack which introduces you to Gunpoint’s most compelling mechanic. By changing to an alternative view mode, you can rewire electric circuits. For example, you can rewire a light switch to open a door or a motion detector to turn off the lights. Later on, you can even purchase a gadget that allows you to rewire the guard’s weapons. This complete freedom of gameplay opens up numerous possibilities and the game never penalizes you for playing the way you want to play. Different clients will have different requests such as minimal violence or leaving no living witnesses, but these are completely optional objectives that only affect how the client rates you, but the mission will still be a success and you will get payed the same.
The only major drawback is that the game is pretty short. It will definitely leave you craving for more content, but at least you can play all the missions again with all the gadgets and abilities you’ve unlocked which is compelling in its own way as it lets you further experiment with all the crazy stuff you can pull off.
Gunpoint is an original and intelligent game that treats players with respect and facilitates emergent gameplay through the use of compelling, innovative and slick mechanics.

Rimworld offers a unique take on the survival game concept, where you take control of a colony of people rather than a single individual. As the benevolent leader of your peon colonists your goal is to survive the planet for as long as possible and eventually make it off, whether you find a space ship or build one is up to you.
The game offers several ways to play with a variety of difficulty levels and a few starting scenarios (which you can edit or download from the community) ranging from relaxing and easy to chaotic and painful. While on the topic of the community, I would be remiss if I did not mention the plethora of mods available to enhance your experience, or just make it easier.
At its core Rimworld offers a perfectly acceptable top down strategy game for fans of the genre, though what keeps me engaged is the constant updates despite being an alpha build, and the user modifications that allow for drastically different methods of play while maintaining a core similarity. Rimworld is a wonderful game that can only get better over time.

Positives:
1- It's resolution is unlocked (Altought you need plugins like Yanfly's Core plugin to anable them for example).
2- Plugin system makes it easier to avoid errors for people who don't know how to code but  want to use someone else's code.
3- It brings features back from RPG Maker 2003 like the sideview battles and event chasing, making this engine like a fusion between RPG Maker VX Ace and RPG Maker 2003.
4- Using Javascript may bring in more coders since it's a more known language than Rubyscript.
5- Assets resolution got increased along with the characters etc. Included sprites are 48x48 for example.
Negatives:
1- This is not a $80 USD egine since outside of the returning features from 2003 and the higther resolution, it's mainly just  a improved version of RPG Maker VX Ace. Most of the value comes from what the community's coders had done and not Enterbrain (Yanfly's Core Engines for example) yet each new engine costs $10 USD more than the previous.  Get this on a steam sale like I did.
2- The Automatic layering is a improvement over VX Ace but I want full control of the layers like I had on RPG Maker XP. This is the only thing that I miss the most of XP. I don't know why they removed this feature.
3- There's not options to make a full scrolling over world map. Many go around this by placing a bunch of teleporters around the map but it shoud not be this way, it should scroll giving the world the form of a donut like RPGs had been in the past. I don't even think it's possible for coders to add this functionality by making a Map Core script.
Conclusion:
This is the strongest of all the PC RPG Maker egines ever released and the only one who can support HD resolutions. (A core plugin is requiered.) Since it's new it will take a while before it is as supported as VX ACE but it is slowly reaching there. Also to get assets you may want to subscribe to their principal page. There's also some resources here on Steam as well, so just browse around.
If I where to rate this game, I would give it 8/10  or 3.5/5
