If you've played any of the lego games you'll have a fair idea of what this one is all about. It follows the LoTR story relatively well (obviously it takes liberties) and the story mode took me about 10 hours on the first play-through.
Essentially, you smash your way across the landscape, picking up lego 'studs' (money) solving puzzles and fighting lego monsters. The story is very linear, and it's not at all difficult. A couple of the puzzles were a bit touch and go... for example, I couldn't figure out how to kill Shelob the giant spider for quite a while... but it generally feeds everything to you on a plate, leaving you with what is essentially a hand-held but enjoyable little play through the LoTR universe... albeit in lego form.
You can play all the way from start to finish unlocking areas as you go, without having to go back and repeat anything... but if you want to, you can unlock characters and go back to do parts of the game that you had trouble with earlier.
If you're even remotely OCD then this one will really wind you up. There are so many little bits and pieces to complete (optional if you're not a completionist) but getting 100% of everything on every level is going to be quite a long haul.
I've unlocked around 25% of the game after 12 hours... and that's just the easy stuff.
The strength of this one is in the ability to go back after you've done the story mode and find all the extra little bits and pieces that you missed the first time. For example - there's a secret level where you get to play Sauron and smash up a miniature Middle Earth. I won't say where.
There are dozens of characters to unlock. You can buy them with the 'studs' as you find them, and go back and collect the lot later on.
There is no character progression to speak of, but there is a very simple crafting system, which allows you to exchange mithril bricks for items that you can discover and unlock on your travels.
I wasn't expecting to enjoy this one as much as I did. I bought it for my little girl to play with, and thought I'd give it a try first. Suddenly, I realised I was hooked.
Cons... the biggest one is the save system, which seems to be rubbish. A few times I had to repeat sections I thought I'd completed, because I hadn't found a statue which acted as a save-point.  Once you're in "free-play" mode after completing the story, however, you can save whenever you want.
Other than that, and a few annoying camera angles, the game is extremely good. A light-weight explorer/platformer in the lego LoTR universe. Much fun.

Before I say anything it's important to note that this game much like is predecessors receives a ton of scrutiny because every fan boy out there thinks they know whats best for a game and how it should be made with unrealistic expectations and broken game mechanics for the sake of their little hearts.
I like this game. I was skeptical upon news of it that it would fall in line with many other attempts to cash in on this franchise and ultimately give a half hearted game without the gameplay we are all looking for. After seeing gameplay for a bit and then actually purchasing myself I'm please I did. The game is not without hiccups though.
The storyline is original and helps bring a personal immersion for the gamer that former titles failed to capitalize on. The ability to make your own character or even play as the Z warriors and even villains allows the nostalgia to come alive for anyone looking to live out there gaming fantasy of being in the Dragonball Universe.
I believe the inclusion of an original story, player immersion, customizability, and a collectibles system make for a game with very good replayability. Different builds, fighting styles with both a PvE and PvP aspect allow for a wider arrange of gaming for the player. If you're the kind of person who is a crazed completionist then there are tons of items and skills to collect in the Parallel Quests, which is probably where the most meat of the game is.
The downsides? Charging is a skill that must be equipped when you get it. You only have 4 skill slots, two super skills, and 1 evasive skill. I believe that charging should have been something native to players or even a passive skill that could be unlocked at a certain ki attribute or something besides eating up a precious skill slot for something so common among the universe.
It would have been nicer to see perhaps a split in the skills where Physical skills and ki skills are seperated so that even a physically adept player could still perform a few signature ki attacks without crippling their build or vice versa. It waters down the gameplay a bit when the reptitive nature of the same techiques are seen. Also each skill doesn't really have a rating and you have to trial and error each one to find out how effective it is, I worry this may lead to some balancing issues.
Transformations, not enough of them. It seems to be something pretty much exclusive to Kaio Ken users, and Saiyans. It would have been nice to see other races get some power increases. (i could be wrong about this, but what I've read thus far says otherwise). Also of note for transformations is that they take up yet again precious skill slots. So if you want to transform and are capable you'll be down another slot which leads to a serious decision making process for your build and once more waters down your options and makes your playstyle a little more generic.
Through it all though I have had a good time with the game throughout, the grinding for collectibles or for a Z rank in missions is something that I can see people getting frustrated with and I'm usually one of those people. The ability to do missions with a friend or even a couple friends though makes that more fun. I haven't had the frustration yet with the game and that leads me to believe that despite the negative remarks on this game I believe the Devs did a good job. There are still things that need to be balanaced or sorted out here and there but nothing that updates can't fix.

Phiranna Bytes may not be earning awards for stability, but they delivered again on a game that explains why they have produced three of my favorite RPGs.  In the spirit of the original two Gothic's, and the original Risen is an open-ended and rather buggy adventure for RPG enthusiasts, with a layer of modern polish and features that really brings it to life.  The game is rough around the edges, but has more personality and charm than you'll get out of the latest Dragon Age.  It harkens back to a time when people were more concerned with what they could do than how it looked to be doing it.
Once you get through the fairly standard 'tutorial' and intro sequence, the game opens up.  You are free to make mistakes and follow the story at your own leisure and choosing.  This means you can go places you shouldn't be and do things that make your life harder.  This isn't a point-and-click follow the dotted line adventure, this time you are in charge with nothing more than your sense of adventure and desire to explore to fuel you.  Thanks PB!  After Risen 2 I was skeptical, but you've put those fears to rest.

You can interpret it the way you like, there is no story line, just that as life starts, it ends at some point. You can view as much energy in a winter landscape as on summer days, it is just your perspective in play. If you know the meaning of wanderlust, you get the idea.
Now, do I recommend full price? Not quite, there has been no update since launch and there could be more content, but if it is on sale and you like the exploration-observation type of games, you bet.

The best way for me to describe Crossout is Mad Max meets Minecraft meets Warthunder. Basically is a tank battling game where you build your own tank minecraft style then battle them out in arena like battles. The vehicle building aspect of the game is one of the best. Building the ultimate death machine is just so incredibly satisfying. If you like crafting and building games such as minecraft and others you'll find lots to love here. Once you're finished you can save your blueprints then easily upload and share them with other players on the "Exhibition." You'll also want to test it out in combat. The gameplay is very solid and combat can be a lot of fun if you can get a competent team. Combat will provide endless joy for those who enjoy chaos and mayhem. It's also a lot of fun just to see what kinds of crazy machines other players are building.
The Likes:
The graphics are quite good but the main draw for me is the art style. I prefer a more realistic yet fantastical art style and this game is just that. This game has a has a sort of steampunk vibe to it and i love it.
The audio quality is quite good but i really wished they'd give me the option to turn down the gun noise as it can be quite tiresome after long gaming sessions. Hopefully it'll come soon.
Matchmaking queues are very quick and they restart quite fast after each round. Longest i've had to wait was maybe a minute or two but it's quite rare. I have yet to run into any noticable bugs although i will note that the hitbox could use some tightening up.
Dislikes:
The gameplay is a lot of fun but I feel like matches are mindless and end way too fast. The problem is that the PVP match timer are set way too short for this type of game. A short timer is great for a fast pace gamemode such as free-for-all where you can respawn but in this game the normal PVP gamemode only allows for one vehicle per match. Why is this a problem? The game modes usually have objectives such as capturing the opposing team’s zone or fight for a central zone. Either way you’re bound to clash in the middle. The short timer prevents teams from playing the objective tactically and instead everyone just rushes to the middle and whichever team has the most kills wins. This is also worsen by the fact that this game fills the lobby with bots if it can’t find enough players. Bots are basically useless in combat and they’re also allowed to take objectives. I personally don’t think bots should belong in any public PvP matches. I think i’d rather lose to human players on an unbalanced team than to lose a game because a bot secretly captured our base.
Vehicle building: The parts descriptions are very confusing especially when it comes to cabin, engine, and wheel parameters. The game does not do a very good job at explaining these things if at all. I found myself in the forums more often than I should. I'm not sure if its just a translation error but like “tonnage, mass, engine speed, cabin speed, max speed and power” needs to be renamed or further explained with more intuitive ui and tooltips. Sometimes games will add some lore to item description but I only find them to be mostly useless and annoying. In this case it's actually just confusing.
PAY-TO-WIN!
Although i’m having a blast in Crossout it is very unfortunate that this game is without a doubt pay-to-win. I understand that this game is free-to-play but Gaijin literally designed every aspect of this game to force players into buying the DLCs.
Where do i start? This game is a grind fest! Basically to unlock new parts you must
either craft them or buy them from the market. In order to craft you must gather for parts and resources such as scrap metal, coppers, wires, and more. You’ll need a lot of it but that isn’t the main problem. The main problem is the resource caps. This limit means that not only do you have to spend hours and hours grinding for parts and resources you'll also be spending a lot of time waiting in between for the next reset. Some things such as copper can only be obtained through “Raids” which is the game’s co-op PVE game mode. These modes can only be accessed by spending fuel similar to other mobile games. Therefore you have a limited amount of fuel to earn a limited amount of coppers and this feature is just more annoying than anything i can imagine. Currently scraps reset on a weekly basis. This game will take weeks if not months to unlock and earn enough resources to craft what you need. Often than not it's much faster and easier to just buy them from the market since you don't have to meet the level requirements to craft them. This also brings me to my next topic.
The "Market." This game has a player market where you can buy or sell parts and resources to other players. The problem is, these things cost Coins. When you first start the game all your parts are precious but are worth mere pennies on the market. It is very difficult to earn Coins and there are no good ways to do so especially with the resource caps in place.
So why do you want want coins anyways? Because as soon as you start gaining a few levels you'll notice that you're getting absolutely slaughtered by high level players. At first i thought i was just bad. This is true but surely i cannot be that terrible. I now know that it wasn’t just me. This is happening because player level is not a factor in matchmaking. In fact high level players gets faction bonus advantage. Instead of factoring in player levels it seems as though matchmaking is completely determined by a vehicle's "powerscore." The game rates each part on your vehicle using powerscore and the total is your vehicle's overall powerscore. The game pairs you against other players of "somewhat" similar powerscore. I say “somewhat” because more often than not i’m matched up against players with a much higher powerscore than my own. I can be using a 1,500 powerscore vehicle and still be matched against players with double my powerscore if not more. This means that a high level player can slap on the best weapons in the game and as long as they meet the powerscore requirement  just absolutely dominates. Then there are also gamemodes where the powerscore is not even accounted for. I can be using a vehicle with a powerscore of 2,000 and be matched against 12,000 powerscore monsters. Hmm i wonder how they afford all those expensive parts? Yep, you guessed it. They paid real money. To me, this is absolutely game breaking and needs to be addressed.
Conclusion:
Even though the game is still in beta it plays wonderfully with very little lag or hiccups. The game is fully playable and it truly is a lot of fun to play. But with that said, there are some major issues in the game’s current state. These issues are not technical issues but rather moral issues. I've never been a fan of microtransaction, never was, and never will be but if i find a game that i really enjoy playing i would much rather buy it for full price and maybe some even consider buying some DLC as long as they're reasonably priced. $160.00 is not reasonably priced for a game that is still in beta. I know that microtransaction isn't going away anytime soon but forcing us to buy DLC just to keep up with the other players is just wrong. So far the game feels more like a human experiment than a videogame beta that bothers me more than anything. The real question here is should it?
I know it sounds like i'm just absolutely hating on this game but in truth far from it. In fact i just really love this game and i have high hopes for it. I just hate to see it ruined by greed. If you make a great game and people love it they will always come back for more, but no matter how good your game is if you fail to respect your fans you will lose their trust and with it their coins.
Crossout is by no means perfect since it still in beta but i still recommend you give it a try and see it for yourself. I hope this review isn’t too boring and thank you for taking the time to read this.

The best Borderlands game in the series & probably Telltales' best point & click adventure to date.  The overall experience is just so amazing that I couldn't put it down from beginning to end.  A must buy game!
-Long engrossing story
-Fun cast of characters
-Improved QTE mechanics
-Choices actually have effects!?
-Can't skip cutscenes after death
-They killed my favorite BL Character :'(
Unlike previous Telltale games this game actually puts you in the roll of two protagonists.  Rhys is the first you meet, a young man who worked for Hyperion.  He starts out in the middle of the desert searching for someone.  He eventually gets ambushed by a lone masked bandit & is dragged off.  During his capture the bandit asks him to tell him a story about how he ended up where he is.  Rhys then starts The Tale from the Borderlands!
One of the more brilliant parts of the story is how each chapter begins.  They all start off in the normal borderlands style of 2D page by page cutscenes but then as you get through the chapter you're treated to a great opening every time.  You could say every opening to a chapter is like getting a new Borderlands intro.  Each one is simply amazing to witness.
As Rhys is dragged off further he is brought to a camp where you meet the second protagonist, Fiona who has also been taken prisoner by the bandit.  She's a professional con-artist who got a job involving Rhys & everything went to hell.  In the aftermath they ended up forming a neccessary alliance in order to survive their ordeals together.
The bandit has captured them both in order to learn what he calls, "The Truth."
If you've played other Telltale games you know what you're in for.  Mostly QTE segments within the cutscenes with choices of dialog.  Inbetween cutscenes you will have small puzzle like elements.  I say "Puzzle-Like" because they're all so easy they barely feel like puzzles at all.  I really wish Telltale would spruce up the puzzle elements of their games & make them more challenging.  They mostly consist of "Find this item" or "Hit this switch".  Actually, that's pretty much all their puzzles consist of & it just feels tacked on to break up the story.
I guess you could say the real puzzles in the game are within the dialog because they effect the outcomes & what happens within the game.  A good example appears in later chapters with Fiona where she is given options to shoot with elemental properties.  These are all pretty easy, though & involve simply choosing the right element for the corresponding color.  You could also say that unlocking specific characters for the final chapter is part of the puzzle element within Telltale games.
The graphics are of typical Borderlands & Telltale style.  It's almost as if Borderlands was meant to be a Telltale game because they're both represented in such similar fashions.  Cellshaded & outlined.  The game does have some graphical glitches every now and then with flashing character models & lip sync issues.  Other than that though the game looks & feels great.  The QTE segments also tend to make cutscenes look off.  Unless you time it properly it will look like you teleport.  This isn't really a big issue but more of a nitpick for me as I'd prefer much more fluid transitions.
The music is fantastic & perfectly entwined with the whole Borderlands world.  Opening cutscenes playback with probably the best music they could use & everything just feels natural for the whole game's aethstetic.Voice acting is also very well done to the point where I have no complaints about it.
If you enjoy Telltale games or Point & Click style gameplay or just an enjoying experience full of laughs, drama, & more laughs then you should probably pick this game up.  I had more fun with this game in particular than I have with any other Telltale game & that says alot.  This is absolutely the best Telltale game currently on the market & I hope there will be more Tales from the Borderlands games in the future or at least something similar to them.

I like what I see. A highly enjoyable game, and I expect to see great things when it comes to it's final release, because this has potential.

I can only begin to try to describe the countless good and bad things about this game, but the bad far outweigh any of the good. Detailed other reasons are noted after the 3 short lists of key factors. Note: I have clocked in several thousand hours over the 5+ years I have played this; before it was available on steam naturally.) Looking back, it was not worth any of the time or money invested.


Thanks to some feedback I remembered those existed. However do not think its that great you now get some basic free pets for travel. The choices they picked for these "beginner" pets are among the worst in combat, they do not have access to their pet inventory feature (so they cannot hold anything, not even things to heal/mend you; mending is EXTREMELY important, as when you are alone, since pets can mend you as you sit down for full effectiveness of each bandage.
I can only begin to try to explain why the cash shop is just among the worst. To save your item's max durability you must repeatedly spend ~$6 USD each time (each item i believe.) This is just unacceptable because you should not be influenced to spend money for something that is such a basic need of the game.
Pets cost between $2.90 and ~$18 ... naturally the more expensive ones are among the only really useful ones, as their cost seems to go hand in hand with how useful they will be in both function, and combat. These are important because of any combination combat, travel, healing, gathering, and inventory functions.
They just go too far tying the cash shop directly into the game,enchantments are among the worst.  Want a good enchantment?  Well enchantments themselves ... when they fail it destroys the item (at higher enchant ranks) lower ranks cost you max durability, and to even get to using higher level enchantments you not only have to do a series of enchantments (going from low ranking to higher ranking enchantment scrolls; you also need the enchantment skill level high enough to be able to do them and up your % of success ... to save an item from a failed enchantment you must purchase an absurdly expensive $$ thing to stop that from happenning.
Character slot availability also suffers, you only have 1 character per account ... luckily they have "assistant" cards given to those humans who choose a race (elves or giants) to ally with (not sure if this still holds true). After that you have to spend $10+ per character for new "character cards."). But this is a problem as it limits the different combat playstyles you can try (as levling up different skills do not always compliment eachother, and they all add to "CP" Combat Power, which makes leveling up skills substantially harder in the long run. There is also the fact that for some end game skills you will have to buy a special "ace" card of ~$6 to !$20 just to keep your progression going. One example being the Merlin talent. Depending how much you spend is how much it gives you to start with.
You will find that it has lots of chances of failure, as if to pad and drag out the experience, some may argue its part of the joy, but I find no join in having an A rank herbalism and struggling to pick even base herbs (the most basic, literally), or blood herbs (for HP potions). Why it costs mana and having to rank up how much mana you have just to batch make potions is stupid (especially for warriors). tailoring and blacksmithing can also feel like a game of chance. And mining is only done within certain dungeons! (only 1 of which being good), There is also of course the obvious fact that Life skills take INSANE amounts of time, grinding, and effort to rank up (literally many hundreds of hours.) Enchanting (although in the magic tab) is the worst of life skill (because of pading and cash-shop tie ins), as you use it to enchant armors/weapons, and of course when those fail ... it destroys the item ... worse yet those scrolls EXPIRE after just a mere 24~48 hours. Basically in laymans terms enchanting is one of the hardest and most drawn out skills to rank up. And the most costly to items, as depending on the enchantment rank (the scroll imbued with the enchantment), you will lose 0~8 max durability to your item ... most have about 10 to 14. Why is this such a big deal? because you will be needing those good enchantments for good gear, especially for later in the game, you will quickly find that the risks for going up only get higher and higher too.
You will notice that humans are the only race that can effectively use pretty much any combat style or skill sets ... yet they are also the slowest movement speeds (which has both travel and combat implications).
Races are all different, they rank up skills at different rates and costs, but also have different stats per rank. For example a giant has better melee skills (costs less to rank up too), than humans, and elves are the weakest at melee (to a point where investing into it is a bad idea for a playstyle.) Giving each race a lean is good, but making them drastic as it is, is terrible. Especially since finding gear for any race other than humans is VERY difficult (gear outside of starting and basic gear.)
The combat and story itself are interesting and wonderful (respectively), but Nexon has just butchered the game into something to milk money from, and the sad part is that its been that way for as long as I remember. So this game is definitely not worth your time, or your money.

Rimworld offers a unique take on the survival game concept, where you take control of a colony of people rather than a single individual. As the benevolent leader of your peon colonists your goal is to survive the planet for as long as possible and eventually make it off, whether you find a space ship or build one is up to you.
The game offers several ways to play with a variety of difficulty levels and a few starting scenarios (which you can edit or download from the community) ranging from relaxing and easy to chaotic and painful. While on the topic of the community, I would be remiss if I did not mention the plethora of mods available to enhance your experience, or just make it easier.
At its core Rimworld offers a perfectly acceptable top down strategy game for fans of the genre, though what keeps me engaged is the constant updates despite being an alpha build, and the user modifications that allow for drastically different methods of play while maintaining a core similarity. Rimworld is a wonderful game that can only get better over time.

VERY mixed feelings, recommended for Risen/Gothic fans - not really for people used to "modern" RPGs.
Game is beautiful for Risen standards, its gameplay is an improvement over Risen 2 but overall I do not believe that people new to the series would appreciate it fully.  Let's be honest paying $50 for a game you expect to get something in line with other games out there - Dark Souls, Skyrim, Bound by flame to name a few.  RISEN ENGINE DOES NOT PROVIDE THIS.
Engine is aged by now, terrain looks choppy, maps are compact and all "sub environments" are right next to each other (nothing new to Risen fans) so this may annoy some people new to the series.
If you haven't played previous Risen games - please watch some gameplay videos before buying to see if this is something you would enjoy.
For Risen fans:  game is definitelly worth it !!!  It is the same oldschool type of gameplay but with improvements and much more polish over old installements.
PROs:
- Interesting Storyline
- Cool quests
- Good character progression
- much more polished shootas (no reload on the pistol anymore)
- Nice environments
- CHEEEEEZY dialogues so common to Risen games
CONS:

Before I say anything it's important to note that this game much like is predecessors receives a ton of scrutiny because every fan boy out there thinks they know whats best for a game and how it should be made with unrealistic expectations and broken game mechanics for the sake of their little hearts.
I like this game. I was skeptical upon news of it that it would fall in line with many other attempts to cash in on this franchise and ultimately give a half hearted game without the gameplay we are all looking for. After seeing gameplay for a bit and then actually purchasing myself I'm please I did. The game is not without hiccups though.
The storyline is original and helps bring a personal immersion for the gamer that former titles failed to capitalize on. The ability to make your own character or even play as the Z warriors and even villains allows the nostalgia to come alive for anyone looking to live out there gaming fantasy of being in the Dragonball Universe.
I believe the inclusion of an original story, player immersion, customizability, and a collectibles system make for a game with very good replayability. Different builds, fighting styles with both a PvE and PvP aspect allow for a wider arrange of gaming for the player. If you're the kind of person who is a crazed completionist then there are tons of items and skills to collect in the Parallel Quests, which is probably where the most meat of the game is.
The downsides? Charging is a skill that must be equipped when you get it. You only have 4 skill slots, two super skills, and 1 evasive skill. I believe that charging should have been something native to players or even a passive skill that could be unlocked at a certain ki attribute or something besides eating up a precious skill slot for something so common among the universe.
It would have been nicer to see perhaps a split in the skills where Physical skills and ki skills are seperated so that even a physically adept player could still perform a few signature ki attacks without crippling their build or vice versa. It waters down the gameplay a bit when the reptitive nature of the same techiques are seen. Also each skill doesn't really have a rating and you have to trial and error each one to find out how effective it is, I worry this may lead to some balancing issues.
Transformations, not enough of them. It seems to be something pretty much exclusive to Kaio Ken users, and Saiyans. It would have been nice to see other races get some power increases. (i could be wrong about this, but what I've read thus far says otherwise). Also of note for transformations is that they take up yet again precious skill slots. So if you want to transform and are capable you'll be down another slot which leads to a serious decision making process for your build and once more waters down your options and makes your playstyle a little more generic.
Through it all though I have had a good time with the game throughout, the grinding for collectibles or for a Z rank in missions is something that I can see people getting frustrated with and I'm usually one of those people. The ability to do missions with a friend or even a couple friends though makes that more fun. I haven't had the frustration yet with the game and that leads me to believe that despite the negative remarks on this game I believe the Devs did a good job. There are still things that need to be balanaced or sorted out here and there but nothing that updates can't fix.

A gritty and realistic, singleplayer Sci-Fi survival horror experience from the top-down perspective. This rogue-like/rogue-lite gem will truly test your ability to adapt and survive, whilst fighting off infected monsters, in an underground base on the inhospitable planet we humans call Mars.
You will need to scavenge for food and water. And when you do eat/drink, you will eventually need to♥♥♥♥♥♥piss. Yeah that's a thing in this game. But the game doesn't force it upon you every 5 minutes like some games would. In about 5 hours of play I only had to find a toilet once or twice if I recall correctly.
You will also need to scavenge materials for crafting. You can craft weapons, clothing, and better basic gear(oxygen, thermal, power.) to increase your odds against the infected hordes you will no doubt face eventually. Crafting is also used to build the components necessary to repair critical systems like heat, oxygen and power to various areas of the underground base. If the infected creatures don't get you, the infection itself will. Finding or crafting enough anti-infection drugs to keep your blood clean will become a priority.
If the infection don't get ya, the cold just might get ya. You'll need to carry a thermal canister(basically a glorified heat pack) in areas that don't have a working temperature regulator. If you can survive the cold, you'll still need to worry about stocking up on food & water. This game's system for hunger/thirst/temperature/sleep/etc may be the best I've seen yet. These needs don't turn you into a walking baby who needs to be fed and burped every 5 seconds(cough cough, DayZ).. It doesn't feel like you have to watch it every second for fear of passing out or something horrible like that. Instead, it keeps you moving, and searching for supplies, because that's the only way you'll survive more than a day in this cold, dark, and forgotten base on Mars.
There are also elements of tower defense in the game, when you must defend the main power reactor for the entire base from advancing infected hordes. But I have not yet survived long enough to be attacked in this way.
This game includes varying difficulty levels, from a normal mode where you are able to manually save, to permadeath hardcore mode, with no manual saves, where damage taken is greater and survival needs are much less forgiving. There's a difficulty for everyone here.
All in all, if you love survival, zombies, and sci-fi horror, give this game a try! You won't regret it.

Risen 3: Titan Lords is a solid RPG with awesome (but cheesy) dialogues, pretty nice story and large world that rewards exploration.
Every other system in the game is somewhat basic:
- Leveling? Yep, just put your XP into your stats.
- Combat? Yep, just 3 buttons - evade, attack and block. You can do riposte by blocking at right time and you can do heavy strikes by holding attack, but that about it. Oh, yeah, there are spells that make combat a bit more enjoyable, but you get them only after ~10h into the game.
- Crafting? Yep, just gather mats and click "craft" to get the item, no random stats or minigames.
- Lockpicking? Yep, no fail state though. Just a lot of annoyance with complex locks >_>
- Naval battles? Yep, but so arcadey that you can actually tell the ship to go forward...
- Other mini-games? Yep, drink game, knife throwing game, arm wrestling game, etc. All come down to either using one button, or just QTE stuff.
All of those are VERY basic, but not bad. They can vary gameplay a bit from time to time, but get boring pretty quick.
If you are looking for fat loots - you won't find them in this game. Items are pretty limited, but getting a new one almost always feels like a large upgrade. No random stats either. (think Witcher 2 style of itemisation)
If you still want to be a pirate and good storyline and quests is what you are searching for - then Risen 3 will deliver in full.
All dialogues are nicely voices, there's tons of quests to do and places to explore. Quests often has several ways to complete them and some of them are pretty amusing. Once again - all of that is pretty cheesy.
So if you don't like cheese or searching for fat loots - this is not the game.
If you want RPG, dialogues and exploration - this is the game, and quite good one.

I have to say this game is a mixed bag, but overall extremely fun. All the core mechanics feel perfect... the RPG mechanics work well for training up a DBZ fighter from zero to hero, the fights themselves are great and are where the game especially shines, and it has a lot of side quests you can embark on as well as the main story that are fun to do. And you can invite people from your Steam friends list to play with you too, so it's not hard to play with friends.
However, the game does have... issues. Basically they perfectly designed all the core mechanics, namely the fighting and leveling up your character and all that, but all the fluff surrounding it seems badly designed. There's a ton of game breaking bugs that pop up more often than you might like in cooperative multiplayer, and it's more than a little frustrating when it gives you a bad ranking on a mission and you have no idea at all WHY your rank is bad.
Not to mention earning many special moves and pieces of equipment requires finishing missions in a special way, earning an extra, harder fight that if you beat you can get something special. Unfortunately, meeting these requirements doesn't always trigger the extra fight and it's a random chance even if you beat the fight whether or not you'll get what you were trying to... it took me 20 tries to get Symphonic Destruction as an example, not counting the times I failed the special conditions to get that fight. So getting what you're looking for can often be pretty frustrating due to the RNG and not knowing how the ranking works or why you got a low rank that makes item drops less likely.
There is essentially no way to find friends in game with any reliability at all, so you will be going through your steam friends list. That said, it is a whole lot of fun just playing... the core mechanics in the quests and fighting system are all really well done and enjoyable, the rest is just fluff. So highly recommended even with its problems.

To start I would like to say that I love indie gaming and am not one of those individuals who feels you truly have to define "what a game" is by scores, or quests. However the trend may have been taken to far with proteus. This is one of those games that is just supposed to lull you to sleep with its calming environments and harmonious sounds, which I can dig. I mean Flower really got the genre off the ground doing the same thing. Proteus is not Flower. It costs the same. But is nothing close to Flower.
Proteus as a whole feels empty to me. It starts of for the first minute as this lush world of beauty and quickly diminishes once you realize that it doesnt go any where from there. The sounds and views wont change at all from what you first see wandering onto the island and only get worse as the seasons pass. Fall and Winter are actually depressing in this depiction. The sounds themselves actually made me more annoyed than anything being high pitched as they were with that 8-bit midi style the game tries to make its own. And even the navigation is empty and lazy you essentially no-clip with gravity the whole time. You will never feel as though you are walking or are an entity at all except when creatures run from you and weather you are swimming, going up or down hill, or running in a grotto your speed will not change.
This lazy half an hour (at best) experience feels as though the developer is screaming at me to appriciate thier work and I feel I could if I weren't asked to cough up 10 bucks for it when games like Cloud are being offered for free by other developers. If you are looking to take some pretty screenshots to make some nice 8-bit wallpapers then maybe this is for you. If you are looking to kick back and relax in an exploratory game then I can definitely recommend something better with a cheaper price tag if not for free.

Atom Zombie Smasher (Steam) (Humble) from Blendo Games is a unique strategy game.  Zombies are invading the 1960s city of Nuevos Aires, and you are tasked with evacuating the populace from each district from your orbital platform.
Each month, you can take on one mission and try to rescue as many civilians as possible.  Everything is procedurally generated, from the city limits to the levels to even the names of your mercenary squadrons.
The city grid is full of little yellow cubes, which represent citizens.  Zombies will come pouring in from side streets in a wave of purple cubes.  If they touch a citizen, it will instantly be turned.  A sure-fire victory can be instantly turned to defeat by one lone zed wandering into a clump of defenseless people.  You’ll need to mitigate this risk by carefully deploying and directing your troops.
As the game goes on, you’ll receive new and interesting units to deploy, though you’ll only get a random assortment of them each round.  This keeps things challenging, as you can’t take on a completely infested level with just a single mortar.  You’ll need to decide each round how hard of a level you think you can complete with your ever-changing arsenal.  Your different units can level up and improve their capabilities, and you can even recruit scientists to give you some bonus powers.  The Llama bombs are especially game-changing.   You only have a set time to evacuate citizens before night falls and zeds come pouring in from every angle, almost ensuring any remaining citizens will die.  This puts a soft cap on the length of time a level can take; most will last 3 minutes or less.
Let’s talk about that music!  A handful of upbeat, cheerful tracks of what I would term “Beach Rock” add a layer of dissonance to the disturbing proceedings taking place below.  Jamming guitars and pounding drums make you so happy to be mowing down zombies and abandoning people to die just so you can save a few others!  But its OK, you’ll say, because they’re just cubes anyway.  They turn purple.  That’s a nice color.
The campaign mode offers a big list of customization options so you can set it to be as hard or as breezy as you’d like.  You can also remove some of the randomization and select your squads at the beginning of each month, which is a feature I really liked.  Oh, and there’s also a set of backstory vignettes you can collect to tell you about the history of Nuevos Aires and how the outbreak occurred.
Atom Zombie Smasher is a weird, cheerful, bright zombie-slaying game.  Sometimes you just need to rescue some little cubes from certain death, blowing up other cubes to buy some time.  AZS lets you do that to a totally rad soundtrack.

There's so much I wanted to talk about mine and other players experiences on this game, but I think there is enough of other reviews that succesfully was capable to pinpoint all of the keypoints about every features in this game; so I will just use as reference an analysis of a thoughtful and experience player about the current version of the product, which is already its release version, since its well known already for most of its playerbase the retrospect of this game, so to don't base my review on previous version, I will just keep my opinion of the nowadays one:
~ By Chinspinner
"A few issues I have found with the direction of Robocraft development
Call me a "salty vet" if you will, but here are the issues I am currently finding that are preventing me from playing Robocraft:
1) Server stability: Disconnects occur to me or people in my queue or players on my team, or players on the opposing team almost every game. This seriously destroys gameplay far too regularly.
2) Match balancing: This has been an issue for some time and remains an issue. If it were just a luck of the draw issue (i.e. one team happened to have better bots than another) then it would not bother me. But often one team has a multitude of a certain type of bot that cannot be countered by the type of bot on the other team. That is poor match-making.
3) Game-changing patches: These occur regularly and constantly alter the meta build. I do not have the time or inclination to rebuild my bots in response to every new patch. The game is not interesting enough.
4) Protonite cores: These are used as a cheap alternative to match balancing. It is the deus ex machina of game design; it is just horrible.
5) The absence of progression: Why did we lose tiers or the ability to unlock new weapon types. What is the point of playing if we are all max level from day one? More importantly, playing in lower tiers with worse gear actually provided an entertaining alternative to fighting with max gear.
6) The tiny maps and base capping mechanics: The larger maps of old and the capping mechanics required far more tactical gameplay. The revised mechanics seem dumbed down.
7) The smaller teams: Smaller teams mean less tactical gameplay; a greater ability for one good, or one bad, or one afk player to seriously alter the course of a match, and; a higher likelihood of a disconnect destroying a match (and as per point 1, this happens far too regularly).
8) The escalation of problems: Rather than solving issues by tweaking or removing game breaking elements, the developers seem intent on adding in a fix (eg. a new weapon), which creates a new layer of problems, and to fix those, they add in another layer of problems. It is hammer to crack nut syndrome, and it is crazy.
Do not get me wrong, there have been many improvements to the game during its development, but there have been equally as many missteps, and unfortunately the missteps have removed the core fun of the game."
---
So, I thought a lot about what do post on review here, and as you can see, I practically only used someone else thoughts, no for laziness or inability, but because he perfectly described what the Robocraft is today; so as summary, the game barely has any PROS that can outshine significatly the CONS, even the basic criativity is totally discarded now on a competitive set up, since its drag out with the new "features" like the "boost" ones, which does exactly the opposes it should do, it doesn't balance builds properly, it most often used to exploit the game mechanics in a allowed method and sadly the glitches/bugs/lags/disconnects & terrible matchmaking is still unsolved.
In the end, this game has too much potencial to grow, but shamefully the develpers tried to walk through a shortcut on the development process, which evidently cost the quality factor on the game, which superficially looks better than old versions, but this "rebuild" after some gameplay time, anyone can see that its broken in multiple layers in the content, and if you don't give up to follow the same route of using copy-paste Min/Max builds, gunbeds or mini/micro robots that exploits the Boost feature, you are certainly doomed, even more if you try any kind of criativity that exceeds the usual "box of blocks" in any robot of yours.
Then, its not a nostalgic feeling, the broken/unstable/ripped off/generic/overly simplified/unbalanced current state say for itself, the version that won many awards from the game industry/journalism/media and acknowledgment from the players 2 years ago, ...is dead.
The feather falls but the rock floats, this game is rocks my boats!

I thought the single player game would be as fun as the Multiplayer game (both of them install completely separating, including a 10 minute tutorial that takes up a third space in your Steam Library), but it doesn't even compare. It doesn't live up to arcade mode. It has a good idea that should have built onto the multiplayer mode by giving the player goals and objectives to complete as a way to escape off the Ship everyone is trapped on, but it adds nothing. With very simple shallow gameplay, there's not a whole lot to this game. All it is, is a long string of repetitive tedious fetch quests, running from to one place to get something and then running back to the exact same place you were at previously only to do this two more times. Getting from point A to B is such a chore even, often getting lost and needing to back track because your location on the map isn't accurate. Your pinpoint is constantly in an area beside your actual location, thus disorientating your sense of direction and making you double check and guess where to go. There are other glitches too that hinder your progress, such as elevators not working. There was a guy even who was completely frozen in front of the door I needed to go through, and it was the only door to that area. There were security cameras so I couldn't even hit him, and when I stood back and threw weapons at him, nothing happened. The game registered him as an object instead of a kill-able person. The voice acting is bad, and the animation is really stiff and bad. The mouths barely move when characters are talking, and in the case of the opening cutscene, the characters were reduced to bean poles. They stood there very lifeless, not even moving, and didn't even react verbally or with facial expressions when the antagonist, Mr. X, revealed that they were trapped on the ship and would be forcing the crew members to murder each other against their will. The opening itself was even very corny, as well as how the story line is executed. A good concept, but done poorly. The way the NPC's react to your character is very odd I thought, and not at all realistic. From the very beginning, a bellboy wants to help you get off the ship, and he chooses you instead of all the other passengers because he says he likes the way you kill, which I thought was very strange. The other NPC's, who offer to give you money in exchange for completing certain tasks (so you can afford the bellboy's 100,000$ ticket to somehow get off the boat) seem by no means distressed or even concerned about Mr. X destroying the boat after all the games are done. They just care about making money. Perhaps the NPC's aren't aware of what's going on, but from my understanding by the cutscene, Mr. X had locked all the crew members inside a room to tell them about what he was doing. It seems eerily and very creepy that none of the NPC's care about the disturbing things going on aboard of the ship or that they'll all be killed. Further more, what also doesn't make sense is that the guards will arrest you if you are seen holding a weapon or hurting someone. These guards are stated in the opening to be hired by Mr. X, who explains that he wants them left out of the killing because the uniforms are expensive. Why would you get taken to the jail cell for murdering when that's exactly what Mr. X is wanting the crew members to do? Yes, it adds to the challenge but plot wise, it makes no sense.

To start off let me say the the The Ship: Singleplayer is an interesting idea, poorly executed...
The Singleplayer addon to the uniquely blended multiplayer game The Ship is a curious one...with many faults.
The Singleplayer part of the game (actually it is more of a mod actually) try's to act as a introduction and tutorial to The Ship.
The opening scene of the game starts with a bunch of captured idiots watching a television in which Mr. X is broadcasting himself. He then proceeds to tell them that he likes to play a game...a game where you shall receive a quarry, in which you must proceed to kill without you yourself getting killed. You receive money for killing your quarry without being killed by your hunter. You earn extra money by killing your quarry with "unusual" weapons (frying pans, syringe, hammer, croquet racket, flare gun etc.). Whoever is left standing at the end is the winner.
Oh, and another thing, you have to eat, sleep, entertain yourself, stay happy, stay clean, pee, poop...
If you don't take care of your "needs" consequences to make things more difficult for you will occur. So for instance if you don't sleep you'll be unable to sprint, and fall asleep at random moments. If you don't eat you will stave and die. If you don't entertain yourself and stay happy, you will commit suicide. If you don't stay clean you'll turn into a pile of dust. If you don't go to the bathroom, you'll either pee, or poop on yourself...or both.
The Singleplayer addition try's to teach you these basic things.
Many parts of the game seems as if it was created by a third party modder, who wanted to make their own version of The Ship without slaughtering general concept.
The graphics are the same as the original game and have not improvements whatsoever. Nothing to complain about here, but nothing to be impressed with.
The sound remains the same, as the repetitive music plays itself over and over and over again...
The worst portion of the game is perhaps is a annoying voice acting. The characters voices are fake and totally unbelievable. They don't bring life to the characters, rather they bring stupidity and gullibility.
The gameplay is boring and very simple. The game will set you up in a situations like, where you have to stalk two unsuspecting women (yeah, REALLY unsuspecting) into the bathroom and slaughter them while they are in the restroom...like...duh! Don't freak out cuz there is a guy with an axe chasing you into the WOMENS' bathroom! They don't even fight back either they just let you hack away...
So the gameplay was a fail. As a game no. As a tutorial, yes.
I must admit I learned a lot about how to play the game though this. Not that I couldn't have learned it myself, but hey, I got the game for free so I can't complain...

This game used to be great but...
what happened?
When they removed tiers it was still fine, it was less confusing, but it wasn't quite the same. Then the updates were pretty good, adding more guns, quality of life changes, it was still a great game.
But then they added mega bots. They were basically the same thing as before but bigger and more powerful. All megabots really added was a change to the scale of the game. I think around that time they also added the healing guns which was one of the good things to come out of this time.
But it was only downhill from here. Update after update it just got worse and worse. It became more based around making money than being a good game. It felt like the developers were no longer passionate about the game. Matchmaking broke, several gimmicky weapons were added, and of course there was a crate system as your main way to get vehicle parts. All in all, it wasn't robocraft anymore. It was a shadow of what it used to be and it kinda breaks my heart to see one of my all time favourite games fall so far. What started out as an awesome, creative, complicated, fast paced, team game turned into the pay to win, uninspired money-maker it is today.
I can't quite say "today" though, which is why I'm hoping they've fixed their mistakes. I haven't played in a while. So I'm hoping for the best and I desperately want this game to come back to its roots.
TL;DR: Used to be great, now it's pay to win and a shell of its former self.

The rain continues to fall as I check my watch. Four hours have passed since last I checked and all I have to show for my time are a brooding unease and a sense of justice as twisted as this review.
ALRIGHT, so I can't write like the people that made Gunpoint, but I had to try. This game is really fantastic. I have had the demo sitting my PC since I built my new living room gaming rig, but in the absense of a decent TV, it was too difficult to play a game with small detailed graphics. Having upgraded my TV, I thought I'd give it a try. The demo was very convincing and shortly after I purchased the game. Four hours after that I had beaten the main storyline. The gameplay really sucks you in and the whole atmosphere and story make it really easy to tell yourself, "Just one more mission"
Pros:
- Great (albeit short) story.
- Simple, yet detailed graphics (reminds me a bit of Canabalt HD, only with a whole lot more going on).
- Quite fun jumping / stealth game mechanic.
Cons or annoyances or whatever:
- The story is short. I want more. DLC missions or a sequel or even some Steamworks user-made missions. I definitely finshed the game wishing it wasn't over.
- Details mean you need an appropriately sized screen to play. Normal laptop or desktop screen should be fine. If played in the living room, you'll probably have trouble if you're 10 feet away from a 32inch TV. (Note this isn't really a flaw of the game, just thought it was worth mentioning.)
- No controller support. Seems like this would've been pretty easy to add (left stick moves, right stick jumps, buttons do things). Maybe it would've sucked compared to mouse/keyboard (Trine, I'm looking at you), but at least it could be an option.
I think that's enough review, don't you? Yes of course it is. Anyway some kind of rating: 4/5
If I gave half points it'd be 4.5 but I don't so it isn't. It's nearly perfect, I just wish there were a lot more of it.

Subterrain seemed really promising: good mars colony horror survival atmosphere, competent crafting/research and polished/responsive UI. I don't really mind the micro-managing (facility power and maintenance) but after having explored 6 of the 16 something areas now,
- crawling through the samey dark corridors and
- being stuck on the same level of research with the same crappy guns,
- fighting the same enemies and always in the same manner,
- having to flee to HQ every 5 minutes to refill O2 and heat,
I begin missing serious progression of any sort. Ultimately, you have very little influence over research and developpment, since it's all tied in to you finding data chips at the end of the explorable areas to upgrade your 4 R&D-levels. And I already know that exploring the next area for a solid 2+ hours, being subjected to the same rinse and repeat formula listed above, I am only gonna get a pointless upgrade for mining level 2 Ore.
Subterrains basic gameplay and different concepts are really well put together but it commits one of the most egregious crimes against its players: wasting your time.

I've recieved this product as a gift- and I have to say, it's the one of the best things I've ever got.
This is a very early review considering I haven't fully delved into the application 100%. It will take a lot of time and patience. Not just one or two or ten hours. This will take houndrets of hours. But with enough practice and experience you'll get while using this engine- Anyone can make a great game from this if they meet a set criteria.
It may be really frustrating from the beginning when you have no idea and you'e literally just browsing through menus and trying to find out what to do and what's going on. It'll take you some hours to figure out how does some things works. once you'll watch couple tutorials, it'll become much easier than on the beginnig. I haven't played loads of it but from the around 10 hours I have spent currently on one project I have learnt many new things that I would've never learnt in a video or in the manual. Its simple and familiar look makes it easily accessible to people who have already used any of the previous engines, but is really approachable to people new to it as well. It contains a lot of features, things you can edit, things you can create on your own. It isn't only map creator and character generator. I've been focusing on character creation, creating classes, skills, items, weapons, all of the above. Like the tagline says: Simple enough for a child, powerful enough for a developer. That tagline 100% applies to the software. If you want to make your game better and create something amazing, you must go through a lot of struggle, manuals and tutorials, but that applies to all of the game engines.
Over $90 for the base game isn't worth it if you are just going to mess around for a short amount of time so if you're really interested in game engines, creating RPG's, just go for it.
This is not a game you play from time to time, it's not something you'd turn on and play for two hours and then get bored with it. This takes a lot of trial and error to get it to make the magic more experienced users can do.
I'll probably add more things to this review as the time pass, but all I can say for now is-
RPG Maker MV is great, simply amazing engine full of opportunities.

Rimworld offers a unique take on the survival game concept, where you take control of a colony of people rather than a single individual. As the benevolent leader of your peon colonists your goal is to survive the planet for as long as possible and eventually make it off, whether you find a space ship or build one is up to you.
The game offers several ways to play with a variety of difficulty levels and a few starting scenarios (which you can edit or download from the community) ranging from relaxing and easy to chaotic and painful. While on the topic of the community, I would be remiss if I did not mention the plethora of mods available to enhance your experience, or just make it easier.
At its core Rimworld offers a perfectly acceptable top down strategy game for fans of the genre, though what keeps me engaged is the constant updates despite being an alpha build, and the user modifications that allow for drastically different methods of play while maintaining a core similarity. Rimworld is a wonderful game that can only get better over time.

Overall this game is really fun. It's kept me playing for a long time, which says more than any other Dragon Ball game that I have played before. I give the game a good 7.5 to 8 out of 10. It's your typical Dragon Ball fighting game however, as after you beat the storyline and most of the parallel quests; it becomes very repeatitive.
The story itself is a cool take on the story of Dragon Ball Z and GT. It gets more than annoying though how Goku always seemingly shows up and takes all your credit for battles going how they should, but then again, it's not like he didn't win them before. Many times throughout the game I'd be sitting there staring at my screen thinking 'and once again, I save your♥♥♥♥♥and yet you somehow get all the credit for my heroics. Typical Goku....typical." That's pretty much the entire storyline, and eventually you get used to it. At least Trunks tells you that you did a good job. Someone sees you for the hero you are.
Multiplayer on this game is actually really fun, and has made my time playing this game worth the money I spent on it and the DLC. One of the more frustrating aspects of multiplayer though, is multiple servers. I have had more than my fair share of "musical servers" with friends from steam, two of us being on the same server; and the other being on a completely different server. This makes making a team with steam friends next to impossible and more than a minor irritation at times. At least you have the ability to invite others to your room makes up for this.
While I do like the fact that there is constant DLC, only getting two to three time patrol quests is more than a little dissapointing. I literally got on after the new DLC, played for about a total of 30 minutes and had beaten the storyline DLC and was left going "oh wait....that's all?"
Once again, it's a great new take on Dragon Ball Z and I'm excited to see what it's going to do and where it is going to go. Hopefully the new DLC will be worth more play time and will give me more than 2 more storymode quests. In all, it's a good game and hasn't dissapointed me much in the many hours I've put into it.

RPG Maker has always been the go-to game maker for those who want to get started in expressing their creativity without learning complex programming languages, and over the course of the last few installments it's grown considerably in flexibility thanks to the introduction of scripting and plugins.
RPG Maker MV's use of JavaScript-based plugins is by far the most elegant solution the developer has come up with to extending the engine's functionality yet. No more accidentally putting scripts in the wrong place -- though in some cases, the order in which you load the plugins matters -- and no more configuration by delving into scary-looking script, thanks to dedicated plugin parameter windows.
Even if you don't want to delve into the more complex aspects of customisation with plugins, RPG Maker MV remains the same easy to use package that it's always been. The mapping and eventing systems will be immediately familiar to series veterans -- though some will miss the "layers" approach to mapping -- and the included resources are of high quality. A particular shout out to the included music, which is particularly good; Shoji Meguro would be proud of the wailing electric guitars on display in some of the battle themes.
Combine all that with the fact that you can now export your games to Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and HTML5 and you have a formidable package for getting started in game development. Even if you never bring your grand designs to the commercial market, if nothing else RPG Maker is a great means of learning the basic logic of programming and how to tell your computer to do things. For some, it will be enough to realise their dreams; for others, it will be a stepping stone to more complex tools and techniques.
Either way, if you have the slightest interest in making games, pick this up. And be sure to check out the community content, too; there's already a ton of great resources and plugins available, many of which are completely free to use in both commercial and non-commercial products.

EVE Online is one of the most expansive games currently in existance. With hundreds if not thousands of individual star systems and plenty of ships to choose from, the world of New Eden is a strange and fanstastic universe. That being said, just about everything is player run. A player probably built the ship you fly, another guy manufactured the ammo you use, and someone else entirely will buy all your loot from you when you want to sell the spoils of your efforts. This means that there's a lot of opportunity for other players to screw you over, and they'll do it without a moment's hesitation. But it also means that there's room to grow and I mean LOTS of room. It is entirely possible, if you have the mettle and the patience, for you to LITERALLY conquer the entire universe of EVE Online. But don't expect to earn your crown within a year, or probably even 5, as there are veteran players who have been playing for a decade or more trying to bring the galaxy under their rule.
tl:dr It's good, but people are jerks.

So, after getting involved with helping out with Subterrain, my opinion is obviously extremely biased. However, I still defend my position by not being involved with Subterrain at the start. The game has improved a bit since I first started playing it, and many aspects of the gameplay have changed considerably based on player feedback. The gunplay is faster, there's an in-game minimap to help players navigate, randomization was expanded and a big chunk of content was added to the game. Even with all these drastic changes, Pixellore managed to preserve what made the game special in the first place. The changes were successes all around, as far as I'm concerned.
I love this game, and I'm proud to have contributed. It's not perfect and it's not going to be for everyone, but if you're looking for a top-down survival horror game with a bunch to read and a bunch to shoot, look no further.
The demo is very out of date, so it's not the best "slice" of the game anymore. I would watch videos of recent builds, as just about everything has been retuned on player feedback.
Subterrain is a top-down survival horror game where you have to manage the health, hunger, thirst, infection level and tiredness of Dr. Albert West while exploring the ravaged MPO Mars base. After escaping their prison cell, players need to research and develop guns, armor and other equipment to bring parts of the base back online while fighting the infection that's taken over while you were in confinement. It doesn't take long before you're thrown into the thick of it!
It takes a bit to get familiar with all the mechanics, but they aren't overly complex and are rather forgiving if managed properly. Dr. West is a rather capable fighter, able to dodge and block while using shotguns, pistols, SMGs, grenades and melee weapons to clobber all sorts of twisted horrors roaming Mars in the various districts with the goal of escaping Mars. To do this, players need to explore districts by connecting them back to the power system and taking a tram to the district of their choosing (similar in design to a dungeon). Unfortunately for the survivabilty of Dr. West, most districts are lacking working oxygen and thermal systems, requiring players to keep an eye on their oxygen and thermals while collecting materials, schematics and gear.
There's a rather robust crafting element to the game, in which players break down items to research them and develop better items as they improve their technologies. Crafting, material producing stations and research systems all have upgrades to expand their range of item creation.
Suberrain offers a bunch of difficulty levels, including one that disables menu saves and has permadeath, but also offers easier difficulty levels (though maybe
easy- stick with at least normal or above!) for those not wanting to weep over their keyboard when their character dies.
Over the course of a month the game has gone through a bunch of stable and impressive changes since I bought it; the developers are very responsive and are invested and proud of their product (as they should be!) and seem to be invested in continuing to update the game as time goes on and players continue to add feedback.
As an ARPG top-down shooter, or as a survival horror game, Subterrain is easily in the top running for both those lists. It's extremely enjoyable, and while there's a goal of escaping Mars, the game is fun enough to attempt to survive as long as possible.

Whether or not you like Xenoverse depends on one of two things:
1) If you like the previous DBZ games, this one is the best one yet. The create a character option is what makes this game the best yet, if you're not looking to create your own character...you may want to skip this purchase.
2) If you enjoy fighting games, you will master this one in minutes. It's very simple and straight forward, you get a handful of basic combos to use which you can use to string together longer combos once you customize your supers. It's what can make this game repetitive, but also fun since you don't need to concentrate to enjoy it.
Is it perfect? Hell no, if a teacher were to grade Dimps they'd likely get a B or B-...but it's the best we've got so far and is worth picking up if you have someone to play with. Single player in this game frankly sucks, the AI is about as helpful as a monkey's♥♥♥♥♥♥much of the time and the enemies you fight will either sit there and accept your punishment or they will make sure you have no chance to block or parry once the first hit lands. If I compare it to mortal kombat...you can go from pwning two characters at once to having your face shoved into humble pie by 3 Shao Khan hammers to the skull.
If you're just worried if you're going to get your moneys worth with this game...in my personal opinion it's worth it. I believe I've got over 70 hours in this game so far and I still haven't managed to unlock all the moves...granted it's mainly because the reward system in this game is based purely on luck once you satisfy the challanges, such as "Beat within 5 mins"...that's where it gets frustrating, when you complete the challenge and the randomized system doesn't give you the opportunity to get an ultimate finish at the end...and when it does you won't always get a new skill. Some like this feature, some hate it. It's really personal preference...same situation that Destiny has going, some enjoy repeating the strikes...others would rather swallow a live scorpion.
I've mentioned some of the most frustrating things in Xenoverse already, so if you're not completely turned off...then you should probably give it a try! It's not bad, by any means...just has it's frustrating moments, but most of those aren't noticable once you've got a friend on the mic with a decent connection.

I've got basically everything I'm going to write below in a video format as follows:
Because MV has Javascript behind it, the engine already has as many if not more plugins than VX Ace did. Now I have never used the engines that came before VX Ace- Ace was my first RPG Maker- but I can already tell you the differences are astounding.
Javascript gives you access to HTML and Canvas elements, which basically allows you to edit absolutely anything you can see. My partner managed to create something in the engine that took an entire scene, calculated what areas has the abilityto step on, and then spawned enemies in random spots any time the player entered the screen. This took him only a few hours.
If that doesn't impress you- and the sheer ease of making a plugin should, because it means you're not being held back from making something OTHER than a JRPG- then the beauty of the engine should.
VX Ace was pretty. It allowed for some very nice looking sprites, lovely areas, and a fine amount of detail. MV spits on that and calls Ace ugly.
MV's tiles and sprites have a good deal more room for detail and looks. I don't recall the exact size difference between the sprite sizes, but I can tell you the sheets are way bigger in resolution than Ace's. But the best part is you can still use VX Ace sprites in MV- in fact, there are ways and places on the internet that explain very simply how you can take your sprites from Ace and turn them into MV compatible sprites. Or you can just use Ace sprites. It works beautifully either way, so your old DLC isn't useless anymore.
AND there are now side battlers for your characters that MV generates in the character creator. Should you use them, that means your tiny 2D characters will be fully animated with correct weapon types based on equipment and attack the enemy. It's beautiful.
One of the best parts of Ace was how beginner friendly it was. When you got the engine, it already had 92 billion spells set up for you, like 500 enemies and troops ready for deployment, and basic classes already filled out and calculated for gameplay. You could seriously just populate a scene and start a game right then and there.
MV doesn't have this.
The four classes it gives you are nearly all identical; you get four-five starter spells for exmple, and a really poor example. You have much nicer sprites for items and spells and weapons... But less. You have less options for customizing characters in the character creator (though the character faces look WAAAAAAAAY better).
And my LEAST FAVORITE part:
Things that I felt should have been a part of the base engine were DLC.
When I got my DLC, I though perhaps I'd actually gotten an Update. It was very difficult to even sus out what the DLC even was, because it felt like it should have been in the engine to begin with. I got five extra face structures, a few new hair styles, and a couple different eyes and clothes, as well as a little music and (atcually quite a few) plugins.
The character creator stuff really should not have been DLC. It really shouldn't have been. Music, new sprite sheets for areas, plugins- those can count as DLC. But for a basic piece of the engine with so little that was given, the DLC felt a bit... Depressing.
Would I still buy MV if I didn't have it? Yes. Do I plan to return to Ace? Not on your life. I have it installed so I have easy access to its DLC.

LEGO The Lord of the Rings is in my opinion the best LEGO adaptation game. I'll admit I'm slightly biased as I'm obessed with Middle-Earth, but it s a perfectly balanced game. The LEGO series is well known by now for creating polished, solid, and extremely fun adaptations of existing franchises, and LEGO The Lord of the Rings is no exception.
This game would have been fun enough if it had just followed the lead of LEGO Star Wars and simply the player a selection of levels based on the movies along with a small hub. However, LEGO LOTR not only provides this, it also includes a full open-world version of Middle-Earth to explore between each level. This open world isn't empty either, it's full of side-quests, collectables, and characters to unlock.
As with pretty much every LEGO game, the gameplay is very casual, and not meant to be very challenging. This may put some people off, but most people know by now how LEGO games work. The gameplay is fun, the twists on the movies' memorable moments are hilarious, and collecting thousands of studs is still so addictive. If you are fan of either LEGO games or The Lord of the Rings, if you are just looking for a bit of casual fun, I couldn't recommend this game enough.

Would anyone like to take a guess at what I just did?
So, here I am, Dayvis2, reviewing this game that I purchased from Steam about a month or two ago while it was on sale for £3.74, which, seeing as the story alone has given me 12 1/2 hours of fun gameplay, is a freaking bargain! Anyway, here's my review.
PLOT
The story follows the plot of The Fellowship of the Ring, The Two Towers and The Return of the King, using cutscenes with sound clips from the films and levels with some brilliant gameplay. There are 18 action-packed levels to play, each about 25-45 minutes depending  on how much time you like to spend fighting, collecting etc.
GAMEPLAY
You can play as loads of different characters from Frodo to Tom Bombadil to an Orc. In the levels, it's obvious that there are some new features, such as Ring Mode, where you can enter the wraith world and discover new objects that only ring-bearers can make, along with horse rides including the frankly epic Ride of the Rohirrim in Return of the King. There are cooking puzzles that require collecting of items that are then put in a pan, and the ability to use the Palantir in both Film 2 and 3 in order to travel between Frodo and Sam's and Aragorn Gimli and Legolas's stories. There is also the Eye of Sauron to look out for when you finish Fellowship, because its sight will cover areas, blocking access until you play a certain level, after which the eye will shift to a different area. This is so you don't just play all of Frodo and Sam's journey and none of Aragorn, Gimli and Legolas's journey.
OPEN-WORLD
One of the best bits is the Open World, a complete map of all the areas explored in the story. You can visit the stone trolls in the Trollshaws, sail down the Great River and then past the Argonath, walk into Mordor, complete quests, forge items and collect gold and red bricks. Areas you can explore include: Hobbiton, Bree, Weathertop, Trollshaws, Rivendell, The Misty Mountains, outside of Moria, Lothlorien, The Great River, Amon Hem, Fangorn Forest, Rohan, Isengard, Helm's Deep, Edoras, Dunharrow, Minas Tirith, Emyn Muil, The Dead Marshes, Ogsgilliath, Minas Morgul, The Stairs, Shelob's Lair, Cirith Ugnol, The Black Gate and Mordor! You'll be able to switch the world from day to night and back again when you've completed the story, and inbetween levels you'll be journeying through the land. I must say that I prefer some aspects of the Hobbit world more than this one (see my LEGO Hobbit review for more detail) because of Eagle travel and the different locations, but that's just my opinion.
GRAPHICS
Graphics are pretty good even with the medium settings I had to use on my seemingly ancient computer.
OTHER
The game doesn't feel rushed, but some levels, such as the Caradhras level, do feel a little stretched out. I particularly like the main menu screen that has four different versions, one with a map of Middle-Earth for the very first one, another with Hobbiton for Fellowship, one with the alignment of Isengard and Bardadur for Two Towers and Baradur with Mordor for Return.
CONCLUSION
This is a great game that feels like an epic bargain if you get it on sale. The LEGO games do go on sale often, so try and grab this one quickly if you see it on sale! Still worth the money at the usual price, too though. All in all 9/10.
