King.)  Random drops will be working against you day one.  If you want to be a super sayian, you better be the luckiest SOB of that month, of that day, of that year, of that second, after you do the all the quest requirements.
Queen.)  The parallel quests will be the DBZ equivalent of From Software's fantasy games.  Especially if you don't have the right lvl or characters.  Pray to what every diety you believe in if the game decides to drop you in a quest againts 2-3 opponents off the bat without getting to support.
Jack.)  The character creation is very limited and I haven't even gotten to the clothes.  For that see King.) and Negatives 2.).
Joker.)  The leveling, soul, and clothing buff systems, will hurt you if you're not careful. (hope you were paying attention during the tutorial)  In honesty, the leveling system should have been like DBZ budokai 3.
Personal score:  A super sayian 2 out of a super sayian god
Once you make it isn't that special anymore.  Something that isn't as fun or rewarding as its older siblings, but still better than it's three other attempts to draw in a wider audience. Lego Lord of the Rings is, guess what, yet another Lego 3d-platformer from Travellers Tales. What a punchline that was. Came out in 2012, after Lego Batman 2. It also was released for consoles Xbox 360, PS3 and Wii. Oh, and had handheld version for NDS, 3DS and Vita, which is kinda somewhat different but same. Well, lesser versions.
PC version doesn't have DLCs that consoles have. Those are three character packs and one tools/stuff pack. I doubt that they are important in Lego game, but it still means that PC version isn't the best one. At least be happy that they still support non-Xbox controllers. Oh, and be happy that they finally implented achievements for Steam.
Technically, it shows that Travellers Tales kept spitting out Lego games pretty much every half/full year. People complain about crashes and bugs, like getting stuck in geometry. Personally I had a bug where I lost control over character aside from jumping when he tried to ride the Warg beast in one of the levels. Had to restart the level. Also had character to jump high into air, like when hobbit was cutting ropes over Gollum's hands. Or when riding the Ent, huge tree character. At least it wasn't anything progress halting.
And hey, it's yet another Lego platformer. Punch stuff to collect studs. Lose studs by dieing, but never have game over. Have simplistic puzzles of using right character to do something. Collect everything you can!
Also, second game that has actual talking character and kinda-free-roam between levels. Lego Batman 2 was the first. Though this one is the first licensed after movie, so have your copy-pasted voice talents. Oh well, having plot still makes it more fun for me. And levels themselves are nicely done that they aren't annoying. When not glitching.
Well, you can also craft. And "crafting" just means another way-around of collecting. Collect recipe, collect mithrill bricks, choose to craft them. And there are quest-givers, which are fetch-quests, mostly involing the crafting. Oh, and developers figured out that since they have split-screen then you can separate characters into two different scenes for some solo actions. Back in previous games they always would have at least two character in same area, slightly altering scenario. Now at least two characters but they can be in two different areas.
Open world portion also seem to be a bit nasty at times. Most often you are probably going to walk by foot and there is only one spot on a map that has blacksmith. Heck, when I set it destination, game for some reason decided to change path mid-way through and showed me the path to bonus level. When I checked this level and quit, I was sent back to where I starter: opposite side of map.
Bah, should have checked forums to see how to fast-travel.
And once you unlock free-play you will notice that sometimes it behaves against players. Like, you climbed this tall tower while AI kept standing on the ground. That AI is Frodo. On top of tower you noticed Campfire that you can light with Sam. And if you change your character to Sam, instead the AI will change character from Frodo to Sam since they are both hobbits and it will change control to this character. Or because both Frodo and Sam are short. So either reclimb the tower or do even more things of changing characters around, selecting different races.
Not to say that there is no positive. Actually, there are a lot. It just that it's so formulic that I got tired of talking about same things all over again. Still fun to whack everything. And such. And collect everything.
I will rather talk about things that really matter. Like, did you know that They Are Taking The Hobbits To Isengard? Whole 10 hours! You don't simply get tired of such classic YouTube video.
But eh. Yet another Lego game. With free-roam and voices.

A battle-royale simulator that takes ques from games like the Sims and Hitman.  A mysterious man threatens the entire people on the ship by enforcing a battle-royale.  Things take a turn the moment you hunt down your first victim as you try to make sense of the insanity aboard.
You have to constantly manage your character's needs from reading, eating, drinking and cleanliness in order to consistently be on top of your performance.  Money is earned depending on what type of weapon you use based on the requirements.
The downside to this game as it lacks core focus, having the gameplay set-up as a farce in favor of the narrative designed by the creator.  Game has fun, but it also lacks balance causing you to find exploits within the game to have the upper hand.  Damage has no indicator for both player and NPC's making the game frustrating when enemies are capable of taking you down instantly with no sense of rhyme or reason.  Saving is automated through chapters which means failing a mission would cause you to restart from the beginning of the chapter.
Despite all this, the game is relatively interesting for it's concept as many of the stealth/assassination games are focused on power-fantasy dudebro market.  This is probably closer to the passive nature of Splinter Cell & Hitman in terms of pacing which may interest those looking for a more focused game.  A little polish could make this game reach its potential but clearly a concept sold as a work-in-progress.
Best check it out for a steam sale if the premise deem to risky for your cash.

If you've played ArcheAge and aren't satisfied by the lack of content, Mabinogi is for you. In Mabinogi, you could have a farm. You can construct a home in an instance which are called "Homesteads". You can do trade-runs (Commerce) for gold and EXP. You can run dungeons and never get bored of the same layout. The make-up of the dungeon is changed every time you enter it. You can quest like any other. There are traditional quests like "Kill X, Kill Y" to quests where story is involved. As you progress through the storyline, you can gain the ability to transform and even gain powers of a god! Not a fan of dungeons & questing? You can cook, go fishing, perform alchemy, dig at beaches for gems, blacksmith, weaving wools, hunt for artifacts, explore for treasure, buy a house, get married, and even make your own music. The great thing about this game is that there is NO LEVEL CAP! That's right. No level cap. Of course, you can grind your way to the highest level, but you can undergo a process called "Rebirth" which will reset your current level to 1. All progress in leveling is added to the total level.
I highly recommend this game! It's worth tossing money into if you are a fan of vanity or want to progress faster. Huge amounts of content. You will never get bored. If you get bored, then you are doing something wrong.

This is a game. This should be obvious. Is it a good game? If you failed to realize this was a game before I told you, you probably won't enjoy this game. Gunpoint is a game where you stealth around hacking a collection of terminals scattered around a building using a fancy gadget called the Crosslink, allowing you to make certain things activate things they shouldn't/ should. It's difficult to explain in words, so I recommend watching a video explaining it. You also have at your disposal a pair of trousers that allow you to jump super high, which is actually quite useful as you can pounce in any direction. There are a few other gadgets that you get later on, and numerous other mechanics, but I don't have room to explain all of them. So, on to the story. The story is funny, dark, intelligent and just all-around good. The art style works well, accomplishing what a lot of pixel art fails to do: not look horrible and ugly. What is there else to say? The controls work well and the level design is great. The story took me 3 hours to finish (though there are multiple endings, etc) and there is a level editor for that bit more content. Overall, this is great. If you want to play a 2D stealth-puzzle game, this is probably the best game on the market for you. As a stealth game, it works great, and overall is something I would highly reccommend.

Proteus is an exceptional and definitive "notgame" that is easier to explain by what it isn't. It isn't about passive story telling. It isn't about objectives or achievements. It isn't about simulating realistic environments. It isn't about efficiency or mastery. Most importantly, it isn't about you, which itself is marvelous for a video game. Proteus doesn't want to thank you for saving it. Instead it wants to offer a glimpse of what was, is, and always will be, with or without your interaction.
So many games are psychological exercises in transitioning chaos into order, weakness into strength, beginner into expert, boring grass into busy city, and at the crux is you as the agent of transition. I am not immune to dopamine's effect when completing these types of games, and I definitely enjoy them. Yet when I think back at what these addictive games have taught me about myself it's that I need to justify my free time with feelings of accomplishment.
Proteus is the antithesis of typical addictive games; there is no feeling of loss and thus no reason to save. It deconstructs the spatial awareness of Doom and the floral and faunal mystery of Super Mario 64. It is about discovery and wonder. It is about recognizing aliens. It is about finding frequencies. It is about turning off sight to focus on sound, and vice versa. It's also a challenge to status-quo game designers to stop being lazy and comfortable. Have we really come that far from Doom and Super Mario 64? Is it benefiting anyone creatively by continuing those types of games ad-nauseum? And the much more interesting question that was raised by Paolo Pedercini: can the industrial rationalization of goal-oriented video game design be replaced by chaotic, paradoxical, and human design within the influence of our capitalist society?
Radiohead and Universal Everything recently published a free app with a very similar design to Proteus called PolyFauna. On their website, Dead Air Space, they clearly and concisely list the app's mechanics, not its plot or objectives - just as music, film, portraits, or sculptures would not have those things. So what if Proteus is considered art? It is beautiful, inspiring, or meaningless depending on your interpretation, not the designers'. You don't need it to have endless appeal like a FPS or RPG. But just like a piece of art, you might feel inclined to hang on to it, occasionally appreciating it by yourself or with others. Even if playing around in Proteus' pixelated ecosystem for only an hour causes you to feel differently about how you spend your free time, then it will have been worth a purchase.

I don't usually review games, but i think this time i'll make an exception.
I really like lego games. they are funny, unique, and creative, and can provide immense fun and enjoyment for everyone.
This one is no exception; in my opinion, the finest of all lego games.
The game spans throughout the entire LotR trilogy (The Fellowship of the Ring, The Two Towers, and The Return of the King), using audio and music directly from it. and of course, it is Lego, and they put their own unique spin on it. of course, the game (And cut - scenes) can't afford to be as long, so the very main points are in the narrative, while adding some well - known Lego homour, and to my surprise, i found that i enjoyed it very much, in it's own way.
If you love lego, or LotR in general, (or both - i know i do), you'll most likely enjoy it very much.
However, I encourage you to play the Demo (can be downloaded from the LEGO site) or see game walkthroughs, to form your own opinion, before you decide to buy it. (Which is always wise before thinking of getting a game). And, maybe the game will get you liking one of them, or introduce you to, if you weren't already. I will admit and confess that this game was my introduction to Tolkien's world, when i got it when it was first released. My love of lego games did that. and i'm so glad i did.
If you identify with the points noted above, do consider getting the game. it is also on sale now at a very low price, until February 12. ($5 i believe).
You really have nothing to lose here, in my opinion. only to gain. at least, i know i did.
I hope very much that my review helped you form an opinion on the game.

I have already put over 50 hours in on Xbox One and just bought this version a few hours ago. My thoughts? VERY much worth it to any DBZ fan, anyone else should wait for a price drop.
Pros:
Amazing storyline. Although not written by Toriyama himself, but rather Dimps, it follows true to the Dragon Ball heart. It stays close enough to what has been presented before so that it remains believable and memorable, but strays just enough to keep you on your toes to see what happens next. Ends up in an ending that is neither overly impressive nor unimpressive, just satisfying.
Large selection of characters. While Base/2nd/3rd form Frieza and base/2nd form Cell are missing, along with characters like Dabura and Androids 16, 19, and 20 (Gero), they still have plenty of characters to choose from, all of them feel unique in their own ways.
Character creation. Not as immersive as some games have it, but you can change your race, gender, hair, facial features, voice, and name. While your character doesn't typically speak outside of yelling attack names, these changes presented are still nice, with enough for them to improve upon in future sequels.
Amount of content. I've played over 50 hours and still have yet to do everything the game has to offer, and I've yet to start the DLC. Grinding for the next move you want or to get the Dragon Balls remains ever fun, training with mentors to learn new skills, and playing through the story as well as battling with friends and taking on quests with people from around the world, the game gives plenty for you to do.
Cons:
Simple battle system. You have light attacks, heavy attacks, ki blasts, 4 swappable Special Moves, 2 swappable Ultimates, and a single swappable Evasive skill. It leaves a lot to be improved upon in future releases, though is passable.
Controls. You'll probably want a gamepad, as the k/m controls are, while functional, a bit awkward. Not deal-breaking IMO, but if you're planning on using your trusty keyboard and mouse, you'll need to get used to the inputs.
Limited options. You can change the resolution, framerate, motion blur, and anti-aliasing, but that's about it. Better than Naruto, but not as good as some big release PC games.
Overall, great game geared towards fans of Dragon Ball Z.

Description: A top-down real-time strategy game (with unlimited planning stage) in which the player must rescue civilians by helicopter from zombies entering by several points surrounding the map. The player places units, barricades, and explosives in the planning stage, then during the real-time portion maneuvers/uses them in order to slow the zombies from reaching the civilians before they can be rescued. As missions go by, the player acquires a larger arsenal, points with which to upgrade the various units, and new mission types. Zombie incursions increase in size and difficulty in discrete stages.
Is it playable? (Barely/Mostly/Completely)
Completely.
Bugs?
None.
User Interface?
Easy to use and straightforward.
How good is it? (Terrible/Bad/0k/Good/Great)
Good
Audio?
Satisfactory explosions, gunfire, sirens, etc. The music had a generally Latin feel. The audio enhanced the gaming experience.
Visuals?
Colorful art style. Comic-style drawings used to help convey story points. Game map visually basic, with zombies and units represented simply for maximum visibility. Not visually impressive.
Story?
Barely there. Your Mileage May Very whether that's a good or bad thing. Personally, I think zombie stories are usually silly, and so the lack of a more substantial treatment is no big loss and even opened room for player-driven narrative stemming from mechanical interaction during missions. Zombies happen. You defend against them and eventually destroy them entirely. 20 lines of story.
Mechanics?
Solid and varied enough for several hours of fun. Sometimes the random selection of units made available in the vanilla game proved frustrating, as it is impossible to win with some combinations. On the other hand, playing with certain of the non-vanilla boxes ticked made the game much too easy (especially the ability to select whichever units you want for every mission).
Verdict:
Recommend

After putting myself through Fifty Shades of Grey, I swore I would never again endure stories about company executives. But, my internet cut out for a week and I had to set about playing my handful of downloaded games, including Tales from the Borderlands.
This was fortuitous. The game resisted my enthusiasm initally (exploring Pandora without a legendary SMG in my hand feels alien) but became immersive fairly quickly. The central plot is good, better than any in the original Borderlands series, and full of nuanced references.
There are compelling twists, some genuinely moving moments, and a welcome return of Handsome Jack on best form. The choices give you a lot of power over shaping the central characters - deciding whether to make Rhys a Hyperion fascist or a moral adventurer, and Fiona either a cold-hearted con artist or a vault hunter in love with Scooter.
All in all, a worthy contribution to an addictive series. Maybe Telltale Games will pick up the task of Half Life 3.

I played this game to death on Xbox and when I saw it for less the £5 on Steam I couldn't pass it up.
Let's not beat about the bush; this is a Mario Kart clone. It is however, the best Mario Kart clone in existence, even surpassing the thing it's shamelessly copying. But what makes it so good?
The track design is fantastic in this game. The transforming gimmick is used to its full potential and many of the tracks themselves change on each lap due to an ongoing battle, a volcanic eruption or a ever changing dreamscape to name but a few. This ensures the tracks never become boring and you have to be prepared for anything. Also a lot of the stuff going on in the background makes the tracks feel alive and action-packed,
The soundtrack adds to the overall experience, with many excellent remixes of old Sega tunes, each perfectly suited to the tracks they accompany.
There are also loads of challenges with four difficulty levels to satisfy the completionists, with good variety testing all your skills.
Speaking of challenge, this game pulls no punches right from the start. Until you get a good feel for it you'll find yourself getting trounced by the AI even on the lower difficulties, and on the harder settings they can be downright brutal. You have to bring your A game to every race if you want to win. Some people might find this a bit offputting but if you like a challenge (like me) you will love attempting a race again and again until you nail it perfectly.
Another downside inherent with the mascot racer genre is the pickups. If you like driving through pure skill then in can be frustrating to be constantly hammered by comedy weapons. But this is a risk of any game of this sort, and you can use it to your advantage.
This is still one of the best racers I have ever played and certainly the best 3D Sonic game since ever. I cannot recommend this enough.

This is a surprisingly complete early access game. If it weren't for the occasional small bug or fairly common typo, I'd think it was a complete game that steam had mistakenly labeled as early access. My first moment with this game was spent wondering whether or not the opening cutscene was supposed to have audio dialogue or not. My second moment was spent getting accustomed to the fairly simple controls and flipping through the brief and fairly straightforeward explaination of the games systems. After that, I spent some time wandering around the facility (in the wrong order because I wasn't paying attention, and noticing that your oxygen supply runs out in an amount of time I'd call &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥all." Your oxygen tank will run out looong before your thermal will. It's an incentive to find and replace the broken filters/fuses in each sector and promotes a sort of "scouting" gameplay where you have to carefully plan your excursions until you get the filter/fuses replaced. I'm not sure, but I believe the filters/fuses can be destroyed or burn out. These filters/fuses are also vital not just for your genral survival, but also to push back the diseased hordes. The contagion that runs them doesn't like a warm, oxygen rich environement. The lower the entire facilities "infection" level, the safer you'll be. You also have to keep an eye on the facilities reactor, which will, apparently, be attacked by monsters occasionally. During that part of the game, it becomes a sort of tower defense. You can collect a wide array of "junk" items that can be broken down to obtain materials to create items you can actually use, and you can take items you have and research them to obtain the blueprints for that item, and the next most powerful version of that item. It's a very easy to use system.
I've gone to many game forums and seen many requests/recommendations. No game of this kind (sandbox/survival) have I ever seen where someone did not ask for the ability to take a♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's well executed in subterrain, and is a far less persistant need than I thought it would be, considering a lot of games with defecation/urination often make you do it all the time. In the five hours I've played at the time of this review, the need for the character to take a♥♥♥♥♥♥has come up a grand total of once. Once. I thought when I got this game that it would be just another of the many pressing needs that had to be managed. It's not exactly tasteful, but it isn't nearly as distasteful as it was in any of the other games i've seen it in. It isn't really worthy of being a selling point though.
Overall, this is a good game, and as an early access game, it is a definete exception to the rule of early access games being garbage.

Nexon saw World of Warcraft, thought "we could probably do better," and then spat out an anime-styled cutesy MMO for the masses to enjoy. I've been around for a good portion of it's lifespan... and through every generation as things grew bigger and I became a smaller and smaller part of the world, I sat back and enjoyed myself more and more. The choices that are there now are expansive and there's so many ways you can build your character. Don't fret, because how you build them doesn't matter! REBIRTH allows for you to start over again at level 0 if you are tired of being range-based. So you can follow your Mabinogi dreams and become a chef or a great mage or even just a fun little bard. Speaking of bards, they have a custom COMPOSING system which allows for one to fashion a song of their choosing/making. The possibilities are endless, especially if you are one for running dungeons like a classic MMO player. One drawback I can see is many parts of the game are locked/hard to get to without paying a bit of cash. Some character customizations are also premium only too, but that's mostly vanity stuff. It doesn't make it pay to win necessarily, it just makes dealing with travel and some skilling much easier, especially with a limited source of inventory slots and hotbars for skills. I still find it worthwhile to pay a little so you can play the game at it's fullest potential. The game is so expansive that I can even recount a time where I was pillowfighting with my sister in Dunbarton as our mounts went nuts trying to devour us. From what I remember, there are Humans, Giants, and Elves for racial picks, but if you buy any pets they not only carry stuff for you/between your characters more fluidly, but they also can be directly playable, so buying a flying mount can make you a taxi as well.
All of that I just typed... Only a small portion of what's in store if you're up for it. Seriously, if you are into WoW, it's definitely worth checking out. Just remember that just like WoW, it's best to play with friends... 'Cept here you can go a step further and marry your friends and make them your family. Then go family dungeoning and recount endless adventures across Iria with them around a warm campfire.
Mabinogi has events all the time, so it's wise to check in on it once in a time so you get LOTS of free stuff and more to pick from.
I give it a 8/10. In comparison, I give a game like WoW a 6/10 due to the lack of a deep and extensive story. Mabi goes, in my opinion, too far to fill the blanks on your experience. Plus with all the events going on, odds are you'll make friends that will explain it all for you. I've had many amazing memories playing this game, and I am SURE you will too!
The game seems well made and so far I enjoy everything but the heavy breathing that lasts forever!! As well I dislike the low bass sound when running.

Sole survivor of a virus outbreak in a colony on Mars...all that stands between you and escape is an army of mutants...
And you have only your bare hands...
And the lights are off...
And all you`re wearing is a thin jumpsuit that barely counts as clothing...
And the heat generators are broken...
And the oxygen generators are broken...
And even if they were working, the reactor to power them is failing...
Find, research, and upgrade a wide range of weapons, armour and equipment to keep you alive and the mutants thoroughly dead as you scavenge for 'stuff' to recycle into useful materials.
The atmosphere and music is suitably creepy, and since you can usually only see what`s in the cone of light from your torch you inevitably get nervous and start waving it around in a manner similar to someone trying to shoo away a wasp, because those grunting and growling mutants sound rreeaallyy close...
At the time of writing the game is still in early access, although the devs intend a full release sometime in January 2016.
The game is fully playable at the moment (out of idle curiosity I tried it on a pc with Windows XP and it seems perfectly happy with it), the devs are active on the Steam forums (and quick to squash any bugs that are reported) and open to constructive criticism and feedback as they add further content and polish what`s already there.
All plus points and promising signs for an early access title. (Yeah, I`ve had my fingers burnt before with games being left in an unfinished state, but I`m satisfied with progress on this one)
There are some bugs crop up, but they tend to be quickly fixed. The level maps are partly random, as they are procedurally generated from various tiles and room types, then slotted together. So there can be a bit of repetition, but as more tiles are added then that should become less noticable.

I love Risen 3 in its current form. My gaming life has revolved around Day of Defeat after my fascination with Half-Life, the mods that came of it, and my family. My brother John (Fuzz) (I use his pseudonym because I look up to my brother and the name is catchy to me) and a few programmers at the time came up with the initial concept of DoD after my brother watched Saving Private Ryan. At an early age (8 or 9) I would watch my brother create sandbox levels within his newly created mod, Day of Defeat. My brother paved the way for Day of Defeat before his departure of the development team (focus on school and relationships) shortly before Valve purchased the mod and turned it into a Valve product.
Soon after my father (Wes) (Fuzzdad) would join in on the efforts to help propel the game forward with level design. My father was a Major in the Army and a helicopter pilot for 13 years, to say he loves history is an understatement. His dedication to the game and meticulous craftsmanship of design with each level was researched, designed, tested, redesigned and re-tested for countless hours. I vividly remember walking downstairs on more than one occasion to his mancave and watching him design what is now known as dod_glider with the Hammer tool, Valve Software's map creation program for their game engine. I am grateful that my father allowed me to playtest his maps and give input. Fuzzdad went on to be a Valve-contracted level designer for dod_glider, dod_flugplatz and dod_falaise. He also created custom maps such as dod_factory and dod_Anvil (Made on Source)
Fuzzdad worked directly with Matt Boone (Main Programmer for DoD/DoD:s and now works on multiple Valve games, also known as Mugsy) with game changes, community map pack releases, updates to stock maps, texture files, sounds, etc. I commend Mugsy for sticking it out as long as he did with DoD/DoD:S by helping the community and working with my father to better the game.
Day of Defeat and Day of Defeat: Source are my favorite multiplayer FPS. It is evident Valve gave up on Day of Defeat: Source after Sourcefilms was tested with DoD:S (The trailers referring to specific maps like Donner) It's hard to blame Valve for lack of content or continuous updates with the game not breaking even on sales. The WW2 era FPS from the 90s and early 2000's has lost the populace favor but that doesn't mean this game is anything less than great.
Do I recommend this game? Yes, yes and yes. DoD:S is a majestic game that has countless replay value and at its core is fun. It's realistic in terms of 1-2 bullet kills. While there is only one "true" gamemode (CTF) they also have demolition style maps, but the majority of what's left of public servers play CTF or realism. I personally wish they would release a steam workshop for the game or add gamemodes, but it would be safe to say DoD:S has lost it's prime motivation that it once had years ago. What's left of public servers is mostly realism units which you may or may not like (I personally find them more like a person trying to relive his/her military past and not fun in terms of gameplay) but you as a player might find that style of play different or fun.
To conclude: Day of Defeat will always be a part of me and my future endeavours in gaming and I hope you the reader give this game a try, even if it's not in its prime anymore. It's still enjoyable to pub once in a while.
I'll always have hope for a new DoD, maybe one day, maybe never, but I'll always have my memories of this great game.

What is and what isn't Risen 3 - A guide for buyers and players
I decided to write this guide/review after all the hate that's been spreading through the forum from people who were expecting something different I think, so here it goes
What is Risen 3?
-It's a Piranha Bytes game, which means you'll be thrown into a world with little to none knowledge of how you're supposed to play, fight and deal with stuff and you'll have to learn by yourself by experimenting tactics and fighting styles
-It's an exploration RPG, which means you'll be spending a big amount of time just roaming through the place to find stuff, people, quests and places, some of what you find will be rewarded, some will just be for your own personal curiosity and pleasure, you'll find yourself saying "Hey I wonder what's in there, let's have a look" a lot.
-It's a piratesque/fantasy mesh game, which means you'll find a mix of both genres in it, you'll have pirates, mages, warriors, musketeers, demons, sea creatures, big ships, big castles, ruins, treasures, etc...
- It's not a game about combat, which mean you'll often find yourself presented with the option to avoid fights by talking, running away, sneaking past enemies, etc. Or, if you so desire, you could smack everyone's teeth inside their skulls, the choice is yours.
- It's a living world, which means NPCs have routines, interact with eachother and have lifes and monsters aren't all out to get you, sometimes you might happen to stumble upon a guy too busy to care about your problems or a dragon snappers killing worthogs to eat them.
-It's a game where you choose your difficulty, which means the game won't get harder the more you progress, but you'll have to shape your character the way you like in order to fit the game, you want fights to be hard but you want every possible shiny coin in the world? Spend all your glory points into dexterity and influence, you want to stomp everything with powerful blows? Focus on melee combat. You want to survive everything and just run through hordes of enemies unscathed? Max out your toughness.
What Risen 3 isn't?
-It's not Gothic, which means that you won't relive your days gone by getting mauled by orcs and wargs, it has some nostalgia easter eggs and it's still a Piranha bytes game which means there are some strong points of connection and if you liked Gothic 1/2/3 you'll most likely like Risen 3 too, but don't expect to play another Gothic because it isn't such.
-It's not Risen 2, which means if you played Risen 2 and didn't like it you should tell so in Risen 2's forum, not here.
-It's not a combat driven action RPG, which means that if you care for insane combos with stunning animations and insanely big numbers flying all over the place you'll have to look elsewhere, fights in Risen 3 are milder and more realistic, you won't launch your enemy in the air and slash him 400 times in 3 seconds before he hits the ground.
-It's not a Sandbox game, which also means it's not Skyrim, you won't have heavy modding, you won't have a world that answer to your bidding, you won't have an immense amount of general sidequests that all look the same and have no soul.
-It's not a game you can understand in a few hours, which means that you'll have to put a bit of time into the game before you start to grasp all the details and untold gimmicks of the game's mechanics.
And last but not least, it's not a game for everyone, which means you shouldn't get mad because people buy it and enjoy it and you shouldn't feel offended if others don't like it, it's a game so peculiar that it can only appeal to a core group of people, just like all PB games so far.
All in all it's a fantastic game and I'd recommend it to anyone who likes RPGs and isn't afraid of a bit of thinking instead of buttonmashing all over the place.

You either love it or you hate it.
If you enjoyed the previous titles you will like this game - a lot.
If you did not enjoy them you will not enjoy this game either.
The advertisments in form of the the game trailers are kind of misleading.
There you are basically promised that you get a " Gothic " experience.
Instead you get a Risen 2 with slight improvements.
The graphics are solid but unimpressive, they look outdated but still fit the game in a strange way.
The game will probably run on less powerful machines as smooth as on high end rigs.
Some animations look incredibly clunky and wooden ( like drawing your weapon ), others look organic and fluent ( agitated animals ).
The Music of the game is beautiful and immersive, it has both a pirate and fantasy vibe.
The ambient sounds are well done as well and add to the immersion.
The Voice acting seems to be a matter of conflict to many people.
Personally I thought it was fine, the voice acting has the typical Gothic / Risen characteristics which I personally enjoyed.
The language is rude and direct most of the time, with its own kind of dark humor.
Lips of the characters are usually out of sync with what they are saying, but I just noticed that because I actively looked for it.
[b}COMBAT[/b]
Combat is a mixed bag.
At the beginning it is frustrating and feels unfair as well as clunky.
Every enemy you encounter appears to be able to attack twice or thrice as fast as you can, constantly interrupting your attacks.
This changes later, once you get a feel for the enemies attack patterns.
The majority of the enemies utilizes a combo of 3 attacks in a row. Which become quite predictable after a short while.
This is later mixed up with enemies that can block your attacks, instead of dodging it, or throwing the occasional stone or fireball at you.
Later in the game you are able to improve your combat skills significantly, you will be able to learn to attack faster, add more attacks to your combos, riposte and interrupt enemies attacks.
Combat feels harsh and unfair at first but quickly becomes menial as you progress in your skills.
This continues to the point where you are basically a demi-god, an almost indestructible force of mayhem.
Some people like it some hate it.
I personally enjoyed it because it instills a feeling of gratification, like you worked hard to get there and now you are able to enjoy the fruits of your labor.
One thing about combat however seems quite annoying, almost all types of enemies are able to knock you on your♥♥♥♥♥
Sending you flying through the air.
It makes sense with certain type of enemies such as big rhinos or Golemts.
However I fail to see how a small spider, a lake lizardman ( which is basically a water-ghoul ) or an over sized chicken ( scavanger ) can constantly send you flying.
Magic seems powerful and satisfying, there is no mana just cooldown rates which you can decrease by unlocking various perks.
There is a good amount of spell variety.
The game offers some mini games to liven things up a little.
You will have to combat other ships and Sea-Monsters.
Combating other ships is very scripted you basically just have to fight some pirates on deck and beat their Leader.
This is accompanied by some shooting the board cannon, which feels quite underwhelming in terms of power and destructive force.
The Sea monster combat allows you to steer your mighty vessel and give the sea monster some broad-sides.
This battles with Sea monsters become progressively more difficult, the last encounter is frustratingly difficult.
Everything about it feels wrong, the monster seems overly powerful and have homing shots.
After I beat it I felt more like it was a stroke of luck than skill.
Many people seem to complain about it, especially since its a " mini game " that you can´t skip.
If you reached that point it basically blocks your progress until you beat it.
There seem 2 ways around this issue :
1. Lower the difficulty, which makes the battle mind numbingly dull and underwhelming
2. Prepare yourself to try it 10-20 times in a row.
Maybe there are some very good players who found a pattern or strategy to use, I personally could not find it.
Any good RPG like game needs vast amounts of Weapons and Armor and othe trinkets to make you feel like a truly mighty Warrior.
The game offers a variety of Armors consting of hats, chests pieces, pants, boots.
Depending on the faction youi will join you get access to 3 exclusive types of Armor.
As you progress in the ranks of your faction you will advance from light armor to medium to heavy.
Armors look good and characeristic for their faction.
You can also get some general pirate themed armor from vendors or as special rewards from quests.
These all look nice but are utterly inferior to your faction armor.
With the exception of something just labeled " Heavy Armor " that you can find on your adventures.
Which is slightly better than your tier 3 Faction armor.
If you own the Adventurer Garb DLC you get a set of armor that is slightly better than your first faction armor.
Which makes quite a bit of a difference at the start of the game.
The armor just looks kind of whacky.
There are various accessoirs to choose from, such as rings, earrings and amulets.
Those basically boost your stats and allow you to specialize your skill sets.
Weapons, there are plenty of weapons to be found.
Swords, Axes and Maces, sabres and fencing weapons.
I personally could not see a big difference between the weapon types.
You get perks for each class, and all seem to do the same amount of damage.
There are slight variations but they make no difference in actual combat.
Wether your weapon does 95, 100 or 110 damage does not matter, you still need at least 2-3 hits to kill an enemy in the end game.
So it just is a matter of taste.
There also is a Musket type of weapon, allowing you ranged combat.
If you choose to use this combat will change slightly but soon falls into the same patterns as meele combat.
Last but not least you are able to utilize dirty tricks, which basically are secondary weapons.
You will be able to throw daggers, fire a pistol or crossbow in the heat of battle.
If you have enough ammunition this can change your combat style a bit.
However it is quite tedious to use in the beginning.
Without proper training your will miss a lot, this has nothing to do with your personal skill however.
It is purely stat based, an enemy can stand point blank and you still will miss with your scatter pistol ( which is like a pumpgun in pistol form ).
There are only 2 components that matter : skill level with your desired dirty trick weapon and range.
The game offers an extensive crafting system.
You can Craft new weapons, repair broken legendary weapons which you can find in your adventures, craft rings and amulets, brew booze ( yay ) and alchemical tinktures.
You also can create your own spell-scrolls / rune stones.
You gather resources by picking them up ( herbs and so on ), ripping them out of defeated enemies ( requires hunting perks ), finding them in chests, or buying them at vendors.
The game plays smooth, you can reach about everything you can see, there are few invisible walls that block you from reaching zones that you are not supposed to reach yet.
I only got stuck once in the environment but could rescue myself with the parrot spell.
Combat becomes boring fast, since its very basic. The old Gothic Combat system is far superior.
Quest / Quest logs are sometimes confusing, leaving you wondering what to do next.
The game does not hold your hand much, which is nice.
You can get additional mini rewards by talking to people that had a part in a quest you completed

All in all, a worthy contribution to an addictive series. Maybe Telltale Games will pick up the task of Half Life 3.

Who remembers this one? Back from the olden days of Winter Sale coal and fresh indie zombie games. Actually, maybe it's more appropriate to ask if you remember that decade-old zombie simulator with the colored dots, because this is the fully gameified version of that. Humanity is on the retreat from the zombie hordes and it's up to you to evacuate the survivors from your region. You can select different infested areas from the strategic map based on the infection level (difficulty), and it takes you to a small city map where you have to plan the evacuation. You get a helicopter that airlifts folks (yellow dots) out every 20 seconds or so, and up to 3 mercenary units to help defend. These units are anything from soldiers and snipers to landmines and barricades. After each mission you AND the zombies get victory points based on the final number of survivors and zombies. New events occur as you both reach certain victory point milestones, and the first side to rack up the target number of points wins.
Sounds solid, right? Unfortunately, this all comes together to form a strategy game that's mostly based on random chance. Just like the old simulator, humans turn into zombies instantly when touched, and you better believe the survivors clump up around the landing zones like delicious stuffing. All it takes is one zombie escaping your best-laid deathtrap to ruin an entire map. This is further exacerbated by the fact that your 3 mercenary units are randomized for each mission. So while you're in good shape if you get your mortars and zombie baits in one mission, you're boned if you get stuck with barricades, mines, and bombs, all of which are one-use tricks. There's also random variance in the performance of your units; soldiers can miss, and your mortars can go off-target, ruining that hail mary shot you needed to save the day. There are a host of other frustrations, like how you and the zombies get points for holding territory, but you only claim territory if you kill ALL the zombies on the map before sundown, which is ludicrously difficult even if you have the right mercs for it.
It's a shame, too, because the presentation is stylish and weird, and there are some neat systems to explore like XP to improve your mercs and rescuing scientists to upgrade your other abilities. The story vignettes are compellingly strange as well and I still can't make heads or tails of the story, but I know Tesla and an antichrist baby are involved. Shame I'll never figure it out, because the game's just too damn discouraging and frustrating to get through.

An MMO that falls just short of perfect, it has basically everything you would want in an MMO:
-free form character creation that lets you constantly build your character's strength, forever
-a wide array of awesome to goofy mounts
-a pretty large open world
-a complex crafting system that provides useful items
-player homesteads where you can craft, farm, decorate, etc
-a long and constantly added to story broken up into arcs that can actually be surprisingly well written
-constant updates that add very significant features
-frequent events that can be pretty fun
-many different ways to play, and fun minigames to play, some for daily bonuses (ie - rafting, alone or with friends try to steer a raft down a river and used ranged abilities to kill goblins on the shores attacking you with magic and arrows, some melee ones will jump onto the raft and attack as well!)
but there's some downsides that you should consider before you get into it:
-pets and mounts cost money, although they do give you some basic ones for free now. limited edition ones can be powerful and extremely useful for certain kinds of crafting and playstyles so it's hard not having them sometimes
-the combat is based on manipulating skills to counter the enemies and when you start it'll be hard to figure out what enemies are good to fight despite a "combat power" system that's supposed to help, it's not really accurate
-it takes a loooong time to build up a decent amount of power, and if you start with magic good luck with that, some of the spells can literally take you years to get if you're trying to get them alone because you need extremely rare drops from hard dungeons
-the game can be extremely confusing at first because almost nothing is explained well, they've started adding more in-depth tutorials but you'll still have a hard time figuring out what to do as a newbie
-some people will be seriously turned off by the goofy cell shaded anime art style, but the screenshots are on the store page so you can see that for yourself. It can be seriously worth a laugh though when you see something like the pelican pet's running animations
in the end though the game's sheer volume of content that's surprisingly high quality overpowers the downsides so once you get into it the game's very good for being mostly free. I've played it since it came out in 2006 and I've probably spent $60 tops on it, and most of that was not needed to be competitive in gameplay.

Proteus is both one of the most interesting and most boring titles I've played.
Interesting for its beautifully rendered world. Designed using blocky, 8-bit era bitmaps, its procedurally-generated islands have a stark and eye-catching beauty to them. The world teems with wildlife, each of which reacts differently to your presence. As you progress, the seasons change from spring, to summer, autumn and finally winter, and each has a noticeably different feel from the last. Every plant and animal has its own signature music and as you approach them, it alters the soundtrack accordingly. It is a wonder to wander through the world and absorb its new-age vibe.
Unfortunately, that is /all/ you can do in the game; there is absolutely no interactivity in this title. The gameplay consists of wandering the island until you find a ring of stones; stand within this ring at night and a shower of stars will whisk you to the next season. Once you have progressed through a full year, you float off into the sky. The idea is that the player will take the opportunity to explore the island and soak in the calming atmosphere. Unfortunately, the dearth of any real content means that you will have seen all the game has to offer in the first few minutes of the game, leaving you little to discover for the rest of the session. This is particularly galling when you realize that most games finish in 15 minutes; in short, Proteus can't even fill up a quarter-hour of gameplay.
No, I get it, I get it; I'm supposed to relax and just wander. Proteus isn't about goals or victory. It's one of those games that are just about the "experience". But the experience Proteus offers is neither particularly innovative or robust; it palls long before the nominal end of the game. Certainly it isn't worth the price of admission. Unique presentation aside, Proteus feels stale and unfulfilling. Better to just install some other open-world game and turn off the AI; you'll get much the same experience and when you're done, at least you get to kill some monsters.

DISCLAIMER: I'd mark this as "Recommended With Reservations" but there isn't an option for it.
This game reminds me of a cross between thatgamecompany's two biggest games, Journey and Flower, in terms of atmosphere and gameplay: simple but well-executed. Proteus consists of a short stroll through a randomly-generated island that, on first impression, seems to have no purpose or any form of progression. In reality, it's a relaxing little treasure hunt in a (rather well rendered) pixelly world. Unlike Flower and Journey, Proteus lacks progression (with the exception of the changing seasons) and a story. There are a few interesting landmarks and creatures on the island, and that's really about it. The environment-generated music was a little on the gimmicky side at first, but it grew on me. The few interactive sites that sometimes appear are neat, though a bit arbitrary. The "snapshot" mechanic is actually quite interesting. Pressing F9 in game saves a special screenshot of the game that can be used to access the same island again (a new island is generated each time you start the game) so that you can return and explore some more. A minor gripe is that, while the snapshots can be used by anyone who owns Proteus to explore the same island, Steam does not recognize them as screenshots so they need to be shared differently. You need to find the Snapshots folder in your game directory to be able to add or share snapshots. Proteus has moderate replayability due to the randomly generated nature of the island, but frankly that's not enough to keep players coming back for dozens of hours of gameplay. Also, some of the "things" (for lack of a better word) in this game may seem confusing and pointless without going through guides, but I believe that it was more fun to explore without spoiling anything, frustration notwithstanding.
Overall, Proteus is relaxing and fun to explore in, but if you are looking for any amount or direction or story, you are going to hate this game and want your money back.
On the subject of price, I bought Proteus for $2 during a sale, and frankly, that's around the maximum amount of money I'd spend on this game. The normal price ($10) is a bit excessive for what feels like a glorified engine demo.
Pros:
-Decent art style
-Snapshot mechanic
-Relaxing
-Surprising amount of exploration capacity
Cons:
-No story
-Steep price for a couple hours of simplistic gameplay
-Niche audience
6/10

This game is great. I bought it off of impulse when it was only $2.50, and I'm VERY glad I did.
Unlike most modern day games, there is no other characters, no monsters, no leveling, no upgrades. The entire game is fully exploration-based. You have to find some stone circles, and they shift you from season to season, until you finish the game.
Even though this game is a pixel-type game, the graphics and dynamics are amazing. The landscapes are everchanging, and beautiful. Clouds move in over the flatlands at night, the sun rises and sets, as does the moon. Heck, there are even shooting stars! The most unique element to this game is the music. Nobody will ever listen to the same music, ever. It all depends where you go. If you go near trees, you'll hear some additions to the music. If you go to a flower field, then you'll hear the music of the flowers. When you're walking through the landscape, it will all just blend together into a great, and truely unique musical score. If you are hesitant about getting this amazing game, don't be. You'll be very glad you did.

If your browsing the reviews looking to see if you should buy this game, I suppose you should ask yourself a few questions...
- do you like games that require you to build, gather goods, and create stuff to survive?
- do you like games that have waves of enemies and random events that can end you?
- do you like games where your characters are the story and you help it develop?
- do you consider graphics to be a huge part of your gaming experience?
If you said yes to all but the last one, I suggest you try this game. It’s a fantastic game currently still being developed. Without a doubt, it still needs many improvements and new content but where it stands, you’ll get plenty of game play for a few days, maybe longer.
Once you get bored of the vanilla version, this game has an amazing modding community constantly creating mods to improve the game in many different ways. There are complete overhaul mods, there are new race mods, new character customization mods, AI mods, mods that create more content... and so much more... it can drive you crazy trying to find mods to make your gameplay way more amazing. The best part is that if you can’t find it, you can make it or ask someone to make it, and chances are (If your idea is a great idea) someone will jump on it. In addition, some mods at times even become part of the original game due to how incredible the ideas are!
In my personal opinion, the game could definitely expand on the tribal age of the game... adding more clothing and structures so a player doesn’t feel rushed to advance technologically... sometimes I want to stick with swords and spears. Adding some primitive armor for that age would be amazing. There are mods out that I feel should be a part of the game for sure... and there are other improvements that could make this an ultimate game for fun.
With all that said, in the end, this game has been incredible. I wish I could play it with other people, but im perfectly fine playing this solo because the game can keep things interesting. I love this game, and hope you enjoy this game as much as I do.

This is a good Action RPG. It stands on it's own even if you've never played any of the Gothic/Risen series.
It's an RPG meaning that if the player tries to melee a golem without putting any points into combat related skills, it will likely end rather badly for that player. Or rather, the player won't do much damage and the fight will be really long and boring. With high skills in Melee, Magic or even Toughness the game is quite easy even on the hardest setting. However, if the player feels the urge for punishing fights, all he/she has to do is not level up.
So it has everything one would expect. It has lots of monsters to kill. It has lots of skills to level that help kill monsters in better and more fun ways. It has skills that help manipulate the world and the people in it, such as lock picking and silver tongue. It even has multiple options to succeed in combat with guns or magic or swords as well as several factions that add combat flair. There is even enough potions to max every single attribute if you're that type of player.
I had fun with it and it was well worth the price tag to me. Buy it if you enjoy RPGs.

I'll start with the cons, because there's a couple of things that really bug me:
This game is NOT MMO - it's a pitched battle game with no open-world gameplay, public areas, or other MMO characteristics. You appear in an arena, you battle, you recieve rewards. You teleport back to your garage, you organise your assets. Repeat.
The crafting - or rather the resource gathering for crafting - is very time-expensive. Some of the crafting materials are easily accessible, but some, like the wires and copper, you only get on average about 10 per battle (if you win) (oh, and you need to do seperate battles for each resource) and you'll need around 400-500 for even the basic-level items (400-500 of each different resource for higher level items). You need multiple basic-level items, plus resources, to build rare-level items, and multiple rare-level items, plus resources, to build legendary-level items, then you'll need multiple legendary-level items, plus resources, to build the relic-level items. Over 75 hours on this game, and I am still working on building a single legendary item. This includes single wheels (most vehicles will require at least 3-4, or more).
What's worse, some of the parts you need to build faction vehicles can only be aquired by paying real-world money. Spiked mudguards anyone? Only if you buy the such-and-such pack... And you'll still need to level up at the normal rate, only you won't recieve many of the rewards throughout the game if the car you bought already has those bits on it.
Despite that, the pros almost make up for it:
Driving around shooting and blowing things up is fun. The vehicles come apart really nicely, and targeting certain areas causes weapons to come away, restricted movement and downgraded buffs.
The vehicle building is a lot of fun, and there's a lot of variety in the styles and restrictions of the various factions. Building an effective battle-machine is a very satisfying feeling, and although it can be time-expensive, it's the good-time kind.
There's a gallery area where you can post your vehicle designs - even better, you can test-drive other people's creations too which can be a lot of fun, especially when demonstrating the game to new players.
Lastly, it's a very solid game-engine. I have yet to see any glitches at all, and it has always loaded and played without any drama whatsoever. Amazing really, for a game with so many moving parts!
Summary:
It's a fun game, and it's free-to-play so it's not all bad, but it badly needs a look-over by a game-designer with a head for economics to balance the time/cost factors of many of the assets.
I would recommend it to anyone looking for short-term fun, or to someone looking to pay to get into the game a bit deeper, but if you want to believe the free-to-play claim it is going to take dozens and dozens of hours just to make a set of nice wheels for your vehicle, and I don't think that's worth it.
tl;dr - time playing versus rewards factor is very low, but it's fun - at least for a while.
Update edit:
Well, it seems they've put the guy who was in charge of the economic balancing in charge of the vehicle re-balancing. The lightening of the vehicles was the starting point for everything going wrong. I now have truck bodies that I can't armor without going over the extremely low weight limit. The more powerful engines that take weeks to make are completely ineffectual, rendering any sort of truck build pointless. Higher level players building rammers have the run of the game right now as they seem to be able to disintegrate your vehicle in seconds, as does anyone with drone setups.
Vehicle control seems to have been affected also, with small adjustments to the steering being ignored - it goes where you want it for a split second, then self-corrects back. Tapping the turn key shouldn't leave your vehicle running in a straight line. The only way to combat it is to hold the key for too long, which more than likely will send you in a direction you don't want to go. I though it might have something to do with how multi-wheel builds handle, but no - it's the same on standard 4-wheel builds as well.
Also, there is now a lot of judder in the graphics - not all the time, but commonly when there are a few AI on screen. This is something that has only started since the update - beforehand, as I said above, there were no glitches at all - it used to run smooth as butter.
As a result, this game is no longer fun at all. They have, whether deliberately or through gross incompetence, made the game strictly pay-to-win and the control/judder factor makes the gameplay frustrating. I can no longer recommend it to anyone.

Steam is SEVERLY flawed when letting other people use your game when playing with a different account on the same computer; somehow Steam doesn't want to remember a save for a friend's use of the game, it always starts from the Prologue.
To see how this happens, share your game with a friend who also has a steam account, or in some cases with a second account you've made for yourself, and then attempt to play the game; when a friend saves the game it never keeps, the second account always starts from scratch.
(Makes it difficult to try a different species for starters without having to go from the very begining every single time. So, be prepared to have a long levelling process before you can have more than one character on the same account. The only advantage is that the Parallel Quests will all be there to help your secondary characters level quicker)

First thing you need to know about Proteus is that it is not a "game" in the classic sense of the word.
It doesn't contain much interaction or any tasks to complete whatsoever, so if this what you are looking for this title may simply not be for you.
What it does offer is an interesting audio-visual experience with the freedom to explore procedurally generated islands made of  stylised 8bit 2D/3D hybrid visuals. It would be right to say that there is simply not much to Proteus, but that is the point of it. It is not meant to provide high octane action or hours of convoluted plot. It simply places you in its world in order to for you to see the sights (with some neat stuff happening at night) and enjoy a relaxing moment. It could best be compared as a pleasant, waking dream.

RPG Maker advertizes itself as being simple enough for a child, but powerful enough for a professional. As someone who has herself programmed games the hard way, I can assure you that this statement is true. For the new game developer, RPG Maker provides a nice framework to understand how mechanics and gameplay can mesh with story and helps learn the basics of game design - how to telegraph things to your players, how to make enemies an appropriate strength, etc.
For those who know how to do that, RPG Maker trims the fat, saving you the time of having to program different elemental types while still giving you the option to modify it if you want.
And that, I think, is the power of this tool. It presents you with so many options to get you started, but can do so much more if you know how to code.

Well. Where I must begin?
Let's start from... mods. A lot of people actually loves dat mods, aren't they?
Without them, any game is a bit less "complete" and a bit more "unfinished".
In Rimworld there is at least one mod for everything: wanna eat trees? We got you covered. Want to squash some zombies? Kiddo, please, we have mods for that. Want to master The Force's powers, shackin' ya lightsaber around yodeling like your favourite pervert krapfen & bauertoast fanatic next door? Splendid idea! Three Star Wars oriented mod are ready to be grabbed from Steam's Workshop.
But 'member, kids: as stated on mods-dedicated part of Ludeon Studios' EULA, "You may not advertise for donations within your Mods themselves". So stop dreaming about offshore yachts!
Sum all it up: there are legions of mods that can add many amazing way you can play this game. If the base game - more on this topic later - don't please Your Highness at 100% fell free to mod-theft the dedicated Workshop pages.
---
The premise is done. Let's talk about Rimworld "as-is". The core game is beatifully complex, like a mesmerizing sheep's curly wool. When you start a new game, you have to choose some details.
1) You can start with one or more "colonists" which have randomized stats (but with mods you can choose every detail of them, from skin colour to badass attributes) and are grumpy tribal people that inhabited the Rim for 4873782348683...1 years or sofisticated but despaired space-faring folks.
Without mods, your colonists will be Humans; but... with another plethora of mods... we have also more fabulous races like Dwarves, Aliens, Predators, Orcs, semi-animals beings, Smurfs, and so on.
2) You can start with a "seed" (useful for generate the same map over and over again - I'm watching you, nostalgic oldie!) that will shape the planet where your colonists will spawn.
3) You decide the explorable percentage (5% for DEV MODE, 100% for roaming gipsies like me) of the world, the climate parameters and the spawning point. Do you like Tundras? Or snowy and mortal icy landscapes? Maybe some hot desert resort? Tropical jungle anyone? I must stop myself, sorry.
4) You decide the storyteller - there are three of them available. But only if you hate mods; instead there are some more... like a... uhm... H. P. Lovecraft in his Rimworld counterpart. Storytellers are the AI entities that will generate random events to keep you entertained. Infamous ones will send you nasty hostile raids every two days or so whilst angelic ones will make you and your colonist a bit more relaxed.
5) You start to play and basically must survive one day after another hunting, farming, researching, crafting, harvesting organs from prisoners, make silver money trading with caravans and outpost, imprisoning poor 86 years grannies and selling them @ pirate slavers and so on. You know what? With a mod you can also wander the world without relocate your permanent colony base.
You can have medicine-oriented colonists that can perform surgical operations on your ill people or against a visiting guest that decide to collapse - you must made him a prisoner prior to operate, but it's a microscopic detail.
You can hunt for exploding animals (like the tiny "boomrat" and the biggest bro "boomalope").
You can raid other Rimworl AI inhabitants' colonies.
There are so many things that you can do in this game and I'm afraid that I'm too lazy to write about all of them.
Some CONS just to finish my review:
* No multiplayer. Not yet, at least. Maybe one day. But let me be honest: I don't miss it. And maybe there is some nice mod that.............
* AI is dumb (there are mods that tries to make it better, of course!). For instance when a colonist is moving in direction of a Steel vein, he can suddenly "decide" to turn back and drink a cold beer instead. Cold beers wins against mining labour, it's a matter of fact. *HIC*!
* Colonists doesn't mate. Nope. They can be lovers, they can do "fiki-fiki" but... no little babies that will do Big Surprise Puke nor poop-like-there-is-no-tomorrow around. You can only pray that soon or less the reluctant AI Storyteller of the moment decides to spawn an Event that hopefully will add a new colonist to your pool. And that colonist may have some kind of relationship with one or more already existing colonists. Sometime you can have "child" (with a minimum age of 15 or 16 years, but better than nothing... it's something) or "mother" or "father" or "brother" or... well, you can have different degrees of parental choices to randomize your newly-added colonist.

So I started out by a free weekend on steam. I started just a silly game to learn the program. RPG Maker MV was so easy to use that this small game started turning into a real RPG very quick. I realized that 4 days were not enough so I went to their website to see if they had another week of free trial or so so I could just finish my half♥♥♥♥♥game. They had a 20 day free trial which was EXACTLY enough time to finish and test my game, and really begin to comprehend the power behind this engine.
I love it. You can only make one style of RPG as best I can tell, however other than that options are limitless. At its base it is a great platform to tell a fantastic story if you have one, but more than that you can install plugins to make your RPG unique and interesting. All of the art is made of PNG files so you can inport your own artwork if the anime style isn't what you are looking for, but for me the built in character generator got the job done well.
Though I am very pleased with this program, I will not be buying it at this time. I want to learn how to make a wide variety of games, and this can not help me in that endeavor. That said, should the day come that I want to make a 2D RPG like this, this program would likely be the first I turn to. And as my son grows up, if he is interested in games as I am, I would gladly buy this program for him so he could begin learning the importance of balancing story arcs and other important mechanics.
All in all, 9/10 this program does all that it says and more, just not much more. It has its restrictions, but definitely worth the price (especially in user friendliness alone!). Thank you so much Kadokawa for letting me try the program.

The problem I have with suggesting this game though is that not everyone in the world is a fan of what is essentially virtual tourism. If you like science fiction survival- type games with depth and a difficulty slider, then this is for you. If you like sci-fi base building with stories, then this is for you. Want drama, even better. Don’t want drama, then kill or banish the colonists you don’t like.
The first thing I thought about when randomizing my pawns (name for the characters) and building their skills was... this game is like the Sims. Yet, it's at a level that isn't afraid to tell you how to get your hands dirty in the name of science and survival. The consequences of ill-thought decisions are significant and impactful to the continued success or spiraling failure of your colony. Your colonists are fragile human beings and won’t survive being shot in the head more than once, just like most people…
There is a game over.  This is not just a dollhouse simulator, it's a mature "build your base, recruit your pawns, heed to their moods, and survive against the natural forces of mayhem and random events that could pretty much spell a fast demise depending on difficulty. All with the appeal of storytelling, something that’s kept me entertained on Reddit and Youtube for hours.
As first impressions go, Rimworld doesn't just remind me of great aspects from other titles like Fallout Shelter and Half-Life, it inspires a megaton of mods to get very immersive as a roleplay experience. Play as tribals, play as the crash survivors, become pirates, become cannibals! The stories you can tell from some of these experiences are just hilarious at times, and the lessons are important--like why not to give a squirrel alcohol, accidentally kill it in an operation to study the effects of go-juice, and then feed it to guard bears, who get a little sick and can’t help their master as he gets stampeded by a herd of muffalo.
I am a masochist when it comes to steep learning curves, so I only play on the highest tier of difficulty with one save-file. Nonetheless, I really enjoyed the brutality of losing a half dozen games before I started to understand how to react to events and make the sacrifices that good leaders sometimes have to.
Highly recommended!

Move or die is a party game that encourages you to rage, most of the gamemodes involve you having to deal with the other players more than the environment, but this doesnt include all, this game is quite a great idea, and is a very fun quick party game, but I believe the game should still be in early access, and this is for quite a few reasons.
In move or die, you can play matches 5-30 minutes long, with each of these matches you get to choose the game modes that YOU want to play and your oppenents do the same. You then play  your match according to the game randomly picking from your collective choices of gamemodes and you playing them in that order.
You earn xp for every match you play with people online, you are however, able to play using AI bots to fill in for other players, but if you play the entire game without another person you earn no xp at all.
Steam items are awarded with every level up of your exp bar and items you earn have different rarities. You earn characters and gamemodes by leveling up, characters are purely cosmetic and provide no in-game benefit, while gamemodes give the player the ability to choose that in thier list of gamemodes to play for any given match! Players can still play gamemodes they dont have, but they have to rely on another player having it and putting it up for individual matches.
There is many different gamemodes (I believe a little over 15 or so)  that challenge the player with moving, each gamemode has a different objective and it is up to you to master them and beat everyone who stands in your way. The devs have said they will continue to release new gamemodes and characters as future updates continue, but really as this game is not in early access, there really should be alot more features by now.
Right now the state of the game is okay, connection can get really bad, and it gives the host a slight advantage every match, which is a big deal, but the devs are working on the feature, and hopefully they will put all effort towards it and stop giving us wierd updates like this "mutator update" that gives more of an RNG taste to the game and veers from the skill aspect of the game a bit.
