Definitely worth the buy if you don't rage at a bit of farming here and there, assuming you like 3D fighting games. This game pulls off the DBZ fighting style really well the way you can do your own flying/teleporting combinations within combat. The story is done well. Each mission has base objectives, such as kill this guy, and don't let you or your partner die. In the side quests/parallel quests, which are most of the game really, there are hidden bonus objectives, conditions for getting an ultimate completion. If you meet all the ultimate conditions, often just beating in a fast time, you get extra drops, and in most cases, there's an extra part to the mission. Sometimes another enemy steps in, or one you just beat comes back stronger. The style of the matchmaking reminds of Phantasy Star Online, where you have a hubworld and missions can be done with 1-3 people. If you go alone, you often are allowed to bring 2 AI with you. As far as the create a character system goes, I think they did it really nicely. You can build your stats as you'd like, and get whichever moves you want too. One thing I'm not fond of is that different clothing has different stat benefits, so often you get something you don't want to wear with great benefits, or what you want to wear wouldn't help you at all. The benefits aren't massive so you can ignore them if you want, it's just a bit annoying. If you think this game is gonna be a level grinder for your created character, that's not really true. Yeah, it takes some time to hit max level, but most of the farming you do is to get some skill you see in the rewards list that sounds cool. One thing I hope is added is a party system. As of right now, you have to set up every mission and invite your friends to join every time. Takes away from the immersion. I wasn't completely sure for the first hour or so because I was so used to Tenkaichi 3, but this game was 100% worth the money. The DLC is good too. Each will give you a few bonus missions to do and characters to play as. Said missions have exclusive rewards too. DLC is $10 per pack too, not the common $15, and it's even less with the season pass. 9/10

This is a fun game, especially if you like Lego's but...
1. Lego games are clearly made with Co-op in mind and this is no exception, so that means you need two controllers or a keyboard and a controller + a friend if you want the full experience, though you can still play alone alright.
2. It is one of the buggier games out there. The bugs are not many but when they do show up they are somewhat game-breaking. For example, the Sauron fight at the very beginning is sometimes bugged to the point that you have to restart the game and you can't skip the long intro to that fight. The Xbox controller suddenly began to cut out every minute or so, killing your character unless you disconnect and reconnect it in time.
3. The game is poorly ported from the consoles. You can quickly tell that you were not supposed to play this with the keyboard and there is no guarantee that it will support a non-xbox controller. Unless you already play games with a controller, you have to ask yourself if you are going to buy one just for this game?
4. This is not a big problem, but you will quickly notice that the actors sound like someone with a cheap mic just recorded Lord of The Rings when it was on TV and put those recordings in the game.
Some of the pro's are:
- Co-op is well integrated into the gameplay for multiple players to feel useful.
- Graphics and sound are...well they are Lego graphics and sound; they are fun if you are into that sort of thing
- There are a lot of secrets, little puzzles and stuff to do. Pleasant level design overall.
- Girls seem to like this game so you may get your partner to co-op
If you enjoy DBZ this game is worth it.

There is a reason Eve Online is aka Spreadsheets in Space, these are required to keep track of information whether you are a miner/industrialist or wormhole explorer or even pve'r.  The thing I love about this game is the amount of detail involved in almost everything, and keeping track of everything and preventing information overload can be challenging.  This game can only be recommended to the experienced MMORPG players in the crowed, and at that not to ones that have played strictly care bear types of games.  By background was from Everquest pre care bear days, back in the late 90's and early 2000's when dying meant you could lose all of you stuff.  That is an important distinction since in Eve the exact same can happen but with even worse odds of not recovering your gear.
In Eve your ships can get very expensive very fast, faster than the isk curve can keep up with.  Most will just buy a couple plex which they exchange on the market for the in game currency isk which is used in all purchases on the in game market.  This will allow them to fund one or two characters for the first little while to get the needed gear, unless you like grinding the old fashioned way for isk.  Most new players though will have issues with this since they want to get into the action right away, that just usually does not happen, unless you have connections already in the game world.
The learning curve is another element of the game that puts most people off, it is with out a doubt the worst in any game ever, yeah including old EQ.  You will be spending long hours reading forums and wikis trying to glean out every last bit of information that you can, especially after losing a few ships and wondering what is wrong with your fits.
And keep in mind after the 21 day free trial your now paying for the privelage of being all the older players favorite new ganks, because that will happen unless you are lucky enough to fall into a good player run corp.  If you are an experienced player and love having to live a game in order to be in the top and receive the just rewards then this game is for you.  You understand that all of this can happen, but with lots of patience and at least 6 months to a years worth of skill training on your character.  Enjoy!

A few points in regards to the mechanics of EVE:
1) The skillpoint system. While it is true that new players may never accumulate the same
number of skillpoints that older players have, everyone can gain the skillpoints necessary to fill a particular role exactly as well as those old players can. Age allows you to branch out more expertly, but a level 5 certified Interceptor pilot will get the same results with their ship whether their character has 5 million skillpoints or 150 million. And for people with limited play time, there is no fear of being left behind by those who would otherwise "grind" their way to the top in a traditional MMO. The system has it's good and bad points, so it's really better to think of it simply as being
2) The players. EVE encourages competition at every level, in every aspect of the game. This naturally makes people competitive outside the game as well, on forums, blogs, and news sites. This is not meant as an excuse, merely an explanation, as to why EVE players seem more monolithically hostile. Whatever you do in the game, there are almost certain to be other players trying to beat you at it, which makes finding the right people to play with far more important than it is in other MMO's.
3) The combat. I can only echo
and say that if you find the PvP combat boring, you've never actually experienced it. To this day no other game has given me the same sort of adrenaline rush you get when your ship is on the line in EVE and only your skill at piloting can win the day.
I recommend this game for a particular kind of gamer. EVE has a rich history, a strange fabric, and a thick shell, and it's rewards are consummate with the amount of effort you put into walking your own path through it's universe. For those who are dedicated (or disturbed) enough to seek it out, there is no other experience like it.

You find yourself coming upon a randomly generated island, with music  that matches the environment and changes with your actions. Proteus is a pixelated, first-person adventure game where you explore the island of Proteus and interact with its inhabitants. The artwork, sounds, and music are very good for the most part, and the first half of the game makes you curious and intrigued as to what different sights there are to see on the island and how to interact with different things that you find (as the game offers no instructions or tutorial, but instead lets you find out how to play and explore Proteus on your own.)
The second half of the game, however, is very dull and boring, and these negative aspects worsen until the game finishes. Also, after 1 or 2 playthroughs, you've pretty much seen everything, as Protues is a very short title that should take less than an hour to complete, and there's no incentive to play again. In fact, the painfully dull second half of the game may DETER players from exploring Proteus again.
In short, the first half of Proteus is quite well done, but considering the boring second half and lack of replay value, the positive qualities of this game are not enough to recommend a purchase.

If you like science fiction survival- type games with depth and a difficulty slider, then this is for you. If you like sci-fi base building with stories, then this is for you. Want drama, even better. Don’t want drama, then kill or banish the colonists you don’t like.
The first thing I thought about when randomizing my pawns (name for the characters) and building their skills was... this game is like the Sims. Yet, it's at a level that isn't afraid to tell you how to get your hands dirty in the name of science and survival. The consequences of ill-thought decisions are significant and impactful to the continued success or spiraling failure of your colony. Your colonists are fragile human beings and won’t survive being shot in the head more than once, just like most people…
There is a game over.  This is not just a dollhouse simulator, it's a mature "build your base, recruit your pawns, heed to their moods, and survive against the natural forces of mayhem and random events that could pretty much spell a fast demise depending on difficulty. All with the appeal of storytelling, something that’s kept me entertained on Reddit and Youtube for hours.
As first impressions go, Rimworld doesn't just remind me of great aspects from other titles like Fallout Shelter and Half-Life, it inspires a megaton of mods to get very immersive as a roleplay experience. Play as tribals, play as the crash survivors, become pirates, become cannibals! The stories you can tell from some of these experiences are just hilarious at times, and the lessons are important--like why not to give a squirrel alcohol, accidentally kill it in an operation to study the effects of go-juice, and then feed it to guard bears, who get a little sick and can’t help their master as he gets stampeded by a herd of muffalo.

Atom Zombie Smasher is a my favorite Blendo Games title. It's a brilliant casual realtime strategy game that's tense, strategic, flexible, and most of all, a lot of fun. I've heard a few people describe it as "tower defense", but that's really pigeon-holing it and doing a disservice to a new player's expectations. It's true that a large portion of the strategy is in controlling the flow of the enemy, but it's not nearly as deterministic and simple as that implies. Also there are no towers. The feel of the game is much more about thinking on your feet, and dealing with disasters as they're unfolding in real (or slowed down) time.
You can play any way you want by modifying the campaign settings, letting you restart levels at no cost for that perfectionist victory, or turning on permadeath and a variety of difficulty mods for more intense and less forgiving sessions.
The entire game takes place in the same universe as Brendon Chung's other tiles, including Gravity Bone, 30 Flights of Loving, and Flotilla. Chung's unique humor and sensibilities come through in the form of a large number of vignettes and background articles describing the characters in and around events of the game, and the whole experience is topped off with an amazing instrumental surf rock soundtrack by The Volcanics.

This is one of my first reviews for a game on steam, so I will try my best to cover the pros and cons of Risen 3. I will bring the conclusion at first, so that people searching for an indicator may find my judgment without reading the whole text.
IMPORTANT: This games has problems with some CPUs or system configurations! - It won't work in some cases!! - Therefore, consult the PB forum for more information!
Conclusion: This game is not worth 50 €/$. Let me be me ore specific: For fans of Risen it may be a must have, but for all others that are looking for a good/excellent rpg game which provides you with tons of quests, variety, a good combat system, polished gameplay and game engine, Risen 3 should not be your choice. The graphics engine is really old, textures are not provided in a high resolution, and even the world design (even if it is really good) cannot hide the shortcomings of the really old engine. The designers tried their best but the engine does not provide enough features to create a fully living world and this is experienced in the very first moments you enter the jungle in Risen 3. This fact is reflected if you take a closer look at the scene. The models are, how shall I say, really really bad; no (face) gestures at all, animations are choppy.  Another very important aspect of an RPG is the combat system. This is the biggest shortcoming of Risen 3. First, it is completely unbalanced. In the early stages of the game each creatures might be your death, later on you feel like god and nothing can really kill (except you head for a coffee and it takes you 5 minutes until you come back ...). Second, the factions are more or less a nice to have but after you have learned the most "skills" the spells earned by the factions are just for fun and do not seriously influence the combat.
Detailed Review:
Impressions/Opinion:
I have to admit, I am a very big fan of Gothic 1 & 2. One reason that I bought the game were the reviews that are provided by computer magazines. In fact it was the "open world" which disappointed me already in the beginning of the game. I felt somehow cheated because the game has not the freedom as a Gothic 1 or 2. It still fells like Risen 2. NO, there is no "open world" or freedom in the game, except the selection of the so-called factions. The game follows a strict chapter system and islands are quite linear. The world does not feel like its living. If you have cleared/killed all creatures on an island, you are done, there is nothing left to kill and there will nothing respawn (that’s it). Sure, there are a lot of side quests but there is no real difference between the main story and the side quests. I have played many RPGs but I seldom come across such a bad story telling. The "quests" are very generic like, "kill x", "bring me xyz". It feels like playing an really old RPG in 2014. If you have seen the 5 (including the first one where you start and are brought back to "life") main islands, which are not that big as it looks like in the beginning, there won't come any more (SPOILER: a sixth island at the end for the very last fight/quests). The combat system is useless at its best. In the early game it feels like every creature may be the last creature you will face and after the first 4 hours you get so strong that fights become just a necessity and does not feel like an epic fight. I won't talk about boss fights because they are not really any better but writing about them may spoiler one or two things. But, bosses are just like events, nice to watch. A real challenge is the gameplay and that you do not fall off some shores or edges if you are hunting for hidden places...
Technical discussion:
There is not much positive to say. As already mentioned in the conclusion the engine is old and the models are far from state-of-the-art, such as in Witcher 2 or BioShock Infinite. The models are definitely missing vertices, such as the terrain and everything in this game. The textures have a really low resolution and sometimes they look awkward and misplaced. Furthermore, the game crashes from time to time (if it even decides to run on your system).  The animations of the models are really choppy and are not that smooth as someone may expect for a game that was released mid 2014.
Last words:
I am just curious why this game got such good review from computer magazines. This game is just a refresh of Risen 2 with some really MINOR improvements. In fact, its more like a joke for 2014. PB you could have done way better and you know it!
Fans will buy it anyway, but all the others should think twice!

5/5
Gameplay:
+ Oriented on Gothic 1&2 and Risen 1
+ Same humor as ever
+ Very much atmosphere, in terms of quests and the game/level/island design.
+ I can not! confirm, that the quests are generic or anything like that. Also every character has it's own personality and position in this game, there are only very few unnamed characters with no kind of background in this world. But this does not only to npcs, but to all items and locations aswell, truly handcrafted!
+ I love the way magic got implemented in this game! No exhausting mana-potion collection or brewing which I always disliked, but just a cooldown-based system. Some critisize that, I love it and think a lot of games should go that direction!
+ I do not find the story boring and do not agree with (most) reviewers.
+ I love flying or gliding around like a parrot.
- Sometimes there's not enough feedback whether a quest is completed, failed or still pending in status, e.g. before being promoted to a guardian you have to talk to your pirate admiral. He then tells you to kill the undead dogs, swirling around the city. Although this is not hard to accomplish, one may still miss out on some dogs and ask him-/herself, why one can't get promoted. Another example would be the "di fuego" related quests.
- Sometimes npcs can't follow you and get stuck, however if you wait long enough they will eventually be back at your position (Teleporting and/or going back to your ship or another island helps in this case).
Graphics:
+ I don't know where to start. All people critizing the graphic of risen 3 can't have played it.
+ I have rarely seen such beautiful sunsets and sunrises as in this game. Just as an example if one stands a bit away from the council hall or tower in antigua and in front of it, and if it's dawn and you look up in the sky, you see the air glimming inside the council hall, with a warm fire enlightening the whole building and if you look up, you have this dark, star filled sky, which at the very edge slowly fades into a warm pink/purpleish kind of color. There were countless moments like that and I can truly say that I have met no game, where the graphic is that atmospheric, some of the steam-screenshots catch very well how beautiful the game looks!
- I mean, yes, sometimes!!! there are very low resolution textures, but most of the time they don't catch the eye.
Sound:
0 Well, there has been written a lot about this part of the game so I will skip the extensive part and sum up that although I also find that the sound is very atmospheric, there are some downsides.
+ The german synchronization however is very well!
To sum it up: If you liked the Gothic series and Risen 1, buy it. The basis for this game may be a pirate setting and of course it plays in the Risen universe, but it catches the Gothic flair from old times quite well and has some (good) adjustments to it.
Also I have not played Risen 2 so I can't say which textures got reused etc.
One last comment I want to make is, that most of the negative reviews seem to be from people that have played the game only a few hours and could not immerse themselfs in it, whether it is because their personal taste of a game is different or because they were not patient enough. I also think that this is reflected pretty well in the metacritics score which has a lot of negative reviews, but just as much positive reviews and nothing in between, so this game really splits based on your personal taste.

Another great Lego game - a very fun way to relive these epic movies. Worth a playthrough.
I have some major qualms about some of the game mechanics though.
The game encourages you to use Free Play to get all the minikits chests, and its a fun way to play the levels again once you have all the necessary types of characters. The problem, however, is in levels like Black Rider and The Secret Stairs - where at the very last part of the level, after at least 15 minutes of using 50 characters with all their little different tools to get to the last sequence you have one VERY small window to get the last minikit. If you miss it - guess what? You have to re-do the WHOLE level for another shot at the last mini-kit. Even with the Mini-kit Finder Extra, those minikits can be difficult to get.
Also, some white bricks require that you hop from very small ledges to other very small ledges. The game is supposed to 'lock on' to the ledges but very often it does not and you have to re-do the whole process. The problem is that you cannot free-jump to use skill and timing to get to the ledges - the game locks you into its supposed-to-be-precise jumping mechanic and causes you to fail. There are two white bricks in the Mordor region that are almost impossible to get unless you spend 30 minutes re-doing it waiting for your jump to randomly lock onto the ledge like it's supposed to.
Also, switching between the characters you prefer is very tedious. You should be able to customize the 'wheel' of characters that you can switch between. I hate having to scroll between the plethora of unlockable characters over and over. Choosing between tools should be better too - again a customizable 'favorites' type function would be better.
With that said - I did really enjoy playing this game and I'd recommend it - but the some of the broken mechanics kept me from achieving 100% game completion which kind of annoys me.

Level 10 and around power level 3000+ Everything changes. 90% of the time you will be so outclassed that you dont stand a chance so you die the instant you encounter an opponent then just wait around hoping your team wins so you can get the reward. I wholeheartedly recommend RPG Maker MV as a starter software for anyone who is interested in making a game.
I see a lot of people recommend Unity or Unreal Engine as "easy" tools for beginners, but both of those require a decent coding knowledge of some sort (well, Unreal Engine 4 not so much). On top of that, you will need to make your own assets for the game to be high-quality, unless you want to purchase an asset pack off someone else.
RPG Maker requires zero coding experience, only patience and understanding. The eventing system, while it takes a bit of time to fully figure out (e.g. self switches and "delete event" commands reset after you change map), is very simple to use, yet allows for (functionally) limitless possibilities.
Improvements over VX Ace, the previous iteration of the software, include:
-Changing the nightmare-inducing front portrait character generator to a side portrait one, allowing you to create much more aesthetically pleasing character portraits.
-Native sideview battle mode, no longer requiring custom scripting.
-Significantly improved OST, with much improved themes for everything.
-Javascript instead of Ruby (kind of a big deal, as plugins are now able to do a lot more).
-Export to pretty much anything (Browser, Android, iOS, Windows, etc.) whereas VX Ace only supported Windows (I think).
-Modern tilesets/assets provided with the base game - no more reliance on custom content for a modern-themed RPG.
-Various QoL improvements (showing you where the dialog window cuts off when editing, so you don't accidentally have your text not showing properly in-game because you forgot to hit enter).
-Native touch/mouse control support.
If you can't afford it at base price, as it is pretty expensive, you can wait for a sale.
This is a brilliant tool for anyone interested in game design, beginner or otherwise. I might go as far as to say it is the tool to start with for those who are interested in game development but have little to zero coding knowledge.
Definitely recommended.

Well. Where I must begin?
Let's start from... mods. A lot of people actually loves dat mods, aren't they?
Without them, any game is a bit less "complete" and a bit more "unfinished".
In Rimworld there is at least one mod for everything: wanna eat trees? We got you covered. Want to squash some zombies? Kiddo, please, we have mods for that. Want to master The Force's powers, shackin' ya lightsaber around yodeling like your favourite pervert krapfen & bauertoast fanatic next door? Splendid idea! Three Star Wars oriented mod are ready to be grabbed from Steam's Workshop.
But 'member, kids: as stated on mods-dedicated part of Ludeon Studios' EULA, "You may not advertise for donations within your Mods themselves". So stop dreaming about offshore yachts!
Sum all it up: there are legions of mods that can add many amazing way you can play this game. If the base game - more on this topic later - don't please Your Highness at 100% fell free to mod-theft the dedicated Workshop pages.
---
The premise is done. Let's talk about Rimworld "as-is". The core game is beatifully complex, like a mesmerizing sheep's curly wool. When you start a new game, you have to choose some details.
1) You can start with one or more "colonists" which have randomized stats (but with mods you can choose every detail of them, from skin colour to badass attributes) and are grumpy tribal people that inhabited the Rim for 4873782348683...1 years or sofisticated but despaired space-faring folks.
Without mods, your colonists will be Humans; but... with another plethora of mods... we have also more fabulous races like Dwarves, Aliens, Predators, Orcs, semi-animals beings, Smurfs, and so on.
2) You can start with a "seed" (useful for generate the same map over and over again - I'm watching you, nostalgic oldie!) that will shape the planet where your colonists will spawn.
3) You decide the explorable percentage (5% for DEV MODE, 100% for roaming gipsies like me) of the world, the climate parameters and the spawning point. Do you like Tundras? Or snowy and mortal icy landscapes? Maybe some hot desert resort? Tropical jungle anyone? I must stop myself, sorry.
4) You decide the storyteller - there are three of them available. But only if you hate mods; instead there are some more... like a... uhm... H. P. Lovecraft in his Rimworld counterpart. Storytellers are the AI entities that will generate random events to keep you entertained. Infamous ones will send you nasty hostile raids every two days or so whilst angelic ones will make you and your colonist a bit more relaxed.
5) You start to play and basically must survive one day after another hunting, farming, researching, crafting, harvesting organs from prisoners, make silver money trading with caravans and outpost, imprisoning poor 86 years grannies and selling them @ pirate slavers and so on. You know what? With a mod you can also wander the world without relocate your permanent colony base.
You can have medicine-oriented colonists that can perform surgical operations on your ill people or against a visiting guest that decide to collapse - you must made him a prisoner prior to operate, but it's a microscopic detail.
You can hunt for exploding animals (like the tiny "boomrat" and the biggest bro "boomalope").
You can raid other Rimworl AI inhabitants' colonies.
There are so many things that you can do in this game and I'm afraid that I'm too lazy to write about all of them.
Some CONS just to finish my review:
* No multiplayer. Not yet, at least. Maybe one day. But let me be honest: I don't miss it. And maybe there is some nice mod that.............
* AI is dumb (there are mods that tries to make it better, of course!). For instance when a colonist is moving in direction of a Steel vein, he can suddenly "decide" to turn back and drink a cold beer instead. Cold beers wins against mining labour, it's a matter of fact. *HIC*!
* Colonists doesn't mate. Nope. They can be lovers, they can do "fiki-fiki" but... no little babies that will do Big Surprise Puke nor poop-like-there-is-no-tomorrow around. You can only pray that soon or less the reluctant AI Storyteller of the moment decides to spawn an Event that hopefully will add a new colonist to your pool. And that colonist may have some kind of relationship with one or more already existing colonists. Sometime you can have "child" (with a minimum age of 15 or 16 years, but better than nothing... it's something) or "mother" or "father" or "brother" or... well, you can have different degrees of parental choices to randomize your newly-added colonist.

Hitman or Houdini: either take the guy out, or create an intricate jouney of events to confuse him and espionage your way to the objective. Tom Francis's brainchild 2D stealth puzzler Gunpoint takes on a vast, open ended approach to making the player formulate ways to complete an objective, however that may be.
Grainy pixel art complements the noir-esque anonymity that comes with espionage - a shady setting but a brightly lit housing that seems impossible to penetrate unless you have a plan. Gunpoint's main character gives the player the means to think of a hundred and one different ways to sly yourself to the end of a level, be it superjumping, window smashing, door slammin', or wire trippin'. I couldn't help but reminded of the frantic formulation of a plan in my brain when playing games such as Monaco or Hotline Miami when confronted with a devious challenge - you have a destination, and you have the means to get to it, but in what order suits your style? Truly, this kind of game can be tackled in any way a player wants - smash a window on the other side of the building and quickly flip a switch to confuse him or maybe jump and hang on to the ceiling and watch his every move for an oppertunity.
Story wise it is a clever peice of work. Witty, RPG-like dialogue is exchanged before each mission through the player's phone (which is coincidentally the menu screen) gives the player an array of responses to NPC storylines that have the player both intrigued and tickled at the same time, whilst the spy-themed bass-driven jazz sountrack gives them an immersion into the noir genre.  Player-chosen dialogue responses have an effect, too: you can either go for the funny guy spy approach and annoy the NPC or interrogate with vindiction about a certain case. On the smartphone-clad menu screen, players will have the option to chooses between missions, deciding how their story will play out.
All in all, it's a very sharey "I did this at this point" kind of game, which takes the user through a brilliant plot orchastated by ingenious mission layouts. Players are allowed to experience this game at their own pace, awarding merits for the amount of violence, stealth, anonymity or time used at the end of the mission (just as a guage, though- completion of further additional objectives allow you to earn extra money to spend on upgrades to your character). Cleverly executed, you'll find yourself conjuring clever schemes to outwit the level in this game. Worth every penny.

If you like science fiction survival- type games with depth and a difficulty slider, then this is for you. If you like sci-fi base building with stories, then this is for you. Want drama, even better. Don’t want drama, then kill or banish the colonists you don’t like.
The first thing I thought about when randomizing my pawns (name for the characters) and building their skills was... this game is like the Sims. Yet, it's at a level that isn't afraid to tell you how to get your hands dirty in the name of science and survival. The consequences of ill-thought decisions are significant and impactful to the continued success or spiraling failure of your colony. Your colonists are fragile human beings and won’t survive being shot in the head more than once, just like most people…
There is a game over.  This is not just a dollhouse simulator, it's a mature "build your base, recruit your pawns, heed to their moods, and survive against the natural forces of mayhem and random events that could pretty much spell a fast demise depending on difficulty. All with the appeal of storytelling, something that’s kept me entertained on Reddit and Youtube for hours.
As first impressions go, Rimworld doesn't just remind me of great aspects from other titles like Fallout Shelter and Half-Life, it inspires a megaton of mods to get very immersive as a roleplay experience. Play as tribals, play as the crash survivors, become pirates, become cannibals! The stories you can tell from some of these experiences are just hilarious at times, and the lessons are important--like why not to give a squirrel alcohol, accidentally kill it in an operation to study the effects of go-juice, and then feed it to guard bears, who get a little sick and can’t help their master as he gets stampeded by a herd of muffalo.
I am a masochist when it comes to steep learning curves, so I only play on the highest tier of difficulty with one save-file. Nonetheless, I really enjoyed the brutality of losing a half dozen games before I started to understand how to react to events and make the sacrifices that good leaders sometimes have to.
Highly recommended!

Firstly, although my game time says 4 hours, my save file says 6. 6 hours of gameplay might not be enough to properly review this game, it seems to be improving, but is all the time I am willing spend here for now. I bought this game based on the various reviews here swearing that the game will get better, but honestly, who wants to go through 5 or 6 hours of gameplay before having fun?
The combat is clunky. The attacks are not responsive, the characters go through pirouettes, leaps and lunges to deliver a single blow. At the beginning of the game the delay between the strikes in your 3-hit combo are long enough to allow the enemy to interrupt you every single time. You will be reduced to using the same hit and roll tactic for next 3 hours, whittling away at the enemy's health while your companion does most of the heavy lifting... Unless the companion AI suddenly decides to stop attacking or has gotten stuck somewhere, in that case whittle away.
On the other hand, as you progress you acquire new types of weapons and skills that really add up to the combat. It can still be frustrating, but after 5 hours or so (your mileage might vary depending on the places you visit first and how you develop your character) you start to see where the combat is trying to go. I do not if it eventually gets there, I will update this review when I revisit the game.
This might be surprising, but the combat isn't what finally pushed me away from the game. It is the conversation that did it for me, and that is quite sad because they went through the effort of voicing pretty much everything. The problem is that the conversations meander so much, there are so many exchanges in one conversation branch that hold no value, they don't develop the characters, they don't introduce lore, nor do they mimic normal conversation. It is really, baffling how much extra effort went where it needed to.
I understand that a complaint for the previous game was the lack of voiced acting or how little voice acting there was, I am not too sure about this, but regardless, there is just too much useless and pointless dialogue in this game, but I might have been able to take if it wasn't for the horrible voice acting.  That's right, there is awkward writing being voiced very badly. This is the first time that this has affected my gameplay so much that I have stopped playing.
All that said, the game has the potential to improve plenty, perhaps by the 15th hour everything else would be sufficiently enjoyable that you can look past the scrip and voice acting, but if that is the case, it would be better to wait for this game to go on sale, currently it isn't worth the asking price.

This game has had a lot of mixed reviews but personally I really enjoy it, Ill give my pros and cons on what i think about it and give a summary on what i think
*Cons
- Not for your casual gamer, you need to grind to get better gear, gear is everything in this game
- Crossout is pay to win format, you will battle people that have paid for OP builds. You will go through a period where you get owned heavily

*pros

An impressive creation that everyone should at least experience. There's a lot of misconceptions surrounding the experience of new players, the learning curve, character progression and such, so I suggest you at least give EVE a fair go before choosing to avoid it. Like all games, it has its issues, but the common complaints, while I see where they are coming from, are frequently over exaggerated and naive. EVE online works much differently than other popular MMOs, so keep that in mind if you see/hear of a mechanic that sounds a bit iffy (such as the time based skill progression).
Downsides to EVE is basically the balance between high, low and nullsec. In highsec, outside of playing the market, there's essentially no way of making money outside of doing L4s, the have other things, but they don't pay anything worth your time. Looting/salvaging in EVE is such a slow and tedious process without a second account or friend it's not worth doing over rushing (blitzing) the mission. Suicide gankers basically kill anyone or anything, anywhere in highsec, I've never been ganked personally and I actually scored a kill on a ganker once, but the concept of being killed through cheesing concorde mechanics, while being incredibly safe from retalitory action by the system you are cheesing, is a bit weird. It's also dangerous to the health of the game, noobs often get caught into being a miner (instead of security) and will get suicide ganked, then they leave the game and post a bad review. Also they basically harass miners all day who are already making next to zero isk per hour. The devs should just remove 90% of high sec if their interest is to make everywhere dangerous or get people into low sec. Problem of low sec is most of the content isn't worth the risk for the reward you are going to get, there's good opportunities for low risk, low reward small group/solo PVP in low sec however. Nullsec is basically controlled by a small number of coalitions, so you aren't going to get anywhere there unless you want to join a blob. You also can't get ships big enough to do PVE content in low or nullsec, so basically most PVE'rs will be buying over 1 bill isk ships to do L4s all day. There's basically gate camps everywhere, with that in mind and suicide ganking in high sec, you get the impression there's nothing to do in the game, why else would you waste your time with that if you had better things to do?
The GINI coefficient of EVE is also absolutely borked, PLEX's are totally overpriced and unfeasible for most people to buy, instead your smartest option is to buy a plex with real money and sell it. This mostly comes from the fact that the large corps control so much money they can buy thousands of ships, an near infinite amount of PLEX and RMT at the same time. I don't really know why corps have been able to become that powerful when RMT is forbidden, is easily tracked by CCP, but suspicously, it is rampant in EVE. The corps control so much of the most (practically only) lucrative areas in the game, their wealth is absurd, and this affects everyone not involved in them. I highly suspect one or two things is at play to explain the imperialism, RMT, and prices in EVE. CCP secretly works with corps to RMT, this is known to have happened at least twice, both times of the same corp/player using a PLEX referral sham that was allowed until there was public outcry, which was incredibly dodgy. Alternatively to this, large corps RMT blatently and CCP turns a blind eye to protect the public image and to avoid reducing the playabase. Either way there's something foul at play, who makes EVE a job by running an ingame company similar to real life, without getting paid?

With Crossout Gaijin repeats allmost all mistakes they made with War Thunder, Targem only appears to be the voiceless contractor doing a generic p2w-MMO order following gaijin handbook.
The good:
- it looks not bad, sound can be decent and there are no performance issues with the graphics even on older machines
- a PvE part included, helps to avoid the PvP frustration
- the vehicle building is easy to do and with quiet a lot of variety
- player controlled market for parts and costumization
The bad:
- Balance is non-existent, in every part of the game (including PvE, own team or teams comparision) there are huge gaps in strength of overall powerscore, builds and abilities unrelated to playerskill, some gamemodes like brawls or races even have no consideration at all for the games own powerscore rating or item specialization ... sealclubbing is everywhere, u are either bored by how easy it is or frustrated by how unfair ... fair competition is the exception
- gameplay design is an outdated, unoriginal, repetitive mashup of things we know for ages, right down to a silly white circle to wait out a far too short timer in
- the game includes massive amounts of AI and AI-controlled / autoaim weapons, often its not Player vs Player, but Cpu vs Cpu
- gameplay is dominated by a fraction of the available weapons and parts, outdated and simplistic mission and map design plus ridiculous short timer also favor speed and agility way too much
- a lot of afk grind bots exploiting the AI controlled parts and little to no effort to fight these accounts
- server performance is poor, during primetime a lot of lag and rubberbanding ruins battles
- outside primetime playerbase is too small, even more AI and even worst powerscore gaps come in
- the pay-/grindwall is huge and the sealclubbing pressures towards the overpriced itemshop, free-to-play is only theoretical for a majority of people as the grind is practicly neverending, and the lack of balancing clearly favors high grade items/skills ... pay-2-win for all who have a real life
- prices in item shop are ridiculous high, packs and coins have no connection to value ... clear exploitation of a few socalled whales, while common gamer are pushed away
- development is disconnected from community wishes and priorities, expansion already implemented long before base gameplay works and is free of most easy to fix failures, design choices clash with the original setup and are in no way coordinates with community wishes/ideas
player numbers already problematic around the day, further stagnation is allmost certain ... money would be wasted on this game.

A fantastic port of a game that's about as close as you can get to Mario Kart without it actually being Mario Kart. But make no mistake; this SEGA variant has its own identity running through it. You'll find tracks and tunes inspired by the classic Sonic, Panzer Dragoon and Afterburner games, as well as the more recent Skies of Arcadia and Jet Set Radio.
There is - admittedly - a shortage of characters to choose from, with Sonic's roster of racing heros and villains being grossly overrepresented compared to those from other SEGA games. Nevertheless, the overall package is a colourful dose of nostalgia, with easy-to-learn and tricky-to-master 'boost' racing mechanisms and a slew of challenge modes that have kept me coming back to achieve those high 'S' ranks.
Some of the track designs are static, but there are also evolving tracks, where the racing landscape disappears to reveal waterways, new roads or airspaces - and that's where the transforming vehicles really shine.
This is pure gaming happiness I'd recommend to anyone who doesn't take racing too seriously and wants to escape life for a while.
I have ONE major caveat: the online multiplayer of this game is a dead zone, so don't expect to race against the world.
HOWEVER, it does have split-screen mode for up to four players. If you've got friends/kids/spare controllers and a decent monitor/TV size, it's a no-brainer and I'm so impressed that the devs thought to include it.
What can I say, it's a great console port. Occasionally miracles do happen.

For a fan of the Naruto series this game is excellent, it tells the story brilliantly with fully voice acted (Japanese and English) cutscenes throughout which is very impressive considering the amount of dialogue and cutscenes in the game. It is mostly faithful to the anime and manga (with the exception of the final fight which I assume was changed to give the game a climactic ending opposed to just continuing as the anime does).
However, there is a huge amount of assumed knowledge about the series. The story of this game cannot be fully appreciated unless you have seen a good amount of Shippuden and in places it references things that happened in the original series without bothering to give you a reminder or fill in those who havnt seen it. The story often takes presidence over gameplay with quicktime events mid-fight with actions representing the fights in the anime.
The combat is what you would expect from an anime spectacle fighter, with alot of charging up attacks, cinematic grapples and finishers. If you enjoy this type of fighting game, then this is one of the best. However, the powers of individual characters seem to be faithful to the series as opposed to being fairly balanced for online multiplayer. For example Madara with annihalate characters like Sakura with ease (however its not nearly as bad as older Dragonball Z games where some characters could 1-shot others).
Overall, for a fan of the Naruto series this game is excellent. However, if you're the type of person to skip cutscenes, dont bother as this game isn't affraid of throwing 40 minute cutscenes your way (not an exageration, the Minato/Kushina flashback midway through the game is around 40 minutes long). The story took me 12 hours to complete including the full burst Kabuto fights, 7-8 hours of which is cutscenes. Regardless, the free-battles and multi-player have so far given me an additional 6 hours and counting.

High resolution graphics are top-notch. Music is filled with emotions. Character generator is amazing. Features are wonderful. In fact, I think the biggest strength of RPG Maker MV is that they made it very convenient for game creators:
1. Plugins system where you can turn on and off instead cutting the whole script into another project.
2. Holding enter key speeds up your whole game, which can be easily disabled by a plugin.
3. Game can be edited while you are in-game, and changes made to maps are live (just open and close menu to update). Event changes will require you to re-enter the map to update. Database and plugin changes require you to close and reload the game.
4. Switches and variables can be controlled in-game. Just press F9. Very helpful for testing events in-game.
5. A lot of support and updates from community.
Criticisms:
Default graphics may be too "squarish" for those who want to map circular stuff. You can find resources for this though.
Auto-shadowing of tiles can be a disaster. Shadowing tool is hard to use. You can't click and drag a rectangle of shadow; you must draw it carefully like a pencil.
Conclusion:
Worth buying. It makes your life a lot easier, and produces high quality games.

This game was on my wishlist for months, just waiting for a sale so I could try it out. But, as months went by, it never once dipped in price, and during a night of unfathomable boredom, I decided to take the plunge, forked over the $29.99, and started to play one of the most awesome games ever. Naturally I set a timer to 2 hours in case I wanted a refund, but that wasn't the case, as I was hooked in before the first hour ended, and knew after looking over the modding community, that this game is a keeper. That first time I played it, I didn't stop until the sun rose and I realized it was almost 6 in the morning, after playing for 8 hours straight.
If you are like me and are waiting for a sale -- it seems like that won't happen anytime soon, or at least, it never seems to happen, and this review is to encourage you to take the plunge and have a good time. It is absolutely worth the $29.99, you don't need to wait for a sale, it's worth it, and, while it may not click with you immediately, it is met with "overwhelmingly positive" reviews for a reason, and it is a ton of fun. Very interesting concept too, and executed in a way that is easy to learn, difficult to master, and incredibly addicting regardless of the outcome of your pawns.
Most of my colonies die at one point or another. Most of yours will too. It is not a bad thing, it is not a sad thing, and it shouldn't make you mad, and I don't think it will unless you are like insane about "losing". It's just how the story unfolds, though, and it's part of the game and part of the fun. Another reviewer put it perfectly, saying "Colonies are here for a good time, not a long time". However, sometimes they do last, and it's cool progressing everything, getting more people to join, and experimenting with what to do next as you make it further and further in the new world you are trying to make. Currently my longest lasting colony started out as a tribe of 5 people, but has grown and thrived and may defeat the odds against them in surviving in the world as a colony to be reckoned with. Maybe someday they'll even make it off the planet, if I choose to make it so.
Point is, this game is worth its price tag. Give it a go, you may find yourself immersed in one of the coolest games with a wonderful modding community aiming to make each run a different, engaging, and exciting experience.

Update 11/13/17: Below, I tell you a tale of a distant Rimworld.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
They started as a group of three, crashlanding in a small patch of temperate forest surrounded by the green hell commonly referred to as "tropical rainforests". Akemi was a builder, and a fine one at that, first prioritized building shelter for his fellow survivors. Akemi was accompanied by Kirschi, a former child star that grew into a seasoned actor, charming as hell and good looking to boot, as well as Mal, a roboticist that some considered "too smart".
The first few days were rough. Akemi worked hard to maintain their shelter and even started to build more, in order to stockpile their goods safely, and even considered expanding their little domicile. He was an optimist after all, and crashlanding could just mean a new beginning. He even wanted to give their home a name, declaring it "Greenhell's Oasis". Meanwhile, Mal studied further technologies and applied her intellect to research ways to improve life on this new Rimworld. Kirschi took care of keeping their area clean, but grew restless, as he started to experience withdrawals from his psychite addiction.
For Kirschi, each day without a hit of yayo was a challenge, but he wouldn't break just yet. It was then that the budding colony got its first visitors, some people from a nearby colony that were interested in seeing what exactly fell out of the sky. It was then that Kirschi showed what he could do. What he was born to do - charm and entertain. He talked with each of the visitors and silvertongued his way into their hearts, causing them to break allegiance with their colony and join his cause and his people.
One of them was Skye, an enforcer, and while she was swooned by Kirschi's charm, she saw that at his core, he was an addict, and that he needed help. She decided to arrest him and force him into rehab, a decision that ended up being the best thing for Kirschi, but caused a lot of berserk rages and psychotic breaks on the path to sobriety.
Their numbers grew from three, to eight, and the colony began to thrive. However, this angered their previous chief, causing tension between them and the rising faction that crashlanded only days earlier. A move that could easily turn into a grave mistake if they decide to send raiders for a siege.
However, days went by, then weeks, then months. The colony only grew and prospered, becoming wealthier and more established each day. Their numbers continued to grow, from eight, to ten, to fifteen, until one day, there was an outbreak of malaria. Six colonists were infected, Akemi among them, and had to be forced to rest in the hospital. Lorne, a recent addition to the colony, was a nurse and Skye's father, and he did his best to treat the condition. However, when it rains, it pours.
A myserious plague started to ravage the populace. Twelve colonists were swept by the plague, including Kirschi and Akemi, as well as some others that already had malaria, and only two colonists were considered healthy, Lorne the nurse among them, as well as Mal, the roboticist.
Lorne did what he could, using up most of the stockpiled medicinal herbs, only to find that his efforts were spread so thin, trying to treat everyone, that it was an impossible battle that could not be won. He wanted to break, but he persevered long enough to bury his friends and his daughter, Skye, a real survivor that was taken too soon by a plague that Lorne couldn't cure. Lorne is a broken man now, teetering on the edge of insanity, often having mental breakdowns and hiding in his room.
The colony is mostly deserted now, with Mal being the only founder to have survived this long. Still, while the colonists are beside themselves with grief, they continue on. They can find new members, surely, and hope that such a plague doesn't come back. After all, Mal now sees that they must make it off this planet, and has started to research ship building and all of its intricacies. It may be some time before this happens, but Mal must make sure her comrades' deaths are not in vain.
It's become all too clear. They must get off this Rimworld, but... Will they be able to? Or is this the place where they are all doomed to perish?

Let's get one thing straight from the beginning - Proteus isn't a game. It's an experience.
It combines two elements - sound and vision - to create a uniquely moving and personal experience as you roam a small island. You don't
anything. You explore your own personal world, one that teems with surprises. You won't forget the first time you walk through a creaking forest at night and an owl hoots at you form a nearby tree. Nor will you forget the first time you stepped atop a mountain. The first sunrise actually set the hairs on my arms on end.
It's about exploring what Proteus has to offer with your eyes and ears. Both sounds and sights are simultaneously abstract and magnificent, drawing the traveller deeper in. You could find yourself chasing a bunny for the strong notes it creates versus a melodic background, or simply sitting under a tree watching a sunset, admiring the view and ambience.
As I said, Proteus is an experience - if you don't give it the time it deserves, you won't feel it as you should, you won't be drawn in as the developers intended. If you want instant gratification, go play CoD. But if you want something a little deeper, a little more personal, something that isn't all about the numbers, give Proteus a try.

(The game took me 35-40 hours to complete, Steam failed to record some of them, so the displayed amount is missing at least 8 hours) If you know Piranha Bytes and their history, you know what you're getting yourself into: A unique and memorable adventure with quirks both major and minor. Virtually everyone would like to see another proper Gothic game, but PB is keeping in mind what the market lacks at any given time and what the publisher may be willing to shell out money for. Back in 2012, it made sense for them to try out a different setting for Risen 2. After all, it had to compete with the likes of Skyrim, and a small studio such as PB has to pick its battles. Risen 2 was a sequel developed from scratch (content-wise) – no easy task, I imagine. They probably could not afford to ditch it all again for Risen 3 and instead opted for a more iterative approach, applying a thin layer of Gothic in the meantime to please the impatient fans. Thus, it feels more like a very large content update to Risen 2 than a true sequel, and PB have not quite delivered on their promise to go back to their roots. I'm not going to talk about story and graphics, as those elements are just solid, do the job and do not stand out to me. What does stand out, is the world.
The world:
The islands can be visited in any order this time around. They have been lovingly crafted, with many small highlights and cheekily placed treasures waiting to be uncovered. Carefully placed objects tell stories without using words, such as skeletons surrounded by bottles of rum in a secluded spot or a monkey messing around among bananas, voodoo dolls and corpses. There were countless occasions of these enriching little things that never failed to make me smile or ask myself "WTF happened here?". The world is teeming with quests (300+ of them) that mostly revolve around fetching and killing stuff. Their presentation through funny and witty dialogue (which does have its cheesy moments) makes them rewarding to complete beyond the glory and loot you get. Swearing is indeed overused, which is a trademark and a welcome recurring theme in the German version, but probably superfluous in the eyes of the English audience. The world and the characters that populate it can suck you in for countless hours at a time. What bothers me is the use of recycled locations from Risen 2 (such as Antigua and Tacarigua), which, apart from the shadow realm's dark taint, retain their Carribean atmosphere.
A thin layer of Gothic, weapons & armor:
PB promised to go back to their roots and create a darker atmosphere. There were indeed (very short) moments where I felt like I was playing a Gothic game again, largely due to the new locations, factions and their armor sets. Roaming through the swamplands in a demon hunter's armor that looks like a beautiful cross between a dragon hunter's armor (G2) and an Old Camp one (G1) felt great. However, once I returned to my ship and met a parrot named Polly that told me to shave, nostalgia was quickly smothered. There are a few reincarnated minor NPCs from the old games, such as Mud (G1), an annoying, needy motormouth following you around for a bit, and Moe (G2), a violent bully demanding a toll from everyone trying to enter a tavern. Such small instances of fan service kindle hope for a more substantial return to Gothic in the future.
Aside from the faction-specific armor sets, there is still a huge emphasis on pirate's clothing. This results in an muddled mixture of epochs and settings in places. Moreover, it's a shame that some stronger versions of armor pieces are just recolorings of the previous ones (e.g. a third-rank demon hunter helmet is a shade lighter than a second-rank one). Re-using assets from within this game and the previous one and applying a different coat of paint to some may be a necessity because of the development team's small size and budget. However, it seriously hurts immersion and they need to apply more polish and care to their equipment in future games.
The types of weapons you'll find are again ripped from different eras and settings. There are Gothicesque axes and maces, there is your typical pirate gear and then there are a few questionable design choices. For example, the strongest musket in the game looks like an overdesigned modern-day (scoped...) air rifle that is made of bright, varnished wood. The fact that it says "way ahead of its time" in the description doesn't help much. By mixing medieval-looking arms, pirate sabers and fancy guns, PB created a rather incoherent set of tools.
Combat:
Serviceable, but still rather quirky. You'll find that monsters essentially teleport to your location from 10 meters away and repeatedly knock you back in a straight line. This gives a very rigid and stiff feel to the whole affair when it comes to sword fighting. Thankfully, you can dodge and pick up more moves along the way, but most of the time surviving melee combat felt more like exploitation of design flaws than standing up to a challenge to me. Many have said that it gets better later on as you get stronger and master your timing, but I really wasn't enticed to put up with sword fighting for that long. The fact that they re-introduced offensive magic abilities (painfully absent in Risen 2) adds some much needed flow and diversity. Muskets still provide an easy way to avoid finicky sword fighting and just shoot s#it in the face Indiana Jones style. I would not call them overpowered per say, as they behave and do damage as you'd expect, but still quite out of place in a Piranha Bytes RPG.
Conclusion:
Piranha Bytes took Risen 2 as a foundation, made it less linear, a little bit better and added a few excellent islands and factions. The result is a fun and engaging, though incoherent pirate game with a hint of Gothic/Risen 1 and plenty of the old PB quirks. That's a little less than I was hoping for, but about what I was expecting. Overall, I'm satisfied with Risen 3 and I can't wait for what future games might have in store.

PB came into this title promising that they'd returned to their roots and had learned from their past mistakes, but have they? Yes and no.
The bad:
-The story drags a bit in the middle. They do things to improve this and try to keep it interesting, but it's easy to do things in an order which can feel like a slog and not a fun progression of events.
-Companions are tanks. This isn't as much of a problem on the hardest difficulty, but on medium it feels like they are more powerful than you for far too long and are neigh unkillable. If you're spending glory on skills you don't have until you join a faction, like magic or voodoo, this is especially true.
-Voice acting is hit-and-miss. Sometimes your main character can sound like a badass that you'd never want to mess with, other times he has a mouth full of gravel for no reason. Also, there are too many times where you'll hear that the voice actors didn't have good direction and say lines with the wrong inflection.
-Combat can be clunky. I actually put this in both the good and the bad because they improved some aspects, but from friends I know who've played the game on a console the controls can be a pain without a mouse and keyboard. This is where you'll really feel the "companions are tanks", because you can often just roll circles around enemies while your friend rips them apart. Seeing enemies get stuck behind a fence or rock and glitch out during can also break immersion.
-Day one DLC. This is more a knock on the publisher and not the developer, but for ♥♥♥♥ sake stop making Devs do this♥♥♥♥♥♥ It only hurts the customer.
The neutral:
-Reused areas. I put this in neutral because PB has done this before to great affect, like in Gothic II. Seeing how areas change over time is fun and they are disimillar enough that I didn't feel it detracted from my experience, but it annoys enough people that it can be a negative.
-Ship combat under utilized. This was one of the most fun parts of the game, but like Assassin's creed 3 it just leaves you wanting more.
The Good:
-Magic system is a blast. Anyone who played Risen 2 can tell you that the voodoo magic left a lot to be desired with a few cool tricks but damage spells that came much too late. Now you have three different schools of magic to play with (rune, crystal, and voodoo) all with fun and unique spells. Instead of a mana pool that gives out over time you have different elements that you can wield like weapons at melee and range supplemented by timed spells with effects like fire rain or summoning. Enemies also have vulnerabilities to elements that you can discover with experimentation.
-Exploration. This has always been a strongpoint of PB games and this iteration is no different. A bevy of secret caves, islands, and treasure to find will keep you wanting to see what is around every corner for hours if you're anything like me.
-Arcane Vision. For anyone who likes collecting every ounce of junk as a metagame this upgradable ability highlights objects so you don't have to worry about missing anything and squinting at every corner. It reminds me of the wisp ability from Gothic II, but much more efficient.
-Huge number of interesting quests. Many may knock this game for having quite a few 'fetch' quests, but it's what you can do within these quests that lets them shine and wash away any tedium. Asked to hand out some crystals to your compatriates? Scam them instead and make them pay for the privelage.
Conclusion:
It's a solid 7/10 RPG, 8/10 if you like the PB style of exploration and questing. For any fan of PB's previous Gothic series I'd recommend buying now, but if you're just a general lover of open world RPGs you might want to wait for a sale. The day one DLC added a lot of content but the it will leave a sour taste in your mouth if you buy full price.

Gunpoint is short. I beat the main campaign in three hours, but I think the developers were going for quality over quantity. The content provided contains fun and unique stealth platforming gameplay that encourages different play styles with controls so fluid you'd think you've spilled your drink on the keyboard. If you want to brutally punch an enemy over 100 times just for fun, you can (and there's even an achievement for doing so). But if you prefer to stay nonviolent, you can avoid confrontation completely, which kind of makes titling the game "Gunpoint" a little strange. A Better title would have been something along the lines of "Sarcasm and Snark: The Video Game", because Gunpoint's writing is some of the most hilariously witty dialogue outside of some of the best Joss Whedon movies. There is also a level editing mode, which I never got to USE because I accidentaly deleted the floor immediatley upon opening the mode, and because the autosave feature is so quick to the punch, whenever I tried to open up that mode again my character just dropped like a sack of bricks off the face of the Earth. Oh well. At least when I try to use that mode I can listen to the game's amazing jazz soundtrack on loop. Did I mention the soundtrack? Yeah, it's some of the best jazz music ever used in video games and it perfectly fits the silly yet simultanously dark noir atmosphere of the game. So, do I recommend Gunpoint? Absolutley. It's a complete blast as long as you don't delete anything necessary. 8/10

PB games are NOT for everyone, the stories won't blow you away, the graphics are usually not up to par with current tech, the camera usually sucks and animations are some of the worst you will come across. Yet there is alot I enjoy with the games PB has made (Gothic 1-3 and Risen 1-3). Risen 3 is here and in my opinion it is the best of the series, Magic is back, melee combat is improved (you still have to go to trainers and learn new moves, improvements,etc.. Some of the series long lasting issues rear there head such as what I mentioned above with the terrible animations and a story that could be alot better). Risen 3 won't win Game Of The Year awards and probably not many RPG of the year awards either with games like Divinity Original Sin, Wasteland, Dragon Age and Pillars of Eternity out or coming out this year, it does have a good amount of issues but for me the good outweighs the bad and overall is my favorite PB game since the wonderful Gothic 2.
The overall combat is a nice improvement from Risen 1/2, you have the option to put points into skills with glory points you have gotten (from doing missions and killing enemies) and also training with trainers in towns for new moves like Parry, Pickpocket,etc.. These improvements help big time for things like combat,etc... Hit a trainer up for Parry, Speed and what ever type of sword you use (Slash, Sword or another) and you will be kicking♥♥♥♥♥in no time. This game does not hold you're hand, it is a very nice challenge, although not quite as hard as Risen 2. Combat is not perfect though, there are still some issues but bringing Magic back and improving the Melee abit has gone a long way. Far from a flawless game but a nice step in the right direction for PB, hopefully they can improve even more in this department for the next game.
The start of the game is a bit slow and can also be very tough, especially for new players. You're character has not leveled up and doesn't have any moves really other than a normal and a heavy attack. Get past the first little bit and things start to pick up quickly. You have lots of trainers to pick from and also a bunch of factions to pick from so make sure to use them. These games don't hold you're hand and you will feel overwhelmed at the start, just make sure to visit trainers and save often and you should be good.
The graphics are improved from Risen 1 and Risen 2, but its still inconsistent. Some of the landscapes, character faces and colors look gorgeous, while other things like buildings up close and animations are laughable. Although for me I dont expect top of the line graphics or animations from PB games, they are much more than just fancy graphics or animations. Sure I would love a Risen game on a Witcher engine or something (speaking of witcher, the devs said they have taken inspiration from the old Gothic games also made by PB, for there upcoming open world game Witcher 3), but this is a smaller dev team and atleast for me animations and graphics are last on my list. Still there are some spots where I was in awe of some of the beauty in the game, come over a mountain at night with you're torch and you will witness a beautiful scene.
The leveling up is very good and you have many options with how you want you're character to go. Want to do some thief aspects? Put tons of points into the categories that support pickpocketing and locksmithy when you level up and also go to some trainers and improve that way to. Also depending on what faction you join you will have access to unique things and missions (I joined the mages, which I am liking alot, especially there island, looks like Risen 1/Gothic style.
The audio and music overall is pretty good, the soundtrack is very good that really kicks in when you are exploring these wonderful levels. The voice acting for the most part is good, it ranges from poor to fantastic, but most are good I will say. The game also has the usual PB humor which I love (Divinity Original Sin also had some good humor to), and the dialogue in general is well done (few cheesy parts but would it be a PB game without a little bit of comedy?).
One of my favorite aspects of PB games is the exploration and scavaging and Risen 3 does these with flying colors. Each island is different from the last and while some of them are frmo Risen 2, they look completely different, this is the game Risen 2 should have been imo. Also the characters are great and interesting once again, where ever I go in the game I always meet characters that I enjoy talking to, some are funny, some are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and some are in the middle. In that sense the writing of the dialogue and characters is good but the writing of the story is not very good impressive.
It really comes down to what you think of PB games in general, yes it is an improvement over the first two games but it still has some of its long lasting issues that might throw some people off. But for me I am 30 hours in and having a blast, findng some new areas have me saying "Just another hour Kozzy". Risen 3 has been fun as all get out so far, but I don't expect everyone to enjoy this game.
The level design is also very well made, each Island I want to explore EVERY INCH. This is something alot of open world rpg devs need to take note of from PB. Sure there is alot of things they can do better, but they have exploring, level design and characters NAILED. What is next for PB? I would love another Gothic game with the improvements made in Risen 3 and hopefully even more improvements down the road. Weither its a new game on a new engine or another Risen or Gothic game I look forward to playing there next game.
Sure I wish we could have a new Risen game on a new engine with the best new tech, a better story and for them to keep improving the combat, but in the end I have had a blast and while it won't be my GOTY from a technical standpoint, it has given me some of the most fun ive had in all of 2014. Sort of like indie foreign flicks in the sense that they might not be the best from a technical standpoint as they don't have as much money or people working on the games as some of the big wigs, but they end up doing some aspects better, while some aspects are not as good.
In the end Risen 3 is a flawed gem that I recomend to anyone who enjoyed Risen 1, Gothic 1-3 to play, it is a nice mix of the old gothic games and Risen 1/2. Will I say it is better made than say Skyrim? From a design perspective, Hell no. What I will say though is that I have had much more fun on this game in 30 hours than I did playing Skyrim 80 hours. For me the characters are much more enjoyable, the exploration is much mroe rewarding, it is much more challening, I have had more FUN and I like the gameworld design better. If you can put up with a slow start, some terrible animations and a meh story, pick this up with the quickness, it is quite enjoyable.
For me this is the best overall PB game since Gothic 2, it is not as open as Gothic 3 and while Risen 1 was a blast, if we are talking best overall package I have to say this is my second favorite PB game. It definatly has its issues and it seems impossible for PB to nail everything perfectly, but I would be lying if I said I havn't been hooked to my computer since I got this game and that a few things have been a nice pleasent surprise. No its not GOTY material or better than the wonderful Divinity Original Sin that we got this year, but I have had a very fun time with Risen 3 so far, a flawed gem indeed. Not quite the masterpeice it could have been, but still my overall experience has been good to great.

First off, I'll say Xenoverse is fairly fun. In most cases, its difficult not to enjoy DBZ games, especially for those of us who find a bit of nostalgia within. However, this game is not without its issues.
The story is fun, if a bit short and predictable, and even though there are some differences in story writing in this game and the original material, it doesn't fail to maintain the feel of Dragonball Z. I suppose in that aspect, one could say it does its job quite well.
The biggest problems I find with this game are purely mechanical. There are several things that occur within this game that, for the life of me, I cannot fathom. To begin with, why must I always be connected, AND THEN make the decsion to play solo? If i want to play offline, why must I be made to log into a server that couldn't stay connected to save its life? I know the whole 'always connected' arguement has had its point in the spotlight and it isn't a new problem, but that still doesn't make it any less pointless and annoying, especially when I'm required to connect just to decide I don't want to play online.  Couldn't the 'offline play' just be a main menu option or something???
To be fair, the servers have been upgraded and no longer drop constantly, but once you get past that, there are plenty of other mechanical gripes to be found. Why the hell is there a solid second lag after EVERY action?! Its rather hard to captialize on combat opportunities when my Kamehameha causes me to wait a solid second before I can act afterwards. And what's the point of an ability having a cutscene that takes my eyes off of my target to flaunt, especially when I can be interrupted in this custscene and proptly stomped to the floor?! Who's idea was this? Did this game even go through a playtest before it dropped? And if It did, has Bandai fired the playtesters yet for missing that part?
All this pails in commarrison, however, to the stupidest thing that has ever hit DBZ Games. Unflinching, untouchable opponenets were a bad idea when it happened in Tenkaichi. A few years passing does not make it any less of a bad choice. I don't care if its supposed to make the game more dynamic or whatever b.s. excuse you've got. When an enemy is five levels lower than me, there is no reason I should be intterupted in EVERY COMBO EVER because Cell Jr. decided to sneeze in my direction. I find the idea that certain opponents being untouchable until their stamina meter is dropped to be a new form of 'fake difficulty', as these opponents do not fight harder or smarter, they simply can't be stopped now.
I guess at the end of the day, having played mostly Fighter Games and RPG's, I had hoped that the newest DBZ game making noises in those two directions would have actually improved upon their past successes, but honestly? I'd rather just boot up my PS2 and play Tenkaichi; and if it weren't for the new story that Xenoverse brings, I honestly think I would...
TL;DR? Game is fun, like most DBZ games, but the mechanic is garbage. 8/10.

With my previous experience with this game (and my current play after recent updates), it is hard to say whether or not I actually enjoyed it. What I liked was the customisability and open world feel to the game, with many different play options to explore.
However, after my terrible experience with paywalls a few years ago, I subsequently quit playing. Downloading it again to see what improvements had been made.
PROS
- The game is up to you how to play and explore.
- There are many different ways to customise your character.
- A devoted fanbase.
- Opportunity to waste many hours.
CONS
- Compatibility and anti-aliasing issues.
- It's an old game, so some textures look very low-res, whilst newer items/areas look far more detailed, which breaks the flow of the game, in my opinion.
- While the fanbase is devoted, the player base is much smaller than it was, leading to the world feeling barren and empty.
- The combat system takes a lot of getting used to, and often made me want to flip the table.
- Some story aspects seem forced to add content (race war, really?)
- Pop up windows, annoying and always at the worst times.
Overall, if you're new, you're a bit late to the party. Has Nexon quality (generally p2p and such). But if you can cope with the cons and somewhat annoying pop up windows, and playing mostly alone, then go for it!
